===== lecture 1: General Intro to XR

1/A0  quiz  1/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q What is the full form of the abbreviation XR?  [1/S0/F0]
    - Augmented reality
    - Virtual reality
    - Mixed reality
    * Extended reality
    because: The facts state that XR stands for extended reality.
  Q Which association is described as the most common perception of VR?  [1/S0/F1]
    - A 3D or 4D movie-theater documentary about extinct animals
    - A visualization of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins
    * A headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world
    - A game in which the real world is visible on a screen and virtual objects are also seen
    because: The facts identify the most common perception of VR as a vision-blocking headset that transports the user to a virtual world.
  Q Why can the terms XR, VR, AR, and MR create ambiguity for different people?  [1/S0/F1]
    * Because hearing them can lead people to think of different examples or scenes
    - Because XR is a single fixed hardware technology
    - Because all four terms refer to one and the same example
    - Because the extended reality market size is growing
    because: Different people may associate these terms with different examples, such as films, games, headsets, or body visualizations.

1/A1  recap  1/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  XR, VR, AR, and MR stand for extended reality, virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality. Different people may associate these terms with various experiences.
  - XR, VR, AR, and MR stand for extended reality, virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality.
  - Different people may associate these terms with various experiences.

1/A2  quiz  1/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What does the term Extended Reality refer to?  [1/S1/F0]
    - A specific technology for fully virtual environments
    - An intermediate state in which reality is augmented
    * An umbrella term for present or future immersive technologies
    - The reality-virtuality continuum
    because: Extended Reality is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers present or future immersive technologies such as AR, VR, and MR.
  Q In XR, what does the X represent?  [1/S1/F1]
    - A fixed part only in the word extended
    * A variable with values such as A, V, and M
    - A point on the reality-virtuality scale
    - A single label for virtual reality
    because: The X in XR can be read as a variable, with values such as A, V, and M denoting augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality.
  Q What makes a technology immersive?  [1/S1/F2]
    - It creates a completely virtual environment with no real content
    - It adds virtual objects to a real environment on a screen
    - It requires the user to recognize the environment as simulated
    * It creates a sensory experience that appears real and is not distinguished from reality
    because: An immersive technology produces an experience through sensory organs that the person fails to distinguish from their real environment, perceiving it as real.

1/A3  recap  1/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term for immersive technologies, with 'X' acting as a variable for technologies like AR, VR, and MR. A technology is immersive if it produces an experience that a person perceives as real through their sensory organs.
  - Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term for immersive technologies where 'X' serves as a variable for technologies like AR, VR, and MR.
  - An immersive experience is one that a person perceives as real through their sensory organs.

1/A4  quiz  1/S2  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q Which pair describes the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum?  [1/S2/F0]
    - A completely real environment with virtual content and a completely virtual environment with real-world content
    * A completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real
    - A completely real environment with nothing virtual and an immersive experience through sensory organs
    - A real environment augmented with virtual content and a virtual environment augmented with real-world content
    because: The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real.
  Q Which intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum is the real environment being augmented with virtual content?  [1/S2/F1]
    - Virtual reality
    - Extended Reality
    - Augmented virtuality
    * Augmented reality
    because: Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  Q Which intermediate state on the reality-virtuality continuum is the virtual environment being augmented with real-world content?  [1/S2/F2]
    - Virtual reality
    - Augmented reality
    - Extended Reality
    * Augmented virtuality
    because: Augmented virtuality is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
  Q In a broad sense, what does mixed reality cover on the reality-virtuality continuum?  [1/S2/F3]
    - Only the intermediate state in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content
    - Only the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content
    - Only the completely virtual environment extreme with nothing real
    * The entire space between the real and virtual extremes, containing different degrees of augmentation in both directions
    because: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

1/A5  recap  1/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale ranging from a completely real environment to a completely virtual environment. Augmented reality and augmented virtuality represent intermediate states where either the real environment is augmented with virtual content or the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content. Mixed reality encompasses the entire space between these two extremes.
  - The reality-virtuality continuum ranges from a completely real environment to a completely virtual environment.
  - Augmented reality is an intermediate state where the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  - Augmented virtuality is an intermediate state where the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
  - Mixed reality is the entire space between the real and virtual environment extremes.

1/A6  put_in_order  1/S2  "Order the positions on the reality-virtuality continuum"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  Order the positions on the reality-virtuality continuum: Completely real environment > Augmented reality > Augmented virtuality > Completely virtual environment  [1/S2/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F2]

1/A7  quiz  1/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Which description best fits the metaverse in relation to VR, AR, and MR?  [1/S3/F5]
    * It is a broader reimagining of human interaction with digital content, not merely an application of one XR technology.
    - It is simply an advanced application of virtual reality.
    - It is only an augmented reality feature for flat screens.
    - It is a specific mixed reality hardware product.
    because: The metaverse is not merely an application of virtual, mixed, or augmented reality technology; a broad view is that it reimagines how humans interact with the digital world.
  Q How does the metaverse envision human interaction with digital content?  [1/S3/F6]
    - People only view three-dimensional video content without natural interaction.
    - People operate through standard keyboard, mouse, and two-dimensional text commands.
    - People mainly use flat two-dimensional screens with occasional three-dimensional interaction.
    * People act as in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment with natural interaction.
    because: In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions.
  Q Why is the metaverse not yet fully realized?  [1/S3/F7]
    - Current technology is advanced enough, but consumers are uninterested.
    * Current technology is not advanced enough and still has technological bottlenecks.
    - Companies are not investing heavily in its development.
    - The hardware and software markets have already reached their limits.
    because: The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, although companies are investing heavily to make it a reality.
  Q What kind of manpower does extended-reality growth create a need for?  [1/S3/F8]
    - Only passive viewers who can consume ready-made XR content.
    - Only artists who can produce two-dimensional video game assets.
    - Only technicians who can repair VR headsets.
    * Knowledgeable and skilled people who can develop and deploy XR systems.
    because: The growth of extended reality creates a need for more knowledgeable and skilled manpower who can develop and deploy systems based on the technology.
  Q What growth pattern is associated with the extended reality market?  [1/S3/F1]
    * An exponential increase in market size.
    - A temporary spike followed by a permanent decline.
    - A slow, steady linear increase.
    - A long-term decline after an early peak.
    because: A market study reports that the extended reality market size was about 20.5 billion US dollars in 2021 and is expected to be about 860 billion US dollars by 2030, an exponential increase.

1/A8  recap  1/S3  "Recap"  (10 facts, 15 concepts)
  The extended reality market is growing exponentially across various application domains. The metaverse reimagines human interaction with the digital world through natural interaction in a three-dimensional environment. Despite current technological bottlenecks, XR is a major emerging area that creates a demand for skilled manpower.
  - The extended reality market is growing exponentially across various application domains.
  - The metaverse reimagines human interaction with the digital world through natural interaction in a three-dimensional environment.
  - XR is a major emerging area that creates a demand for skilled manpower despite current technological bottlenecks.

1/A10  recap  1/S5  "Recap"  (1 facts, 2 concepts)
  The seminal reference for the reality-virtuality continuum is the 1994 paper 'A Taxonomy of Mixed Reality Visual Displays' by Paul Milgram and Fumio Kishino. This one of the earliest papers in the field significantly influenced the development of mixed reality visual displays.
  - The reality-virtuality continuum is based on a seminal 1994 paper by Milgram and Kishino.

1/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q How are augmented reality and mixed reality positioned on the reality-virtuality continuum, and how does extended reality relate to both?  [1/S1/F0, 1/S2/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F3; extended reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, virtual reality, reality-virtuality continuum]
    A Extended reality is an umbrella term that covers augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality. The reality-virtuality continuum has a completely real environment at one extreme and a completely virtual environment at the other. Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between those extremes.
  Q Why can a headset that transports a user to a virtual world be understood as an example of immersive technology?  [1/S0/F1, 1/S1/F2; virtual reality, headset, virtual world, immersive experience, immersive technology]
    A A user wearing a headset that blocks vision and is transported to a virtual world is the most common perception of virtual reality. An immersive experience occurs when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the real environment, perceiving it as the real environment. Therefore, a technology that produces such an indistinguishable virtual experience is an immersive technology.
  Q How does the metaverse connect to the growth of extended reality, and why is it not simply an application of virtual reality, augmented reality, or mixed reality?  [1/S3/F4, 1/S3/F5, 1/S3/F6; metaverse, extended reality, virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, three-dimensional environment, natural interaction]
    A The metaverse has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field. It is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality; one broad view is that it reimagines how humans interact with the digital world. In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction with digital content, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions.
  Q How do the reported market size and the hardware-software split of the extended reality market point to the need for more skilled workers?  [1/S3/F1, 1/S3/F2, 1/S3/F8; extended reality, market size, hardware, software]
    A The extended reality market size was about 20.5 billion US dollars in 2021 and is expected to be about 860 billion US dollars by 2030, an exponential increase. Within that market, the hardware market is about 60 percent and the software market is about 40 percent. The growth of extended reality creates a need for more knowledgeable and skilled manpower who can develop and deploy systems based on the technology.

===== lecture 2: Application Domains and System Categories

2/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is immersive technology? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

2/A1  quiz  2/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Why can a relatively small share of XR applications in defense still be commercially important?  [2/S0/F0]
    - Defense is expected to have the largest percentage share of XR applications.
    * Worldwide military budgets are large, so even a small percentage can represent a large monetary amount.
    - Defense is commercially promising because its application share is expected to shrink.
    - Defense is commercially promising because it uses only headsets, making it cheaper.
    because: The segment says that, because worldwide military budgets are huge, even a small percentage of defense applications can be a large monetary amount, so commercial penetration can be expected.
  Q Why are VR or MR particularly useful in medical education and training?  [2/S0/F3]
    - They let patients visit faraway hospitals without traveling or physical effort.
    - They let buyers inspect upcoming properties before spending large amounts.
    * They let trainees explore body organs, their appearance, function, and parts even when cadavers are difficult to obtain.
    - They let soldiers practice combat training with wireless weapon controllers.
    because: Healthcare is a prominent VR/MR domain for medical education and training, where immersive simulations help potential doctors learn about organs and are useful when obtaining cadavers is difficult.
  Q What is a main benefit of using immersive technologies in education for an appropriate duration?  [2/S0/F4]
    * They can improve learner engagement and learning outcomes compared with standard teaching methods.
    - They are most beneficial when used for excessive durations.
    - They replace standard teaching methods without changing learning outcomes.
    - They are beneficial only at the tertiary education level.
    because: Appropriate exposure to immersive technologies in education can improve engagement and learning outcomes compared with standard methods, although excessive duration may create problems.
  Q Why is digital heritage preservation a suitable application for immersive technologies?  [2/S0/F7]
    - It lets large numbers of users physically enter restricted areas of the site.
    - It stops physical decay by making the entire heritage site fully virtual.
    - It requires every part of the heritage site to be physically accessible to visitors.
    * It allows users to explore heritage spaces that cannot be physically visited by large numbers, while preserving parts digitally.
    because: Digital heritage preservation is suitable because heritage places may not be physically visited by large numbers or in all parts, and immersive technologies can preserve the space digitally despite physical decay.

2/A2  recap  2/S0  "Recap"  (10 facts, 38 concepts)
  Extended reality has commercial potential in various sectors, and penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise. Gaming, healthcare, and education are prominent or emerging domains that use immersive technologies to improve popularity, training, and engagement, although excessive duration may create problems. The automobile, travel, tourism, and digital heritage sectors are evolving or emerging areas that use immersive experiences for virtual exploration. Finally, real estate and architecture allow for the exploration of properties, while defense provides simulations for specialized military training.
  - Extended reality has commercial potential in various sectors, and penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.
  - Gaming and entertainment is a current VR domain that uses immersive technologies to make gaming more acceptable and popular.
  - Healthcare is a prominent domain for training, and education is an emerging domain that can improve engagement and outcomes, although excessive duration may create problems.
  - The automobile, travel, tourism, and digital heritage sectors are evolving or emerging areas that use immersive technologies for virtual exploration.
  - Real estate and architecture allow for exploring properties, while defense is a major area for simulations used in specialized military training.

2/A3  quiz  2/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q In virtual reality, what does immersion require of the user's sensory input?  [2/S1/F0]
    * The user's senses are blocked so input comes only from the virtual world.
    - The user's eyes are blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real signals.
    - The user is psychologically engaged while physically attached to the real world.
    - The user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open to the real world.
    because: Immersion in VR means the user's senses are blocked so that no input comes from the real-world environment, and input comes only from the virtual world.
  Q Why are VR systems categorized as non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive?  [2/S1/F1]
    - The price of the hardware alone determines the sensory blocking level.
    - Commercial VR systems must block all senses to be fully immersive.
    * Market applications offer different degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.
    - Each category is defined by a different real-world application domain.
    because: VR systems are categorized this way because market applications provide varying degrees of immersion instead of all being fully immersive.
  Q How does a non-immersive VR application affect the user?  [2/S1/F3]
    - It blocks all senses, making the user feel physically present in the virtual world.
    - It blocks the eyes while leaving ears and skin exposed to the real world.
    * It captures attention, but sensory organs remain open and the user stays physically attached to the real world.
    - It uses gloves, body connectors, and body suits to detect physical movements.
    because: A non-immersive VR application can completely take the user's attention, but the eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user remains physically attached to the real world.
  Q A three-dimensional virtual tour that is experienced through a headset with no real physical movement is an example of which VR system type?  [2/S1/F6]
    - Non-immersive VR
    * Semi-immersive VR
    - Augmented reality
    - Fully immersive VR
    because: Semi-immersive VR can be a three-dimensional virtual environment experienced through a VR headset, with examples including virtual tours using only a headset, while users typically have no real physical movements.

2/A4  recap  2/S1  "Recap"  (8 facts, 11 concepts)
  Immersion in virtual reality means that the user's senses are blocked from the real-world environment so they receive input only from the virtual world. Systems are categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive based on the degree of sensory blocking. Non-immersive and semi-immersive systems are common and cost-effective, while fully immersive systems are the costliest and rarest because they completely block all senses.
  - Immersion in VR means the user's senses are blocked from the real world so they only receive input from the virtual world.
  - VR systems are categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems based on the degree of sensory blocking.
  - Non-immersive systems allow users to control virtual activities while remaining physically attached to the real world.
  - Semi-immersive systems provide partial immersion by blocking some senses while leaving the user free to sense the real world.
  - Fully immersive systems completely block all senses but are the costliest and rarest systems.

2/A10  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (10 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why can an immersive experience that is perceived as real be useful in both healthcare and travel and tourism?  [2/S0/F3, 2/S0/F6, 1/S1/F2; immersive experience, virtual reality, mixed reality, healthcare, travel and tourism, virtual tourism]
    A An immersive experience appears real because the user perceives it as the real environment. In healthcare, virtual reality and mixed reality simulations let potential doctors explore body organs, see their parts, and learn when cadavers are difficult to obtain. In travel and tourism, virtual tours let users visit faraway places without physically going there, saving money and physical effort.
  Q Why are most commercial immersive applications semi-immersive rather than fully immersive?  [2/S1/F5, 2/S1/F7, 2/S1/F10; semi-immersive virtual reality system, fully immersive virtual reality system, immersion]
    A A semi-immersive virtual reality system gives a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses. It is the most cost-effective and commonly used form of virtual reality, so most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive. A fully immersive virtual reality system is the costliest and commercially rare because it is difficult to afford.
  Q How does a non-immersive virtual reality system differ from a semi-immersive virtual reality system in the user's sensory connection to the real world?  [2/S1/F2, 2/S1/F3, 2/S1/F5; non-immersive virtual reality system, semi-immersive virtual reality system, virtual environment, immersion]
    A A non-immersive virtual reality system is a specific, limited class of computer application in which the user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user. The user may be psychologically engaged while the eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open, so the user remains physically attached to the real world. A semi-immersive virtual reality system instead blocks some but not all senses, for example the eyes, while other senses remain exposed to real-world signals.
  Q Why do virtual boot camp and combat training systems use motion trackers, full-body tracking systems, and wireless weapon controllers in addition to head-mounted displays?  [2/S0/F9, 2/S1/F9; virtual boot camp, combat training, head-mounted display, motion tracker, full-body tracking system, wireless weapon controller, fully immersive virtual reality system]
    A Defense training includes virtual boot camp and combat training that simulate vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments with constraints. Such training uses head-mounted displays with motion trackers, full-body tracking systems, and wireless weapon controllers. Fully immersive virtual reality systems detect actual movements, reactions, and even a blink of an eye and translate them into actions in the virtual world.

===== lecture 3: Application Domains and System Categories

3/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.
  What is metaverse? (lecture 1) -> The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.

3/A1  quiz  3/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q What distinguishes augmented reality from virtual reality in the type of experience it requires?  [3/S0/F1]
    - It is defined mainly by the user's psychological level of immersion.
    * It emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content instead of requiring immersion.
    - It requires a fully immersive experience by replacing the real environment.
    - It occupies the entire space between the real and virtual environment extremes.
    because: Augmented reality does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes adding digital content to real-world content.
  Q How can augmented reality be used in archaeology?  [3/S0/F3]
    - It can let a customer try cosmetic looks on a digital face before purchase.
    - It can scan a patient's vein network to support a medical treatment decision.
    * It can display things not visible to the naked eye and reconstruct lost structures.
    - It can measure room heights and lengths using a mobile phone.
    because: In archaeology, augmented reality can show things that are not visible to the naked eye and can reconstruct lost structures.
  Q How can augmented reality assist a worker in industrial manufacturing?  [3/S0/F4]
    - It can let a customer digitally paint walls on a screen before buying paint.
    * It can let a person see things while repairing or troubleshooting an industrial component.
    - It can place digital furniture in a scanned image of a customer's room.
    - It can trigger digital content when a device detects a QR code.
    because: In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
  Q Which augmented reality application area is a motivation for the metaverse concept?  [3/S0/F5]
    - Gaming, particularly well-known mobile augmented reality titles.
    - Archaeology, particularly reconstruction of lost structures.
    - Industrial manufacturing, particularly repair of industrial components.
    * Commerce, particularly e-commerce.
    because: The presence of many augmented reality applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.

3/A2  recap  3/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 5 concepts)
  XR technologies have huge application potential in many domains. AR does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content. Applications include reconstructing lost structures, troubleshooting industrial components, and providing one motivation for the metaverse through commerce.
  - XR technologies have huge application potential in many domains.
  - AR does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content.
  - AR applications include archaeology, architecture, manufacturing, commerce, gaming, and medicine.
  - AR can reconstruct lost structures, troubleshoot industrial components, and provide one motivation for the metaverse.

3/A3  quiz  3/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q How can an augmented reality passenger app help someone moving through a large airport terminal?  [3/S1/F0]
    - It can create a fully virtual terminal where the passenger can move before departure.
    - It can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside the terminal.
    * It can show the passenger's exact location and the direction to take to reach a desired terminal.
    - It can let the passenger virtually try on luggage or accessories before buying them.
    because: The passenger app can use beacons at different points in the terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal.
  Q What can an augmented reality product-visualization app do before a customer buys a product?  [3/S1/F1]
    * It can let the customer digitally place or apply the product in a real-world view, such as furniture in a scanned room or paint on a wall.
    - It can let the customer measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room with a mobile phone.
    - It can let medical professionals interact with patients through telemedicine sessions.
    - It can let the customer virtually try cosmetic looks on a digital face or watch models on a digital hand.
    because: AR customer-experience product-visualization examples let a user scan a room and place IKEA objects in the digital image, or digitally paint walls on a screen, to see the effect before deciding whether to buy.
  Q What task can an augmented reality virtual tape measure application perform with a mobile phone?  [3/S1/F2]
    - It can tell a passenger their exact location and direction to a desired terminal.
    - It can visualize a patient's internal vein network by pointing at the skin surface.
    * It can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room without a physical tape.
    - It can place digital watches on a customer's hand to compare models.
    because: The virtual tape measure application can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room using a mobile phone, so a physical tape is not needed.
  Q What is the main purpose of an augmented reality virtual try-on application for retail?  [3/S1/F3]
    * It can let a customer preview cosmetic looks on a digital face or watch models on a digital hand before deciding to buy.
    - It can show a passenger the exact location and direction to a desired terminal.
    - It can let a customer preview furniture or wall paint in a digital view of their room before deciding to buy.
    - It can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room with a mobile phone.
    because: Virtual try-on examples let customers try different cosmetic looks on a digital face or different watch models on a digital hand, and decide whether to buy based on look and feel.
  Q What can the handheld AccuVein device do in a healthcare setting?  [3/S1/F5]
    - It can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room.
    - It can tell a passenger their exact location and direction to a desired terminal.
    - It can let a customer digitally paint walls on a screen before buying paint.
    * It can scan and visualize the patient's internal vein network to help decide a treatment course.
    because: AccuVein is a handheld AR device that scans a patient's vein network and, when pointed at the skin surface, allows the internal vein network to be visualized so the treatment course can be decided.

3/A4  recap  3/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 20 concepts)
  AR can be used to help users navigate large terminals and to preview products or measure objects in physical spaces. It also offers virtual try-on experiences for various products. Additionally, AR supports healthcare through training, telemedicine, and the visualization of internal structures.
  - AR can help users navigate large terminals by showing exact locations and directions.
  - AR allows for virtual product previews and measuring objects in physical spaces.
  - AR provides virtual try-on experiences for various products.
  - AR is used in healthcare for training, telemedicine, and visualizing internal structures.

3/A6  quiz  3/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What is the primary basis for categorizing augmented reality systems?  [3/S2/F0]
    * The technology used to develop and deploy them
    - The type of input hardware used
    - The position of the system on the reality-virtuality continuum
    - The level of immersion experienced by the user
    because: Augmented reality systems are categorized by the technology used rather than by psychological or immersive experience.
  Q Which four subcategories are used for markerless augmented reality applications?  [3/S2/F1]
    - Location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and immersive-based
    - Location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and marker-based
    * Location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based
    - Location-based, superimposition-based, fiducial-based, and outlining-based
    because: Markerless augmented reality applications are divided into location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based subcategories.
  Q In marker-based augmented reality, where does digital content appear after a marker is detected?  [3/S2/F2]
    * At the marker's position in the real-world view
    - On a surface selected by a light projector
    - At the center of the device's display
    - At the user's current GPS location
    because: When a marker-based AR device detects a placed marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
  Q What do markerless augmented reality applications allow that marker-based applications do not?  [3/S2/F2, 3/S2/F5]
    - Users to receive content only at a GPS location
    - Users to view graphics projected onto a surface by a light projector
    * Users to place virtual objects without physical markers
    - Users to trigger content by scanning a fiducial marker
    because: Markerless AR does not require physical markers and allows users to decide where to place virtual objects, while marker-based AR relies on markers to trigger content.
  Q Which markerless augmented reality subtype uses light projectors to place digital content on an object, surface, or space?  [3/S2/F8]
    * Projection-based augmented reality
    - Superimposition-based augmented reality
    - Outlining-based augmented reality
    - Location-based augmented reality
    because: Projection-based markerless AR uses light projectors to project digital graphics, characters, or other content onto an object, surface, or space.

3/A7  recap  3/S2  "Recap"  (9 facts, 15 concepts)
  Augmented reality applications are categorized into marker-based and markerless systems. Marker-based applications trigger content at specific markers but can be difficult to maintain, whereas markerless applications are more versatile and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects. Markerless systems include location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based subcategories that use sensors, computer vision, and projectors to augment the real-world view.
  - AR applications are categorized into marker-based and markerless systems.
  - Marker-based applications trigger content at specific markers but can be difficult to maintain.
  - Markerless applications are more versatile and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.
  - Markerless systems include location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based subcategories.
  - These subtypes use location sensors, object recognition, or light projectors to augment the real-world view.

3/A8  quiz  3/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What do virtual reality system categories primarily distinguish?  [3/S3/F0]
    - The display hardware used by the system
    * The user's experience or psychological aspect
    - The application domain of the system
    - The technology used to develop and deploy the system
    because: VR system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, comprising non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.
  Q What do augmented reality system categories primarily distinguish?  [3/S3/F1]
    * The technology used to develop and deploy the systems
    - The user's psychological or immersive experience
    - The type of immersive display used
    - The application domain of the systems
    because: AR system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the systems rather than on the psychological aspect.
  Q Why are markerless augmented reality techniques used to address a limitation of marker-based systems?  [3/S3/F2, 3/S3/F3]
    * Markers are difficult to maintain unless the environment is very sanitized
    - Markers depend on GPS sensors for placement
    - Markers prevent digital content from appearing in the real-world view
    - Markers require complex computer-vision algorithms
    because: Marker-based AR systems are easier to make because they rely on simple algorithms, but their markers are hard to maintain unless the environment is very sanitized. Markerless techniques are used to overcome this maintenance difficulty.
  Q What do markerless augmented reality techniques rely on primarily?  [3/S3/F4]
    * Computer vision, with other sensors such as GPS in location-based applications
    - Physical markers, such as QR codes and fiducial markers
    - Fully immersive virtual environments without a real-world view
    - Psychological immersion levels, such as semi-immersive experience
    because: Markerless AR techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as GPS sensors, in location-based applications.
  Q What is the main difference in how VR and AR applications are characterized?  [3/S3/F7]
    - AR applications are categorized by psychological immersion, whereas VR applications are categorized by display technology
    * VR applications are immersive, whereas AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view
    - VR and AR have completely different application domains
    - VR applications rely on markers, whereas AR applications rely on GPS sensors
    because: VR and AR have broadly similar application domains. VR applications are characterized as immersive, while AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than being immersive applications.

3/A9  recap  3/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  VR systems are categorized by psychological experience into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems, while AR systems are categorized by technology into marker-based and markerless systems. Markerless AR techniques rely on computer vision and other sensors to overcome the difficulty of maintaining markers. While VR and AR have similar application domains, VR is characterized as immersive and AR emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view.
  - VR systems are categorized by psychological experience into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.
  - AR systems are categorized by technology into marker-based and markerless systems.
  - Markerless AR techniques rely on computer vision and other sensors to overcome the difficulty of maintaining markers.
  - VR is characterized as immersive while AR emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view.

3/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q How does augmented reality differ from virtual reality in the kind of experience it aims to provide to the user?  [3/S0/F1, 3/S3/F7, 1/S1/F2; augmented reality, virtual reality, immersive experience]
    A Augmented reality does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content. Virtual reality applications are characterized as immersive, and an immersive experience is one perceived through the senses as real rather than distinguishable from the user's real environment. Thus augmented reality adds digital content to the real-world view, whereas virtual reality applications aim to provide an immersive experience.
  Q Why can markerless augmented reality techniques be useful for augmented reality systems that would otherwise rely on physical markers?  [3/S2/F2, 3/S2/F4, 3/S3/F2, 3/S3/F3, 3/S3/F4; marker-based augmented reality system, markerless augmented reality technique, marker, computer vision]
    A Marker-based augmented reality systems use markers placed in the environment, and those markers are prone to damage, making the systems difficult to maintain unless the environment is very sanitized. A damaged marker may make the application not work, especially in outdoor or less well-attended settings. Markerless augmented reality techniques overcome this maintenance difficulty by not requiring physical markers and by relying primarily on computer vision or other sensors such as GPS.
  Q How do augmented reality applications in commerce and retail connect to the metaverse idea in extended reality?  [3/S0/F0, 3/S0/F2, 3/S0/F5, 1/S3/F4; extended reality, augmented reality, application domain, metaverse]
    A Extended reality technologies have application potential in domains such as retail, and augmented reality has applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce. The presence of many augmented reality applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept. The metaverse has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field, so these commerce-oriented augmented reality applications help show why the metaverse idea became relevant.
  Q How do location-based and superimposition-based markerless augmented reality applications use different sensor or recognition methods to add digital content to the real world?  [3/S2/F6, 3/S2/F7, 3/S3/F4; location-based markerless augmented reality application, superimposition-based markerless augmented reality application, location sensor, global positioning system, computer vision technique]
    A Markerless augmented reality techniques can rely primarily on computer vision, and they may also rely on sensors such as GPS in location-based applications. Location-based markerless augmented reality applications rely on a location sensor such as GPS to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame and augment digital content when the user is at a specific location. Superimposition-based markerless augmented reality applications recognize one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimpose digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.

4/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (1 facts, 1 concepts)
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

4/A1  quiz  4/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  Q What does the term virtual mean?  [4/S0/F0]
    - Something that exists independently of ideas concerning it
    - An artificial environment experienced through computer-provided sensory stimuli
    - A real or actual thing distinguished from something merely apparent
    * Something present in essence or effect but not in fact
    because: Virtual is defined as being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, present but not attributable to factual things.
  Q What does the term reality mean?  [4/S0/F1]
    - An artificial environment shaped partly by a person's actions
    - Something present in essence or effect but not in fact
    * The state or quality of being real and existing independently of ideas
    - A thing that is merely apparent rather than an actual thing
    because: Reality is defined as the state or quality of being real, existing independently of ideas, or an actual thing distinguished from the merely apparent.
  Q What is virtual reality in its dictionary definition?  [4/S0/F2]
    - An artificial environment experienced through computer-provided sights and sounds, where user actions fully determine every event
    * An artificial environment experienced through computer-provided sights and sounds, where user actions partially determine events
    - A real environment experienced through natural sights and sounds, where user actions partially determine events
    - An artificial environment experienced through computer-provided sights and sounds, where user actions do not affect events
    because: Virtual reality is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, with sights and sounds playing a primary role and user actions only partially determining what happens.
  Q How do the dictionary meanings of virtual and reality differ?  [4/S0/F0, 4/S0/F1]
    - Virtual means an artificial environment; reality means a real environment experienced through sensory stimuli
    - Virtual means actual and existing independently of ideas; reality means present in essence or effect but not in fact
    - Virtual means a real or actual thing; reality means something present in essence or effect but not in fact
    * Virtual means present in essence or effect but not in fact; reality means actual and existing independently of ideas
    because: The meaning 'in essence or effect but not in fact' belongs to virtual, while the meaning 'real, actual, and independent of ideas' belongs to reality.

4/A2  recap  4/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  Virtual means something that is there in essence or effect but not in fact, while reality is something that exists independently of ideas. Virtual reality is an artificial environment provided by a computer through sensory stimuli, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  - Virtual means something that is there in essence or effect but not in fact.
  - Reality is something that exists independently of ideas.
  - Virtual reality is a computer-provided artificial environment where user actions partially determine what happens.

4/A3  quiz  4/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Which combination of characteristics is required for a system to be defined as a virtual reality system?  [4/S1/F0]
    - An artificial environment, passive observation, and fixed playback
    * An artificial environment, sensory immersion, and user interaction
    - A real environment, sensory immersion, and user interaction
    - An augmented real environment, sensory immersion, and no interaction
    because: A VR system is defined by an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment.
  Q What does the artificial environment of a VR system consist of?  [4/S1/F1]
    - A real environment augmented with virtual content
    - A real-time video presentation of the user's actual surroundings
    * A computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world
    - A physical location populated with actual objects
    because: The artificial environment is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.
  Q Why can a virtual tour that uses real-world imagery still count as a VR system?  [4/S1/F2]
    - Because the viewer physically enters the actual location being shown
    - Because it presents the real environment directly without computer generation
    * Because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time
    - Because it updates the environment in real time as the user moves
    because: A virtual environment can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, but it still counts as VR because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.
  Q Which statement describes the sensory experience characteristic of a VR system?  [4/S1/F3]
    - The user interacts with physical objects in an actual room
    - The system shows a real-time camera feed of the user's room
    * Computer-generated stimuli reach the user's sensory organs and create immersion
    - The user perceives only unaltered real-world sights and sounds
    because: The sensory experience characteristic means the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user immersively experiences the artificial environment.
  Q What does user interaction mean in a VR system?  [4/S1/F4]
    - The user interacts with real objects in the physical world
    - All changes are controlled by the system without user input
    - The user only watches a fixed sequence of displayed events
    * User actions partially determine what happens in the environment
    because: A VR system must be interactive: the user can act on elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens, producing dynamic changes.

4/A4  recap  4/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  A virtual reality system is defined by an artificial environment, sensory experience, and user interaction. The artificial environment is a computer-generated representation of a real or imaginary world. Sensory experience involves computer-generated stimuli for immersion, while user interaction allows users to interact with elements to produce dynamic changes.
  - A virtual reality system is defined by an artificial environment, sensory experience, and user interaction.
  - An artificial environment is a computer-generated representation of a real or imaginary world.
  - Sensory experience involves computer-generated stimuli to provide an immersive experience.
  - User interaction allows users to act on elements to produce dynamic changes in the environment.

4/A5  quiz  4/S2  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q What must a system satisfy to be classified as a virtual reality system?  [4/S2/F0]
    - Only two characteristics: virtual environment and immersive sensory experience
    * All three VR characteristics: virtual environment, immersive sensory experience, and interaction
    - Only two characteristics: immersive sensory experience and interaction
    - Only two characteristics: virtual environment and interaction
    because: A VR system must satisfy all three characteristics, and a system that does not satisfy at least one is not a VR system.
  Q Why is a CAD system not a VR system?  [4/S2/F1]
    - It does not support a virtual environment
    - It does not support interaction
    - It presents a real-world environment in real time
    * It does not support an immersive experience
    because: A CAD system supports a virtual environment and interaction, but it does not provide an immersive experience because the user interacts with screen content while still seeing the real world.
  Q Why is a video conferencing system not a VR system?  [4/S2/F2]
    * It is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience
    - It is a virtual environment, but not interactive
    - It is immersive, but not a virtual environment
    - It is not interactive
    because: Video conferencing is interactive, but it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen, so it is neither a virtual environment nor an immersive experience.
  Q Why is a 3D movie experience not a VR system?  [4/S2/F3]
    - It does not provide any immersive experience, because it uses only ordinary two-dimensional images
    - It does not provide a virtual environment, because it shows only a real location
    * It is not interactive, because the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content
    - It is not a sensory experience, because it gives only visual content without other senses
    because: A 3D movie provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, but it is not interactive.

4/A6  recap  4/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  A system is a virtual reality (VR) system if it satisfies three characteristics: a virtual environment, an immersive experience, and interaction. CAD, video conferencing, and 3D movies are not VR systems because they each fail to meet at least one of these three requirements.
  - A system is a virtual reality (VR) system if it satisfies three characteristics: a virtual environment, an immersive experience, and interaction.
  - CAD, video conferencing, and 3D movies are not VR systems because they each fail to meet at least one of these three characteristics.

4/A12  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (8 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q Why can a computer-aided design system support a virtual environment and interaction, yet still not be classified as a virtual reality system?  [4/S1/F0, 4/S2/F0, 4/S2/F1; virtual reality system, virtual environment, interaction, computer-aided design system, mouse, immersive experience]
    A A virtual reality system must satisfy three characteristics: an artificial environment, an immersive sensory experience from computer-generated stimuli, and user interaction that partially determines what happens. A computer-aided design system can provide a virtual environment and interaction, but the user interacts through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen. Therefore it lacks the immersive experience required for virtual reality.
  Q How can a virtual tour that uses real-world imagery or video still be considered a virtual reality system?  [4/S1/F1, 4/S1/F2, 4/S2/F0; virtual tour, virtual reality system, artificial environment, real time, sensory experience, interaction]
    A The artificial environment in a virtual reality system is a computer-generated scenario, not a real environment, even when it recreates a real world. A virtual tour can therefore use real-world imagery or video while remaining a computer-generated scenario, because its changes are not happening in real time. If the system also provides the required sensory and interaction aspects, it can be categorized as a virtual reality system.
  Q Why does a three-dimensional movie experience not qualify as a virtual reality system even though it can provide a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience?  [4/S1/F0, 4/S2/F0, 4/S2/F3; three-dimensional movie experience, virtual reality system, virtual environment, immersive experience, user interaction]
    A A virtual reality system requires an artificial environment, an immersive sensory experience, and user interaction in which user actions partially determine what happens in the environment. A three-dimensional movie experience provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, but the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content. Because it lacks this interaction, it is not a virtual reality system.
  Q How does the use of computer-generated stimuli in virtual reality relate to the idea that an experience is immersive when sensory organs make an environment appear real?  [4/S1/F3, 1/S1/F2; virtual reality, virtual reality system, computer-generated stimuli, sensory experience, immersive experience, artificial environment]
    A An immersive technology produces an experience through sensory organs that appears real, so the person cannot distinguish it from their real environment. A virtual reality system gives the user computer-generated stimuli to sensory organs such as eyes and ears, enabling an immersive experience of an artificial environment. Thus, the sensory immersion in virtual reality is what makes the artificial environment feel real.

===== lecture 5: Definitions

5/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is reality-virtuality continuum? (lecture 1) -> The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

5/A1  quiz  5/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q According to the Merriam-Webster definition, what is augmented reality?  [5/S0/F0]
    * An enhanced version of reality that overlays digital information on an image of something being viewed
    - An artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli
    - The entire space between a completely real and a completely virtual environment
    - A medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments
    because: The dictionary definition describes augmented reality as an enhanced version of reality created by technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.
  Q According to the systemic definition of augmented reality, what must happen when a user interacts with digital content added to the real-world view?  [5/S0/F1]
    - The interaction must be performed on a separate interface
    * The interaction is reflected immediately in real time
    - The interaction is reflected only after the interaction ends
    - The interaction must replace the real-world view
    because: The systemic definition states that an AR system is interactive in real time, so interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately.
  Q According to the four-characteristic account of augmented reality, how must the digital enhancement be experienced?  [5/S0/F2]
    - Through a separate interface from the environment
    - Through a static display with no real-world view
    * Through the user's sensory organs
    - Through a completely virtual environment
    because: One of the four AR characteristics is that the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs.
  Q What conclusion follows if a system does not satisfy one of the four characteristics of augmented reality?  [5/S0/F3]
    - It is automatically a mixed reality system
    - It is automatically a virtual reality system
    * It is not an augmented reality system
    - It can still be called an augmented reality system
    because: A system is identified as an AR system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.

5/A2  recap  5/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 5 concepts)
  Augmented reality is an enhanced version of reality created by overlaying digital information on a real-world view. An AR system enhances the real world with digital content that is registered in 3D, experienced through the senses, and allows for interaction with that content. A system is only classified as augmented reality if all four of these characteristics are satisfied.
  - Augmented reality is an enhanced version of reality created by overlaying digital information on a real-world view.
  - An AR system enhances the real world with digital content, registers it in 3D, provides a sensory experience, and supports interaction with that content.
  - A system is only identified as an augmented reality system if all four of these characteristics are satisfied.

5/A3  quiz  5/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q How do augmented reality and virtual reality differ in their effect on the user's experience of reality?  [5/S1/F0]
    - AR and VR both completely replace the user's real-world perception with a virtual environment.
    * AR alters the ongoing perception of the real world, while VR completely replaces it with a virtual environment.
    - VR alters the ongoing perception of the real world, while AR completely replaces it with a virtual environment.
    - AR and VR both only alter the ongoing perception of the real world.
    because: AR alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas VR completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.
  Q Why can a VR system present an object or place that does not physically exist?  [5/S1/F1]
    - Because it superimposes non-existent digital content over a real-world view.
    - Because it requires the experienced place to exist and then enhances it with digital content.
    - Because it only alters the ongoing perception of a physically real room.
    * Because it creates a virtual environment instead of requiring the experienced place to exist.
    because: A VR system does not require the physical existence of an object or place because it creates a virtual environment.
  Q How can an AR system display digital content in a view of a real room?  [5/S1/F2]
    - It can remove the real-world view and present a separate virtual scene.
    - It can show furniture only if that furniture physically exists in the room.
    - It can replace the room with a virtual environment so the real room is no longer visible.
    * It can superimpose non-existent furniture as digital content over the real-world view of the room.
    because: An AR system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

5/A4  recap  5/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  AR alters the perception of the real world, while VR replaces it with a virtual environment. VR systems do not require a physical place to exist, but AR and MR systems require the place being experienced to exist. AR can superimpose extra information, such as digital content, over a real-world view.
  - AR alters the perception of the real world, while VR replaces it with a virtual environment.
  - VR systems do not require a physical place to exist, but AR and MR systems require the place to exist.
  - AR can superimpose digital content over a real-world view.

5/A5  quiz  5/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What is the state of agreement on a precise definition of mixed reality?  [5/S2/F0]
    - Practitioners and the literature agree on one precise definition.
    - A single developer-oriented definition is universally adopted.
    - Only the dictionary definition is accepted by all practitioners.
    * There is no agreement among practitioners and the literature.
    because: The segment states that practitioners and the literature do not agree on the precise definition of mixed reality.
  Q What limitation does the dictionary definition of mixed reality have?  [5/S2/F1]
    - It does not mention any combination of physical and virtual elements.
    - It excludes interaction with digital content in the view of reality.
    - It treats mixed reality as completely replacing the real world.
    * It is not categorical about how mixed reality differs from VR or AR.
    because: The dictionary definition combines physical and virtual elements but does not clearly state how MR differs from VR or AR.
  Q According to one definition, how is augmented reality related to mixed reality?  [5/S2/F2]
    * AR is included in MR, which spans everything between the real and virtual extremes.
    - AR is an extreme separate from the MR range.
    - MR is only the virtual extreme and excludes AR.
    - AR replaces MR as the broader category.
    because: One definition places MR as everything in between the real and virtual extremes, so AR is included in that broader MR.
  Q From a developer's point of view, what can make an application mixed reality in one definition?  [5/S2/F3]
    * Combining AR and VR technologies in the same application or on the same device.
    - Requiring the place being experienced to exist physically.
    - Creating a fully immersive environment without any physical reference.
    - Overlaying digital content on a view of reality and allowing interaction with it.
    because: One definition treats an application as MR when it combines AR and VR technologies in the same application or device.
  Q Why may mixed reality be used as a synonym for augmented reality by many people?  [5/S2/F5]
    - Because both combine augmented and virtual reality technologies in one device.
    - Because both describe every point between the real and virtual extremes.
    * Because both let users see reality enhanced with overlaid digital content and interact with it.
    - Because both replace the user's view of reality with a virtual environment.
    because: In many people's usage, MR is a synonym for AR because both involve viewing reality augmented with digital content and interacting with that content.

5/A6  recap  5/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 6 concepts)
  There is no consensus on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR), with various definitions describing it as a range between real and virtual environments, a combination of AR and VR technologies, or a more capable version of AR. Because many people use mixed reality synonymously with augmented reality, this course treats the two terms as interchangeable.
  - There is no agreement on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR).
  - Definitions of MR vary, ranging from a continuum between real and virtual environments to a combination of AR and VR technologies or a more capable version of AR.
  - Mixed reality is often used as a synonym for augmented reality (AR).
  - This course treats mixed reality and augmented reality as the same technology.

5/A7  quiz  5/S3  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 2 concepts)
  Q How does the course treat the terms mixed reality and augmented reality?  [5/S3/F0]
    - It treats augmented reality as a subset of mixed reality.
    - It treats mixed reality as a combination of augmented reality and virtual reality.
    - It treats mixed reality as a subset of augmented reality.
    * It treats them as interchangeable terms for the same technology.
    because: The course assumes mixed reality is the same technology and idea as augmented reality and uses that assumption to keep the later discussion simple.

5/A8  recap  5/S3  "Recap"  (1 facts, 2 concepts)
  In this course, mixed reality is assumed to be the same technology and idea as augmented reality for simplicity in subsequent discussions.
  - Mixed reality is treated as the same technology as augmented reality in this course.

5/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q How do augmented reality and virtual reality differ in their relationship to the physical environment being experienced?  [5/S1/F0, 5/S1/F1; augmented reality, virtual reality, physical environment, virtual environment]
    A Augmented reality alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment. A virtual reality system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality system requires the place being experienced to exist.
  Q Why is it not enough for a system to overlay digital content on a real-world view in order to be an augmented reality system?  [5/S0/F0, 5/S0/F1, 5/S0/F2, 5/S0/F3; augmented reality, augmented reality system, real time, three-dimensional, sensory organ, interaction]
    A The dictionary definition describes augmented reality as overlaying digital information on an image of something viewed through a device. The systemic definition requires an augmented reality system to combine the real world with virtual content, be interactive in real time, and be registered in 3D. The four-characteristic identification test requires the enhancement to be registered in 3D, experienced through sensory organs, and supported by interaction in the enhanced environment, and a system is an augmented reality system only if all four characteristics are satisfied.
  Q How do definitions of mixed reality relate to augmented reality and the reality-virtuality continuum, and why does the course use mixed reality and augmented reality interchangeably?  [5/S2/F0, 5/S2/F2, 5/S2/F5, 5/S2/F6, 5/S3/F0, 1/S2/F3; mixed reality, augmented reality, reality-virtuality continuum]
    A There is no agreement on a precise definition of mixed reality. In a broad sense, mixed reality is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, and one definition says it comprises everything in between those extremes, so augmented reality is included. Another definition treats mixed reality as a synonym for augmented reality. Because the definitions are confusing, the course assumes mixed reality is the same technology and idea as augmented reality and treats the terms as interchangeable.

===== lecture 6: Historical Evolution

6/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.
  What is immersive technology? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.
  What is metaverse? (lecture 1) -> The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

6/A2  recap  6/S0  "Recap"  (1 facts, 6 concepts)
  The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases. These include the early era before the advent of digital computers, the formative years from roughly 1950 to 1990, the modern phase from 1991 to 2015, and the current growth phase from roughly 2016 onwards.
  - The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases.
  - The phases are the early era, formative years (roughly 1950 to 1990), the modern phase (1991 to 2015), and the current growth phase (roughly 2016 onwards).

  Q Why can a virtual reality headset create immersion from a flat display?  [6/S1/F2]
    - The headset adds smell and wind feedback
    * Stereoscopic vision lets the user perceive 2D images as 3D objects and space.
    - Head tracking makes the display generate true 3D light fields
    - Multiple sensors make the user feel motion
    because: VR headsets or display devices present 2D images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as 3D objects and space, which is immersion.

    - It showed that head-mounted displays were the defining feature of the era
    * It contained key developments that were conceptually similar to immersive VR experiences.
    - It already included complete immersive virtual environments
    because: The early era was before modern digital computers, but a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.
  Q How did an early compact stereoscope advance earlier stereoscopic devices?  [6/S1/F3]

    * It created the illusion of depth in viewed images in a compact display.
    - It added head tracking with computer-generated images
    - It introduced smell, wind, and vibration feedback

    - It popularized the term virtual reality
    - It introduced the compact stereoscope

6/A4  recap  6/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  The early era of virtual reality occurred before modern digital computers and featured key developments like Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device. This device proved that the human brain can process 2D images as 3D objects, which is how modern headsets create immersion. Further developments, such as David Brewster's 1860 compact stereoscope and Edwin A. Link's 1928 flight simulator, served as precursors to modern multi-sensory immersive experiences.
  - The early era of virtual reality occurred before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s.
  - Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device demonstrated that the human brain can process 2D images as 3D objects.
  - Stereoscopic vision is the mechanism where headsets present 2D images that the brain perceives as 3D objects and space.
  - David Brewster's 1860 compact stereoscope was an advancement toward practical immersive experiences.
  - Edwin A. Link's 1928 flight simulator was a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality.

6/A6  recap  6/S2  "Recap"  (11 facts, 35 concepts)
  The formative years of virtual reality began in the 1950s with the development of head-mounted displays (HMDs). These technologies progressed into immersive systems featuring haptic feedback and the first commercially viable stereoscopic head-tracked HMD. By the late 1980s, the terminology shifted from "artificial reality" to the modern term "virtual reality."
  - The formative years of virtual reality began in the 1950s with the development of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
  - Immersive systems and haptic feedback technologies were introduced in the 1960s.
  - The first commercially viable stereoscopic head-tracked HMD was launched in 1985.
  - The term "virtual reality" was proposed in the late 1980s as an evolution of "artificial reality."

6/A9  recap  6/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 23 concepts)
  The modern phase of virtual reality lasted from approximately 1990 to 2015, during which systems like CAVE and software tools like WTK were developed. Modeling languages were introduced in 1994, while head-mounted displays evolved into more portable and usable designs. The availability of affordable headsets like the Oculus Rift eventually made virtual reality accessible to the masses.
  - The modern phase of virtual reality lasted from approximately 1990 to 2015.
  - New systems like CAVE and software tools like WTK were developed in the early 1990s.
  - Modeling languages such as VRML, X3D, and Java 3D were introduced in 1994.
  - Head-mounted displays evolved from bulky models into more portable and usable designs.
  - Affordable headsets like the Oculus Rift made virtual reality accessible to the masses.
