6/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 30 concepts)
  Q How does Sir Charles Wheatstone's stereoscopic demonstration connect to the way a VR headset creates immersion?  [6/S1/F1, 6/S1/F2; Sir Charles Wheatstone, stereoscopic device, virtual reality, headset, stereoscopic vision, immersion]
    A Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device established that the human brain can process two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. In VR, headsets present two-dimensional images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional objects and space, and that perception is immersion.
  Q Why can Sensorama be treated as the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality?  [6/S2/F3, 6/S2/F4, 1/S1/F2; Morton Heilig, Sensorama, immersive virtual reality system, virtual reality, immersive experience, three-dimensional, stereo sound, haptics]
    A Morton Heilig introduced Sensorama in 1962, and it can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality. It was publicized as having 3D, wide vision, motion, color, stereo sound, smell, wind, and vibrations, and it stimulated all sensory organs. An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real because the person cannot distinguish the environment from the real environment, so multi-sensory stimulation like Sensorama's fits that definition.
  Q How did the availability of inexpensive headsets such as the Oculus Rift help VR move from the end of its modern phase into its current growth phase?  [6/S3/F6, 6/S3/F7, 6/S3/F8, 6/S4/F0; Oculus Rift, Palmer Luckey, Facebook, virtual reality, headset, modern phase, current growth phase, virtual reality headset, immersive experience]
    A The Oculus Rift was an inexpensive VR headset created by Palmer Luckey in 2012, and Facebook's purchase of it in 2014 helped try to popularize the headset and make VR affordable. The availability of inexpensive headsets such as the Oculus Rift greatly spurred interest in VR towards the end of its modern phase. The growth phase then began roughly in 2016, when many well-known companies released commercial VR headsets that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population.
  Q How do the 2016 commercial headset releases and the 2021 popularization of the metaverse connect within the current growth phase?  [6/S4/F0, 6/S4/F2, 1/S3/F4; current growth phase, virtual reality headset, metaverse, Zuckerberg, Meta, immersive experience]
    A The current growth phase began roughly in 2016 when many well-known companies released commercial virtual reality headsets, making immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurring growth in the field. The metaverse term had been in use for more than 30 years and had existed in the research community since the 1990s, but in 2021 Zuckerberg of Meta popularized it. After that, people began taking an interest in the metaverse and interpreting it in different ways, which spurred further activity.

===== lecture 7: Historial Evolution

7/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

7/A2  recap  7/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  The historical evolution of augmented reality can be broadly divided into four overlapping phases from before the 1980s to the present. These phases progressed from early experimentation and basic research into the development of tools and widespread commercial applications.
  - The historical evolution of augmented reality can be broadly divided into four overlapping phases from before the 1980s to the present.
  - These phases progressed from early experimentation and basic research into the development of tools and widespread commercial applications.

  Order the phases of augmented reality historical evolution: Experimental phase > Basic research phase > Tools or applications phase > Commercial application phase  [7/S0/F0]

    - An LCD-based see-through hand-held display
    * A CRT-based optical see-through head-mounted display
    - A CRT-based fully immersive head-mounted display
    - A projection-based desktop see-through display
    because: The first Sutherland-Sproull AR prototype combined a CRT-based optical see-through head-mounted display with a ceiling-mounted tracking system.
  Q What did the tracking system in the first computer-generated AR prototype register?  [7/S1/F1]
    - Eye movements in a virtual display
    - Hand movements in two dimensions on a hand-held display
    - Body orientation in an aircraft cockpit
    * Head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display
    because: The mechanical tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display.
  Q In the super cockpit prototype, when was the real-world view replaced by computer-generated imagery?  [7/S1/F3]
    - During daylight
    - Only when the aircraft was on the ground
    - Only during takeoff and landing
    * At night or in bad weather
    because: In daylight, computer-generated imagery was superimposed over the real-world view; at night or in bad weather, it replaced the real-world view.
  Q Which hardware category was an outcome of early AR experiments?  [7/S1/F4]
    - Shared multi-user AR room systems
    - Projection-based desktop AR displays
    - Hand-held mobile AR displays
    * Input and tracking hardware
    because: Early AR experiments led to head-mounted AR displays used in modern aircraft, VR displays such as the VIVED HMD, and input and tracking hardware.

7/A5  recap  7/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 21 concepts)
  Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first computer-generated augmented reality prototype in 1968. This prototype used a head-mounted display and a tracking system to register head movements in three dimensions. The US Air Force super cockpit program produced technologies where pilots saw computer-generated imagery through a head-mounted display. These early experiments led to modern aircraft displays, virtual reality systems, and tracking hardware.
  - Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first computer-generated augmented reality prototype in 1968.
  - This prototype used a head-mounted display and a tracking system to register head movements in three dimensions.
  - The US Air Force super cockpit program produced technologies where pilots saw computer-generated imagery through a head-mounted display.
  - These early experiments led to modern aircraft displays, virtual reality systems, and tracking hardware.

    because: The basic research phase came after the experimentation phase and included influential 1990s work that shaped augmented reality.

    * See-through head-mounted displays
    - Handheld liquid-crystal displays
    because: University of North Carolina research during the basic research phase included early work on see-through head-mounted displays, which are typically used in augmented reality.
  Q How did Chameleon present virtual content to a user?  [7/S2/F5, 7/S2/F7]
    - By superimposing virtual tags on real objects
    - By using GPS to locate outdoor markers
    - By overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video
    * By moving an LCD over paper
    because: Chameleon allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display over a piece of paper and see virtual content, making it an early handheld or mobile augmented-reality system.
  Q What did NaviCam superimpose on real objects?  [7/S2/F6]
    * Virtual tags
    - Shared augmented content
    - Outdoor navigation information
    - Virtual cues
    because: NaviCam was a handheld or mobile augmented-reality system that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.
  Q What is often credited with introducing the term augmented reality into academic work?  [7/S2/F1]
    - The first handheld AR system
    - The first see-through head-mounted display
    * The first academic article containing the term
    - The first mobile AR publication
    because: Tom Caudell is often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality because he published the first academic article containing the term AR.

7/A7  recap  7/S2  "Recap"  (8 facts, 17 concepts)
  The basic research phase of augmented reality came after the experimentation phase and shaped the field during the 1990s, including the coining of the term "augmented reality" in 1992. Research during this phase focused on tracking techniques, head-mounted displays, and interaction methods. Early systems like Chameleon and NaviCam were true augmented reality applications and precursors to the kind of AR applications seen today.
  - The basic research phase of augmented reality came after the experimentation phase and shaped the field during the 1990s.
  - Tom Caudell coined the term "augmented reality" in 1992.
  - Research during this phase focused on tracking techniques, head-mounted displays, and interaction methods.
  - Early systems like Chameleon and NaviCam were true augmented reality applications and precursors to the kind of AR applications seen today.

    - Image-guided surgery, video conferencing with surgeons, and marker-based outdoor navigation
    * Visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.
    because: Medical AR applications from that phase included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.
  Q Why was viewpoint tracking a significant challenge in augmented reality?  [7/S3/F8]

    * It had to be addressed so that three-dimensional registration of content could happen accurately.
    - It had to be addressed so that shared AR content could be displayed on separate screens.
    - It had to be addressed so that users could hear immersive audio more clearly.
    because: Viewpoint tracking was significant because it enabled accurate three-dimensional registration of AR content.

7/A9  recap  7/S3  "Recap"  (12 facts, 42 concepts)
  Research in the mid-1990s focused on key technologies like tracking, display, and interaction, leading to developments in shared AR content, medical applications, and wearable computing. By 1997, computer vision and GPS were used to register 3D content in the real world. In the early 2000s, wearable AR systems were developed for various applications but remained bulky and difficult to use. Viewpoint tracking challenges were eventually addressed by systems like the AR Toolkit, which was later ported to mobile phones in 2004.
  - Mid-1990s research focused on key enabling technologies like tracking, display, and interaction.
  - This period saw the development of shared AR content, medical applications, and wearable computing using head-mounted displays.
  - By 1997, tracking techniques using computer vision markers and GPS were used to register 3D content.
  - In the early 2000s, wearable AR systems were developed for various applications but were bulky and difficult to use.
  - Viewpoint tracking was addressed by tools such as the AR Toolkit, which was later ported to mobile phones in 2004.

7/A10  put_in_order  7/S3  "Order the tracking and mobile AR milestones"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  Order the tracking and mobile AR milestones: Printed-matrix computer-vision tracking > AR Toolkit tracking library > Mobile-phone-based AR application  [7/S3/F9, 7/S3/F10, 7/S3/F11]

7/A11  quiz  7/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q What marked the beginning of the commercial application phase of augmented reality?  [7/S4/F0]
    - A laboratory-only AR tool became widely adopted
    - An outdoor GPS-based wearable AR interface was first shown
    * A widely used consumer AR experience became available
    - An open-source marker tracking library was released
    because: The segment says the commercial application phase began when a widely used consumer AR experience was released, after AR had been neither very popular nor easily available.
  Q What factors helped augmented reality move from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology?  [7/S4/F1, 7/S4/F2]
    * Web-browser AR authoring, smartphone-based AR, and global marketing campaigns
    - Backpack computers, HMD displays, and GPS outdoor navigation
    - Virtual reality headsets, haptic feedback, and metaverse platforms
    - Computer-vision marker tracking, shared AR content, and image-guided surgery
    because: AR became widely available because AR authoring tools made web-browser AR possible, smartphones had become common, and global marketing campaigns used AR to promote products.
  Q What did the launch of AR development platforms for major mobile platforms help achieve?  [7/S4/F3]
    - AR development required only custom computer hardware in a backpack
    - Only simple AR applications could be created
    * Many developers could create AR applications, increasing apps from simple to complex ones
    - AR was restricted to specialist research laboratories
    because: These development platforms further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and by increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.
  Q Which developments are expected to support continued growth of the AR commercial application phase?  [7/S4/F4]
    - Better AI and computer vision that make 3D tracking feasible only on high-end devices
    * More AR applications and tools, hardware improvements, and better algorithms, AI, and computer vision for 3D tracking on low-end devices
    - Only more marker-based AR applications and bulky wearable computers
    - More complex AR applications, but without hardware or tracking improvements
    because: The segment says the phase is expected to keep growing through more applications and tools, improved wearable, mobile, and holographic hardware, and better algorithms, AI, and computer vision that make 3D tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

7/A12  recap  7/S4  "Recap"  (5 facts, 24 concepts)
  The commercial application phase of augmented reality began in October 2007 and moved from research laboratories to widely available technology by 2009, driven by new authoring tools, smartphones, and marketing campaigns. The launch of ARKit and ARCore in 2017 further stimulated growth by enabling developers to create complex applications. This phase is expected to continue growing as hardware improves and AI and computer vision technologies advance.
  - The commercial application phase of augmented reality began in October 2007 and made the technology popular among consumers.
  - In 2009, augmented reality moved from research laboratories to widely available commercial technology.
  - This shift was driven by Adobe Flash-based authoring tools, the start of the smartphone era, and global marketing campaigns.
  - The launch of ARKit and ARCore in 2017 stimulated growth by enabling developers to create more complex applications.
  - The commercial application phase is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing through improvements in hardware, AI, and computer vision.

7/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 39 concepts)
  Q How does the historical framing of augmented reality differ from the historical framing of virtual reality's formative years?  [7/S0/F0, 6/S2/F0; augmented reality, virtual reality, experimental phase, basic research phase, tools or applications phase, commercial application phase]
    A The formative years of virtual reality are described as roughly 1950 to 1990, ending with the popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s. In contrast, the historical evolution of augmented reality is divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap. Those AR phases are the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present.
  Q What does the Sutherland-Sproull prototype show about how an early augmented reality system could satisfy the systemic requirements of combining real and virtual content and being registered in 3D?  [7/S1/F0, 7/S1/F1, 5/S0/F1; Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality prototype, Ivan Sutherland, Bob Sproull, optical see-through head-mounted display, mechanical tracking system, three-dimensional registration, augmented reality system]
    A Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality prototype in 1968, using a CRT-based optical see-through head-mounted display and a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware. The tracker registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display. The systemic definition of an augmented reality system says that it combines the real world with virtual content and is registered in 3D, and the prototype's see-through HMD with 3D head registration corresponds to those characteristics.
  Q What connection can be drawn between early handheld augmented reality systems such as NaviCam and the later commercial growth of mobile augmented reality?  [7/S2/F6, 7/S2/F7, 7/S4/F2, 7/S4/F3; NaviCam, mobile augmented reality system, smartphone-based augmented reality, ARKit, ARCore]
    A NaviCam was a 1995 handheld or mobile augmented reality system that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays. Early handheld systems like NaviCam were true augmented reality applications and precursors to the kind of AR applications seen today. In 2009, augmented reality moved to widely available commercial technology partly because of smartphone-based augmented reality, and Apple's ARKit and Google's ARCore further stimulated growth by enabling many developers to create augmented reality applications.

===== lecture 8: Issues & Challenges

8/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.
  What is artificial environment? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

  Q What is the main objective of any virtual reality system?  [8/S0/F0]
    - To let the user experience a virtual world through computer-provided stimuli for sight and sound only
    - To let the user experience a virtual world through a surrounding and plot-informing display
    * To let the user experience an artificial environment through computer-provided stimuli for all sensory organs
    - To let the user experience a virtual world through a headset that matches user movements
    because: A VR system aims to let the user experience an artificial environment via computer-provided sensory stimuli, not only for sight and sound.
  Q What are the two major issues involved in experiencing virtual reality?  [8/S0/F1]
    - How to generate suitable sensory stimuli and how to measure immersion objectively
    * How to generate suitable sensory stimuli and how to perceive those stimuli suitably
    - How to create a vivid virtual environment and how to match user movements
    - How to build a surrounding display and how to make the virtual world plot-informing
    because: The issues are technological generation of suitable stimuli and human, psychological perception of those stimuli suitably.
  Q Which two major concerns arise from the technological and psychological issues in virtual reality?  [8/S0/F2]
    - Surrounding and plot-informing
    - Matching and interactivity
    - Extensiveness and vividness
    * Immersion and presence
    because: The technological and psychological issues give rise to immersion and presence, which appear in almost every VR literature.

8/A2  recap  8/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  The main objective of a virtual reality system is to let users experience artificial environments through sensory stimuli provided for all sensory organs. VR involves technological issues in generating stimuli and psychological issues in how users perceive them. These issues give rise to the two major concerns of immersion and presence.
  - VR aims to let users experience artificial environments through sensory stimuli for all sensory organs.
  - VR involves technological issues in generating stimuli and psychological issues in how humans perceive them.
  - These issues give rise to the two major concerns of immersion and presence.

In virtual reality, immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.
  - Immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality system projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users.
  - Immersion is defined by six qualities: extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.
  - Immersion is the technological issue, while presence is the psychological issue.

    * It captures whether the user perceives generated immersive qualities.

    - It describes a system's technological capacity to stimulate sensory organs.
    - It measures the objective degree to which a system projects stimuli.
    because: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  Q In the definition of presence, what happens in the user's perception?  [8/S2/F1]
    - Part or all of perception accurately acknowledges the role of technology.
    * Part or all of perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of technology.
    - The entire current experience must be generated by human-made technology.
    - The user must consciously recognize that the experience is filtered through technology.
    because: Presence is defined as a subjective perception in which part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of technology in the experience.
  Q Why does a user perceive computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world during presence?  [8/S2/F2]
    - Because they stimulate more sensory organs than real-world stimuli.
    - Because they match the user's physical movement in the virtual world.
    - Because they provide a wide panoramic field of view.
    * Because the user cannot distinguish them from real-world stimuli.
    because: In presence, computer-generated stimuli are perceived as real-world stimuli because the user cannot distinguish them from real-world stimuli.

    - The ability to accurately identify the role of technology in the experience.
    because: Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

8/A6  recap  8/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 3 concepts)
  Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives immersive qualities while failing to acknowledge the role of technology in the experience. This occurs when computer-generated stimuli are perceived as coming from the real world rather than a computer. Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.
  - Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives immersive qualities.
  - It is a psychological state where a user fails to acknowledge the role of technology in their experience.
  - Computer-generated stimuli are perceived as coming from the real world rather than a computer.
  - Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

8/A7  quiz  8/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q How do immersion and presence differ?  [8/S3/F0, 8/S3/F1]
    * Immersion is an objective system property, while presence is a subjective state in the user's mind.
    - Presence is the measurable description of what a system can provide
    - Immersion is the psychological sense of being in the virtual environment
    - Presence is an objective system property, while immersion is a subjective state in the user's mind
    because: Immersion is described as objective and quantifiable, whereas presence is a psychological sense that exists in the user's mind and requires subjective experience.
  Q What does the relationship between immersion and presence say about causing presence?  [8/S3/F2]
    - Immersion always guarantees presence when it is sufficiently high
    * Immersion can aid and produce presence, but it does not guarantee presence.
    - Presence is only a function of the system's technological experience
    - A user's subjective experience cannot affect presence
    because: Presence can depend on both the user's subjective experience and the system's immersion, so immersion can support presence but does not ensure it.
  Q What effect does a greater degree of immersion have on presence?  [8/S3/F3]
    - It guarantees that the real and virtual worlds cannot be distinguished
    - It decreases the likelihood that the user feels present
    * It increases the potential for a user to feel present.
    - It removes the need for the user's subjective experience
    because: The greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world.
  Q What is the overall goal of a virtual reality system?  [8/S3/F4, 8/S3/F5]
    - To make the virtual world objectively identical to the real world
    - To provide the highest possible objective immersion alone
    * To create a high degree of presence, making users unable to distinguish the real from the virtual world.
    - To measure the user's psychological state as accurately as possible
    because: The goal is a high degree of presence, and creating that presence requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion.

8/A8  recap  8/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 4 concepts)
  Immersion is an objective description of what a system provides, while presence is a subjective psychological sense of being in a virtual environment. Immersion can aid and produce presence, but it does not ensure it, and the potential for presence is limited by the level of immersion provided. The goal of a virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, which is a systemic issue requiring the system to provide a high degree of immersion.
  - Immersion is an objective description of what a system provides, while presence is a subjective psychological sense of being in a virtual environment.
  - Immersion can aid and produce presence, but it does not ensure it, and the potential for presence is limited by the level of immersion provided.
  - The goal of a virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence.
  - Creating a high degree of presence is a systemic issue that requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion.

8/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q Why are immersion and presence treated as different kinds of issues in virtual reality, and what does that mean for what a virtual reality system must provide to achieve its overall goal?  [8/S0/F1, 8/S1/F7, 8/S3/F0, 8/S3/F1, 8/S3/F2, 8/S3/F4, 8/S3/F5; virtual reality, immersion, presence, sensory stimuli, virtual reality system, virtual environment]
    A Virtual reality involves two major issues: the technological issue of generating suitable sensory stimuli and the psychological issue of perceiving those stimuli. Immersion corresponds to the technological side, giving an objective and quantifiable description of what a system provides, while presence is the psychological, subjective sense of being in the virtual environment. The overall goal is high presence, so a system needs high immersion to increase the potential for presence, but immersion does not ensure presence.
  Q How do the objective qualities of immersion explain the way a virtual reality system presents the artificial environment described in the definition of virtual reality?  [8/S1/F0, 8/S1/F1, 8/S1/F2, 8/S1/F3, 8/S1/F4, 8/S1/F5, 8/S1/F6, 4/S0/F2, 4/S1/F0; virtual reality, virtual reality system, artificial environment, sensory stimuli, immersion, extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactivity, plot-informing]
    A A virtual reality system is an artificial or synthetic environment in which computer-generated sensory stimuli provide the experience and user actions partially determine what happens. Immersion is the objective degree to which such a system projects stimuli, and its qualities name the dimensions of that projection. Extensive and vivid describe the range and energy of the sensory modalities, surrounding makes cues panoramic, matching and interactivity connect stimuli to user movement and action, and plot-informing makes the world's behavior understandable.
  Q How does the description of immersion as blocking real-world input relate to the objective qualities used to evaluate a virtual reality system's stimulus projection?  [8/S1/F0, 8/S1/F1, 8/S1/F3, 8/S1/F4, 2/S1/F0; immersion, sensory stimuli, virtual world, extensive, surrounding, vivid, field of view, resolution, lighting, frame rate, audio bit rate]
    A Immersion can be described as blocking real-world input so that the user receives input only from the virtual world. The objective qualities describe how the system projects that virtual input. Extensive covers more sensory modalities, surrounding makes cues more panoramic through a wider field of view, and vivid increases stimulus energy through factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, or audio bit rate.


===== lecture 9: Issues & Challenges

9/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

9/A1  quiz  9/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q What is the overall design goal of a virtual reality system?  [9/S0/F0]
    - Creating a high degree of photorealism
    - Creating a high degree of interaction fidelity
    - Creating a high degree of representational fidelity
    * Creating a high degree of presence
    because: The goal of any VR system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning users believe they are in a real world while actually in a virtual one.
  Q For a user who treats real-world perception and sensation as the gold standard, what should a VR system do?  [9/S0/F1]
    * Match real-world experience as closely as possible
    - Avoid exact mimicry of the real world
    - Surpass the user's day-to-day reality
    - Use only abstract, non-objective environments
    because: When reality is the gold standard, reality is what is perceived and sensed in the real world, so the VR goal is to match that experience closely.
  Q For a user who expects VR reality to go beyond lived day-to-day reality, what is the design goal?  [9/S0/F2]
    - Match the real world exactly
    - Present only familiar real-world places
    * Surpass the user's idea of reality
    - Limit the experience to lived day-to-day reality
    because: For this conception, reality in VR should be beyond or surpassing day-to-day reality, not an exact mimicry of the real world.
  Q Why do different conceptions of reality make VR evaluation ambiguous?  [9/S0/F3]
    - Because surpassing reality is always easy to comprehend
    - Because a single fixed definition of reality is universally accepted
    - Because all users share the same gold standard of reality
    * Because a system that matches one group's sense of reality may be poor by another group's standard
    because: Different users define reality differently, so a system can satisfy one group while seeming bad, creepy, or hard to comprehend to another.

9/A2  recap  9/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  The goal of a virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence. Some people want to match real-world experience as closely as possible, while others want to surpass it. These differing conceptions of reality make the evaluation of a VR system ambiguous.
  - The goal of VR systems is to create a high degree of presence.
  - Some people want VR to match real-world experience as closely as possible.
  - Others want VR to surpass their daily reality rather than mimic it.
  - These differing conceptions of reality make evaluating VR systems ambiguous.

9/A3  quiz  9/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q Which best describes the uncanny valley effect?  [9/S1/F0]
    - Familiarity caused by fully realistic digital humans
    * Unease caused by almost-human digital figures with subtle imperfections
    - Comfort caused by clearly non-human virtual objects
    - Preference caused by abstract virtual environments
    because: The uncanny valley effect is that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections.
  Q In the uncanny valley plot, how does familiarity change for moving objects as human likeness increases?  [9/S1/F1]
    - It falls first, then rises to a peak, then falls again
    - It falls steadily throughout the range of human likeness
    * It rises, then falls more sharply to a minimum, then rises again
    - It rises steadily throughout the range of human likeness
    because: As an artificial object becomes more human-like, familiarity first increases, then decreases more sharply for moving objects, reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region, and then increases again.
  Q What is the main design implication of the uncanny valley effect for VR content?  [9/S1/F2]
    - Use only abstract objects to guarantee a comfortable experience
    - Always match reality exactly to maximize user familiarity
    - Avoid all human-like figures in every VR experience
    * Balance realism because exact human likeness can reduce familiarity
    because: Trying to match reality exactly may not produce a good VR experience if human-like figures fall in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.

9/A4  recap  9/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first. Familiarity with human-like objects first increases, then decreases in the uncanny valley region, typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness, and then increases again. When creating a VR experience, trying to match reality exactly may not produce a good experience if figures fall in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.
  - Digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first.
  - Familiarity with human-like objects first increases, then decreases in the uncanny valley region (typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness), and then increases again.
  - There is a trade-off over how much realism to include because matching reality exactly may not produce a good experience if figures fall in the uncanny valley.

9/A5  put_in_order  9/S1  "Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases"  (1 facts, 4 concepts)
  Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases: Familiarity increases for moving and stationary objects > Familiarity decreases, more sharply for moving objects > Familiarity reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley > Familiarity increases for highly human-like objects  [9/S1/F1]

9/A6  quiz  9/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q Representational fidelity in a virtual reality experience refers to  [9/S2/F2]
    * how familiar the experience is with real or possible Earth places
    - how closely virtual task actions match real-world task actions
    - how well the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience
    - how much photorealism is required for virtual presence
    because: Representational fidelity is the degree to which a VR experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth. The other options describe interaction fidelity, experiential fidelity, or a false requirement for photorealism.
  Q Which of these is an example of high interaction fidelity?  [9/S2/F5]
    - Sitting still and pressing a button to move forward
    - Presenting purely abstract, non-objective virtual places
    * Translating intense, realistic physical activities into virtual activities
    - Letting every user roam freely so each session differs
    because: High interaction fidelity involves intense realistic physical actions, in which real-world physical activities are translated into virtual activities. Sitting and moving by button press is very low interaction fidelity, while the other options relate to different fidelity concerns.
  Q Experiential fidelity in virtual reality describes  [9/S2/F6]
    - the degree to which digital humans are perceived as familiar
    * the match between the user's personal experience and the creator's intended experience
    - the match between a virtual place and familiar Earth places
    - the match between virtual physical actions and real-world physical actions
    because: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. The other options describe interaction fidelity, representational fidelity, or the uncanny valley.
  Q Why can a free-roaming virtual world with endless possibilities have low experiential fidelity?  [9/S2/F7]
    - It requires users to perform intense physical actions
    * It can make every usage lead to a different experience
    - It places real-world constraints on virtual navigation
    - It makes every usage lead to the same intended experience
    because: A free-roaming virtual world with endless possibilities can lead every usage to a different experience, which is not what happens in the real world and lowers experiential fidelity. Placing real-world constraints on navigation, movement, and interaction makes the experience closer to the real world.
  Q Why should virtual reality developers maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity as high as possible?  [9/S2/F8]
    - So every user in a free-roaming world has the same experience
    - So photorealism or human-like objects become necessary for presence
    - So the system no longer needs to consider immersion and presence
    * So the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience
    because: Developers should maintain the three fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience. Presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects, and developers should still consider immersion and presence.

9/A7  recap  9/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 8 concepts)
  Presence does not require photorealism, but developers should consider representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities. Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual experience conveys familiarity with a place on Earth, while interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for virtual tasks correspond to real-world actions. Finally, experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's experience matches the creator's intent, and maintaining high fidelities helps ensure the uncanny valley effect does not affect the experience.
  - Presence does not require photorealism, but developers should consider representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities.
  - Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual experience conveys familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth.
  - Interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for virtual tasks correspond to equivalent real-world actions.
  - Experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's experience matches the creator's intended experience.
  - Developers should maintain high fidelities to ensure the uncanny valley effect does not affect the experience.

9/A8  quiz  9/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Why are the main challenges of AR systems described as mostly technological rather than psychological?  [9/S3/F0]
    * Because immersion is not a major concern in AR and psychological effects are less important than in VR.
    - Because AR depends only on the user's sense of presence in a virtual world.
    - Because AR removes the need for display and interaction technology.
    - Because psychological effects are stronger in AR than in VR.
    because: The segment states that AR challenges are mostly technological because immersion is not a major concern and psychological effects are less important in AR than in VR.
  Q Why is suitable display technology needed to combine real and virtual content in AR?  [9/S3/F2]
    - To replace the real-world representation with a fully virtual scene.
    - To determine the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor.
    * To overlay virtual content on the device's representation of the real world.
    - To provide the only possible input modality for real-time interaction.
    because: Combining real and virtual content in AR requires display technology that can overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on the device.
  Q What does real-time interaction in AR require?  [9/S3/F3]
    - A high degree of immersion to make the experience psychologically convincing.
    - A complete virtual environment that hides the real-world representation.
    - Only a display that overlays virtual content without user input.
    * Suitable input devices and input modalities for interacting with overlaid virtual content.
    because: Real-time interaction in AR requires suitable forms of interaction, including input devices and input modalities, so the user can interact with digital content overlaid on the real world.
  Q What does three-dimensional registration mean in an AR system?  [9/S3/F4]
    - Showing virtual content on a screen without aligning it to real-world objects.
    - Replacing real-world objects with virtual objects in a virtual environment.
    - Recording the user's eye movements to estimate where they are looking.
    * Anchoring virtual content in the real world so it appears part of the physical environment.
    because: 3D registration in AR means anchoring virtual content at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.
  Q What role does pose determination play in AR registration and tracking?  [9/S3/F5, 9/S3/F6]
    - It provides the input devices and modalities needed for real-time interaction.
    - It removes the need to align virtual content with the physical environment.
    * It establishes the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor and updates that pose as the user moves.
    - It selects the display technology used to overlay virtual content on the real world.
    because: Pose means the viewer's position and orientation relative to a real-world anchor. Conceptually, pose determination includes a registration phase that sets the initial pose and a tracking phase that updates it as the user moves.

9/A9  recap  9/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  AR challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological because psychological effects are less important than in VR. AR requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the real world and suitable interaction modalities for users. Furthermore, 3D registration anchors virtual content in the real world through pose determination, which consists of both a registration phase and a tracking phase.
  - AR challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological.
  - AR requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the real world.
  - Real-time interaction requires suitable forms of interaction and input devices.
  - 3D registration anchors virtual content in the real world so it mixes seamlessly.
  - Pose determination includes both a registration phase and a tracking phase.

    * Presence
    - Representational fidelity
    - Tracking

  Q What does the uncanny valley effect in virtual reality refer to?  [9/S4/F1]
    - Uneasiness caused by using virtual input actions that do not match real-world task actions
    - Uneasiness caused by making augmented reality virtual content difficult to register in the real world
    - Uneasiness caused by making the virtual environment completely abstract and unfamiliar to real-world experience
    * Uneasiness caused by making the virtual environment as familiar as possible to real-world experience
    because: The uncanny valley effect is the uneasiness or creepiness that can occur when a VR environment is made too familiar to the user's real-world experience.
  Q Which three fidelities should a virtual reality developer consider to help avoid the uncanny valley effect?  [9/S4/F2]
    * Representational fidelity, experiential fidelity, and interaction fidelity

    - Display technology, representational fidelity, and interaction fidelity

9/A11  recap  9/S4  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  VR systems are defined by technological immersion and psychological presence. To avoid the uncanny valley effect where familiarity causes uneasiness, developers should be aware of representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity. Conversely, the major issues in augmented reality are mostly technological and consist of display technology, input mechanisms, and tracking.
  - VR systems involve technological immersion and psychological presence.
  - Making VR environments too familiar can cause the uncanny valley effect of uneasiness.
  - Avoiding the uncanny valley requires awareness of representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.
  - AR issues are mostly technological, involving display, input mechanisms, and tracking.

9/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q Why can increasing photorealism in a virtual reality system reduce rather than improve the user's sense of presence?  [9/S0/F0, 9/S1/F0, 9/S1/F2, 9/S2/F0; virtual reality system, presence, photorealism, uncanny valley effect, realism, immersive experience]
    A A virtual reality system aims to create presence, and the closer it is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides. Presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects. The uncanny valley effect shows that almost-real digital representations can evoke unease, so making figures more human-like creates a trade-off over how much realism to include.
  Q How can representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity help a virtual reality system avoid the uncanny valley effect?  [9/S2/F1, 9/S2/F8, 9/S4/F1; virtual reality system, representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, experiential fidelity, immersion, presence, uncanny valley effect]
    A A virtual reality system developer should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity along with immersion and presence. Maintaining these fidelities helps keep the uncanny valley effect from affecting the virtual world experience. This is important because making environments as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience can cause uneasiness or creepiness.
  Q Why are the major issues in augmented reality systems described as mostly technological, whereas virtual reality systems also raise psychological concerns?  [9/S3/F0, 9/S4/F0, 9/S4/F3; augmented reality, virtual reality, display technology, input mechanism, pose estimation, tracking, immersion, presence]
    A Augmented reality challenges are mostly technological because immersion is not a major concern and psychological effects are less important in augmented reality than in virtual reality. The major augmented reality issues are proper display technology, proper input mechanisms, and pose estimation and updating, which is popularly called tracking. In virtual reality, the two major concerns are technological and psychological, leading to immersion and presence.
  Q Why is pose determination essential for three-dimensional registration in augmented reality, and how do the registration and tracking phases differ?  [9/S3/F4, 9/S3/F5, 9/S3/F6, 7/S3/F4; three-dimensional registration, augmented reality, pose, position, orientation, anchor, registration phase, tracking phase, tracking]
    A Three-dimensional registration anchors virtual content in the real world at a suitable place so that it appears to mix seamlessly with physical objects. To do this, the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor must be determined. Conceptually, the registration phase determines that pose at the start, while the tracking phase updates the pose as the user moves. Earlier augmented reality systems used tracking to register content in three dimensions by overlaying it on real-world markers.

===== lecture 10: Cybersickness

10/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.
  What is stereoscopic vision? (lecture 6) -> In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.
  What is non-immersive virtual reality system? (lecture 2) -> From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

10/A2  recap  10/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Cybersickness (CS), also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality. It can be caused by many factors and is indicated by symptoms such as nausea, headache, and dizziness. Reducing the impact of cybersickness is very important for the usability and acceptability of VR systems.
  - Cybersickness (CS) is a condition that affects individuals interacting with virtual reality.
  - Symptoms such as nausea, headache, and dizziness indicate the onset of cybersickness.
  - Cybersickness can be caused by many different factors.
  - Reducing the impact of cybersickness is important for the usability and appeal of VR systems.

    - Evaluation and mitigation

  Q Which of the following is an internal user-related factor that can increase the likelihood of cybersickness?  [10/S1/F2]
    - VR content
    - Display resolution
    - Headset latency
    * Motion sickness susceptibility
    because: Internal factors are individual characteristics or conditions such as motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition; hardware factors and VR content are external.
  Q How are motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness generally related?  [10/S1/F10]
    - Motion sickness susceptibility is unrelated to cybersickness risk
    * Higher motion sickness susceptibility is associated with higher cybersickness risk
    - Motion sickness susceptibility only matters when VR content is controllable
    - Lower motion sickness susceptibility is associated with higher cybersickness risk
    because: There is a positive correlation between motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness risk, so higher motion sickness susceptibility is likely to lead to more severe cybersickness symptoms.
  Q Why might female users of head-mounted displays be associated with increased cybersickness?  [10/S1/F6, 10/S1/F7]
    * Inter-pupillary distance fit may be harder to find, affecting stereoscopic vision
    - They usually have greater retinal eccentricity
    - They are more likely to use a standing posture
    - They usually have higher headset latency
    because: A possible reason is inter-pupillary distance fit because inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit.
  Q How does physical position affect cybersickness susceptibility when using the same VR system?  [10/S1/F15]
    - A sitting posture is likely to induce more cybersickness than standing
    - Physical position has no effect on cybersickness
    * A standing posture is likely to induce more or more severe cybersickness than sitting
    - A standing posture matters only for users with neurological conditions
    because: Using a VR system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cybersickness, or more severe cybersickness, than using the same system while sitting.

10/A4  recap  10/S1  "Recap"  (13 facts, 28 concepts)
  Cybersickness is caused by both internal factors, such as age, gender, and motion sickness susceptibility, and external factors like hardware and VR content. Specific physical conditions, including poor sleep quality, greater retinal eccentricity, and neurological conditions can increase susceptibility. Additionally, physical posture and negative emotional conditions can heighten the risk, though repeated exposure may reduce the severity of symptoms.
  - Cybersickness is caused by internal and external factors, with external factors including hardware and VR content.
  - Internal factors include individual characteristics like age, gender, motion sickness susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.
  - Age-related sensitivity varies and is more notable in controllable content, while gender differences remain inconclusive.
  - High motion sickness susceptibility, poor sleep quality, greater retinal eccentricity, and neurological conditions increase the risk of cybersickness.
  - Using a system in a standing posture or experiencing negative emotions can also increase the likelihood of cybersickness.

10/A5  quiz  10/S2  "Quick quiz"  (8 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q How does increasing VR display resolution from 1K to 4K affect cybersickness?  [10/S2/F2]
    * It is substantially reduced from 1K to 2K, with little further reduction at 3K or 4K.
    - It increases substantially from 1K to 2K, then remains stable.
    - It is reduced only when moving from 3K to 4K.
    - It is substantially reduced at each step from 1K to 4K.
    because: A resolution study found a substantial reduction in cybersickness from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or 3K to 4K.
  Q In HMD-based VR, what is the effect of higher latency?  [10/S2/F3, 10/S2/F4]
    - It affects only users with low motion-sickness susceptibility.
    - It decreases the likelihood of cybersickness.
    * It increases the likelihood of cybersickness.
    - It has no effect unless latency jitter is high.
    because: Latency is the time gap between a physical movement and its virtual-world change, and in HMD-based VR, more latency makes cybersickness more likely.
  Q What is latency jitter in VR?  [10/S2/F5, 10/S2/F6]
    * Variability in the time gap between a physical movement and its virtual reflection.
    - A user’s susceptibility to motion sickness.
    - A fixed time gap between a physical movement and its virtual reflection.
    - The difference in cybersickness between HMD and monitor users.
    because: Latency jitter is variability in latency, which can create irregular timing and lead to discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness.
  Q Which display comparison is associated with more cybersickness?  [10/S2/F7]
    - Using a panoramic screen instead of a VR headset.
    - Using a flat-screen display instead of a VR headset.
    * Using a VR headset instead of a flat-screen display.
    - Using a non-immersive display instead of an HMD-based display.
    because: HMD-based or VR headset displays are associated with more cybersickness than conventional monitors or non-immersive systems, and a study found VR headset users experienced more cybersickness than flat-screen users.
  Q Which VR input comparison is associated with less cybersickness?  [10/S2/F9, 10/S2/F10]
    - Using steering with handlebars instead of a joystick.
    * Using a gamepad instead of a hand controller.
    - Using a gamepad and a hand controller equally.
    - Using a hand controller instead of a gamepad.
    because: Input method can influence cybersickness, and a gamepad causes less cybersickness than a hand controller, while motion controls such as handlebars may cause more than non-motion controls such as a joystick.

10/A6  recap  10/S2  "Recap"  (11 facts, 24 concepts)
  Hardware is a category of external factors that can induce cybersickness in virtual reality. Display resolution reduces cybersickness up to 2K, but shows no significant reduction from 2K to 3K or 4K. Additionally, latency and its variability increase the likelihood and severity of cybersickness, while the display type, its quality, and the input method used also influence these levels.
  - Hardware is a category of external factors that can induce cybersickness in virtual reality.
  - Display resolution reduces cybersickness up to 2K, but shows no significant reduction from 2K to 3K or 4K.
  - Latency and its variability, known as jitter, increase the likelihood and severity of cybersickness.
  - The display type, its quality, and the input method used can influence cybersickness levels.

10/A8  recap  10/S3  "Recap"  (2 facts, 11 concepts)
  Cybersickness is caused by internal factors like age and gender, as well as external factors like hardware and content. Virtual reality content is specifically identified as one of these external factors.
  - Cybersickness is caused by internal factors like age and gender, and external factors like hardware and content.
  - Virtual reality content is an external factor that contributes to cybersickness.

10/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 39 concepts)
  Q Why does reducing cybersickness matter for a virtual reality system that is defined as an interactive computer-generated sensory environment?  [10/S0/F3, 4/S1/F0; virtual reality system, cybersickness, usability, acceptability, user experience, virtual reality application]
    A A virtual reality system is a system with an artificial environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens. Reducing cybersickness is important for such systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and supports usability and acceptability. It also makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.
  Q How does prior or repeated exposure to virtual reality relate to the link between motion sickness susceptibility and cybersickness?  [10/S1/F8, 10/S1/F9, 10/S1/F10, 10/S1/F11; motion sickness, virtual reality, motion sickness susceptibility, cyber sickness susceptibility, cybersickness, cyber sickness risk, cyber sickness symptoms, prior exposure to virtual reality systems, repeated exposure to virtual reality, cybersickness severity]
    A Motion sickness occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, and virtual reality recreates realistic movement and visual environments, so motion sickness susceptibility tends to co-occur with cyber sickness susceptibility. Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, with higher susceptibility likely producing more severe cyber sickness symptoms. Prior or repeated exposure to virtual reality can reduce that effect and reduce cybersickness severity over time.
  Q How do latency and display resolution differ as hardware factors that can cause cybersickness?  [10/S2/F2, 10/S2/F3, 10/S2/F4, 10/S2/F5, 10/S2/F6; latency, latency jitter, display resolution, cybersickness, head-mounted display, virtual reality, hardware factor]
    A Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world, and in head-mounted display-based virtual reality cybersickness increases as latency increases. Latency jitter is variability in that latency and can create irregularities, inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness. Display resolution reduces cybersickness only up to a point: a study found substantial reduction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.
  Q How can inter-pupillary distance fit explain why female head-mounted display users may experience more cybersickness?  [10/S1/F6, 10/S1/F7, 6/S1/F2; stereoscopic vision, inter-pupillary distance, inter-pupillary distance fit, head-mounted display, cybersickness, virtual reality display, inter-pupillary distance adjustable range, gender]
    A Stereoscopic vision makes users perceive two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects and space, and inter-pupillary distance determines stereoscopic vision. Female head-mounted display use is associated with increased cybersickness, possibly because a greater proportion of female users have trouble finding a good inter-pupillary distance fit. This suggests that virtual reality displays should have a wider inter-pupillary distance adjustable range for female users.

===== lecture 11: Cybersickness

11/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

11/A1  quiz  11/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q Which of the following is one of the six VR-content factors that affect cybersickness?  [11/S0/F1]
    * Field of view
    - Audio loudness
    - Headset type
    - User's age
    because: The six VR-content factors are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.
  Q How does visual motion relate to cybersickness?  [11/S0/F2]
    - Higher visual motion is irrelevant to risk, and the way content moves determines severity.
    - Higher visual motion can increase risk, but the way content moves does not affect severity.
    * Higher visual motion can increase risk, and the way content moves affects severity.
    - Lower visual motion can increase risk, and the way content moves affects severity.
    because: Visual motion is a primary cause of cybersickness: higher visual motion can increase risk, and the way the content moves also affects cybersickness and its severity.
  Q What is vection?  [11/S0/F3]
    * The sensation of self-motion
    - The preference for adventurous virtual content
    - The rate at which visual motion changes
    - The sensation of the virtual environment rotating
    because: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus.
  Q What does brief exposure to turbulent visual motion do to cybersickness?  [11/S0/F6]
    * Alone it is not enough to induce it, but longer exposure can induce it.
    - Alone it is enough to induce it immediately.
    - Alone it matters only when combined with faster speed.
    - Alone it prevents it, and longer exposure reduces it.
    because: Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cybersickness, but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce it.
  Q How does rotation affect cybersickness?  [11/S0/F7]
    - It increases with angular velocity and is more intense around the z axis than the x and y axes.
    * It increases with angular velocity and is more intense around the x and y axes than the z axis.
    - It is unaffected by angular velocity and is more intense around the z axis than the x and y axes.
    - It decreases with angular velocity and is more intense around the x and y axes than the z axis.
    because: Cybersickness increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

11/A2  recap  11/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 22 concepts)
  The design of virtual environments can have a significant impact on the likelihood and severity of cybersickness. Six content factors affect cybersickness, with visual motion being a primary cause influenced by the amount and manner of movement. Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest in peripheral stimuli and correlates with visual motion. Additionally, factors such as height, speed, duration of exposure, viewpoint, and angular velocity also influence cybersickness.
  - The design of virtual environments can have a significant impact on the likelihood and severity of cybersickness.
  - Six content factors affect cybersickness: visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.
  - Visual motion is a primary cause of cybersickness, and higher visual motion can increase the risk while the manner of movement affects its severity.
  - Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest in peripheral stimuli and correlates with visual motion.
  - Cybersickness is also influenced by height, speed, duration of exposure, viewpoint, and angular velocity.

  Locomotion is a content-related factor because sensory mismatches between virtual and physical movements can cause cybersickness.   - Locomotion is a content-related factor where sensory mismatches can cause cybersickness.
  - Control over motion affects presence, and more control generally leads to less cybersickness.
  - Hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.
  - Teleportation is found to reduce cybersickness compared to naturalistic free movement.

11/A6  recap  11/S2  "Recap"  (9 facts, 19 concepts)
  Field of view (FOV) determines how much of the user's vision is captured and impacts susceptibility to cybersickness. While a larger FOV increases immersion, reducing it can alleviate symptoms, although an excessively narrow FOV may increase head movement and exacerbate cybersickness. Furthermore, action content, horror genres, bumpy terrain, and stormy weather are more likely to induce cybersickness, though users accustomed to adrenaline sports may experience less severity from action content.
  - Field of view (FOV) determines how much of the user's vision is captured and affects susceptibility to cybersickness.
  - While a larger FOV increases immersion, reducing it can help alleviate cybersickness.
  - An excessively narrow FOV can decrease immersion and increase head movement, which may exacerbate cybersickness.
  - Action content, horror genres, bumpy terrain, and stormy weather are more likely to induce cybersickness.
  - Users accustomed to adrenaline sports may experience less cybersickness from action content.

11/A10  recap  11/S4  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)

The measurement technique can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time evaluation, while the output can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a numerical sickness score. Questionnaire-based inputs are a common method that uses self-report questionnaires or scales to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.

  - The output of CS measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.
  - Questionnaire-based inputs are common methods that use self-report questionnaires or scales to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.

11/A23  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (6 facts, 20 concepts)
  *manual evaluation | binary classes | multiple classes | sickness score  (Binary classes, multiple classes, and a sickness score are possible outputs of cybersickness measurement, whereas manual evaluation is an evaluation technique rather than an output.)  [11/S4/F3, 11/S7/F0]
  *nausea scale | disorientation subscale | nausea subscale | oculomotor subscale  (The oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales are the three subscales of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire, while the Nausea Scale is a separate questionnaire for assessing discomfort.)  [11/S4/F8, 11/S4/F14]
  z axis | *angular velocity | y axis | x axis  (The x, y, and z axes are the axes around which rotation can take place in the cybersickness discussion, whereas angular velocity is a motion parameter that increases cybersickness, not a rotation axis.)  [11/S0/F7, 11/S0/F4]

11/A24  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 25 concepts)
  Q Why can giving a user more control over movement in a virtual world reduce their risk of cybersickness?  [11/S1/F1, 8/S2/F0; control over motion, presence, cybersickness, virtual world]
    A Control over motion in a virtual world directly affects presence, the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. Greater presence in virtual reality generally reduces cybersickness, while more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence. Therefore, giving users more movement control can lower cybersickness through increased presence.
  Q Why is changing the field of view of a virtual reality headset a trade-off between immersion and cybersickness?  [11/S2/F0, 11/S2/F1, 11/S2/F2, 11/S2/F3; field of view, virtual reality headset, immersion, cybersickness, head movement, field of vision]
    A A field of view is the extent to which the display captures the user's field of vision, and a larger field of view generally results in greater immersion. Reducing the field of view can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness. However, an excessively narrow field of view can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness.
  Q Why can longer exposure to turbulent visual motion induce cybersickness while brief exposure alone may not?  [11/S0/F2, 11/S0/F3, 11/S0/F6; visual motion, vection, self-motion, peripheral stimulus, turbulent visual motion, cybersickness]
    A Visual motion is one of the primary causes of cybersickness, and higher visual motion can increase the risk, while the way the content moves also affects severity. Vection, the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus. Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cybersickness, but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cybersickness.
  Q Why can physiological or biometric signals complement questionnaire-based reports when measuring cybersickness?  [11/S4/F4, 11/S5/F0, 11/S6/F5; questionnaire-based input, physiological and biometric information, cybersickness]
    A Questionnaire-based input uses self-report ratings and is a subjective category of input for measuring cybersickness. Physiological or biometric inputs are objective, and they can detect cybersickness because questionnaires can be subjective, prone to inaccuracies, and may not always be reliable. Using them together can combine user-reported discomfort with objective signals.

12/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is field of view (FOV)? (lecture 11) -> Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
  What is sickness score? (lecture 11) -> The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.
  What is optical flow? (lecture 11) -> Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.
  What is transparent model? (lecture 11) -> One way to perform machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) is to use transparent models, which provide clear insight into the decision-making process and whose inner workings can easily be understood.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
