12/A10  recap  12/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Users need personal countermeasures because cybersickness is subjective and individual. To reduce risk, users should limit exposure to a safe maximum of 55 to 70 minutes or use habituation through repeated short-duration exposures. Additionally, techniques like controlled breathing, background music, and airflow can help soothe the mind and reduce symptoms.
  - Users need personal countermeasures because cybersickness is subjective and individual.
  - Users should avoid long exposure, as a safe maximum for many is between 55 and 70 minutes.
  - Habituation can be achieved through repeated short-duration exposures.
  - Controlled breathing, background music, and airflow can help soothe the mind and reduce symptoms.

  Order the stages of a user habituation approach: Short-duration repeated exposures > Full recovery from symptoms > Longer-duration repeated exposures  [12/S4/F3]

12/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q Why might a developer of a machine-learning cybersickness evaluator need to weigh prediction accuracy against understandability when comparing transparent, interpretable, and black-box models?  [12/S0/F1, 12/S0/F4, 12/S0/F7, 11/S7/F3; transparent model, interpretable model, black-box model, prediction accuracy, machine learning, cybersickness]
    A Transparent models provide clear insight into the decision-making process, and interpretable models are similar, offering more flexibility in customization and more precise details about the relationship between input and output. Black-box models cannot easily be understood or explained because they take an input and produce an output without revealing how or why that output is generated. Black-box models generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but they require large amounts of data and processing power.
  Q How does prediction differ from detection in cybersickness evaluation, and why can prediction still support mitigation even though most evaluation work focuses on detection?  [12/S1/F0, 12/S1/F1, 12/S2/F0; detection, prediction, cybersickness evaluation technique, mitigation measures, cybersickness mitigation, cybersickness]
    A Detection uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, whereas prediction occurs before the experience to determine whether it will occur. Most cybersickness evaluation focuses on detection, but prediction is important because it can enable mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs. Because complete prevention is generally not possible, mitigation uses measures to reduce or eliminate cybersickness or at least lessen its impact.
  Q Why can a field-of-view adjustment reduce cybersickness while also creating a cost for user experience?  [12/S2/F1, 12/S3/F1, 12/S3/F2, 12/S3/F4; field of view, field of view adjustment, peripheral optical flow, presence, user experience, cybersickness]
    A Field of view is the amount of virtual environment visible at any moment, and adjusting it can mitigate cybersickness because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow. However, this restriction can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks. Since mitigation strategies often affect presence, and presence affects user experience, field-of-view adjustment can improve comfort while degrading user experience.
  Q How do hybrid cybersickness-evaluation models try to balance the higher accuracy of black-box models with the transparency of transparent or interpretable models?  [12/S0/F7, 12/S0/F8, 12/S0/F10; hybrid model, transparent model, interpretable model, black-box model, prediction accuracy, machine learning, cybersickness]
    A Black-box models generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but they require large amounts of data and processing power. Hybrid models are combinations of different machine learning models designed to provide high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process. They can combine the strengths of transparent and black-box models by providing good predictive accuracy and some interpretability, which is useful in application domains where both high accuracy and transparency are essential.

===== lecture 13: VR Hardware

13/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

13/A2  recap  13/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 7 concepts)
  A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. Data flow from the organism to the hardware is tracking, while data flow from the hardware to the organism is stimulation, with bidirectional data flows also existing between the hardware, the physical world, and the organism. The organism is an equally important component of the system that cannot be omitted because the user is always present.
  - A VR system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the physical world.
  - Data flows are categorized as tracking from the organism to the hardware and stimulation from the hardware to the organism.
  - The organism is an equally important component of the system that cannot be omitted.

13/A3  quiz  13/S1  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Which data flow in a VR system carries hardware-generated stimuli to the user?  [13/S1/F0]
    - Surrounding-world output flow
    - Tracking data flow
    * Stimulation data flow
    - Surrounding-world input flow
    because: In a VR system, the stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli to the user, while tracking data flow carries user motion information to the hardware.
  Q What role does the tracking data flow play in a VR system?  [13/S1/F0]
    - It supplies computer-generated sensory experiences directly to the user's organs
    - It blocks real-world sensory inputs from reaching the user's sensory organs
    - It measures how fully immersed the user feels in the virtual environment
    * It lets VR hardware adjust its stimuli using tracked user motions
    because: The tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so that the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.
  Q Which tracked user action is described as commonly used and the most important to track in VR?  [13/S1/F1]
    * Head tracking
    - Controller movements
    - Button presses
    - Eye movements
    because: Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important tracking target, although button presses, eye movements, controller movements, and other body movements may also be tracked.

13/A4  recap  13/S1  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Data flow in a VR system is bidirectional: stimulation data carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data uses sensors to track user motions. Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.
  - Data flow between VR hardware and the user is bidirectional.
  - Head tracking is the most important thing to track, though other motions and button presses may also be tracked.

    * Real-world stimuli can affect user behavior while interacting with the virtual world
    - Head movements are the main data needed to update the display
    - The environment supplies the virtual graphics that the HMD displays

    - By receiving stimulation data from the VR hardware

    because: A robotic arm can change the position of objects in the environment, showing that VR hardware may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than being limited to the computer, HMD, or controller.

  - The virtual reality system consists of the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

13/A7  quiz  13/S3  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q Which three categories are the major components of VR hardware?  [13/S3/F0]
    * Displays, sensors, and computers
    - Hand input devices, non-hand input devices, and displays
    - Displays, cameras, and robotic arms
    - User, hardware, and physical environment
    because: VR hardware is described as having displays as output devices, sensors as input devices, and computers as processing devices.
  Q In VR hardware, what does a display or output device mean in the broad sense?  [13/S3/F1]
    - Any device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user
    * Any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
    - Only a screen that shows visual content
    - Any device that tracks the user's movements

  Q Why are sensors classified as input devices in VR hardware?  [13/S3/F2]
    - They process inputs and produce outputs for the user
    - They require the user's hands to operate
    - They produce output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
    * They track the user's input and extract information from the real world
    because: A sensor/input device is a tracking device that tracks user input and extracts real-world information, with the discussion restricted to sensors tracking user movements.
  Q What is a computer or processing device in VR hardware?  [13/S3/F3]
    * A device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world
    - A device that tracks the user's movements in the real world
    - A device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs
    - A device that changes the surrounding physical environment
    because: The computer/processing device processes inputs and produces outputs so that the user can perceive the world.

13/A8  recap  13/S3  "Recap"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers. Displays are output devices that stimulate the user's sensory organs, while sensors are input devices that track user movements and real-world information. Computers act as processing devices that process inputs and produce outputs for the user to perceive the world.
  - VR hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers.
  - Displays are output devices that stimulate the user's sensory organs.
  - Sensors are input devices that track user movements and extract information from the real world.
  - Computers are processing devices that process inputs and produce outputs.

13/A9  quiz  13/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which of the following is one of the five broad categories of VR hand input devices?  [13/S4/F1]
    * Tracked handheld controllers
    - Body-movement sensors
    - Eye-tracking devices
    - Head-mounted displays
    because: VR hand input devices are divided into world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.
  Q What capability of tracked handheld controllers helps avoid the break-in presence that can occur with non-tracked handheld controllers?  [13/S4/F4, 13/S4/F5]
    - They require the user to keep hands in front of an IR camera
    - They provide only discrete button and trigger input
    * Six-degree-of-freedom tracking of their movement in 3D space
    - They are worn on the fingers instead of held in the hand
    because: Non-tracked handheld controllers are not tracked in 3D space, so virtual hands may not move with the user. Tracked handheld controllers have 6DoF tracking, so their movement can be reflected in the virtual world.
  Q Why may tracked handheld controllers not let users fully touch and feel passive virtual objects?  [13/S4/F6]
    - The controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space
    - The user does not hold any device in the hand
    - The user must keep the hands in front of a camera
    * The user’s hands are occupied with the controller
    because: Because the hands are occupied with the controller, users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction.
  Q What problem is specifically tied to recognizing many gestures with hand-worn input devices?  [13/S4/F11]
    - The fingers are restricted to fingertip-only sensors
    - The device must be attached to a low-cost HMD to work
    * Users may need to recalibrate often or learn and remember many gestures
    - The user’s hands must remain visible to a wide-angle camera
    because: When many gestures are possible, hand-worn devices may require frequent recalibration or force users to remember many gestures, which can be difficult for some users.
  Q What enables bare-hand input to leave the user’s hands completely free?  [13/S4/F12]
    - A tracked controller reports six degrees of freedom
    - A data glove processes continuous bend-sensor data
    - An HMD uses head yaw, roll, and pitch to infer hand gestures
    * Computer vision detects the hand gestures and converts them into commands
    because: In bare-hand input, the system tracks the user’s bare hand with computer vision and translates detected gestures into virtual-environment commands, so no wearable or controller is needed.

13/A10  recap  13/S4  "Recap"  (15 facts, 50 concepts)
  VR hand input devices fall into five broad categories: world-grounded, non-tracked handheld, tracked handheld, hand-worn, and bare-hand. While world-grounded and non-tracked handheld devices have limitations regarding portability and presence, tracked handheld controllers provide 3D tracking but may limit physical interaction. Hand-worn devices like data gloves offer natural interaction but can require frequent recalibration, while bare-hand inputs like Leap Motion leave the user's hands completely free but may cause fatigue or require line-of-sight.
  - VR hand input devices fall into five broad categories: world-grounded, non-tracked handheld, tracked handheld, hand-worn, and bare-hand.
  - World-grounded devices like joysticks have portability issues, while non-tracked handheld controllers may cause break-in presence.
  - Tracked handheld controllers, such as VIVE controllers, provide 3D tracking but may limit the ability to feel passive virtual objects.
  - Hand-worn devices like data gloves provide natural interaction but can require frequent recalibration and may cause discomfort.
  - Bare-hand inputs like Leap Motion leave the user's hands completely free but may require line-of-sight and can cause fatigue.

13/A11  put_in_order  13/S4  "Order the signal steps of a Leap Motion hand-tracking sensor"  (1 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the signal steps of a Leap Motion hand-tracking sensor: IR LEDs emit infrared light > Infrared light reflects from the user's hands > Cameras pick up the reflected light > Software converts the signals into gestures  [13/S4/F13]

13/A12  quiz  13/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What does non-hand-based input mean for VR input devices?  [13/S5/F0]
    - Input from hand-worn devices only
    - Input from hand-held controllers only
    - Input from tracked hand gestures only
    * Input from body parts other than the hand
    because: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.
  Q How does an HMD that doubles as a head-tracking device infer input to change the view?  [13/S5/F1]
    * It uses sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch
    - It uses sensors that detect hand pinch gestures
    - It uses sensors that record the user's voice
    - It uses sensors that track where the user is looking
    because: A head-mounted display can double as a head tracking device when its sensors detect yaw, roll, and pitch to infer input that changes the view.
  Q What information do eye tracking devices help a system understand?  [13/S5/F2]
    - The exact position of a tracked handheld controller
    - The user's head yaw, roll, and pitch
    - The user's hand posture and gestures
    * Where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving
    because: Eye tracking devices track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, so the system can infer what action to take.
  Q What is the Midas touch problem in eye-tracking-based input?  [13/S5/F3]
    - The system cannot distinguish an intentional hand gesture from a habitual hand rest
    - The system cannot distinguish an intentional head turn from a habitual head rest
    - The system cannot distinguish an intentional controller press from a habitual grip
    * The system cannot distinguish an intentional selection gaze from a habitual blank gaze
    because: The Midas touch problem is the inability to differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, which can cause unintended selections or actions.
  Q Why is multimodal input generally preferable to eye-tracking-only input?  [13/S5/F4]
    - It removes eye tracking from the interaction entirely
    - It makes head tracking the only way to change the view
    * It adds other input forms to avoid unintentional gaze-based selections
    - It prevents users from using hand-based input
    because: Multimodal input uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, which is preferable because eye tracking alone can select objects or perform actions from unintentional gazes.

13/A13  recap  13/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hands, such as head motion and eye gaze. Head-tracking and eye tracking allow a system to change the view and infer actions, but eye tracking can suffer from the Midas touch problem where actions are performed from habitual gazes. Consequently, multimodal input is generally preferred over eye tracking alone to avoid actions performed from unintentional gazes.
  - Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hands.
  - Head-tracking devices use head motion to change the view.
  - Eye tracking devices track eye movements to help the system infer actions.
  - The Midas touch problem is the inability to distinguish intentional gazes from habitual gazes.
  - Multimodal input is generally preferred over eye tracking alone to avoid unintentional actions.

13/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q Why does a complete view of a virtual reality system include the surrounding physical environment in addition to the user and the virtual reality hardware?  [13/S0/F0, 13/S2/F0, 13/S2/F1, 13/S2/F2, 13/S2/F4; complete view, organism, virtual reality hardware, surrounding physical environment, user motion, robotic arm]
    A The complete view of a VR system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. The environment is included because the user may respond to real-world stimuli and is not completely detached, so it can affect the user's behavior. The user's physical movement can change the environment, and VR hardware can also change it, for example by moving objects with a robotic arm.
  Q How does the tracking data flow help a virtual reality system satisfy the requirement that a user's actions partially determine what happens in the environment?  [13/S1/F0, 13/S1/F1, 4/S1/F0; virtual reality system, tracking data flow, stimulation data flow, sensor, user motion, head tracking, button press, controller movement, eye movement, body part movement]
    A A virtual reality system is defined by an artificial environment in which the user's actions partially determine what happens. The tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motion, so the hardware can adjust the stimulation data flow carrying stimuli to the user. Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important tracked motion, while tracking may also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.
  Q Why can a tracked handheld controller reduce break-in presence while still limiting the user's tangible interaction with passive virtual objects?  [13/S4/F4, 13/S4/F5, 13/S4/F6, 8/S2/F0; presence, non-tracked handheld controller, three-dimensional space, break-in presence, tracked handheld controller, six degrees of freedom tracking, tangible interaction, passive virtual object, force feedback controller]
    A Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. A non-tracked handheld controller is not tracked in three-dimensional space, so the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the virtual hands, causing break-in presence and affecting presence. A tracked handheld controller has six degrees of freedom tracking, so break-in presence is avoided, but the user's hands are occupied with the controller and cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.
  Q What makes bare-hand input more natural than controller-based hand input, and what practical problems can a Leap Motion device introduce?  [13/S4/F12, 13/S4/F13, 13/S4/F14, 13/S4/F15; bare-hand input, computer vision, gesture, Leap Motion device, infrared, hand-tracking sensor, light-emitting diode, wide-angle camera, head-mounted display, low-cost head-mounted display, fatigue, line-of-sight issue]
    A Bare-hand input is the most natural hand input because computer vision tracks the user's bare hand, detects gestures, and leaves the hands free without any worn device. The Leap Motion device is an infrared hand-tracking sensor with light-emitting diodes and wide-angle cameras, and it can be attached to a head-mounted display to support low-cost head-mounted displays. However, it can cause fatigue if the hands are held in front of its sensor, requires the hand to be in the line of sight of its camera, and may have inconsistent gesture recognition across users.

===== lecture 14: VR Hardware

14/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.
  What is visual motion? (lecture 11) -> The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

14/A2  recap  14/S0  "Recap"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality include head, eye, full-body, and sound-based tracking. Full-body tracking captures movement beyond the head, hands, and eyes to enhance self-embodiment and social presence, and can be implemented through motion capture suits or camera-based systems. Sound-based tracking captures voice and other sounds using microphones or microphone arrays for interaction.
  - Non-hand input techniques in VR include head, eye, full-body, and sound-based tracking.
  - Full-body tracking captures movement beyond the head, hands, and eyes to enhance self-embodiment and social presence.
  - Full-body tracking can be implemented through motion capture suits or camera-based systems.
  - Sound-based tracking captures voice and other sounds using microphones or microphone arrays for interaction.

14/A3  quiz  14/S1  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q What is the role of the processing part or computer in a virtual reality system?  [14/S1/F0]
    * It processes data from input sensors and actuates output devices.
    - It actuates output devices and replaces the input sensors.
    - It processes data from output devices and actuates input sensors.
    - It processes data from input sensors and stores output data.
    because: The processing part processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.
  Q Which factors determine the selection of the processing element in a virtual reality system?  [14/S1/F1]
    - The application, target users, chosen XR engine's RAM requirement, and required immersion level.
    - The application, target users, number of GPU cards, and assumed audio output quality.
    - The required immersion level, target users, assumed display resolution, and headset type.
    * The application, target users, availability of the assumed input and output devices, and required immersion level.
    because: The processing element is selected based on the application, target users, assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.
  Q Which three components are major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality system?  [14/S1/F2]
    - The central processing unit, random access memory, and headset.
    * The graphics processing unit, central processing unit, and random access memory.
    - The graphics processing unit, central processing unit, and motion platform.
    - The graphics processing unit, random access memory, and XR engine.
    because: The major components of the computer used as the VR processing element are the GPU, CPU, and RAM.
  Q Why is GPU support preferable in a virtual reality processing system?  [14/S1/F3, 14/S1/F4, 14/S1/F6]
    - A GPU performs the middleware functions required by an XR engine.
    - A GPU reduces the minimum RAM requirement of each XR engine.
    - A GPU removes the need for a CPU in the VR processing system.
    * A GPU's parallel processing abilities speed up the rendering of complex graphics and scenes.
    because: GPUs speed up rendering because of parallel processing, and CPU-only VR processing with minimal GPU support can have performance issues.
  Q What is an extended reality engine?  [14/S1/F7]
    - It is a motion platform that adds haptic feedback.
    - It is a head-mounted display used for virtual reality output.
    * It is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality experiences.
    - It is an eye-tracking input technique for virtual reality.
    because: An XR engine is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality experiences.

14/A4  recap  14/S1  "Recap"  (9 facts, 31 concepts)
  The processing part of a VR system processes data from input sensors to activate output devices, with hardware selection depending on the application, users, and immersion level. The major components of the processing element are the GPU, CPU, and RAM. GPUs are useful for rendering complex graphics and speed up the rendering process due to their parallel processing abilities. GPU support is preferable for performance, multicore processors increase capacity, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable for XR engines.
  - The processing part of a VR system processes data from input sensors to activate output devices.
  - Hardware selection depends on the application, target users, available devices, and the required immersion level.
  - The major components of the VR processing element are the GPU, CPU, and RAM.
  - GPUs are useful for rendering complex graphics and speed up the rendering process due to their parallel processing abilities, and multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for VR applications.
  - Multicore processors increase computational capacity, but GPU support is preferable for performance, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable for XR engines.

14/A5  put_in_order  14/S1  "Order the steps of VR data processing"  (1 facts, 5 concepts)
  Order the steps of VR data processing: Input sensors provide data > Computer processes the data > Output devices are activated  [14/S1/F0]

14/A6  quiz  14/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q What are the three broad types of visual displays?  [14/S2/F3]
    - Non-see-through HMDs, optical see-through HMDs, and video see-through HMDs
    - Monoscopic displays, stereoscopic displays, and cave displays
    - Tablet displays, smartphone displays, and monitor displays
    * Head-mounted displays, world-fixed displays, and regular displays
    because: Visual displays are divided into head-mounted displays, which are wearable and mobile; world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and stationary; and regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary.
  Q How does a world-fixed display differ from a head-mounted display?  [14/S2/F3, 14/S2/F9]
    - A world-fixed display is a wearable device, while a head-mounted display is a stationary screen.
    * A world-fixed display is stationary, while a head-mounted display is wearable and mobile.
    - A world-fixed display places images directly in front of the eyes, while a head-mounted display renders graphics onto a fixed surface.
    - A world-fixed display moves with the user's head, while a head-mounted display remains fixed in space.
    because: A world-fixed display renders graphics onto a fixed surface and does not move with the user's head, whereas a head-mounted display is wearable and mobile.
  Q Although an HMD can be used to track head motion, what is its primary role?  [14/S2/F4]
    - It is primarily an audio output device.
    - It is primarily a haptic output device.
    - It is primarily a motion-platform device.
    * It is primarily a display device.
    because: Although an HMD can be used as input to track head motion, its primary use is as a display device.
  Q Which HMD category is typically used for augmented virtuality?  [14/S2/F7, 14/S2/F8]
    - Optical see-through HMDs
    * Video see-through HMDs
    - Stereoscopic HMDs
    - Non-see-through HMDs
    because: Video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, where real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.
  Q Which visual display type usually refers to common tablets or smartphones and is mostly used for AR?  [14/S2/F13]
    - World-fixed displays
    * Regular displays
    - Head-mounted displays
    - Cave displays
    because: Regular displays refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, and are mostly used for augmented reality.

14/A7  recap  14/S2  "Recap"  (10 facts, 24 concepts)
  Output devices for virtual reality include visual, audio, haptics, motion, and sensory outputs for taste and smell. Visual displays are categorized into head-mounted displays, world-fixed displays, and regular displays. Head-mounted displays are sophisticated wearable devices that more commonly provide stereoscopic viewing and come in non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through types. World-fixed displays are stationary surfaces, while regular displays are mobile devices mostly used for augmented reality.
  - VR output devices include visual, audio, haptics, motion, and sensory outputs for taste and smell.
  - Visual displays are categorized into head-mounted displays, world-fixed displays, and regular displays.
  - Head-mounted displays are sophisticated wearable devices that more commonly provide stereoscopic viewing.
  - Head-mounted displays can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.
  - World-fixed displays are stationary surfaces, while regular displays are mobile devices mostly used for augmented reality.

14/A8  quiz  14/S3  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why are headphones preferred for audio in a fully immersive VR system?  [14/S3/F0]
    - Because the sound source should not change when the user moves.
    - Because the speakers are fixed in space.
    * Because the sound source can change with head movement.
    - Because they provide tactile stimulation through the skin.
    because: Audio output can provide specialized 3D sound, and headphones are preferred for full immersion because the sound source can change with head movement.
  Q How do passive and active haptic devices differ?  [14/S3/F1, 14/S3/F2]
    - Passive devices move with the user, while active devices are attached to the world.
    - Passive devices provide tactile vibration, while active devices provide proprioceptive force.
    * Passive devices are uncontrolled objects matching virtual shapes, while active devices are computer-controlled.
    - Passive devices are computer-controlled, while active devices are static objects.
    because: Passive haptic devices are static real-world objects that are not controlled by the computer, whereas active haptic devices provide computer-controlled physical feedback.
  Q Which haptic type provides a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance?  [14/S3/F3, 14/S3/F4]
    - Electrotactile stimulation
    - Vibrotactile stimulation
    - Tactile haptics
    * Proprioceptive force-based haptics
    because: Proprioceptive force-based haptics use forces that activate joints or muscles to create a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance.
  Q What distinguishes self-grounded haptic devices from world-grounded haptic devices?  [14/S3/F5]
    - Self-grounded devices provide fully solid objects, while world-grounded devices move with the user.
    - Self-grounded devices are static real-world objects, while world-grounded devices are computer-controlled.
    - Self-grounded devices use skin vibration, while world-grounded devices use joint forces.
    * Self-grounded devices are worn or held and move with the user, while world-grounded devices are fixed to the real world.
    because: Self-grounded haptics, such as handheld controllers, move with the user, while world-grounded haptics are physically attached and cannot move.
  Q Which VR output device provides the sense of walking or running while staying in one place?  [14/S3/F9]
    - Head-mounted displays
    - Haptic rendering systems
    * Treadmills
    - Motion platforms
    because: Treadmills provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different inputs to the feet or legs.

14/A9  recap  14/S3  "Recap"  (11 facts, 29 concepts)
  Audio output provides specialized 3D audio, with headphones being preferred for a fully immersive system. Haptic devices provide touch sensations and are categorized as active versus passive, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded. Motion platforms move the body to produce a sense of physical motion, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness. Treadmills provide the sense of walking or running in place and can be either active or passive.
  - Audio output provides 3D audio, with headphones preferred for a fully immersive system.
  - Haptic devices provide touch sensations and are categorized as active versus passive, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded.
  - Motion platforms move the body to produce a sense of physical motion, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness.
  - Treadmills provide the sense of walking or running in place and can be active or passive.

14/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 44 concepts)
  Q Why is graphics processing unit support generally preferable in a virtual reality system even though modern central processing units are quite powerful?  [14/S1/F3, 14/S1/F6; graphics processing unit, central processing unit, virtual reality system, rendering, parallel processing]
    A A graphics processing unit is used to speed up rendering because it has inherent parallel processing abilities and the rendering process has inherent parallelism, making it useful for complex graphics and scenes in realistic virtual reality experiences. Modern central processing units are powerful but have many other tasks, so a CPU-only virtual reality processing system with minimal GPU support can have performance issues, and GPU support is preferable.
  Q How do the two broad full-body tracking approaches differ in the data they rely on, and why can full-body tracking strengthen the user's sense of being present in a social virtual environment?  [14/S0/F2, 14/S0/F3, 14/S0/F4, 14/S0/F5; full-body tracking, motion capture suit, camera-based tracking, self-embodiment, social presence, inertial measurement unit, fiducial marker]
    A Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves. One broad approach uses a motion capture suit, where sensors such as inertial measurement units capture and transmit raw movement data that are combined into full-body movement. The other broad approach uses multiple surrounding cameras that observe fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from their motion.
  Q How does a cave system apply the general virtual reality system idea that user movement is tracked and visual output is returned to the user?  [14/S2/F9, 14/S2/F12, 13/S0/F1; virtual reality system, tracking, world-fixed display, cave]
    A In a virtual reality system, data flow from the organism to the hardware is labeled tracking, and data flow from the hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation. A cave is a world-fixed display because it renders graphics onto a fixed surface or screen that does not move with the user's head, while the user can move within a physical space. A cave typically has three to six large surrounding screens and requires elaborate tracking of user movement, while it is usually driven by powerful graphics engines.
  Q How do the three head-mounted display categories differ in their typical use for virtual reality, augmented reality, and augmented virtuality?  [14/S2/F7, 14/S2/F8, 1/S2/F1; head-mounted display, non-see-through head-mounted display, optical see-through head-mounted display, video see-through head-mounted display, virtual reality, augmented reality, augmented virtuality]
    A Head-mounted displays can be categorized as non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through. Non-see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in virtual reality, optical see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in augmented reality, and video see-through head-mounted displays are typically used in augmented virtuality. Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while augmented virtuality is the case in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

===== lecture 15: AR Hardware

15/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.
  What is field of view (FOV)? (lecture 11) -> Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
  What is display? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

15/A9  recap  15/S3  "Recap"  (13 facts, 27 concepts)
  Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices use projectors to overlay virtual content onto the physical environment. These systems are not tied to the user and allow multiple people to interact with the content simultaneously. Implementing these systems requires understanding the geometry and lighting of the environment, which is why they are used in various domains like education, art, and entertainment.
  - Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices use projectors to overlay virtual content onto the physical environment.
  - These devices are not tied to the user and allow multiple people to interact with the content simultaneously.
  - Implementing these systems requires understanding the geometry and lighting of the environment using sensors or computer vision.
  - Categories of spatial AR include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.
  - Spatial AR systems are used in various fields such as education, medical training, and entertainment.

15/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 29 concepts)
  Q Why is field of view both a design advantage of AR headsets over AR smart glasses and a display factor that was linked to cybersickness in VR?  [15/S1/F0, 15/S2/F0, 11/S2/F0; augmented reality headset, augmented reality smart glasses, field of view, virtual reality]
    A AR headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view. AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, less powerful, and usually have a smaller field of view, making them more comfortable to wear for extended periods. Field of view was described as a content-related factor affecting susceptibility to cybersickness in VR, so the size of the displayed view matters for both immersion and comfort.
  Q How does the need to present a real-world view shape the component differences between an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens and a VR headset?  [15/S1/F1, 15/S1/F4, 15/S1/F5, 5/S0/F1; augmented reality, augmented reality headset, virtual reality headset, camera, depth sensor, Microsoft HoloLens, hologram]
    A An AR system is expected to combine the real world with virtual content, interact in real time, and register in 3D, so an AR headset may include cameras and depth sensors to obtain a real-world view. A VR headset does not need to provide a real-world view, so it may omit some advanced AR features and typically has fewer components than an AR headset. For example, the Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.
  Q Why can spatial augmented reality support simultaneous multi-user interaction more directly than AR headsets, smart glasses, and handheld AR devices?  [15/S3/F0, 15/S3/F1, 15/S3/F2; spatial augmented reality, augmented reality headset, smart glasses, handheld device, interaction]
    A Spatial augmented reality systems overlay digital content directly on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's own view. Their display element is not tied to or held by a single user, which can make the interface more natural and intuitive. This shared augmented physical content allows multiple users to interact simultaneously, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices where each user interacts only with content on that user's own device.
  Q Why are AR contact lenses considered a future wearable display that can be placed directly on the eye without being visible to outsiders, and what unresolved user-effect issue remains with them?  [15/S4/F3, 15/S4/F4, 15/S4/F8; augmented reality contact lens, wearable technology, field of vision]
    A AR contact lenses are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, and are not visible to outsiders, making them an emerging future wearable display technology. They superimpose digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision. Their effect on the user is not well known or researched, and seeing a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.

===== lecture 16: Understanding Tracking I

16/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is augmented virtuality? (lecture 1) -> Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.
  What is pose? (lecture 9) -> To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.
  What is Microsoft HoloLens? (lecture 15) -> The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

16/A1  quiz  16/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What is tracking in an extended reality system?  [16/S0/F0]
    - A type of virtual content
    * An integral hardware component
    - An optional software component
    - A form of immersive technology
    because: Tracking is described as an integral hardware component of an extended reality system.
  Q Keeping track of motion in the physical world is especially important in which XR area?  [16/S0/F1]
    - Augmented reality
    - Both virtual and augmented reality
    * Virtual reality
    - Mixed reality
    because: Tracking physical-world motion is crucial in any XR system, and it is more important in virtual reality systems.
  Q In virtual reality, what is tracking primarily used for?  [16/S0/F2]
    - Registering virtual content to a real-world anchor
    - Alerting the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world
    * Translating the user's physical motion into virtual motion
    - Tracking only moving objects in the user's field of view
    because: In VR, tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so it can be translated into virtual motion.
  Q In augmented reality, what is tracking primarily about?  [16/S0/F3]
    - Translating the user's physical motion into virtual motion
    - Replacing the real environment with a virtual scene
    * Registering virtual content in 3D space with respect to a real-world anchor
    - Tracking only the user's head orientation
    because: In AR, tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor, while also tracking the user's pose and moving real-world objects.

16/A2  recap  16/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system, and tracking motion in the physical world is crucial, more importantly in VR systems. In VR, tracking translates physical motion or input into virtual motion, while AR tracking registers virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor by tracking user pose and moving objects. Tracking is also called sensing, but the devices are more often called sensors than trackers.
  - Tracking is an integral hardware component of an XR system.
  - Tracking motion in the physical world is crucial, more importantly in VR systems.
  - In VR, tracking translates physical motion or input into virtual motion.
  - AR tracking registers virtual content in 3D space relative to a real-world anchor by tracking user pose and moving objects.
  - Tracking is also called sensing, but the devices are more often called sensors than trackers.

16/A3  quiz  16/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q What are the three categories of tracking based on what is being tracked?  [16/S1/F0]
    - Virtual reality, augmented reality, and telepresence
    * The user's sense organs, the user's other body parts, and the surrounding environment not related to the user
    - Outside-in tracking, inside-out tracking, and hybrid tracking
    - Head tracking, eye tracking, and hand tracking
    because: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.
  Q Why does an XR system need to track the position and orientation of the user's sense organs?  [16/S1/F1]
    - To capture live video of the physical world for telepresence
    - To register digital content to a real-world anchor
    * So a display attached to them can be perceived as attached to the surrounding world
    - To convert a button press into a predetermined virtual hand grasp
    because: Sense organs have body-controlled degrees of freedom, and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.
  Q In VR, which sense-organ tracking is mostly sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears?  [16/S1/F2]
    - Facial expression tracking
    - Environmental object tracking
    * Head tracking
    - Eye tracking
    because: In VR, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.
  Q When is tracking of a user's other body parts required?  [16/S1/F4]
    - When a moved physical object must be registered in three-dimensional space
    - When the user needs to be alerted to a wall not represented in the virtual world
    * When the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands
    - When live capture of the real world is added to the virtual world
    because: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and gestures or facial expressions may be reproduced for interaction.
  Q In VR, why is tracking the surrounding environment useful for safety?  [16/S1/F9]
    * It can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall
    - It reproduces a user's hand gestures as virtual hands
    - It replaces head tracking for updating the virtual view
    - It registers digital content to a moved physical object
    because: In VR, tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, helping to reduce harm.

16/A4  recap  16/S1  "Recap"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Tracking in XR systems is categorized into sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment. Sense organs are tracked so that displays are perceived as attached to the world, while other body parts can be tracked approximately or through simple input signals for virtual representations. Tracking the environment allows for the registration of digital content in AR and provides safety alerts or touch feedback in VR.
  - Tracking is categorized into sense organs, other body parts, and the surrounding environment.
  - Sense organs are tracked so that displays are perceived as attached to the world.
  - Other body parts can be tracked approximately or via explicit input signals for virtual representations.
  - Tracking the environment registers digital content in AR and provides safety alerts or touch feedback in VR.

16/A5  quiz  16/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which factors determine the choice of tracking method or technique?  [16/S2/F0]
    - Tracking process, user age, and headset weight
    - Tracker position, display resolution, and application domain
    - Tracker types, room size, and network latency
    * Tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types
    because: The choice of tracking depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.
  Q Inside-out and outside-in tracking are categorized based on which feature?  [16/S2/F1]
    * The position of the tracker or sensor that provides input
    - The number of body parts being tracked
    - The type of display used for the experience
    - The domain in which the system is deployed
    because: Tracking is categorized into outside-in and inside-out based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input.
  Q In outside-in tracking, where are the tracking sensors located?  [16/S2/F2]
    - In the experience device worn by the user
    * In external sensors or trackers in the real world
    - In the virtual world shown to the user
    - In the user's eyes only, using eye tracking
    because: In outside-in tracking, the experience device does not contain the tracking sensors; external real-world sensors or trackers provide the data.
  Q Why can inside-out tracking avoid the area restriction of outside-in tracking?  [16/S2/F4]
    - It uses a higher-resolution head-mounted display
    - It tracks only virtual objects in the environment
    * Its tracking sensors are worn by or attached to the user
    - It removes the need for any user motion data
    because: Outside-in tracking works only within the range of its external sensors, while inside-out tracking avoids that restriction because the sensors are worn or attached to the user.
  Q Which tracking category includes most VR headsets that use external sensors?  [16/S2/F3]
    - Body-part tracking
    - Environment tracking
    * Outside-in tracking
    - Inside-out tracking
    because: Most VR headsets that use external sensors are described as falling under outside-in tracking.

16/A6  recap  16/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  The choice of tracking depends on tracker position, process, and types, and is categorized as outside-in or inside-out. Outside-in tracking uses external sensors but is limited to a specific area. Inside-out tracking uses sensors within the device and has no such restriction.
  - The choice of tracking method depends on tracker position, process, and types.
  - Tracking is categorized as outside-in or inside-out based on sensor position.
  - Outside-in tracking uses external sensors but is limited to a specific area.
  - Inside-out tracking uses sensors within the device and has no such restriction.

16/A7  quiz  16/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What are the four broad steps of the tracking process?  [16/S3/F1]
    - Calibration, registration, integration, and pose correction
    * Calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction
    - Calibration, localization, integration, and drift correction
    - Calibration, registration, interpolation, and drift correction
    because: The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  Q In tracking, what does calibration primarily do?  [16/S3/F2]
    * Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    - Estimates the sensor's initial position and orientation, setting the start point
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
    because: Calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.
  Q In tracking, what is the purpose of registration?  [16/S3/F3]
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    * Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors at discrete time points
    because: Registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.
  Q In tracking, what does integration do?  [16/S3/F4]
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    * Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
    - Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation
    - Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    because: Integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.
  Q In tracking, what does drift correction do?  [16/S3/F5]
    - Transforms imperfect sensor output toward the real value, reducing sensor error
    - Determines the sensor's initial position and orientation before movement is tracked
    * Compensates for differences between estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error
    - Aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or data sources at discrete time points
    because: Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

16/A8  recap  16/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Tracking input can be obtained via inside-out or outside-in methods. The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms sensor output to behave as closely as possible to natural values, while registration determines the initial position and orientation. Integration combines measurements from multiple sources, and drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual positions to reduce error.
  - Tracking input can be obtained using inside-out or outside-in methods.
  - The tracking process consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  - Calibration transforms sensor output to behave as closely as possible to natural values.
  - Registration determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor.
  - Integration combines measurements from multiple sources, while drift correction compensates for differences between estimated and actual positions.

16/A9  put_in_order  16/S3  "Order the steps of the tracking process"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Order the steps of the tracking process: Transform imperfect sensor output > Estimate sensor position and orientation > Combine measurements from multiple sensors > Compensate position and orientation drift  [16/S3/F1, 16/S3/F2, 16/S3/F3, 16/S3/F4, 16/S3/F5]

16/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q How do pose estimation and environment tracking together support the registration of digital content in augmented reality?  [1/S2/F1, 9/S3/F5, 16/S0/F3, 16/S1/F8, 16/S1/F7; augmented reality, pose, anchor, environment tracking, digital content, physical object, three-dimensional space, field of view, real-world view, virtual reality]
    A Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content. To register virtual content in augmented reality, the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, because without proper pose estimation three-dimensional registration is difficult or impossible. In augmented reality, tracking also requires moving real-world objects in the field of view, and a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered. Environment tracking is more important in augmented reality for this purpose, although it is also important in virtual reality.
  Q How does the position of a sensor determine the two broad ways to obtain tracking input, and why does that affect where outside-in tracking can work?  [16/S2/F1, 16/S2/F2, 16/S2/F4, 16/S2/F5; tracking, tracker position, outside-in tracking, inside-out tracking, external sensor, sensor range, head-mounted display, pose, motion]
    A Tracking is categorized based on the position of the tracker or sensor into outside-in and inside-out tracking. In outside-in tracking, the experience device does not contain the sensors; external sensors such as cameras or markers provide data to identify and track motion, pose, and orientation. Outside-in tracking works only within the sensor range where those external sensors are placed. Inside-out tracking locates cameras or other sensors within the experience device, such as a head-mounted display, so no external devices are needed and there is no such placement restriction.
  Q What different errors are reduced by calibration and drift correction in the tracking process?  [16/S3/F1, 16/S3/F2, 16/S3/F5; tracking, tracking process, calibration, drift correction, sensor error, estimation error, position, orientation]
    A The tracking process broadly consists of calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error. Drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation, reducing estimation error.
  Q How does sense-organ tracking support a display attached to a user's sense organ, and when might eye tracking be added to head tracking in virtual reality?  [16/S1/F1, 16/S1/F2, 16/S1/F3; sense-organ tracking, sense organ, display, body-controlled degree of freedom, virtual world, user experience, head tracking, eye tracking, rendering, display technology, eye movement]
    A Sense organs such as eyes and ears have body-controlled degrees of freedom, and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience. In virtual reality, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears. Eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movement, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.

===== lecture 17: Understanding Tracking - I

17/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
