  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.
  What is registration? (lecture 16) -> The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  What is calibration? (lecture 16) -> The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  What is integration? (lecture 16) -> The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  What is drift correction? (lecture 16) -> The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

17/A1  quiz  17/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Which three sensors are mainly contained in an inertial measurement unit?  [17/S0/F0]
    - An accelerometer, a microphone, and a magnetometer
    - A gyroscope, a camera, and a projector
    * A gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer
    - A gyroscope, an actuator, and a compass
    because: An inertial measurement unit is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer.
  Q In an inertial measurement unit, what does a gyroscope capture?  [17/S0/F1]
    - Magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes
    * Angular velocity
    - Linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes
    - The initial orientation of the headset
    because: In an inertial measurement unit, a gyroscope captures angular velocity, while an accelerometer captures linear acceleration and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength.
  Q Which sensor readings does inertial measurement unit sensor tracking rely mainly on?  [17/S0/F2]
    - Magnetometer readings of magnetic field strength
    - Registration readings of initial orientation
    * Gyroscope readings of angular velocity
    - Accelerometer readings of linear acceleration
    because: IMU sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity; the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation.

17/A2  recap  17/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 10 concepts)
  An inertial measurement unit (IMU) mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer. The gyroscope captures angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer capture linear acceleration and magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes. Tracking relies mainly on the gyroscope, while the accelerometer and magnetometer detect drift errors and take corrective measures.
  - An inertial measurement unit (IMU) mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer.
  - A gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.
  - Tracking relies mainly on the gyroscope, while the accelerometer and magnetometer detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

17/A3  quiz  17/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q How is gyroscope measurement error defined when calibrating an IMU?  [17/S1/F0]
    - As the actual angular velocity minus the measured angular velocity, omega_a - omega_g.
    - As the squared difference between the measured and actual angular velocities.
    - As the calibrated angular velocity minus the measured angular velocity, omega_cal - omega_g.
    * As the measured angular velocity minus the actual angular velocity, omega_g - omega_a.
    because: The measured angular velocity may differ from the actual angular velocity, and the measurement error is defined as omega_g minus omega_a.
  Q What is the goal of calibrating IMU sensor readings?  [17/S1/F1]
    * To bring the measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity as close together as possible.
    - To replace the gyroscope with an accelerometer or magnetometer.
    - To reduce cybersickness by occluding the visual periphery.
    - To make the expensive benchmark sensor exact and ideal.
    because: Calibration aims to reduce the measurement error, making the measured and actual angular velocities as close as possible.
  Q What two types of sensors provide the paired samples used for calibration?  [17/S1/F3]
    - A head-mounted display and a computer used for rendering.
    - A magnetometer and a camera used for drift correction.
    * A cheap, inaccurate IMU sensor and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor.
    - A gyroscope and an accelerometer inside the same IMU.
    because: The calibration uses many paired samples from an inexpensive IMU sensor for measured values and a highly accurate benchmark sensor for actual values.
  Q What quantity does the simple calibration method minimize when finding C1 and C2?  [17/S1/F4]
    * The sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual angular velocities omega_a.
    - The sum of squared differences between the fitted constants C1 and C2 and the ideal constants a = 0 and b = 1.
    - The sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_a and the measured angular velocities omega_g.
    - The sum of squared differences between the measured angular velocities omega_g and the actual angular velocities omega_a.
    because: The method uses linear least squares regression to minimize squared errors between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a.
  Q After C1 and C2 are determined, how is a cheap gyroscope reading used?  [17/S1/F5]
    - It is mapped in the opposite direction, omega_g = C1 + C2 omega_a.
    * It is transformed into a calibrated value, omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g.
    - It is replaced by the actual benchmark value, omega_a, at every sampling instant.
    - It is added to the initial orientation theta_0 to compute the current orientation.
    because: Calibration mathematically maps the inexpensive measured angular velocity to a calibrated angular velocity that approximates the actual value.

17/A4  recap  17/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Calibration aims to minimize the measurement error between a measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity. A linear model can estimate the relationship between many paired samples from a cheap sensor and an accurate benchmark sensor. Linear least squares regression identifies constants to mathematically transform the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value.
  - Calibration aims to minimize the measurement error between a measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity.
  - A linear model can estimate the relationship between many paired samples from a cheap sensor and an accurate benchmark sensor.
  - Linear least squares regression identifies constants to mathematically transform the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value.

17/A5  put_in_order  17/S1  "Order the steps of IMU sensor calibration"  (3 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the steps of IMU sensor calibration: Collect paired samples from cheap and benchmark sensors > Minimize squared differences to find calibration constants > Map measured angular velocity to a calibrated value  [17/S1/F3, 17/S1/F4, 17/S1/F5]

17/A6  quiz  17/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q In XR sensor tracking, what is the main role of registration?  [17/S2/F0]
    - Reduces measurement error by matching a cheap gyroscope to a benchmark sensor
    - Blends gyroscope and camera orientations to reduce drift over time
    - Computes the current orientation by adding calibrated gyro samples to the initial orientation
    * Sets the initial orientation and alignment of the real and virtual worlds
    because: Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds.
  Q Under the simplified registration assumption, what determines the initial headset orientation?  [17/S2/F1]
    - The direction from the headset to a nearby fiducial marker
    - The direction of the magnetic field sensed by a magnetometer
    - The direction indicated by the first calibrated angular velocity sample
    * The direction the headset is facing when tracking is turned on
    because: The simplified understanding takes the direction the headset is facing when tracking starts as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to forward.
  Q What is true about using fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags during registration?  [17/S2/F2]
    * They can simplify registration, but it can also be done without them using computer vision
    - They provide calibrated angular velocity samples for integration
    - They correct drift by blending two sensor orientations
    - They are required whenever a tracking system is turned on
    because: Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags, but it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and is simpler when such aids are present.
  Q How does integration obtain the current sensor orientation at a discrete time step?  [17/S2/F3]
    - It replaces the initial orientation with the latest calibrated angular velocity sample
    - It blends the gyro-derived orientation with the camera-derived orientation at each step
    * It adds the accumulated calibrated angular-velocity changes to the initial orientation
    - It multiplies the initial orientation by the elapsed sampling interval
    because: Integration computes the current orientation by adding to the initial orientation the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval.
  Q In orientation integration, what does one calibrated angular velocity sample represent?  [17/S2/F4]
    - The absolute orientation of the headset at that instant
    - The linear acceleration of the headset along one axis
    - The measurement error between a cheap and a benchmark gyroscope
    * A change in orientation equal to the sample multiplied by the sampling interval
    because: A calibrated angular velocity sample from the gyroscope indicates a change in orientation equal to that sample multiplied by the sampling interval.

17/A7  recap  17/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Registration sets the initial orientation and alignment between the real and virtual worlds, which can be aided by external tools or performed using computer vision. For simplicity, the direction the headset faces when turned on can be taken as the initial orientation. Integration then computes the current orientation by adding the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples to that initial orientation. Each sample indicates a change in orientation based on the sensor's velocity and the sampling interval.
  - Registration sets the initial orientation and alignment between the real and virtual worlds.
  - For simplicity, the direction the headset faces when turned on can be taken as the initial orientation.
  - Registration can be aided by external tools or performed using computer vision.
  - Integration computes the current orientation by adding the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples to the initial orientation.
  - A calibrated angular velocity sample indicates a change in orientation based on velocity and the sampling interval.

17/A8  quiz  17/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What is generally needed for drift correction that blends sensor values?  [17/S3/F0]
    * At least two sensors whose values are blended
    - A single high-accuracy sensor working alone
    - A fiducial marker and an initial pose
    - A benchmark sensor and a calibration model
    because: Drift correction usually uses extra sensors and generally requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.
  Q Besides a gyroscope, which sensors are mentioned as usable for drift correction?  [17/S3/F1]
    - Benchmark sensors, raw movement data, and markers
    * Cameras, accelerometers, and magnetometers
    - Displays, energy sources, and tracking devices
    - Yaw, roll, and pitch
    because: A gyroscope may be used together with other sensors such as cameras, and in an IMU accelerometer and magnetometer readings can be used in addition to gyroscope values.
  Q In the classic drift-correction expression, what is the role of the gain parameter alpha?  [17/S3/F2]
    * It is a normalized gain used to blend the gyroscope and camera orientations.
    - It is a sampling interval used to integrate angular velocity samples over time.
    - It is a measurement error value obtained from comparing two angular velocity sensors.
    - It is an initial orientation value established when the tracking system is turned on.
    because: alpha is the gain parameter in the weighted combination of the gyroscope orientation and the camera orientation.

17/A9  recap  17/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  Drift correction is usually done with the help of extra sensors and, in general, requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift. A gyroscope may be used together with other sensors such as cameras, and IMU accelerometer and magnetometer readings can be used in addition to gyroscope values. A classic approach combines the two individually computed orientations at the same instant using a gain parameter between 0 and 1.
  - Drift correction is usually done with extra sensors and generally requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.
  - A gyroscope may be used together with cameras or IMU readings for drift correction.
  - A classic approach combines the orientations from two sensors at the same instant using a gain parameter between 0 and 1.

17/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q How do the four tracking stages build on one another to produce a usable orientation estimate in an XR system?  [16/S3/F1, 17/S1/F5, 17/S2/F0, 17/S2/F3, 17/S3/F0; tracking, calibration, registration, integration, drift correction, calibrated value, initial orientation, current sensor orientation, calibrated angular velocity sample, sampling interval, drift]
    A The tracking process is described as four stages: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction. Calibration transforms a measured sensor reading into a calibrated value, and registration supplies the initial orientation. Integration computes the current sensor orientation by adding calibrated angular velocity samples multiplied by the sampling interval to that initial orientation. Drift correction then uses values from at least two sensors to estimate and correct drift.
  Q Why is the gyroscope the main sensor used for orientation tracking in an inertial measurement unit, while the accelerometer and magnetometer serve a different role?  [17/S0/F0, 17/S0/F1, 17/S0/F2; inertial measurement unit, gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, angular velocity, tracking, drift error]
    A An inertial measurement unit mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer. The gyroscope captures angular velocity, and IMU tracking relies mainly on those angular velocity readings. The accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to tracking estimation, but they can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.
  Q How do paired samples from a cheap inertial measurement unit and a benchmark sensor allow calibration to reduce measurement error?  [17/S1/F0, 17/S1/F1, 17/S1/F3, 17/S1/F4, 17/S1/F5; calibration, measured angular velocity, actual angular velocity, measurement error, paired samples, inertial measurement unit, benchmark sensor, linear least squares regression, calibrated value]
    A Calibration aims to make the measured angular velocity and the actual angular velocity as close as possible, which reduces the measurement error. It uses many paired samples from a cheap IMU sensor that produces the measured values and a highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values. It finds constants by linear least squares regression that minimize the sum of squared differences between C1 + C2 omega_g and omega_a, then maps omega_g to the calibrated value omega_cal.
  Q How does a classic drift-correction method combine a gyroscope-based orientation with a camera-based orientation, and what does the gain parameter do?  [17/S3/F0, 17/S3/F1, 17/S3/F2; drift correction, sensor, gyroscope, camera, orientation, drift-corrected orientation, gain parameter, drift]
    A Drift correction generally requires at least two sensors, and it can use a gyroscope together with a camera. In the classic approach, the drift-corrected orientation is theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values and theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the same time instant. The gain parameter alpha is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in that combination.

  What is accelerometer? (lecture 17) -> An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).
  What is magnetometer? (lecture 17) -> An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

  Q How does an electromagnetic tracker obtain the real-time position of the receiver?  [18/S2/F0]

    - From infrared light reflected by targets in the room
    - From the angles of serial or parallel mechanical joints
    * From the direction of the magnetic field produced by a stationary transmitter

    * Alternating current or direct current signals
    - Infrared pulses for an optical camera
    - Mechanical motion in a kinematic arm

    - Visible light from optical cameras

    * Stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or body

    * Acoustic tracking requires an unobstructed line of sight, whereas electromagnetic tracking does not
    - Both require an unobstructed line of sight
    - Neither requires an unobstructed line of sight
    because: Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking requires line of sight between transmitter and receiver with no obstacle in between, while electromagnetic tracking does not require this line of sight.

18/A6  recap  18/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Electromagnetic trackers use a stationary transmitter and a headset receiver to measure position by generating currents through three antennas. Acoustic tracking uses stationary speakers and headset microphones to determine position and orientation. While both methods use stationary transmitters and moving receivers, acoustic tracking requires a line of sight while electromagnetic tracking does not.
  - Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact devices that use a stationary transmitter and a headset receiver to measure position via a magnetic field.
  - These transmitters use three antennas to generate currents in the receiver to track the head's position.
  - Acoustic tracking uses stationary speakers and headset microphones to determine position and orientation.
  - Both systems use stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the user.
  - Acoustic tracking requires a line of sight, while electromagnetic tracking does not.

    - It measures magnetic fields produced by three antennas
    * It is mounted with the user and detects external targets
    - It is placed in the environment and detects targets attached to the object
    - It emits ultrasonic signals that reflect from a fixed transmitter
    because: In inside looking out infrared tracking, the camera is mounted with the user and estimates poses from external targets.

18/A8  recap  18/S3  "Recap"  (8 facts, 18 concepts)
  Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses using optical sensors or cameras. The three main categories of optical sensors are infrared, visible light, and 3D structure sensors. Infrared tracking is considered to be among the earliest vision-based techniques, using bright targets to ensure easy and robust detection. It can be configured as "outside looking in" using cameras in the environment or "inside looking out" using a camera mounted with the user.
  - Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses using optical sensors or cameras.
  - The three main categories of optical sensors are infrared, visible light, and 3D structure sensors.
  - Infrared tracking is considered to be among the earliest vision-based techniques, using bright targets to ensure easy and robust detection.
  - Infrared tracking can be configured as "outside looking in" using cameras in the environment or "inside looking out" using a camera mounted with the user.

18/A11  quiz  18/S5  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 10 concepts)

    * The camera pose
    - The virtual environment model
    - The user's hand gesture
    - The fiducial marker position

    * Points, corners, and line intersections
    - Multi-ring fiducial markers
    - Virtual objects generated by the software
    - Small colored LEDs and pieces of paper
    because: The image processing algorithms detect features unique to the surroundings, such as points, corners, and line intersections.
  Q What role do unique feature descriptors serve in natural feature tracking?  [18/S5/F2]
    - They detect points, corners, and line intersections
    * They identify and differentiate one feature from other features.
    - They create the virtual environment to be rendered
    - They add artificial landmarks to the environment

  Q How is the camera pose estimated in natural feature tracking?  [18/S5/F3]
    - By tracking the user's gestures
    - By comparing the camera image with a rendered virtual scene
    - By adding fiducial markers to the environment
    * By matching features in the scene with features in the object using their descriptors

18/A12  recap  18/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features in the natural environment and requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques. These algorithms detect features that are unique to the surroundings, and unique descriptors are calculated to identify and differentiate them. Camera pose is estimated by matching features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked using the calculated descriptors. Popular algorithms for this include SIFT, SURF, BRIEF, and BRISK.
  - Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features in the natural environment and requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.
  - Advanced algorithms detect features that are unique to the surroundings, such as points, corners, and line intersections.
  - Unique descriptors are calculated for each detected feature to identify and differentiate them.
  - Camera pose is estimated by using descriptors to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked.
  - Popular algorithms for natural feature detection and description include SIFT, SURF, BRIEF, and BRISK.

18/A13  put_in_order  18/S5  "Order the stages of natural feature tracking"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Order the stages of natural feature tracking: Environmental and object features are detected > Unique descriptors are computed for each feature > Scene features are matched with object features > Camera pose is estimated from matched features  [18/S5/F1, 18/S5/F2, 18/S5/F3]

18/A14  quiz  18/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q Which process is described by Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM)?  [18/S6/F1]
    - It uses artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid registration.
    - It matches scene feature descriptors with feature descriptors on a tracked object.
    * It creates and updates a map of a real environment while localizing positions within it.
    - It uses structured-light depth data to build 3D models of structures.
    because: SLAM simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it.
  Q Which tracking capability is attributed to SLAM?  [18/S6/F3]
    - Drift-free tracking of already mapped environments only
    - Feature matching between the scene and a tracked object
    - Pose estimation using artificial fiducials in the environment
    * Drift-free tracking of unknown environments
    because: SLAM allows drift-free tracking of unknown environments.
  Q How does Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) optimize SLAM?  [18/S6/F4]
    - It matches scene features to features on the tracked object for pose.
    * It tracks the camera and maps the environment as separate activities.
    - It tracks the camera and maps the environment as a single combined activity.
    - It adds artificial landmarks to the environment to guide camera tracking.
    because: PTAM is a further optimization of SLAM that allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.
  Q What improvement is associated with PTAM?  [18/S6/F6]
    - Improved tracking accuracy but not overall performance
    - Reduced computational requirements for larger environments
    * Improved tracking accuracy and overall performance
    - Improved overall performance but not tracking accuracy
    because: PTAM improved both the accuracy of tracking and the overall performance.
  Q Why is PTAM more suitable for smaller environments?  [18/S6/F7]
    - Its computational requirements for smaller environments are quite high
    - It cannot map the environment while tracking the camera
    * Its computational requirements for larger environments are quite high
    - It requires artificial fiducials to be placed in the environment
    because: PTAM is more suitable for smaller environments because the computational requirements for larger environments are quite high.

18/A15  recap  18/S6  "Recap"  (8 facts, 14 concepts)
  Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing. SLAM creates and updates a map while localizing positions for real-time, drift-free tracking in unknown environments. PTAM optimizes SLAM by treating tracking and mapping as separate activities to improve accuracy and performance in smaller environments.
  - Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing.
  - SLAM creates and updates a map while localizing positions for real-time, drift-free tracking.
  - SLAM was originally developed for robot navigation and adapted for augmented reality.
  - PTAM optimizes SLAM by treating tracking and mapping as separate activities.
  - PTAM was designed for augmented reality to improve accuracy and performance in smaller environments.

18/A26  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (6 facts, 29 concepts)
  Electromagnetic tracking | Electromechanical tracking | *Hybrid tracking | Inertial tracking  (Electromechanical, electromagnetic, and inertial tracking are listed as separate tracking technology categories, while hybrid tracking is placed in the others category because it combines two or more basic tracking systems.)  [18/S0/F0, 18/S9/F6]
  Fiducial tracking | Natural feature tracking | Model-based tracking | *Infrared tracking  (Fiducial, natural feature, and model-based tracking are the three techniques classified under visible light tracking, whereas infrared tracking relies on infrared sensing rather than visible light sensing.)  [18/S4/F1, 18/S3/F4]
  Point | Line intersection | Corner | *Fiducial  (Points, corners, and line intersections are natural features used in natural feature tracking, while a fiducial is an artificial landmark added for fiducial tracking.)  [18/S5/F1, 18/S4/F2]

18/A27  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (18 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How are electromagnetic tracking and acoustic tracking similar in their sensor placement, and what practical difference matters when obstacles may be present?  [18/S2/F0, 18/S2/F2, 18/S2/F3, 18/S2/F4; electromagnetic tracker, acoustic tracking, transmitter, receiver, line of sight, head-mounted display]
    A Both use a stationary transmitter in the environment and a receiver that moves with the head-mounted display. In electromagnetic tracking, position is obtained from the magnetic field direction and the system does not require line of sight. Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking uses ultrasonic signals and requires an unobstructed line of sight between transmitter and receiver.
  Q How can a hybrid tracking system improve on the limitation of an inertial tracker found in many head-mounted displays?  [18/S8/F0, 18/S8/F1, 18/S9/F6, 18/S9/F7; inertial tracker, head-mounted display, hybrid tracker, single-technology-based tracking]
    A Inertial trackers measure changes in orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration rather than absolute values. They are typically MEMS-based and can be part of a head-mounted display. A hybrid tracker combines two or more basic tracking systems, and hybrid trackers typically perform better than single-technology-based tracking.
  Q Why can fiducial tracking and natural feature tracking both be part of visible light tracking, yet one requires added landmarks while the other depends on existing scene features?  [18/S4/F0, 18/S4/F1, 18/S4/F2, 18/S5/F0, 18/S5/F1, 18/S5/F2, 18/S5/F3; visible light tracking, optical camera, fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, fiducial, feature, feature descriptor, camera pose]
    A Visible light tracking uses optical cameras, which are common in consumer and wearable devices, and it includes fiducial and natural feature tracking. Fiducial tracking adds artificial landmarks, called fiducials, to aid registration and tracking. Natural feature tracking uses features already present in the environment, such as points, corners, or line intersections, and uses feature descriptors to match them and estimate camera pose.
  Q How does 3D structure tracking support the idea of augmented reality as a state that augments the real environment?  [1/S2/F1, 18/S7/F0, 18/S7/F2; augmented reality, three-dimensional structure tracking, three-dimensional model, real-world view, Kinect Fusion, structured light depth sensor]
    A Augmented reality is the intermediate state where the real environment is augmented with virtual content. 3D structure tracking obtains 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view. Kinect Fusion uses structured light depth sensor data to create such models and also tracks the pose of the Kinect.

===== lecture 19: VR Software

19/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM)? (lecture 18) -> Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
  What is display? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

19/A1  quiz  19/S0  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q What is the role of virtual reality software in producing a virtual reality experience?  [19/S0/F0]
    - To replace VR or AR hardware by generating output data directly
    - To convert high-level developer descriptions into device drivers only
    - To track the surrounding physical environment instead of the user
    * To drive VR or AR hardware so it generates appropriate stimuli for human sense organs
    because: VR software drives VR or AR hardware so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a VR experience.

19/A2  recap  19/S0  "Recap"  (1 facts, 6 concepts)
  VR software drives virtual reality or augmented reality hardware to generate appropriate stimuli. These stimuli are received by human sense organs to create a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.
  - VR software drives hardware to generate stimuli that stimulate human senses.

19/A3  quiz  19/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In a VR system, which pair of processes occurs between the user and the VR hardware?  [19/S1/F0]
    - Interaction and rendering
    - Environment modeling and object modeling
    * Tracking and stimulation
    - Input queuing and output synchronization
    because: The VR data-flow description states that tracking and stimulation occur between the user and the VR hardware.
  Q How does data move between a user and a VR hardware system?  [19/S1/F1]
    - The physical world generates data, the system processes it, and the hardware generates stimuli for the sense organs.
    - Input devices generate stimuli, the system processes them, and output devices generate data for the sense organs.
    - Output devices generate data, the system processes it, and input devices generate stimuli for the sense organs.
    * Input devices generate data, the system processes it, and output devices generate stimuli for the sense organs.
    because: The user operates input devices to generate data that is processed by the VR system, and the processed data is sent back to output devices that generate stimuli for the sense organs.
  Q What design and software support is required for the data flow between a user and VR hardware?  [19/S1/F2]
    - Interaction design, rendering, and software that processes input and generates output.
    * Interaction design, perceptual design, and software that processes input and generates output.
    - Interaction design, perceptual design, and software that tracks the head.
    - Environment modeling, perceptual design, and software that processes input and generates output.
    because: The data flow requires interaction design and modeling for input devices, perceptual design and modeling for output stimuli, and software to process input data and generate output data.
  Q Which two components represent the software part of the VR data-flow diagram?  [19/S1/F3]
    - The virtual world generator and a middleware component
    - The software-and-database component and a renderer component
    - The VR engine and a head-tracker component
    * The VR engine and a software-and-database component
    because: The software part of the VR data-flow diagram is represented by the VR engine and a software-and-database component.

19/A4  recap  19/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Virtual reality systems involve bidirectional data flows between the hardware, the physical world, and the user. This data flow works by processing user input data to generate output data that suitably affects the user's sense organs. These flows require proper interaction design for inputs, perceptual design for stimuli, and software for processing. The software part specifically includes a virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.
  - Virtual reality systems involve bidirectional data flows between the hardware, the physical world, and the user.
  - The data flow works by processing user input data to generate output data that suitably affects the user's sense organs.
  - Data flow requires proper interaction design for inputs, perceptual design for stimuli, and software for processing.
  - The software components include a virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

19/A5  put_in_order  19/S1  "Order the steps of VR data flow"  (1 facts, 8 concepts)
  Order the steps of VR data flow: User operates input devices to generate data > Data is sent to the virtual reality system for processing > Processed data is sent to output devices > Output devices generate stimuli for the sense organs  [19/S1/F1]

19/A6  quiz  19/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q Which three activities are involved in creating a VR experience?  [19/S2/F0]
    - Generating visual output, aural output, and haptic output
    - Queuing input events, maintaining virtual reality, and synchronizing displays
    * Creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions
    - Capturing a physical world, applying SLAM, and mapping textures
    because: Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering the stereoscopic view, and incorporating interactions that use tracking hardware.
  Q In VR experience creation, what do the terms view or rendering broadly refer to?  [19/S2/F1]
    - Only stereoscopic visual output
    * Output for the visual sense and other senses
    - Only input from tracking hardware
    - Only the modeled virtual environment
    because: View or rendering is used broadly to include not only visual output but also output for other senses.
  Q What kind of support ideally should VR software provide to a developer?  [19/S2/F3]
    * High-level descriptions generate low-level details, while middleware or original from-scratch functions can also be used
    - Developers must directly implement device drivers, head tracking, and display output
    - Low-level instructions generate high-level details, and developers must write all middleware
    - Developers can only call middleware functions and cannot design original functions
    because: Ideally, VR software lets developers provide high-level descriptions from which low-level details are determined, using middleware and libraries or designing functions from scratch.
  Q In practical VR development, what role can an SDK for a particular headset or platform play?  [19/S2/F5]
    - It automatically turns every high-level description into low-level VR details
    - It is platform independent across different hardware and operating systems
    * It handles lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output
    - It lets the developer avoid understanding any platform-specific operations
    because: A practical VR developer may use a platform-dependent SDK to handle lowest-level platform-specific operations, while still needing to understand that SDK.
  Q What is a practical trade-off of using a game engine as middleware for VR development?  [19/S2/F6, 19/S2/F7]
    - It guarantees full flexibility for ideas not part of standard video games
    - It must be a VR-specific engine before it can be used as middleware
    * It can reduce initial effort but may limit flexibility for ideas outside standard video games
    - It removes the need for any platform SDK or lowest-level operations
    because: A game engine can be adopted as VR middleware and save initial effort, but if it is not VR-specific it can be cumbersome and less flexible for non-standard VR ideas.

19/A7  recap  19/S2  "Recap"  (8 facts, 23 concepts)
  Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering, and incorporating interactions. While ideal software would let developers provide high-level descriptions, practical development often requires implementing functionality from scratch or using platform-specific SDKs. Game engines can be used as middleware, but they may be cumbersome and less flexible for ideas that fall outside of standard video games.
  - Creating a VR experience involves environment modeling, rendering, and incorporating interactions.
  - Ideal VR software would allow developers to provide high-level descriptions while still allowing for original work from scratch.
  - In practice, developers may need to implement much functionality from scratch using platform-specific SDKs.
  - Game engines can be used as middleware, but they may be cumbersome and less flexible for non-standard ideas.

19/A8  quiz  19/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 31 concepts)
  Q In the virtual reality software model, what is the virtual world generator treated as?  [19/S3/F0]
    * A black-box abstraction of the entire VR software system
    - An internal model of every hardware driver
    - A renderer that sends data to one display
    - A queue that orders simultaneous input events
    because: The virtual world generator is an abstraction of the whole VR software system and is treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.
  Q In a virtual world generator, why are simultaneous input events from a head tracker, keyboard, mouse, or game controller placed in a queue?  [19/S3/F1]
    * So they can be processed systematically
    - To synchronize output devices with input data
    - To convert input events into renderer output
    - To make the internal reality appear real
    because: Simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.
  Q Which set lists output renderers that a virtual world generator can use?  [19/S3/F3]
    * Visual, aural, and haptic renderers
    - Input queue, internal reality, and display output
    - Head tracker, keyboard, and game controller
    - SLAM, texture mapping, and mesh generation
    because: The virtual world generator can use several output renderers, including visual, aural, and haptic renderers.
  Q In creating a virtual world, what does texture mapping do?  [19/S3/F7]
    - Captures the real world using SLAM techniques
    * Maps camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object
    - Keeps output devices synchronized with incoming input data
    - Defines a triangular mesh in three-dimensional space
    because: Texture mapping is a way of creating a virtual world by mapping camera images of a real object onto a synthetic object.
  Q What must be defined and maintained for a completely synthetic virtual world?  [19/S3/F4]
    - Camera capture, computer vision, and SLAM techniques
    * A triangular mesh and material/physical surface properties
    - An aural renderer, haptic renderer, and input queue
    - A head tracker, keyboard, and game controller
    because: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in 3D and maintaining material and physical surface properties.

19/A9  recap  19/S3  "Recap"  (8 facts, 37 concepts)
  The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the virtual reality software system that receives and systematically processes inputs from various devices. It maintains an internal reality and synchronizes these inputs with visual, aural, and haptic renderers. Additionally, VR software supports the creation of synthetic worlds through computer-graphics operations and recorded physical worlds using computer vision and SLAM techniques.
  - The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the virtual reality software system.
  - The VWG receives inputs from various devices and processes them systematically in a queue.
  - The VWG maintains an internal reality and synchronizes inputs with visual, aural, and haptic renderers.
  - VR software supports synthetic worlds through computer-graphics operations and recorded physical worlds using computer vision and SLAM techniques.

19/A10  quiz  19/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What is matched motion in virtual reality?  [19/S4/F0]
    - A menu operation that sends a user to a selected virtual location
    - A place where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align
    - Moving oneself in the virtual world while real physical motion is not matched
    * Maintaining correspondence between a user's real-world motions and virtual-world motions
    because: Matched motion is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.
  Q What is a matched zone in VR?  [19/S4/F1]
    - A virtual obstacle without a corresponding physical obstacle
    * A safe real-world region with restricted physical movement where real and virtual worlds align
    - A selected virtual location reached without physical movement
    - A visual viewpoint chosen by the renderer for a head motion
    because: A matched zone is a place where the real world and virtual world perfectly align, corresponding to the safe real-world region where physical movement is restricted.
  Q Which situation describes an obstacle mismatch in an immersive VR application?  [19/S4/F2]
    - A user remains seated while their avatar walks through the virtual world
    * A virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone
    - A user's physical movement is translated to another part of the virtual world
    - A physical obstacle in the matched zone has a corresponding virtual obstacle
    because: An obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle lacks a corresponding virtual obstacle.
  Q What is user locomotion in VR?  [19/S4/F5]
    - Maintaining correspondence between real-world and virtual-world motions
    * Moving oneself in the virtual world while the real-world physical motion is not matched
    - Translating movement within a safe region to movement elsewhere in the virtual world
    - Pointing to a desired virtual location and being sent there without physical movement
    because: User locomotion is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched.
  Q Why should VR software include support for different sorts of user locomotion?  [19/S4/F8, 19/S4/F9]
    - So that virtual obstacles always correspond to physical obstacles in the matched zone
    - So that matched motion can be maintained for every body part
    * So that cyber sickness can be addressed
    - So that the visual renderer can always use the correct head viewpoint
    because: Locomotion operations that avoid physical movement may lead to cyber sickness, and support for different locomotion sorts should be part of VR software so that cyber sickness can be addressed.

19/A11  recap  19/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 13 concepts)
  Matched motion maintains correspondence between real-world and virtual motions. A matched zone is an area where physical movements are translated into virtual motions, and VR software helps developers manage these correspondences. User locomotion allows movement in the virtual world without matching physical movement, with VR software providing options like teleportation or vehicle metaphors to address cybersickness.
  - Matched motion maintains correspondence between real-world and virtual motions.
  - A matched zone is an area where physical movements are translated into virtual motions.
  - VR software helps developers manage matched-motion challenges and correspondences.
  - User locomotion is moving in the virtual world without matching physical movement.
  - VR software supports locomotion methods like teleportation and vehicle metaphors to address cybersickness.

19/A12  put_in_order  19/S4  "Order the steps of VR teleportation"  (1 facts, 3 concepts)
  Order the steps of VR teleportation: User pulls up a menu > User points to a desired virtual location > User is sent to that location  [19/S4/F6]

19/A18  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (21 facts, 69 concepts)
  Q How does virtual reality software turn the bidirectional data flow between a user and hardware into a controlled virtual reality experience?  [19/S0/F0, 19/S1/F0, 19/S1/F1, 19/S1/F2; virtual reality software, data flow, input device, output device, human sense organs, virtual reality experience]
    A In a virtual reality system, data flows bidirectionally between the hardware, the physical world, and the user, with tracking and stimulation occurring between the user and the hardware. The user operates input devices to generate data for the system, and the system sends processed data back to output devices that generate stimuli affecting the user's sense organs. Proper interaction and perceptual design and modeling, plus software, ensure the data flow drives the hardware so the stimuli suitably stimulate the human sense organs and create a virtual reality experience.
  Q How does the virtual world generator coordinate a virtual reality system's inputs, internal world, and multiple sensory outputs?  [19/S3/F0, 19/S3/F1, 19/S3/F2, 19/S3/F3; virtual world generator, black box, head tracker, input event, queue, renderer, visual renderer, aural renderer, haptic renderer, synchronization, input-output match]
    A The virtual world generator is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality software, treated as a black box. It receives low-level input from devices such as a head tracker, keyboard, mouse, and game controller, and queues simultaneous input events. It maintains an internal reality, converts incoming input into renderer output, and keeps output synchronized with input to maintain an input-output match. It can drive visual, aural, and haptic renderers for different displays.
  Q How do matched motion and user locomotion differ in virtual reality, and why can teleportation be a useful locomotion choice?  [19/S4/F0, 19/S4/F1, 19/S4/F5, 19/S4/F6, 19/S4/F8, 19/S4/F9, 11/S1/F3; matched motion, matched zone, user locomotion, teleportation, cybersickness, locomotion operation]
    A Matched motion maintains correspondence between a user's real-world motions and the virtual world, with a matched zone where real and virtual worlds align and physical movement is restricted. User locomotion moves the user through the virtual world while the user's real motion is not matched, often to move outside the matched zone. Some locomotion operations that avoid physical movement may lead to cybersickness, but teleportation sends the user to a selected virtual location without physical movement and, as an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement. Software should support different locomotion operations so cybersickness can be addressed.
  Q Why might a virtual reality developer use a headset software development kit together with a game engine as middleware, and what limitation does a non-virtual-reality game engine have?  [19/S2/F2, 19/S2/F3, 19/S2/F4, 19/S2/F5, 19/S2/F6, 19/S2/F7; virtual reality software, software development kit, platform, device driver, head tracking, display output, game engine, middleware, virtual reality engine, high-level description, low-level detail]
    A Virtual reality software should help a developer create a virtual environment, render the stereoscopic output view, and incorporate interaction, ideally from high-level descriptions that determine low-level details automatically. A platform-dependent software development kit can handle lowest-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output, while a game engine can act as middleware to avoid substantial initial effort. In practice the developer may still implement functionality from scratch, and if the game engine is not specifically a virtual reality engine it can be cumbersome for ideas outside standard video games and reduce flexibility.

===== lecture 20: VR Software

20/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is software development kit (SDK)? (lecture 19) -> In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
  What is middleware? (lecture 19) -> Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.
  What is matched zone? (lecture 19) -> A matched zone is a place where the real world and the virtual world perfectly align; it corresponds to the safe real-world region where a user's physical movement is restricted, although the virtual world is not similarly confined, and movement within that region is translated to movement in other parts of the virtual world.
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.
  What is game engine? (lecture 19) -> A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed.

20/A1  quiz  20/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What is the basic purpose of physics support in a virtual world generator?  [20/S0/F2]
    - To make the virtual world align with a user's matched zone.
    - To make locomotion replace the basic laws of mechanics.
    * To make real-world events have similar virtual-world events.
    - To make rendering depend only on computer vision techniques.
    because: Physics support is meant to make the virtual world appear to behave like the real world.
  Q How should a virtual world generator usually treat object motion?  [20/S0/F3]
    - With rendering support only, because graphics can determine motion.
    - With matched-motion tracking data alone, without physical laws.
    * With basic laws of mechanics, adding advanced laws when more realism is desirable.
    - With advanced laws of mechanics only, because basic laws are insufficient.
    because: Support for basic mechanical laws should be good enough, and advanced laws may be added for extra realism.
  Q What should physics support do to a dropped ball in a virtual world?  [20/S0/F4]
    - Move it at a constant speed toward the ground.
    - Keep it still until another body causes a collision.
    - Rotate it to match the user's rotational movement.
    * Make it accelerate toward the ground due to gravity.
    because: A dropped ball should not be moved at constant speed; gravity should make it accelerate toward the ground.
  Q Which two capabilities should ideally be included in collision support?  [20/S0/F5]
    * Collision detection and collision response.
    - Graphics support and computer vision support
    - Rendering support and collaborative VR support
    - Locomotion support and matched motion support
    because: Collision detection determines whether bodies intersect, and collision response determines their behavior after a collision.
  Q Besides object motion and collisions, what should physics support replicate?  [20/S0/F6]
    * Light propagation, surface interaction, illumination, sound, and smell.
    - Triangular meshes, rendering, and panoramic video
    - Matched zones, facial expressions, and body language
    - SLAM positioning, translational movement, and rotational movement
    because: Physics support should also replicate phenomena such as how light propagates and interacts with surfaces, illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

Object motion should be governed by basic laws of mechanics, while collision support requires both detection and response. Physics support should also replicate phenomena such as how light, sound, and smell propagate.
  - Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator.
  - The purpose of physics support is to make the virtual world behave like the real world.
  - Object motion should be governed by basic laws of mechanics, while support for advanced laws can make motion more realistic.
  - Collision support should include both collision detection and collision response.
  - Physics support should also replicate phenomena like how light, sound, and smell propagate.

20/A5  quiz  20/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q Compared with using a ready-made virtual world generator, what is a key advantage of building a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit?  [20/S2/F3]
    - It provides built-in collision and physics support out of the box.
    * It gives maximum control and performance optimization by letting the developer choose physics algorithms.
    - It requires the developer to use fixed algorithms supplied by a package.
    - It avoids the need to implement physics support from scratch.
    because: Building from a basic SDK lets the developer choose and implement physics support algorithms according to performance, giving maximum control and optimization.
  Q When a developer builds a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit, what must they build at the very least?  [20/S2/F2]
    - The tracking APIs that access tracking data.
    - The menu options used to customize a ready-made virtual world generator.
    - The basic drivers that drive the headset or device hardware.
    * The physics support, including avatar movement, collision detection and response, lighting models, and audio support.
    because: A developer building a virtual world generator from a basic SDK must build at least the physics support of the virtual world, handling avatar movement, collisions, lighting, and audio.
  Q How does a ready-made virtual world generator both help and limit a developer creating a virtual reality experience?  [20/S2/F6, 20/S2/F7]
    - It increases effort by requiring the developer to build all physics support from scratch, but it gives full algorithmic control.
    - It provides only low-level drivers and tracking APIs, so the developer must write all high-level scripts.
    - It is best for highly original experiences because it avoids any preexisting function supports or algorithms.
    * It reduces effort by including collision and physics support, but its own function supports and algorithms can restrict highly original experiences.
    because: A ready-made virtual world generator makes creation easier by providing supports such as collisions or physics, but the developer must use its existing supports and algorithm implementations, which can restrict highly original experiences.
  Q What is a basic software development kit for a headset, device, or platform typically expected to provide?  [20/S2/F1]
    * Basic drivers, APIs for accessing tracking data, and APIs for calling graphical rendering libraries.
    - Menu options and high-level scripts for customizing a ready-made virtual world generator.
    - Complete support for locomotion, matched motion, physics, and networked collaborative virtual reality.
    - A shared virtual world maintained by a server for all connected users.
    because: A basic SDK typically provides drivers, tracking-data APIs, and rendering-library APIs, but it does not normally take care of every aspect of locomotion, matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality.

20/A6  recap  20/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Developers can build VR experiences from scratch using an SDK or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG). While building from an SDK provides maximum control and performance optimization, it requires building physics and audio from scratch and imposes a difficult implementation burden. In contrast, ready-made VWGs allow for faster creation because they include built-in supports, though they may restrict the development of highly original experiences.
  - Developers can build VR experiences from scratch using an SDK or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG).
  - Building from an SDK provides maximum control and performance optimization, but requires building physics, collision, and audio from scratch.
  - Building from an SDK imposes a difficult implementation burden and requires a lot of effort.
  - Ready-made VWGs make it easy to create experiences in little time because they include built-in supports.
  - Ready-made VWGs can restrict highly original experiences because the developer must use the engine's existing functions and algorithms.

  - A game engine is middleware that abstracts hardware functionalities for XR applications.
  - It is a software development environment where applications are built on top of the engine.
  - Game engines comprise various components such as rendering, physics, audio, and networking support.
  - Authoring tools allow developers to access these functionalities and configure logic through scripting.

    - Providing software abstractions of the central processing unit

    - Software abstractions of the central processing unit

    * Software abstractions of the graphics processing unit
    - Software abstractions of system memory
    because: A rendering engine is typically built on rendering APIs that provide software abstractions of the GPU.

    - It requires the GPU to modify and generate sound in real time
    - It depends on the GPU to synchronize sound with three-dimensional motion
    because: An audio engine can perform its calculations on a CPU or a dedicated ASIC and does not require a GPU, while GPUs are generally associated with graphics or rendering.

    - The audio engine
    - A rendering API

    - Both engines are fully open source and available without licensing restrictions

20/A10  recap  20/S4  "Recap"  (13 facts, 36 concepts)
  Rendering engines generate 3D graphics using methods like rasterization or ray tracing by using APIs to provide software abstractions of the GPU. Audio engines manage sound generation and processing using a CPU or ASIC, while physics engines simulate physical forces and collisions. These components are often found in game engines, where Unity 3D and Unreal Engine are the market leaders with different licensing and market shares.
  - Rendering engines generate 3D graphics using methods such as rasterization or ray tracing.
  - A rendering engine is typically built on APIs which provide software abstractions of the GPU.
  - Audio engines manage sound generation and processing using a CPU or ASIC rather than a GPU.
  - Physics engines simulate physical forces and collisions within the application.
  - Unity 3D and Unreal Engine are the most popular game engines, with different licensing and market shares.

  Order the layers of a typical VR system that uses a game engine: Hardware layer > Rendering application programming interfaces > Game engine > Application software  [20/S4/F4]

20/A12  quiz  20/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q How does web application deployment for a VR experience differ from native application deployment?  [20/S5/F0]
    - Native deployment can be used remotely without a specific device, whereas web deployment requires platform-specific SDKs.
    - Native deployment is categorized only by whether the SDK is for VR or AR applications.
    - Web deployment is an installable package of tools for designing, building, and testing VR experiences.
    * Web deployment can be used remotely without a specific device, whereas native deployment requires platform-specific SDKs.
    because: Web application deployment allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device, while native deployment requires SDKs tailored to the platform and hardware.
  Q What is a VR software development kit?  [20/S5/F2]
    - A game-engine component that simulates physical forces and collisions at runtime.
    * An installable collection of tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination to design, build, and test VR experiences.
    - A hardware component that speeds up the rendering of animated 3D graphics.
    - A rendering API that provides a software abstraction of a graphics processing unit.
    because: An SDK is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system combination, providing tools to design, build, and test VR experiences.
  Q In VR deployment, what does the term platform usually mean?  [20/S5/F1]
    - The rendering APIs used by a rendering engine.
    - The application software above the game engine.
    - The head-mounted display that presents the virtual environment.
    * The operating system together with the hardware.
    because: In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system plus the hardware, such as Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.
  Q Native VR SDKs can be categorized according to which two criteria?  [20/S5/F3]
    - Game-engine market share and HMD popularity.
    - Operating system and application-software layer.
    * Application type and availability.
    - Hardware layer and rendering method.
    because: Native deployment SDKs can be categorized by application type, as VR or AR applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.
  Q Which native VR SDK is associated with the Samsung Gear VR?  [20/S5/F5]
    - PSVR SDK
    - OpenVR SDK
    - Google VR SDK
    * Oculus Mobile SDK
    because: The Samsung Gear VR uses the Oculus Mobile SDK.

20/A13  recap  20/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 33 concepts)
  VR applications can be deployed natively using software development kits (SDKs) or over the web. A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system, while SDKs provide the tools needed to build experiences for those platforms. Native SDKs are categorized by application type and availability, and different head-mounted displays use different VR software development kits.
  - VR applications can be deployed natively or over the web.
  - A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.
  - SDKs provide the tools to build VR experiences for specific platforms.
  - Native SDKs are categorized by application type and availability.
  - Different head-mounted displays use different VR software development kits.

20/A14  quiz  20/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q What is the main function of cloud hosting and rendering support tools for web deployment?  [20/S6/F1]
    - They compile and package native mobile applications.
    * They provide hosting and rendering over a network.
    - They create 3D models locally on the user's device.
    - They supply hardware-specific SDKs for head-mounted displays.
    because: Cloud hosting and rendering support tools only provide hosting and rendering over a network.
  Q WebXR, Three.js, AFrame, and Babylon.js are examples of which kind of web deployment tool?  [20/S6/F3]
    - Cloud hosting and rendering over a network tools.
    - Native software development kits for specific VR platforms.
    - Complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.
    * Libraries for development support for deployment over the web.
    because: WebXR, Three.js, AFrame, and Babylon.js are listed as popular libraries for development support for deployment over the web.
  Q ZappAir, 8thWall, InstaVR, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of which category of web deployment tools?  [20/S6/F7]
    - Cloud hosting and rendering over a network tools.
    - Generic development editors for writing code for web-based deployment.
    - Libraries for development support for deployment over the web.
    * Complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.
    because: These are listed as complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.
  Q What role does Three.js play with WebGL in web-based development?  [20/S6/F5]
    - It replaces WebGL with a Vulkan rendering pipeline.
    * It makes WebGL easier to use and is used for rendering.
    - It provides a hardware-specific SDK for head-mounted displays.
    - It hosts the finished experience on a cloud server.
    because: Three.js makes WebGL easier and is used for rendering.

20/A15  recap  20/S6  "Recap"  (6 facts, 25 concepts)
  Web deployment tools can be broadly categorized as cloud hosting and rendering, development support libraries, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, and SDK support. Cloud hosting and rendering support tools only provide hosting and rendering over a network. Development support libraries include WebXR, which uses WebGL, and Three.js, which makes WebGL easier for rendering. There are also complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web.
  - Web deployment tools can be broadly categorized as cloud hosting and rendering, development support libraries, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, and SDK support.
  - Cloud hosting and rendering support tools only provide hosting and rendering over a network.
  - Development support libraries include WebXR, which uses WebGL, and Three.js, which makes WebGL easier for rendering.
  - Complete development and deployment tools are available for applications on the web.

20/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (19 facts, 64 concepts)
  Q Why can building a virtual world generator from a basic software development kit give a developer more control over performance than using a ready-made generator, while also creating a larger implementation burden?  [20/S2/F1, 20/S2/F2, 20/S2/F3, 20/S2/F4, 20/S2/F6, 20/S2/F7; virtual world generator, software development kit, physics, performance, collision detection, collision response, audio support, lighting model]
    A A ready-made virtual world generator or engine comes with physics and collision support and its own algorithm implementations, which reduces effort but restricts the developer. A basic SDK typically provides drivers, tracking-data access, and calls to graphical rendering libraries, but it does not typically cover every aspect of locomotion, matched motion, physics, or collaborative virtual reality. Therefore the developer must build physics-related support such as avatar movement, collision detection and response, lighting models, and audio support from scratch, can choose and implement physics algorithms according to performance, but must understand and implement the overall system, which is a difficult burden.
  Q In a networked collaborative virtual reality experience, why must the virtual reality system still manage virtual collisions even when users are in separate real-world matched zones, and what should collision support include?  [20/S0/F5, 20/S1/F1, 20/S1/F2; networked collaborative virtual reality experience, matched zone, shared virtual world, virtual reality system, collision, physical collision, collision support, collision detection, collision response, body]
    A Each user has a distinct matched zone, and unwanted physical collision must be avoided when users are close, while users spread around the globe have no possibility of physical collision. Within the shared virtual world, however, user interactions, including collisions, must be managed by the virtual reality system whether users are close or spread around the world. Collision support should therefore include collision detection, which determines whether bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.
  Q Why are a game engine's rendering engine and audio engine associated with different kinds of hardware even though they can be components of the same engine?  [20/S3/F2, 20/S4/F0, 20/S4/F2, 20/S4/F3, 20/S4/F5, 20/S4/F6; game engine, rendering engine, audio engine, three-dimensional graphics, rendering method, application programming interface, graphics processing unit, central processing unit, application-specific integrated circuit]
    A A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising components such as a rendering engine and an audio engine. The rendering engine helps generate animated three-dimensional graphics by methods such as rasterization or ray tracing and is typically built on rendering APIs that provide software abstractions of a graphics processing unit, which is the hardware used for speeding up rendering. The audio engine uses algorithms for loading, modifying, and generating sound, and it can perform its calculations on a central processing unit or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit, so it does not require a graphics processing unit.
  Q How does native deployment of a virtual reality application depend on a platform-specific software development kit, and how does web deployment change the deployment options available to a developer?  [20/S5/F0, 20/S5/F1, 20/S5/F2, 20/S6/F0; deployment, native application deployment, web application deployment, software development kit, platform, operating system, hardware, web deployment tool]
    A Native application deployment requires SDKs tailored to the platform and hardware, and a platform typically means the operating system plus the hardware. An SDK is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating-system combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality experiences. Web application deployment allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device and can use web deployment tools such as cloud hosting and rendering tools, libraries for development support, complete development and deployment tools, generic development editors, or SDK support.
