===== lecture 21: AR Software

21/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.
  What is authoring tool? (lecture 20) -> An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

21/A1  quiz  21/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Which way of organizing AR software tools distinguishes desktop AR applications from mobile AR applications?  [21/S0/F0]
    - Marker-based application type
    - Developer skill
    - Tracking technology
    * Target application platform
    because: AR software tools can be categorized by target application platform, such as desktop AR applications or mobile AR applications.
  Q In the AR skill-based hierarchy ordered by decreasing programming skill, which category is placed last?  [21/S0/F1, 21/S0/F2]
    - Plugins for existing developer tools
    - Low-level software libraries or frameworks
    * Standalone AR authoring tools
    - Rapid prototyping tools
    because: The skill-based hierarchy ends with standalone AR authoring tools, which assume no programming ability and can be used without any knowledge.
  Q Which AR software category requires strong programming or coding ability and understanding how to call library functions?  [21/S0/F2]
    - Standalone AR authoring tools
    * Low-level software libraries or frameworks
    - Rapid prototyping tools
    - Plugins for existing developer tools
    because: Low-level software libraries or frameworks require strong programming or coding ability and an understanding of how to call library functions.
  Q What skill is specifically required for plugin-based AR software tools?  [21/S0/F2]
    - Some programming ability and design prototyping skills
    * Skill with the original developer tool
    - No programming ability
    - Strong programming or coding ability
    because: Plugins require skill with the original developer tool with which the plugin is used.

21/A2  recap  21/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 21 concepts)
  AR software tools can be categorized by developer skill, target platform, or tracking technology. There are four categories of AR software tools arranged by decreasing programming skill: low-level libraries, rapid prototyping tools, plugins, and standalone authoring tools. These range from libraries requiring strong coding to standalone tools that require no programming knowledge.
  - AR software tools can be categorized by developer skill, target platform, or tracking technology.
  - AR software tools are arranged in four categories according to decreasing programming skill: low-level libraries, rapid prototyping tools, plugins, and standalone authoring tools.
  - The requirements range from low-level libraries requiring strong coding to standalone authoring tools requiring no programming.

21/A3  quiz  21/S1  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Why do low-level AR libraries or frameworks demand the most developer skill?  [21/S1/F0]
    - They expose plugin features that mainly require knowledge of an existing developer tool.
    * They expose core tracking and display functionality needed to build an AR application.
    - They expose authoring tools that assume no programming ability.
    - They expose only simple prototype visuals that can be shared with clients before coding.
    because: Low-level AR libraries and frameworks require the maximum skill because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.
  Q What is ARToolKit mainly designed to provide?  [21/S1/F3, 21/S1/F4]
    - Realistic scene rendering and interaction support for a complete AR application.
    - A standalone AR authoring tool that requires no programming.
    * Tracking support that lets a developer perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.
    - Mobile-only computer-vision tracking without any desktop support.
    because: ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library, and by itself it gives only primitive OpenGL rendering without built-in interaction or complex realistic graphics.
  Q What is the main benefit of combining ARToolKit with a scene-graph library?  [21/S1/F9]
    * ARToolKit handles tracking while the scene-graph library handles low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction.
    - The scene-graph library handles tracking while ARToolKit handles realistic rendering.
    - The combination provides only low-level OpenGL rendering and still requires writing interaction from scratch.
    - The combination removes the need for tracking because the scene graph can detect markers.
    because: When ARToolKit is combined with a scene-graph library, the scene graph takes care of low-level object rendering while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.
  Q What is a scene graph in computer graphics?  [21/S1/F7]
    - A GPS sensor stream used for outdoor tracking of a mobile AR device.
    * A node-based tree of nodes and links that represents a graphics scene and lets developers manipulate selected nodes.
    - A low-level OpenGL function that renders a 3D object directly to the screen.
    - A marker image used by ARToolKit to recognize the camera position.
    because: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene and allows selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene.
  Q In the marker-cow AR example, what are the separate roles of ARToolKit and OSG?  [21/S1/F14]
    - ARToolKit tracks the marker, while OSG performs 3D registration and creates the rendered cow.
    - Both ARToolKit and OSG jointly track the marker and jointly render the cow.
    - OSG tracks the marker and performs 3D registration, while ARToolKit creates and renders the AR scene.
    * ARToolKit tracks the marker and performs 3D registration, while OSG creates and renders the AR scene with the cow.
    because: In the marker-cow example, ARToolKit handles tracking and 3D registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

21/A4  recap  21/S1  "Recap"  (14 facts, 44 concepts)
  Low-level AR libraries provide core tracking functionality but require high developer skill and often lack built-in realistic rendering or interaction support. Developers can overcome these limitations by combining tracking-focused libraries like ARToolKit with scene graph libraries like Open Scene Graph to manage 3D graphics. These combinations are used in various frameworks and mobile-specific toolkits.
  - Low-level AR libraries provide core tracking but require high developer skill and often lack realistic rendering or interaction support.
  - Scene graph libraries, such as Open Scene Graph (OSG), organize 3D graphics scenes as node-based trees to manage rendering, visibility, and state.
  - Combining a tracking library like ARToolKit with a scene graph library allows developers to focus on interaction while the scene graph handles low-level object rendering.
  - Various frameworks and mobile-specific toolkits integrate these tracking and rendering technologies for different platforms.

21/A5  quiz  21/S2  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q Why are rapid prototyping and development tools used for an AR idea before major development?  [21/S2/F1]
    - To provide maximum development flexibility through low-level library access
    - To build a final high-performance AR application with realistic graphics
    - To replace a tracking library with a complete scene graph renderer
    * To visualize the idea with simple means and show it to end users or clients
    because: Rapid prototyping tools are used to visualize an AR idea simply and show it to users or clients before major development, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.
  Q What is FLAR Toolkit in relation to AR Toolkit?  [21/S2/F3]
    - A scene graph library used to manage rendering nodes
    - A 3D graphics library that can be paired with FLAR Tracker
    * A version of AR Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash
    - A non-Flash authoring tool for desktop and mobile AR
    because: FLAR Toolkit is described as a version of AR Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash, allowing an AR experience to run from within a web browser.
  Q What can a user accomplish in FLAR Toolkit with a few lines of code?  [21/S2/F4, 21/S2/F5]
    * Activate a camera, track AR markers, and overlay virtual content onto the tracked image
    - Combine an AR tracking library with a 3D graphics library for full development
    - Generate markerless AR content using natural feature tracking
    - Write interaction from scratch for a complete realistic AR system
    because: FLAR Toolkit lets a user activate a camera, track AR markers, and load and overlay virtual content onto the tracked image for 3D registering with minimal effort.
  Q What is FLAR Manager primarily designed to do?  [21/S2/F6, 21/S2/F7]
    - Provide low-level AR functionality with maximum development flexibility
    * Combine AR tracking libraries with 3D graphics libraries for prototyping
    - Supply markerless tracking and interaction support in a low-level library
    - Replace Adobe Flash with a non-Flash authoring tool for final production
    because: FLAR Manager is a framework that combines various AR tracking and graphics libraries, and such combinations are used primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.
  Q Why might non-Flash-based AR authoring tools be less popular than Flash-based AR prototyping tools?  [21/S2/F8]
    * Flash-based tools have greater market penetration
    - Flash-based tools require more programming skill
    - Non-Flash tools cannot visualize an AR idea before major development
    - Non-Flash tools are limited to markerless augmented reality
    because: Non-Flash-based authoring tools for AR prototyping exist, but they may be less popular than Flash-based tools because Flash-based tools have greater market penetration.

21/A6  recap  21/S2  "Recap"  (8 facts, 28 concepts)
  Low-level AR libraries provide maximum flexibility but require significant programming skill and time, while rapid prototyping tools allow for the visualization of ideas before major development. Adobe Flash can be used with plugins like FLAR Toolkit or FLAR Manager to prototype AR experiences in a web browser with minimal effort using a few lines of code. FLAR Manager combines tracking and 3D graphics libraries primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.
  - Low-level AR libraries provide maximum flexibility but require significant programming skill and time.
  - Rapid prototyping tools allow for the visualization of ideas before major development so that unsuitable ideas do not require further coding.
  - Adobe Flash can be used with plugins like FLAR Toolkit or FLAR Manager to prototype AR experiences in a web browser with minimal effort using a few lines of code.
  - FLAR Manager combines tracking and 3D graphics libraries primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

21/A7  put_in_order  21/S2  "Order the steps of using FLAR Toolkit"  (1 facts, 5 concepts)
  Order the steps of using FLAR Toolkit: Activate a camera > Track AR markers in the camera view > Load and overlay virtual content on the tracked image for 3D registering  [21/S2/F4]

21/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 48 concepts)
  Q Why can a tracking-focused low-level AR library by itself produce only a rudimentary AR system, and what role can a scene graph library take in a combined AR framework?  [21/S1/F4, 21/S1/F5, 21/S1/F9; low-level library and framework, AR Toolkit, scene graph, tracking, rendering, interaction]
    A Low-level AR toolkits such as ARToolKit primarily provide tracking and only low-level primitive OpenGL rendering, with no built-in interaction or complex realistic graphics, so a complete realistic application requires writing interaction from scratch. A scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, allowing the developer to focus on interaction while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.
  Q How does the skill-based hierarchy of AR software tools order categories from the most to the least programming skill, and why can rapid prototyping tools be useful before major development?  [21/S0/F1, 21/S0/F2, 21/S2/F1; skill-based hierarchy, low-level software library or framework, rapid prototyping tool, plugin, standalone augmented reality authoring tool, programming skill, programming ability, design prototyping skill, prototype]
    A The hierarchy places low-level software libraries or frameworks first, then rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools, according to decreasing programming skill. Low-level tools require strong programming or coding ability and understanding of library functions, while rapid prototyping tools need some programming or design prototyping skill, plugins require skill with the original developer tool, and standalone authoring tools assume no programming ability. Rapid prototyping tools are useful because they let an AR idea be visualized with simple means and shown to users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.
  Q How do tracking and three-dimensional registration work together in a marker-based AR example where a phone detects a marker and a 3D cow appears, and how can ARToolKit and Open Scene Graph be assigned to those tasks?  [3/S2/F2, 21/S1/F13, 21/S1/F14; marker, augmented reality, tracking, three-dimensional registration, AR Toolkit, Open Scene Graph, three-dimensional object]
    A In marker-based AR, a marker placed in the real environment triggers the augmented experience when a device detects it, so digital content appears at the marker's position. In the marker-cow example, tracking recognizes the marker and its position, while three-dimensional registration creates and renders the cow at that position. Combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph can assign tracking and three-dimensional registration to ARToolKit and the creation of the rendered AR scene with the cow to Open Scene Graph.
  Q How can AR software tools be categorized by platform and tracking technology, and what do DroidAR and Vuforia show about mobile AR tracking choices?  [21/S0/F0, 21/S1/F17, 21/S1/F18; augmented reality software tool, application platform, mobile augmented reality application, tracking technology, computer vision-based tracking, computer vision, sensor, global positioning system, DroidAR, Vuforia, ARToolKit for mobile, Open Scene Graph, iPhone operating system, Android]
    A AR software tools can be categorized by target application platform, such as desktop or mobile AR applications, or by tracking technology, such as computer-vision-based tracking or other sensors like GPS. Mobile-specific AR frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia. DroidAR uses sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support. ARToolKit for mobile is a mobile version of ARToolKit available for the iPhone operating system and Android and integrated with Open Scene Graph.

===== lecture 22: AR Software

22/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is three-dimensional registration? (lecture 7) -> In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.
  What is rapid prototyping tool? (lecture 21) -> In a skill-based hierarchy, Augmented Reality (AR) software tools are arranged in four categories according to decreasing programming skill: low-level software libraries or frameworks, rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools.
  What is plugin? (lecture 21) -> In a skill-based hierarchy, Augmented Reality (AR) software tools are arranged in four categories according to decreasing programming skill: low-level software libraries or frameworks, rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools.
  What is marker-based tracking? (lecture 21) -> ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.
  What is framework? (lecture 21) -> Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

    - A standalone no-coding authoring tool that includes content authoring and AR support

22/A2  recap  22/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 33 concepts)
  Non-flash-based browser tools allow developers to create fast AR prototypes using web technologies like HTML and WebGL. Open Frameworks serves as a C++ middleware library that combines multiple libraries for tracking, rendering, and interaction. Wikitude provides a mobile prototyping tool where computation occurs on backend servers, and it supports both custom and default content.
  - Non-flash-based browser tools allow developers to create fast AR prototypes using HTML or WebGL.
  - Open Frameworks is a C++ middleware that combines multiple libraries to support tracking, rendering, and interaction.
  - Wikitude is a mobile browser tool for AR prototyping that performs computation on backend servers.
  - Wikitude allows for faster prototyping with custom content but can use default content if needed.

22/A3  quiz  22/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q In an AR software plugin for an existing content authoring tool, what does the plugin mainly add?  [22/S1/F0]
    - A complete standalone authoring package that does not need another tool
    - A web prototype written directly in HTML and WebGL
    - Backend computation that lets the mobile device render only
    * AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration over the real-world view
    because: A plugin is added to an existing interactive 2D or 3D authoring tool and supplies AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration. The main authoring tool remains responsible for content authoring.
  Q Why can using an AR plugin be easy and quick for a developer?  [22/S1/F1]
    * The developer already knows the host authoring tool and only needs to understand the plugin
    - The developer avoids learning any part of the host tool or the plugin
    - The developer avoids dependence on proprietary player software
    - The approach remains sensible even if the developer has never used the authoring tool
    because: The plugin approach is easy and quick when the developer can rely on existing knowledge of the host authoring tool and only needs to learn the plugin. If the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch.
  Q What is a limitation of adding AR support through a plugin to an existing authoring tool?  [22/S1/F5]
    * The user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides
    - The plugin can provide any interaction not already supported by the host tool
    - The content is usually independent of proprietary player software
    - The software and hardware configuration is independent of the underlying tool
    because: Plugins are constrained by the underlying authoring tool for user interface, interaction design, and software and hardware configuration. Content produced with the authoring tool usually also becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.
  Q What approach can resolve the limitations of higher-level AR tools or plugins?  [22/S1/F6]
    - Use higher-level plugins and continue depending on a third-party tool
    * Use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch
    - Use low-level software libraries while still leaving the system dependent on a third-party tool
    - Use a higher-level tool only to avoid building any part of the system from scratch
    because: A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level AR tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch. This avoids depending on a third-party tool.

22/A4  recap  22/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 18 concepts)
  Plugins to existing tools add AR-specific functions to 2D or 3D content authoring tools that may not natively support AR. This method is easy and quick for developers familiar with the host tool, but it can limit user interface design and usually make content dependent on proprietary player software in most cases. Building a system from scratch using low-level software libraries can resolve these limitations.
  - Plugins to existing tools add AR-specific functions to 2D or 3D content authoring tools that do not natively support AR.
  - This method is easy and quick for developers who know the host tool, but it makes no sense if the tool is unknown.
  - Using these plugins can limit user interface design, depend on specific hardware configurations, and usually make content dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.
  - Building a system from scratch using low-level software libraries can resolve the limitations of high-level tools and plugins.

22/A5  quiz  22/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What distinguishes standalone AR authoring tools from AR plugins?  [22/S2/F1]
    - They require a basic authoring tool to provide scene editing
    - They are low-level libraries that require building an AR system from scratch
    * They are complete packages that include content authoring and AR support without depending on another tool
    - They add AR functions to an existing content authoring tool
    because: Standalone AR authoring tools are complete packages that include both content authoring and AR support, unlike plugins that depend on an existing tool.
  Q Why can non-programmers use most standalone AR authoring tools?  [22/S2/F0, 22/S2/F3]
    * They provide drag-and-drop graphical interfaces for creating experiences without coding
    - They require only command-line scripting languages
    - They demand knowledge of a host 3D authoring package
    - They rely on HTML and WebGL expertise to build prototypes
    because: Most standalone AR authoring tools use drag-and-drop GUIs so users with basic PC skills and no programming experience can create AR experiences.
  Q What range of features do standalone AR authoring tools typically support?  [22/S2/F2]
    * Scene construction, animation, and interactive behavior, from simple scenes to complex interactions
    - Only low-level rendering and device sensor access
    - Only static 2D image tracking and marker registration
    - Only audio mixing and haptic feedback
    because: Standalone AR authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from simple scene construction to complex interactive systems.
  Q What is a limitation of building an AR application with no coding in a standalone authoring tool?  [22/S2/F4]
    - It makes mobile deployment impossible
    - It prevents the use of drag-and-drop interfaces
    - It requires a host 3D authoring package
    * Its utility is limited compared with an advanced system that uses scripting for more flexibility
    because: Applications built with absolute zero coding have limited utility compared with advanced systems that use scripting-language support for more flexibility.

22/A6  recap  22/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 10 concepts)
  Standalone authoring tools allow users to create AR experiences without programming experience because they are complete packages that do not depend on any other software. They support scene construction, animation, and interactive behavior. Most provide drag-and-drop interfaces for non-programmers but can also support scripting for more flexibility.
  - Standalone authoring tools allow users to create AR experiences without programming experience.
  - These tools are complete packages that do not depend on any other software.
  - They support scene construction, animation, and interactive behavior.
  - Most provide drag-and-drop interfaces for non-programmers but can also support scripting for more flexibility.

22/A7  quiz  22/S3  "Quick quiz"  (1 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q How are augmented reality software categories ordered by the programming skill required?  [22/S3/F0]
    - Plugins to existing systems require the most skill, low-level libraries and frameworks require the least, and standalone authoring tools and rapid prototyping tools fall between these extremes.
    - Standalone authoring tools require the most skill, low-level libraries and frameworks require the least, and rapid prototyping tools and plugins fall between these extremes.
    - Low-level libraries and frameworks require the least skill, standalone authoring tools require the most, and rapid prototyping tools and plugins fall between these extremes.
    * Low-level libraries and frameworks require the most skill, standalone authoring tools require the least, and rapid prototyping tools and plugins fall between these extremes.
    because: AR software tools and packages fall into four categories based on programming skill: low-level libraries and frameworks require the highest skill, standalone authoring tools require the least, and rapid prototyping tools and plugins to existing systems lie between these extremes.

22/A8  recap  22/S3  "Recap"  (1 facts, 7 concepts)
  Augmented reality (AR) software tools and packages are available in four categories based on the programming skill required. Low-level libraries and frameworks require the highest programming skill, while standalone authoring tools require the least. Rapid prototyping tools and plugins to existing systems fall between these extremes.
  - AR software tools are categorized by the programming skill required.
  - Categories range from high-skill low-level libraries to low-skill standalone authoring tools.

22/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 42 concepts)
  Q When a developer adds an augmented reality plugin to an existing interactive three-dimensional graphics authoring tool, what makes the approach quick, and what aspects of the final augmented reality system can still be constrained by the host tool?  [22/S1/F0, 22/S1/F1, 22/S1/F5; plugin, content authoring tool, tracking, augmented reality visualization, three-dimensional registration, user interface, interaction design, software configuration, hardware configuration, proprietary player software]
    A A plugin is added to an existing content authoring tool and adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and three-dimensional registration, while the host tool handles content authoring. It is quick when the developer already knows the host authoring tool because they only need to understand the plugin. However, user interface and interaction design, software and hardware configuration, and in most cases dependence of the content on proprietary player software are constrained by the underlying authoring tool.
  Q Why might a developer choose low-level software development tools instead of a higher-level augmented reality tool or plugin, and what does that choice demand of the developer?  [22/S1/F6, 21/S1/F0; low-level software development tool, software library, low-level library, low-level framework, higher-level tool, plugin, third-party tool, programming skill, tracking, augmented reality application]
    A Low-level software development tools such as software libraries can resolve limitations of higher-level tools or plugins by letting the developer build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool. They demand the highest programming skill because low-level libraries and frameworks provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an augmented reality application.
  Q How does Wikitude's client-server structure shape the role of the mobile device in augmented reality prototyping, and how does available content affect its usefulness?  [22/S0/F3, 22/S0/F4, 22/S0/F5; Wikitude, browser application, mobile device, client, rendering device, backend server, user interface element, mobile prototyping tool, prototyping]
    A Wikitude is a free augmented reality browser application that runs on mobile devices and can be used as a mobile prototyping tool. It treats the mobile device primarily as a client or rendering device, connecting to backend servers for content and user interface elements, with computation possibly taking place on the backend server. It makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, developers depend on default content, which may reduce flexibility but is still usable.
  Q How do standalone augmented reality authoring tools differ from plugins in what they provide to a developer, and what user skills are enough to begin using many of them?  [22/S2/F0, 22/S2/F1, 22/S2/F2, 22/S2/F3; standalone authoring tool, plugin, content authoring tool, content authoring, augmented reality, scene construction, animation, interactive behavior, graphical user interface, personal computer]
    A Standalone authoring tools allow users to create augmented reality experiences without programming experience and are complete packages that include content authoring and augmented reality support, unlike plugins, which require a basic content authoring tool on which augmented reality support is provided. They typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior. Most provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces, so users with basic personal computer skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

23/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why are extended reality systems treated as interactive systems, and what does that classification imply about the user they should serve?  [23/S0/F0, 23/S1/F0, 23/S1/F1; extended reality system, interactive system, interaction, lay person]
    A Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of interactive systems, in which interaction takes place between the system and the user. Because the user in such systems is a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and wants to use the system rather than understand how it works, the design implication is that the system should serve the user's use of it rather than expose technical internals.
  Q How do disappearing technology and presence point to the same design goal?  [23/S0/F1, 23/S0/F2, 23/S0/F3, 8/S2/F0; disappearing technology, presence]
    A Weiser's claim that the most profound technologies disappear means that a very advanced technology should ideally not be visible to the user, and the user should feel like dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. The disappearing-technology ideal and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.
  Q What can happen when an interactive system intended for lay users gives an error message containing terms such as event log, safe mode, or a hexadecimal status code?  [23/S1/F2, 23/S1/F3, 23/S1/F4; error message, lay person, event log, safe mode, hexadecimal status code, interactive system]
    A Technical terms in an error message, such as event log and safe mode, are not expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user, and a hexadecimal status code is generally incomprehensible to a layperson. A jargon-based error message can make the user anxious, leave the user not knowing what is wrong or how to get out of it, and may lead the user to refrain from using the system further and lose motivation. Designers of such interactive systems should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.
  Q Why do human factors considerations in system design lead to a user-centric approach, and what design decisions does that approach shape?  [23/S2/F0, 23/S2/F1, 23/S4/F0; human factors, system design, user-centric approach, user characteristic, interface element, layout, system state, interaction, goal state, interface]
    A Human factors in system design requires designers to know users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills and therefore require different interfaces. The user-centric approach starts by understanding user characteristics and what users need and expect, and then designs the system based on that. It shapes interface elements, layouts that organize interface elements, ways for users to perceive system state from their own point of view, and interactions that take users to desired system states or goal states.

===== lecture 24: XR as Interactive Systems

24/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is middleware? (lecture 19) -> Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.
  What is human factors? (lecture 23) -> Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.
  What is user-centric approach? (lecture 23) -> The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

24/A1  quiz  24/S0  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q Why might designers use the novice, intermittent, and expert user classes instead of always beginning with empirical or field studies?  [24/S0/F0, 24/S0/F3, 24/S0/F6]
    - Because field studies are inexpensive and usually require no elaborate planning
    * Because field studies are time-consuming and require elaborate planning, while the classes give a design starting point
    - Because users in all three classes behave exactly the same way
    - Because the three classes are the only possible user categorization
    because: Empirical or field studies can be time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning. The novice, intermittent, and expert classes give a broad starting point when the design process starts.
  Q In the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, what does an expert user mean?  [24/S0/F2]
    - A person who uses the system only for the first time
    - A person who uses the system only occasionally
    - A person with advanced technical knowledge about system hardware
    * A person who is an expert in using the system and can use it efficiently
    because: An expert user is not a technology expert but a person who is an expert in using the system and can use it efficiently.
  Q Which user class uses an interactive system occasionally?  [24/S0/F1]
    - The expert user
    * The intermittent user
    - The technology expert
    - The novice user
    because: The three-class classification includes novice users who use the system for the first time, intermittent users who use it occasionally, and expert users who use it regularly over a long period.
  Q For a novice first-time user saving a file, why might a menu option be preferred over a hotkey combination?  [24/S0/F5]
    - Because menu options are faster than hotkey combinations
    * Because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them
    - Because novices cannot see menu options on a display
    - Because hotkeys are always preferable for novice users
    because: A menu option may take longer than a hotkey combination, but it is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them.
  Q Why can a word processing or similar application provide both a hotkey combination and a menu option for the same task?  [24/S0/F4]
    * To cater to different user groups
    - To make the menu option unavailable for first-time users
    - To force intermittent users to use the same option as experts
    - To reduce the number of ways the task can be performed
    because: An application can provide multiple options for the same task, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, to cater to different user groups.

24/A2  recap  24/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Interactive-system designers can rely on novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization as a starting point for design decisions instead of always beginning with time-consuming and laborious field studies. This classification distinguishes users by how regularly they use the system, where an expert is defined by system efficiency rather than general technology expertise. Because users in different classes are likely to behave differently, this broad categorization is useful when the design process starts.
  - Designers can rely on novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with time-consuming and laborious field studies.
  - Users can be classified into three categories: novice users, intermittent users, and expert users.
  - An expert user is defined as someone who can use the system efficiently rather than a general technology expert.
  - These categories provide a starting point for design decisions because users in different classes are likely to behave differently.
  - This broad categorization is useful when the design process starts, even though more fine-grained categorizations are possible.

24/A3  quiz  24/S1  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q For an electronic engineer, what does user-centric design mainly concern?  [24/S1/F0]
    - A software development lifecycle that accounts for users' needs
    - The physical form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look
    - Creative design of interface elements and layouts
    * Hardware-level features such as more sensors, smaller chips, and a more power-efficient battery
    because: For an electronic engineer, user-centric design concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.
  Q How does an application software developer building a VR or AR system incorporate user characteristics?  [24/S1/F1]
    * By following a development lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations
    - By specifying the physical shape, size, and look of the product
    - By designing the interface elements and layouts of the system
    - By adding more sensors, smaller chips, and a power-efficient battery
    because: An application software developer incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations.

24/A4  recap  24/S1  "Recap"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, whether it concerns interface elements, product form, or hardware features. Application software developers incorporate user characteristics by following a development lifecycle that accounts for user needs and expectations. This ensures the system is easier to use and better matches the users' needs and expectations.
  - The meaning of user-centric design varies depending on the designer's specific role.
  - Software developers use a development lifecycle that accounts for user characteristics, needs, and expectations.

24/A5  quiz  24/S2  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q Which three measures are used to evaluate usability?  [24/S2/F3]
    * Effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction
    - Effectiveness, efficiency, and control
    - Effectiveness, efficiency, and functionality
    - Effectiveness, efficiency, and interaction
    because: The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
  Q In the ISO definition of usability, a product is evaluated with respect to which three specified details?  [24/S2/F1, 24/S2/F2]
    - Specified users, every conceivable feature, and a specified context of use
    - All users, specified goals, and a specified context of use
    * Specified users, specified goals, and specified context of use
    - Specified users, specified goals, and all usage scenarios
    because: The ISO usability definition is limited to specified users, specified goals, and a specified context of use.
  Q In usability, what does effectiveness refer to?  [24/S2/F3]
    - How many specified users can use the product
    - How fast the user can do what they want to do
    * Whether the user can do what they want to do
    - How satisfied the user is when using the system
    because: Effectiveness means whether the user can do what they want to do.
  Q In usability, what does efficiency refer to?  [24/S2/F3]
    - Whether the user can do what they want to do
    * How fast the user can do what they want to do
    - How satisfied the user is when using the system
    - How many specified contexts of use are supported
    because: Efficiency means how fast the user can do what they want to do.
  Q In usability, what does satisfaction refer to?  [24/S2/F3]
    - How fast the user can do what they want to do
    - Whether the user can do what they want to do
    - How well specified goals are supported
    * How satisfied the user is when using the system
    because: Satisfaction means how satisfied the user is when using the system.

24/A6  recap  24/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user. The ISO 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals in a specified context of use. These qualities are measured through effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.
  - Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.
  - The ISO 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability based on specified users, goals, and a context of use.
  - Usability is measured by effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

24/A7  quiz  24/S3  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In user-centered design, what is involved in building a usable software application?  [24/S3/F0]
    * Involving users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle
    - Involving users only as final evaluators of the product
    - Involving users only after the software application is released
    - Involving users only through post-deployment feedback
    because: User-centered design involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
  Q What is the stated objective of user-centered design?  [24/S3/F2]
    * To design products that increase usability
    - To design products for every possible context of use
    - To design products with every conceivable feature
    - To design products for every possible user
    because: The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability.
  Q What do cooperative design, participatory design, contextual design, and human-centered design have in common?  [24/S3/F3]
    - They are measures of usability in a specified context of use
    - They are user categories chosen before a virtual tour begins
    * They are related terms for taking users into the design process
    - They are stages of the interactive system development life cycle
    because: These terms are related to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.
  Q In user-centric software design and software development, what is the core design concern?  [24/S3/F4]
    - Designing usable systems that cover all possible usage scenarios
    - Designing usable systems that serve every possible user group
    - Designing usable systems that include every conceivable feature
    * Designing usable systems that meet lay users' needs and expectations
    because: The core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users.

24/A8  recap  24/S3  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  User-centered design involves users in the development lifecycle to build usable software with the objective of increasing usability. Related terms like human-centered or participatory design also refer to including users in the design process. A core concern of this approach is creating usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of layperson users.
  - User-centered design involves users in the development lifecycle to build usable software.
  - The main objective of user-centered design is to increase usability.
  - Related terms like human-centered or participatory design also refer to including users in the design process.
  - Software design focuses on creating usable systems for layperson users.

24/A9  quiz  24/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q What does a user-centered software development approach require of users?  [24/S4/F0]
    - Involvement only after the software is released
    - Involvement only by expert users
    * Active or passive involvement in the chosen software development lifecycle
    - Involvement only during final testing
    because: The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.
  Q Why should interaction design and user-input modeling in an XR system follow a user-centered design approach?  [24/S4/F5]
    - So the XR engine can use hardware resources to generate output data faster
    - So the output devices can stimulate the user's senses more easily
    * So the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily
    - So the input devices can track the user's positions with less effort
    because: Interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.
  Q Why is user-centered design needed for perceptual design and modeling of output in an XR system?  [24/S4/F6]
    - So the input devices can track the user's positions more accurately
    - So the XR engine can use fewer hardware resources
    * So generated output stimuli match the user's perception and are easily understood
    - So the output devices can stimulate the user's senses with less effort
    because: Perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because generated output stimuli must match the user's perception of them, so the user can perceive and understand the output easily.
  Q In the operation of an XR system, what is the role of the XR engine as middleware?  [24/S4/F4]
    - It stimulates the user's senses directly
    - It tracks the user's actions and positions
    - It collects the user's input data
    * It uses hardware resources to generate output data
    because: The XR engine acts as middleware that uses hardware resources to generate output data, while input devices track actions and positions and output devices stimulate the user's senses.
  Q Which option lists the parts that an XR system comprises?  [24/S4/F3]
    - Hardware, the application layer, and the user
    * Hardware, the XR engine as middleware, and the application layer
    - Input devices, output devices, and the XR engine
    - Hardware, the XR engine, and the user
    because: An XR system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

24/A10  recap  24/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 24 concepts)
  XR systems are highly interactive, and human factors are important to understand how users provide input and perceive output. These systems use hardware, middleware, and application layers to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment. By applying a user-centered approach to both input interaction and output perception, developers can ensure that providing input is seamless and that output stimuli match the user's perception.
  - XR systems are highly interactive, making human factors important for understanding how users provide input and perceive output.
  - XR software aims to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment using both hardware and software.
  - XR systems use hardware, middleware, and an application layer to track user actions and process them into output data.
  - Input interaction design should follow a user-centered approach to ensure that providing data is seamless, effective, and easy.
  - Output perception design requires a user-centered approach to ensure that generated stimuli match the user's perception.

24/A11  put_in_order  24/S4  "Order the data-flow stages of an XR system"  (1 facts, 10 concepts)
  Order the data-flow stages of an XR system: User actions and positions are tracked > Actions and positions are sent as input data > Input data is processed and the environment is rendered > XR engine uses hardware resources to generate output data > Output devices stimulate the user's senses  [24/S4/F4]

24/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q Why is the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization useful at the start of interactive-system design when empirical field studies are not always practical?  [24/S0/F0, 24/S0/F1, 24/S0/F3; field study, novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, novice user, intermittent user, expert user, interactive-system design]
    A Empirical or field studies are typically needed to understand users and their behavior, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so designers can rely on the categorization instead of always starting with field studies. The categorization separates first-time, occasional, and regularly using long-term users, and because users in different classes are likely to behave differently, it provides a starting point for understanding users and making design decisions.
  Q Why might a word processing application provide both a menu option and a hotkey combination for the same task, such as saving a file?  [24/S0/F1, 24/S0/F3, 24/S0/F4, 24/S0/F5; word processing application, menu option, hotkey combination, task, file, novice user, intermittent user, expert user]
    A A word processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups. The novice, intermittent, and expert classes consist of first-time, occasional, and regularly using long-term users, and users in different classes are likely to behave differently. The menu option takes longer but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be better for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.
  Q How does user-centered design build on the user-centric approach when developing software for virtual reality or augmented reality systems?  [24/S1/F1, 24/S3/F0, 24/S3/F2, 23/S2/F0; user-centered design, user-centric approach, design lifecycle, development lifecycle, usability, virtual reality, augmented reality, software, user characteristic]
    A The user-centric approach starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that. User-centered design results from applying this approach and involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle, with the objective of increasing usability. An application software developer building virtual reality or augmented reality software therefore incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations, so the system is easier to use and better matches their needs and expectations.
  Q Why should an extended reality system use user-centered design for both interaction design and perceptual design?  [24/S4/F1, 24/S4/F5, 24/S4/F6; extended reality system, human factors, interaction design, user input modeling, perceptual design, output modeling, user-centered design, input, output, input data, output stimulus, perception]
    A Extended reality systems are highly interactive, and human factors are important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output. Interaction design and modeling of user input should follow user-centered design so the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily. Perceptual design and modeling of output also requires user-centered design because output stimuli must match the user's perception so the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

===== lecture 25: Human Factors in XR

25/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.
  What is extended reality system? (lecture 24) -> Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is immersion? (lecture 2) -> Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

These designs aim to create an illusion of reality to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world. Creating this illusion is crucial for VR, while it is less significant but not totally insignificant for AR or MR.
  - Interaction and perceptual designs are both important for usability in an XR system.
  - XR systems create an illusion of reality to enhance presence.
  - Creating an illusion of reality is more crucial for VR than for AR or MR.

25/A11  recap  25/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 23 concepts)
  Sensory system selectivity allows receptors to target particular stimuli and activate only when specific types arrive. While eyes use photoreceptors for visible light, mechanoreceptors sense motion, vibration, and gravitational force for hearing, touch, and balance.   - Sensory system selectivity means receptors target particular stimuli and activate only when those specific types arrive.

  - Chemoreceptors provide signals based on chemical composition for taste and smell.

25/A18  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (5 facts, 31 concepts)
  Balance | Touch | Vision | *Ear  (Vision, touch, and balance are human senses, while the ear is the sense organ for the auditory sense, not a sense itself.)  [25/S5/F2, 25/S3/F1]
  *Stimulus | Mechanoreceptor | Photoreceptor | Chemoreceptor  (A photoreceptor, chemoreceptor, and mechanoreceptor are types of receptors, whereas a stimulus is the input that activates a receptor, not a receptor.)  [25/S5/F4, 25/S4/F0]
  Ear | Skin | Eye | *Photoreceptor  (The eye, ear, and skin are sense organs, while a photoreceptor is a receptor contained in the eye and is not itself a sense organ.)  [25/S3/F1, 25/S4/F1]

25/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 28 concepts)
  Q How do interaction design and perceptual design work together to support presence through an illusion of reality?  [25/S0/F0, 25/S0/F1; interaction design, perceptual design, presence, illusion of reality, perceptual stimuli]
    A Interaction design deals with input and the ease of interacting, while perceptual design deals with output and the perceptual stimuli generated by the system. In an XR system, these designs are used to create the best possible illusion of reality rather than actual reality. That illusion of reality is intended to enhance presence, the sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.
  Q What kinds of virtual-world output questions can perceptual psychology help an interactive system designer answer?  [25/S2/F0, 25/S2/F2; perceptual psychology, interactive system, virtual world, video resolution, pixel, frames per second, virtual sound]
    A Perceptual psychology is the science of how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena. It helps answer questions such as how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, and where virtual sound appears to come from.
  Q How can generally inconsistent sensory signals in virtual reality lead to either adaptation or cybersickness?  [2/S1/F0, 25/S1/F1, 25/S1/F3, 25/S1/F4, 25/S1/F5; virtual reality, sensory signal, adaptation, non-adaptation, cybersickness]
    A In virtual reality, the user receives input only from the virtual world, and artificial stimulation affects biological mechanisms that evolved for the real world. The virtual system generally provides sensory signals that are inconsistent with real-life experience. If the body adapts, the user may become unaware of flaws and believe the virtual system is the real world; if it does not adapt, fatigue, headaches, or cybersickness such as dizziness or nausea may result.
