===== lecture 26: Human Factors in XR

26/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is node? (lecture 21) -> A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.
  What is sensory organ? (lecture 25) -> For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ.
  What is smell? (lecture 25) -> The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).
  What is receptor? (lecture 25) -> Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

26/A1  quiz  26/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q In the perceptual process, what must happen before perception can occur?  [26/S0/F0]
    - The cerebral cortex receives the external stimulus directly
    - Neural impulses are generated before any sense organ is stimulated
    * Sense organs are stimulated and convert the stimulus into neural impulses
    - Long-term memory alone interprets the stimulus before any sensing
    because: Perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.
  Q Which part of the brain is responsible for perception and also for attention, memory, language, and consciousness?  [26/S0/F1]
    - The axon terminals
    * The cerebral cortex
    - The dendrites
    - The receptors
    because: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness.
  Q Why is the cerebral cortex described as a folded sheet of neurons?  [26/S0/F2]
    - The folding creates the gap where electrical or chemical signals pass
    - The folding allows the cortex to generate all sensory input directly
    - The folding separates sensing from perception
    * The folding helps fit the sheet into the skull
    because: The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons folded to fit into the skull.

26/A2  recap  26/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 13 concepts)
  Perception occurs only after sense organs are stimulated by a stimulus and convert that input into neural impulses. The cerebral cortex, containing roughly 20 billion neurons, is the part of the brain responsible for perception and other functions. It is a heavily folded sheet of neurons about 3 millimeters thick, folded to fit into the skull.
  - The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which converts stimuli into neural impulses, to abstract perception.
  - The cerebral cortex contains roughly 20 billion neurons and is responsible for perception and other functions.
  - The cerebral cortex is a heavily folded sheet of neurons about 3 millimeters thick.

26/A3  quiz  26/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q What is the basis for perception and overall cognitive ability?  [26/S1/F0]
    - The isolated activity of individual neurons
    - The thickness of the cerebral cortex
    * The interconnection of neurons
    - The amount of muscular effort sensed by the body
    because: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
  Q In the directed-graph model of neuron interconnection, what does the nucleus or cell body correspond to?  [26/S1/F1, 26/S1/F2]
    - A gap where electrical or chemical signals pass
    - An input edge carrying impulses toward the cell body
    - An output edge carrying impulses away from the cell body
    * A node that processes input
    because: In the directed-graph model, the nucleus or cell body is the node that processes input, while dendrites and axons are edges.
  Q In the directed-graph model of neuron interconnection, what do dendrites correspond to?  [26/S1/F2]
    - Nodes that aggregate information in the cell body
    - Gaps through which electrical or chemical signals pass
    - Output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body
    * Input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body
    because: Dendrites are modeled as input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body.
  Q How does a neuron aggregate and transmit information in the neuron-interconnection network?  [26/S1/F3]
    - It gathers only already-aggregated information and never receives direct neural impulses
    * It gathers information from other neurons through dendrites and sends the processed signal through axons
    - It gathers information from other neurons through axons and sends the processed signal through dendrites
    - It receives and sends signals only when two cell bodies are physically connected
    because: A neuron aggregates information from other neurons through its dendrites, and the processing in the cell body is transmitted through its axons.
  Q How does communication occur between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of the next neuron?  [26/S1/F4]
    - By direct physical fusion of the axon and dendrite
    - By merging axon terminals from the two neurons
    * Across a gap called the synapse, without physical connection
    - By contact between the cell body of one neuron and the next
    because: An axon is paired with a dendrite, but the two are not physically connected; signals pass across the synapse.

26/A4  recap  26/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 24 concepts)
  Perception and cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons, which consist of a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, and axons. The nucleus processes input from dendrites and transmits information to other neurons through axons. Neurons communicate across a gap called a synapse, with each neuron having about 7,000 connections to form a network of 10^15 edges in the human brain.
  - Perception and cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
  - A neuron consists of a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, axon branches, and axon terminals.
  - The nucleus processes information from dendrites and transmits it to other neurons through axons.
  - Neurons communicate across a gap called a synapse using electrical or chemical signals.
  - Each neuron has about 7,000 synaptic connections, forming a network of 10^15 edges in the human brain.

26/A5  put_in_order  26/S1  "Order the path of a neural signal"  (3 facts, 17 concepts)
  Order the path of a neural signal: Dendrites carry neural impulses to the cell body > The cell body processes the input > Axons carry neural impulses from the cell body > A synapse passes electrical or chemical signals  [26/S1/F2, 26/S1/F3, 26/S1/F4]

26/A6  quiz  26/S2  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q What is hierarchical processing?  [26/S2/F0]
    - The propagation of signals from the cerebral cortex back to sense organ receptors
    * Neural processing as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through a neural network to the cerebral cortex
    - The combination of real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory
    - The conversion of input stimuli into neural impulses by sense organ receptors
    because: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing that occurs while receptor signals move through the neural network toward the cerebral cortex.
  Q How does staged aggregation work in hierarchical processing?  [26/S2/F1]
    - Signals are divided into lower-level details at successive levels before reaching the cerebral cortex
    * Signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached
    - Signals from receptors are combined only at the cerebral cortex
    - Signals from a single receptor type are copied without change until the cerebral cortex is reached
    because: Staged aggregation combines signals from many receptor types at successive neural levels, producing higher-level information rather than repeating the same lower-level information.
  Q What does hierarchical processing make possible in perception?  [26/S2/F2]
    - Detection of patterns before any neural aggregation occurs
    * Detection of increasingly complex patterns in the stimulus
    - Detection of only simple, low-level patterns in the stimulus
    - Detection of the same pattern complexity at every processing level
    because: Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

26/A7  recap  26/S2  "Recap"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex. It works by staged aggregation, in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels to produce higher-level information. This allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.
  - Hierarchical processing is the neural processing of signals from sense organ receptors to the cerebral cortex.
  - Staged aggregation combines signals from various receptors at successive levels to create higher-level information.
  - Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in a stimulus.

26/A8  quiz  26/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q Once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, what is combined to produce the interpretation of a stimulus?  [26/S3/F0]
    * Real-time sensory input and long-term memory
    - Real-time sensory input alone
    - Motor cortex efference copies
    - Hierarchical processing alone
    because: Interpretation is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone.
  Q Why can a newborn and an aged person interpret the same stimulus very differently?  [26/S3/F1]
    - They have different hierarchical processing stages
    - They have different receptor selectivity
    - They have different proprioception signals
    * They have different long-term experience
    because: The interpretation of a stimulus depends on the interpreter's long-term experience.
  Q Overall perceptual processing is the outcome of which combination?  [26/S3/F2]
    - Real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge alone
    * Hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge
    - Hierarchical processing and long-term knowledge alone
    - Hierarchical processing and real-time sensory input alone
    because: Overall perceptual processing results from hierarchical processing together with the combination of real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge or experience.

26/A9  recap  26/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 12 concepts)
  Interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory. This interpretation depends on a person's long-term experience. Overall, perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time input with long-term knowledge.
  - Interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with knowledge stored in long-term memory.
  - Interpretation of a stimulus depends on a person's long-term experience.
  - Perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time input with long-term knowledge.

26/A10  quiz  26/S4  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What is proprioception?  [26/S4/F0]
    - The ability to feel external touch through specialized receptors in the sense organs
    - The ability to interpret visual patterns by combining receptor signals in the cerebral cortex
    * The ability to sense relative body-part positions and the muscular effort used in moving them
    - The ability to detect chemical stimuli through chemoreceptors in the nasal passage
    because: Proprioception is the perception of the relative positions of body parts and the muscular effort involved in moving them.
  Q Why can proprioception be called a sixth sense?  [26/S4/F0]
    - Because the motor cortex sends efference copies to it
    * Because it lacks a direct sensory organ or receptor
    - Because it relies on chemoreceptors in the nasal passage
    - Because it creates a mismatch with visual input in VR
    because: It is called a sixth sense because, unlike direct perception through sensory organs, it has no direct sensory organ or receptor.
  Q How does the motor cortex support proprioception?  [26/S4/F1]
    * By sending efference copies to other brain regions to report executed motions
    - By balancing the various sensory inputs to prevent cybersickness in VR
    - By storing executed motion information in long-term memory for later use
    - By receiving and processing visual receptor signals in the cerebral cortex
    because: The motor cortex sends efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand body-part positions and muscular effort.

26/A11  recap  26/S4  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Proprioception is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them. The motor cortex sends signals called efference copies to communicate what motions have been executed, which are then processed to understand position and effort.
  - Proprioception is the ability to sense body positions and muscular effort.
  - The motor cortex sends efference copies to communicate motions and help understand body position.

26/A12  quiz  26/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q Why can an immersive virtual reality system create a sensory mismatch?  [26/S5/F1]
    - Because the cerebral cortex instantly learns new familiar interpretations
    * Because the brain cannot quickly retune its long-term learned sensory processing to new inputs
    - Because immersive virtual reality replaces hierarchical neural processing with a simpler signal path
    - Because real-time sensory input alone is enough to override long-term memory
    because: An immersive VR system can interfere with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing. The brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time.
  Q What can a sensory mismatch in virtual reality cause for a user whose brain does not adapt to it?  [26/S5/F2]
    * Cybersickness, including fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea
    - A permanent retuning of the brain's sensory processing
    - Uniform acceptance of the artificial experience by all users
    - Conscious awareness that the experience is more natural than expected
    because: A sensory mismatch may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness. Symptoms include fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.
  Q In vection, which combination of signals creates the sensory conflict?  [26/S5/F4]
    - Visual input reports stillness while proprioception reports acceleration
    - Auditory input reports acceleration while visual input reports stillness
    * Visual input reports movement or acceleration while proprioception reports no motion
    - Proprioception reports movement while visual input reports no motion
    because: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration. The balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.
  Q How can a sensory mismatch compromise presence in a virtual reality experience?  [26/S5/F3]
    - By letting the brain retune quickly and accept the experience as natural
    * By making the user consciously aware of the conflict and understand the experience is artificial
    - By strengthening the user's familiar learned sensory processing
    - By making the user feel the virtual environment is more real than expected
    because: A mismatch between sensory inputs and familiar processing can make the user consciously aware of the conflict. That awareness makes the user immediately understand that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real.
  Q What design implication follows from the need to avoid sensory conflicts in extended reality?  [26/S5/F5]
    * Balance the experiences presented by the various senses so the brain processes them as intended
    - Remove proprioceptive input so no motion can be reported
    - Prioritize visual stimulation alone to reduce the chance of sensory conflict
    - Present deliberately conflicting sensory signals to train rapid adaptation
    because: Extended reality design should carefully balance the experiences presented by the various senses. This can create an immersive experience by fooling the brain into processing information in the intended way.

26/A13  recap  26/S5  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  The brain processes perception by combining sensory signals with long-term learned experiences, but VR systems can create sensory mismatches because the brain cannot quickly adapt to new inputs. These mismatches may be insignificant for some but can cause cybersickness or compromise the sense of presence, such as with vection where visual motion conflicts with the balance sense. XR design should balance various senses to ensure the brain processes information as intended.
  - The brain processes perception by combining sensory signals with long-term learned experiences.
  - VR systems can create sensory mismatches because the brain cannot quickly adapt to new inputs.
  - Sensory mismatches may be insignificant for some users but can cause cybersickness or compromise the sense of presence.
  - Vection is a sensory conflict between visual motion and the balance sense.
  - XR design should balance various senses to ensure the brain processes information as intended.

  9 down: The sensation of self-motion highest when sensed in peripheral stimuli. (7) = VECTION

26/A18  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  axon | cell body | *synapse | dendrite  (A cell body, dendrite, and axon are parts of a neuron; a synapse is the gap between an axon and a dendrite.)  [26/S1/F1, 26/S1/F4]
  perception | attention | *cybersickness | memory  (Perception, attention, and memory are functions of the cerebral cortex; cybersickness is a condition caused by sensory mismatch.)  [26/S0/F1, 26/S5/F2]
  *presence | fatigue | headache | dizziness  (Fatigue, headache, and dizziness are symptoms of cybersickness; presence is an immersive psychological quality, not a symptom.)  [26/S5/F2, 26/S5/F3]

26/A19  put_in_order  lecture  "Order the steps of perceptual processing"  (4 facts, 21 concepts)
  Order the steps of perceptual processing: A stimulus activates sense organs > Sense organs convert the stimulus into neural impulses > Signals propagate through the neural network > Signals are aggregated at successive levels > Cortex combines input with long-term memory > Interpretation of the stimulus is produced  [26/S0/F0, 26/S2/F0, 26/S2/F1, 26/S3/F0]

26/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q How do a sense organ and the cerebral cortex work together to turn a stimulus into a perception, and why is the final interpretation not determined by sensory input alone?  [26/S0/F0, 26/S2/F1, 26/S3/F0, 26/S3/F2; perceptual process, sense organ, stimulus, neural impulse, hierarchical processing, signal, receptor, cerebral cortex, interpretation of a stimulus, sensory input, long-term memory, perception]
    A A stimulus first stimulates a sense organ, which converts that input into neural impulses, so sensing is the lowest level of the perceptual process. Hierarchical processing then combines receptor signals at successive levels until the cerebral cortex is reached, where the interpretation of the stimulus is produced. This interpretation combines real-time sensory input with long-term memory or experience, so perception is an outcome of more than the raw sensory signal alone.
  Q How does proprioception differ from direct perception through the five senses, and what neural signal supports it?  [26/S4/F0, 26/S4/F1; proprioception, perception, sensory organ, vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, taste, muscular effort, body motion, motor cortex, efference copy, cerebral cortex]
    A Direct perception comes through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste, whereas proprioception has no direct sensory organ. It is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them. The motor cortex sends efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to report executed body motion, and this information is processed to support proprioception.
  Q How do presence and cybersickness explain why a VR user who is visually moving while physically stationary can feel sick or aware that the experience is artificial?  [26/S5/F4, 26/S5/F2, 26/S5/F3, 8/S2/F0, 10/S0/F0; presence, cybersickness, virtual reality system, virtual environment, vection, visual input, acceleration, balance sense, proprioception, sensory mismatch]
    A Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated, and cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness, is primarily relevant to virtual reality. Vection is an illusion of self-motion in which visual input reports movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory mismatch. If the user's brain cannot adapt, the mismatch can cause fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea, or it can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware that the experience is artificial.


===== lecture 27: Visual Perception & Displays I

27/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is sensor? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
  What is tracking? (lecture 13) -> In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.
  What is receptor? (lecture 25) -> Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.
  What is vision? (lecture 25) -> The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).
  What is photoreceptor? (lecture 25) -> The eyes contain photoreceptors, which are activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light and therefore target only visible light.

27/A3  quiz  27/S1  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q The photon view of light is mainly useful for which of the following?  [27/S1/F1]
    * Understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor
    - Explaining the spectrum of color
    - Explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility
    - Explaining whether a surface transmits, absorbs, or reflects light
    because: The photon view treats light as tiny energy particles and is helpful for understanding or calculating how much light is received by a sensor or receptor.
  Q The wave view of light is mainly useful for explaining what aspect of light?  [27/S1/F2]
    - The amount of light received by a sensor or receptor
    - The trajectory of a single hypothetical photon
    * The spectrum of color
    - How lenses work and the concept of visibility
    because: The wave view describes light as ripples through space and is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color.
  Q The ray view of light is mainly useful for explaining what?  [27/S1/F3]
    - The amount of light received by a sensor or receptor
    - The spectrum of color
    - How light is absorbed, transmitted, or reflected by a material surface
    * How lenses work and the concept of visibility
    because: The ray view describes light as trajectories or paths and is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

27/A4  recap  27/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 14 concepts)
  Light can be described by three views: the photon, wave, and ray views. The photon view describes light as energy particles useful for calculating light received by sensors, while the wave view describes light as ripples that help explain the color spectrum. Finally, the ray view describes light as trajectories to explain how lenses work and the concept of visibility.
  - Light can be described by the photon, wave, and ray views.
  - The photon view describes light as energy particles and is useful for calculating light received by sensors.
  - The wave view describes light as ripples and helps explain the color spectrum.
  - The ray view describes light as trajectories and is useful for explaining lenses and visibility.

27/A5  quiz  27/S2  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 5 concepts)
  Q When light rays strike a material surface, which interactions can occur?  [27/S2/F0]
    * Transmission, absorption, and reflection
    - Transmission, emission, and reflection
    - Refraction, absorption, and reflection
    - Transmission, absorption, and emission
    because: The possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection.
  Q In light transmission at a material surface, what happens to some of the striking rays?  [27/S2/F1]
    - They terminate inside the material and do not propagate outside
    - They are reflected from the surface without entering the material
    - They are emitted by the material after striking it
    * They pass through the material and come out of it
    because: Transmission means some rays pass through the material and emerge from it.
  Q In absorption at a material surface, what happens to some of the striking rays?  [27/S2/F2]
    - They are reflected from the surface without entering the material
    - They are emitted by the material after striking it
    * They are absorbed, terminate inside the material, and do not propagate further outside
    - They pass through the material and come out of it
    because: Absorption means the rays are taken up by the material and stop inside it.
  Q What characterizes reflection of a light ray from a material surface?  [27/S2/F3]
    * It is reflected without entering or penetrating the material
    - It passes through the material and comes out
    - It is emitted by the material after striking it
    - It is absorbed and terminates inside the material
    because: Reflection occurs when a ray strikes the surface and is reflected without entering the material.

27/A6  recap  27/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 5 concepts)
  When light rays strike a surface, they can be transmitted, absorbed, or reflected. Transmission occurs when light passes through a material, while absorption happens when light terminates inside it. Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface without entering it.
  - Light rays can interact with surfaces through transmission, absorption, and reflection.
  - Transmission occurs when light rays pass through a material.
  - Absorption occurs when light rays terminate inside a material.
  - Reflection occurs when light rays bounce off a surface without entering it.

    - The cornea
    - The retina
    - The lens
    because: The iris dilates or constricts the pupil, admitting more light in dark surroundings and less light in bright surroundings.
  Q Which structures of the eye refract light so that images are focused on the retina?  [27/S4/F1]
    - The rods and cones
    * The cornea and lens
    - The iris and pupil
    - The retina and optic nerve fibers
    because: The material of the cornea and the lens refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.
  Q How are rods and cones distributed in the human retina?  [27/S4/F4]
    * Rods are more numerous in the peripheral retina, while cones are mainly in the fovea.
    - Cones are more numerous in the peripheral retina, while rods are mainly in the fovea.
    - Cones are mainly in the peripheral retina, while rods are mainly in the fovea.
    - Rods and cones are evenly distributed across the entire retina.
    because: Rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina, whereas cones are mainly located in the small central region called the fovea.
  Q What functional difference is supported by the way rods and cones connect to optic nerve fibers?  [27/S4/F5]
    * Shared rod fibers aid low-light sensitivity, while cone fibers support image acuity.
    - Shared cone fibers aid image acuity, while dedicated rod fibers support color perception.
    - Rods and cones share optic nerve fibers equally to improve central vision.
    - Dedicated rod fibers aid color perception, while shared cone fibers support low-light sensitivity.
    because: Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas about one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.
  Q Which statement correctly distinguishes photopic and scotopic vision?  [27/S4/F6, 27/S4/F7]
    - Photopic vision is rod-based and supports color, while scotopic vision is cone-based and sees weak lights as grays.
    - Both photopic and scotopic vision rely on rods and provide the same color perception.
    * Photopic vision is cone-based and supports color, while scotopic vision is rod-based and sees weak lights as grays.
    - Scotopic vision is cone-based and supports color, while photopic vision is rod-based and sees weak lights as grays.
    because: Cones accomplish photopic vision, in which color is perceived, while rods accomplish scotopic vision, in which weak lights are perceived as grays.

27/A10  recap  27/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 21 concepts)
  Light enters the eye and is refracted by the cornea and lens to focus on the retina, where it is processed by rods and cones. Cones are primarily located in the central fovea to provide color and image acuity during photopic vision, while rods are more numerous in the periphery to aid sensitivity during scotopic vision.
  - Light passes through the cornea, pupil, and lens, which refract the light to focus it on the retina.
  - The retina contains two types of photoreceptors: rods, which are more numerous in the periphery, and cones, which are mainly in the central fovea.
  - Rods share optic nerve fibers to aid sensitivity to lower light levels, whereas each cone has its own fiber to aid image acuity.
  - Photopic vision uses cones for central color vision, while scotopic vision uses rods for peripheral vision in weak light.

  Order the path of light through the human eye: Light crosses the cornea > Light crosses the pupil > Light crosses the lens > Light reaches the retina  [27/S4/F0]

    * Red has a lower frequency and a longer wavelength than violet
    - Red has a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength than violet
    - Violet has a lower frequency and a longer wavelength than red

    - Neither visible light nor outside-spectrum light can excite cones
    - Outside-spectrum light can excite cones, but visible light cannot
    * Visible light can excite cones, but outside-spectrum light cannot
    because: Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing color perception, while waves outside the visible spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception.

    - Vision that uses rods and gives gray perception

27/A13  recap  27/S5  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength. Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing photopic vision, which is color perception. Light waves outside the visible light spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception.
  - Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies and wavelengths ranging from red to violet light.
  - Visible light waves excite cones in the eye to produce photopic vision, which is color perception.

27/A14  quiz  27/S6  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Human eyes support central and peripheral vision mainly because:  [27/S6/F0]
    - the cornea and lens bend side rays more than central rays
    - the optic nerve is stronger in the peripheral retina
    * photoreceptor density varies greatly across the retina
    - the pupil changes size to admit different amounts of light
    because: The two types of vision arise because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.
  Q Which retinal region is primarily associated with central, sharp color vision?  [27/S6/F1, 27/S6/F3]
    * The fovea, the central retinal region with the greatest cone concentration
    - The retinal area where rods are most numerous
    - The blind spot, where the optic nerve fibers leave the eye
    - The peripheral retina, where side-entering rays land
    because: The fovea has the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, particularly cones, and central vision uses it when the eyes are focused and pointed straight at an object.
  Q Compared with central vision, peripheral vision:  [27/S6/F4, 27/S6/F5]
    - has a higher cone concentration than the fovea
    * detects movement better but has weak color perception
    - provides sharper color images when the eyes are focused
    - requires the eyes to be pointed straight at an object
    because: Peripheral vision is supported by a retinal region with lower photoreceptor density and a mix of rods and fewer cones. It is better at detecting movement but does not provide effective color perception.
  Q What is required for central vision to produce a sharp color image?  [27/S6/F3]
    * The eyes must be focused and pointed straight at the object
    - The peripheral retina must receive rays from the sides
    - The optic nerve must serve multiple cones in the fovea
    - The pupil must be fully dilated in dark surroundings
    because: Central vision requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.
  Q Why is there a blind spot?  [27/S6/F6]
    - The pupil constricts when light falls on the central fovea
    - The fovea contains no rods, so it cannot see side stimuli
    * The optic nerve spreads around the retina, leaving a region with no photoreceptors
    - The cornea stops light from reaching the peripheral retina
    because: The blind spot is a retinal region with no photoreceptors. It is caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy and the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so visual stimuli there produce no perception.

27/A15  recap  27/S6  "Recap"  (7 facts, 19 concepts)
  Human eyes support central and peripheral vision because photoreceptor density varies across the retina. Central vision requires the eyes to be focused on the fovea to perceive sharp color images, while peripheral vision is supported by regions with lower photoreceptor density and is better at detecting movement. The blind spot is a region with no photoreceptors where visual stimuli produce no perception.
  - Human eyes support central and peripheral vision because photoreceptor density varies across the retina.
  - Central vision requires the eyes to be focused on the fovea to perceive sharp color images.
  - Peripheral vision is supported by regions with lower photoreceptor density and is better at detecting movement.
  - The blind spot is a region with no photoreceptors where visual stimuli produce no perception.

27/A20  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (7 facts, 25 concepts)
  Absorption | Reflection | Transmission | *Refraction  (Transmission, absorption, and reflection are the possible interactions when a light ray strikes a material surface, while refraction is described as the bending of light by the cornea and lens.)  [27/S2/F0, 27/S4/F1]
  Cornea | Lens | Pupil | *Iris  (The cornea, pupil, and lens are the structures light passes through in the given path through the human eye, whereas the iris controls the amount of light by changing the pupil.)  [27/S4/F0, 27/S4/F2]
  Blind spot | Fovea | *Optic nerve | Peripheral region  (The fovea, blind spot, and peripheral region are regions of the retina, while the optic nerve is a structure that spreads out around the retina.)  [27/S6/F1, 27/S6/F4, 27/S6/F6]

27/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 43 concepts)
  Q How do light propagation through the lenses of a virtual reality headset and the human eye connect display output to visual perception?  [27/S0/F0, 27/S4/F1, 27/S0/F1; virtual reality headset, display, lens, human eye, light propagation, visual perception, retina, cornea]
    A In a virtual reality headset, light emitted by the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye. The cornea and lens of the human eye refract light so that images are focused on the retina. Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is therefore important for understanding how virtual reality headsets lead to visual perception.
  Q Why are central vision and peripheral vision different in acuity and color perception?  [27/S4/F4, 27/S6/F1, 27/S6/F3, 27/S4/F7, 27/S4/F6, 27/S6/F4, 27/S6/F5; central vision, peripheral vision, fovea, cone, rod, photopic vision, scotopic vision, color perception, photoreceptor density]
    A The fovea is the small central retina where cones are mainly located and where the concentration of cones is greatest, and central vision requires the eye to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image. Photopic cone vision is the mode in which color is perceived, while scotopic rod vision is more related to peripheral vision and does not provide good color. Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral retina, where photoreceptor density and cone density are lower, and it is better at detecting movement but does not provide effective color perception.
  Q How do the photon, wave, and ray views of light support different parts of building a virtual reality experience?  [27/S1/F0, 27/S1/F1, 27/S1/F2, 27/S1/F3, 27/S0/F2, 27/S0/F3, 27/S0/F4; photon view, wave view, ray view, sensor, receptor, color spectrum, lens, visibility, light propagation, virtual world, rendering, camera, human eye, panoramic video, tracking hardware, tracking software]
    A The photon view of light is helpful for calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor, the wave view helps explain the color spectrum, and the ray view helps explain how lenses work and the concept of visibility. In constructing a virtual world, modeling light propagation is used to determine what should be rendered, while understanding light propagation, lenses, the human eye, and cameras helps choose camera positions and present panoramic video. Understanding how cameras work also helps build tracking hardware and tracking software.

===== lecture 28: Visual Perception & Displays II

28/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (3 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is photoreceptor? (lecture 25) -> The eyes contain photoreceptors, which are activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light and therefore target only visible light.
  What is virtual reality headset (VR)? (lecture 27) -> In virtual reality (VR) headsets, light emitted from the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye, a combined system that helps the user perceive immersive visual content.
  What is retina? (lecture 27) -> Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
  What is lens? (lecture 27) -> Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
  What is human eye? (lecture 27) -> Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.
  What is cornea? (lecture 27) -> Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

28/A1  quiz  28/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Which two parts of the human eye act as convex lenses that together provide enough optical power to focus images of faraway objects on the retina?  [28/S0/F5]
    - The cornea and the retina
    * The cornea and the natural lens
    - The natural lens and the vitreous fluid
    - The aqueous fluid and the vitreous fluid
    because: The eye effectively contains two convex lenses: the cornea and the natural lens. Their combined optical power focuses faraway objects onto the retina.
  Q Compared with an artificial lens setup, what feature of the human eye replaces a focal plane?  [28/S0/F1]
    - Its liquid-filled vitreous fluid
    - Its flat focal plane behind the cornea
    - Its variable-power natural lens
    * Its non-planar, spherically curved retina
    because: The human eye has no focal plane as such. Its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.
  Q What is the main role of the convex lens in a VR headset when the screen is placed very close to the eye?  [28/S0/F6]
    - To let the screen fill the eye's field
    * To focus the screen's light on the retina
    - To increase the visible pixel count
    - To replace the eye's natural lens
    because: A VR headset uses a convex lens, like reading glasses, to focus the close screen's light on the retina. After that, normal eye operation takes over.
  Q Why is the screen in a VR headset placed at the focal length of its engineered lens for the best experience?  [28/S0/F7]
    - So the screen's light can pass only through air
    - So the user's natural lens can be bypassed
    * So the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance
    - So a real image is formed in front of the user's face
    because: Placing the screen at the focal length makes it appear to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.
  Q Although a VR headset screen can appear to the user as a virtual image, what must happen for the person to perceive it?  [28/S0/F8]
    - A virtual image must be formed on the retina
    - A flat pixel grid must be projected onto the retina
    * A real image must be formed on the retina
    - A stereoscopic image must be formed in the air
    because: In a VR headset, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina. A person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

28/A2  recap  28/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  The human eye converts light into neural pulses using the cornea, natural lens, and a non-planar retina, with light passing through five different media with specific refractive indices. The cornea and natural lens provide a combined optical power of about 60 diopters to focus images onto the retina. VR headsets use a convex lens to focus light from a nearby screen onto the retina. This makes the screen appear as a virtual image at an infinite distance, while a real image is still formed on the retina for perception.
  - The human eye converts light into neural pulses using the cornea, natural lens, and a non-planar retina.
  - Light passes through five different media with specific refractive indices within the eye.
  - The cornea and natural lens provide a combined optical power of about 60 diopters to focus images.
  - VR headsets use a convex lens to focus light from a nearby screen onto the retina.
  - While the screen appears as a virtual image at an infinite distance, a real image must be formed on the retina for perception.

28/A3  put_in_order  28/S0  "Order the path of light through the human eye"  (2 facts, 12 concepts)
  Order the path of light through the human eye: Light passes through air > Light passes through the cornea > Light passes through aqueous fluid > Light passes through the natural lens > Light passes through vitreous fluid > Light falls on the retina  [28/S0/F0, 28/S0/F3]

28/A4  quiz  28/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What is the field of view (FOV) in visual perception?  [28/S1/F0]
    - A linear measure of the distance to visible objects
    * An angular measure of the region visible at a single point in time
    - A count of the objects visible at a single point in time
    - A fixed property of a display screen's size
    because: FOV is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is measured angularly at one point in time.
  Q When both eyes focus on infinity in binocular vision, what is seen in the common region?  [28/S1/F2]
    - Only the right eye sees the common region
    - The left and right eyes see two completely different images
    - Only the left eye sees the common region
    * The same image is seen by both eyes
    because: In binocular vision, both eyes see the same image over a common region when focusing on infinity.
  Q How does binocular vision support perception of three-dimensional space?  [28/S1/F3]
    * It enhances depth perception and relationships between objects
    - It increases the angular width of the field of view
    - It makes the retina act as a flat focal plane
    - It replaces peripheral vision with central vision
    because: Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand relationships between objects in 3D space.
  Q In stereoscopy, how are the two images assigned to the eyes?  [28/S1/F4]
    - Both eyes process only the right image
    - The left eye processes the right image and the right eye processes the left image
    * The left eye processes the left image and the right eye processes the right image
    - Both eyes process only the left image
    because: Stereoscopy involves the left eye processing the left image and the right eye processing the right image simultaneously.
  Q What result is produced when the left and right 2D images are processed simultaneously in stereoscopy?  [28/S1/F5]
    - A single flat two-dimensional image
    - Only the right two-dimensional image
    - Only the left two-dimensional image
    * A three-dimensional view of the objects
    because: Simultaneous processing of the left and right 2D images generates a 3D view, helping stereoscopic vision perceive 3D objects.

28/A5  recap  28/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Field of view is the angular measure of the region visible to the human eye at a single point in time, and the human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal and 150-degree vertical field of view. Binocular vision allows both eyes to see a common region of about 120 degrees while seeing different images in the outer areas, which enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional space. Stereoscopy processes two 2D images simultaneously to generate a three-dimensional view of objects.
  - Field of view is the angular measure of the region visible to the human eye at a single point in time.
  - The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal and 150-degree vertical field of view.
  - In binocular vision, both eyes see a common region of about 120 degrees while seeing different images in the outer areas.
  - Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional space.
  - Stereoscopy processes two 2D images simultaneously to generate a three-dimensional view of objects.

28/A6  quiz  28/S2  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q What is translational movement used for in a virtual world?  [28/S2/F0]
    - Moving at different angles along the translational axis
    - Mapping the environment while localizing positions in it
    * Navigating in the three-dimensional virtual space
    - Aligning a real-world region with a virtual region
    because: Translational movement is used for navigating in three-dimensional space, while rotational movement is used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.
  Q What does the term degrees of freedom describe?  [28/S2/F1]
    * The different ways an object can move in space
    - The simultaneous mapping and locating of a real environment
    - The process of seeing two images at the same time
    - The region visible to the human eye at one time
    because: Degrees of freedom indicate the different ways an object can move in space.
  Q In three-dimensional space, an object's degrees of freedom are divided into which two groups?  [28/S2/F2]
    * Rotational and translational degrees of freedom
    - Translational and navigational degrees of freedom
    - Rotational and visual degrees of freedom
    - Rotational and binocular degrees of freedom
    because: In 3D space, an object has six degrees of freedom: three rotational degrees of freedom and three translational degrees of freedom.
  Q In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to which factor?  [28/S2/F3]
    * The supported degrees of freedom
    - The pixels per square area of a display
    - The human eye's horizontal field of view
    - The real-world region where virtual content aligns
    because: Motion in a virtual world is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

28/A7  recap  28/S2  "Recap"  (4 facts, 15 concepts)
  A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional space: translational movement for navigating and rotational movement for moving at different angles along the translational axis. Degrees of freedom indicate the different ways an object can move in space. In three-dimensional space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom (yaw, roll, and pitch) and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes. Motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.
  - A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement: translational movement for navigating and rotational movement for moving at different angles along the translational axis.
  - Degrees of freedom indicate the different ways an object can move in space.
  - In three-dimensional space, an object can have six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees (yaw, roll, and pitch) and three translational degrees (x, y, and z axes).
  - Motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

  Q Which three display characteristics are highlighted as important for making a VR display match human visual sense?  [28/S3/F0, 28/S3/F1]
    - Spatial resolution, temporal resolution, and color gamut
    * Spatial resolution, intensity resolution and range, and temporal resolution.
    - Spatial resolution, field of view, and intensity resolution
    - Intensity resolution, frame rate, and field of view
    because: The important considerations for matching the human visual sense are spatial resolution, intensity resolution and range, and temporal resolution.
  Q What does aliasing refer to in a display?  [28/S3/F2]
    - An image appearing to have a screen-like grid over it
    - The minimum pixel density needed for a display to be called a retina display
    - A frame rate too low to make displayed motion appear smooth
    * A sharp diagonal line appearing jagged when individual display lights are visible.
    because: Aliasing is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible.
  Q Why is the usual distant-display retina resolution criterion less suitable for VR headsets?  [28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6]
    - AR displays are close to the eye, so the distant-display criterion is too high
    - VR headsets rely on LCD projectors, which produce a screen door effect
    - VR displays need lower pixel density because immersive motion needs higher frame rates
    * A magnifying lens places the display close to the eye, increasing required pixel density.
    because: For displays close to the eye, such as VR headsets, the traditional distant-display retina criterion is not very suitable because a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, requiring much higher pixel density.
  Q Besides increasing spatial resolution, what method can help reduce aliasing or screen door effect in VR headsets?  [28/S3/F7]
    - Increasing the number of producible intensity values
    - Lowering frame rates to ordinary television or movie standards
    - Designing the display to be used at a distance from the eye
    * Adjusting field of view or using foveated rendering.
    because: Corrective mechanisms include adjusting field of view, foveated rendering, and other content-rendering approaches, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.
  Q What does motion perception in an immersive VR environment require of temporal resolution?  [28/S3/F8]
    - A frame rate determined by the display's spatial resolution
    - Frame rates comparable to ordinary television or movie standards
    * Frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards.
    - Only a frame rate high enough to avoid diagonal-line aliasing
    because: Temporal resolution for VR motion perception requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards, with higher frame rates preferred.

28/A9  recap  28/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 30 concepts)
  VR displays should be designed to match the performance of human visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors, focusing on spatial, intensity, and temporal resolution. Wearable XR displays require much higher pixels per linear inch (ppi) than traditional retina displays. Aliasing and screen door effects can be mitigated by adjusting the field of view, using foveated rendering, or increasing spatial resolution, while VR headsets need much higher frame rates than standard television or movies to allow motion to be perceived smoothly.
  - VR displays should be designed to match the performance of human visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.
  - Key considerations for display performance are spatial resolution, intensity resolution and range, and temporal resolution.
  - Wearable VR and AR displays require much higher pixels per linear inch (ppi) than traditional retina displays.
  - Aliasing and the screen door effect can be reduced by adjusting the field of view, using foveated rendering, or increasing spatial resolution.
  - VR headsets require frame rates much higher than standard television or movies to allow motion to be perceived smoothly.

28/A14  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (5 facts, 32 concepts)
  Roll | Yaw | Pitch | *Axis  (Yaw, roll, and pitch are rotational degrees of freedom, while an axis is associated with a translational degree of freedom.)  [28/S2/F2]
  Television | Smartphone | *Headset | Laptop  (A television, laptop, and smartphone are distant displays for which the 326 ppi retina display criterion is suitable, but a headset is a close-to-eye display for which it is not very suitable.)  [28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6]
  *Screen | Lens | Cornea | Retina  (The cornea, lens, and retina are parts of the human eye, while a screen is part of a virtual reality headset.)  [28/S0/F0, 28/S0/F6]

28/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q How does a virtual reality headset use its engineered lens and close screen to make a virtual image that the eye still perceives as a real visual scene?  [28/S0/F6, 28/S0/F7, 28/S0/F8; virtual reality headset, screen, engineered lens, virtual image, real image, retina]
    A A virtual reality headset places a screen very close to the eyes and uses a convex lens to focus the screen's light on the retina. For the best experience, the screen is placed at the focal length of the engineered lens, so the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. Even though the user perceives a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and perception requires real images on the retina.
  Q Why can two flat two-dimensional images shown to the left and right eyes produce a three-dimensional view in an immersive display?  [28/S1/F2, 28/S1/F3, 28/S1/F4, 28/S1/F5; binocular vision, left eye, right eye, stereoscopy, two-dimensional image, three-dimensional view, stereoscopic vision, depth perception, three-dimensional object, three-dimensional space]
    A In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, they see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside that region are seen by only one eye. In stereoscopy, the left eye processes the left two-dimensional image and the right eye processes the right two-dimensional image. When those images are processed simultaneously, the result is a three-dimensional view; this stereoscopic vision, aided by binocular vision, helps perceive three-dimensional objects and enhances depth perception of object relationships in three-dimensional space.
  Q Why is the 326 pixels per linear inch retina display criterion useful for some augmented reality experiences but not for virtual reality headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye?  [28/S3/F4, 28/S3/F5, 28/S3/F6; retina display, pixels per linear inch, retina display criterion, augmented reality, head-mounted display, virtual reality headset, wearable display, magnifying lens, display]
    A A retina display is defined as a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch. Because augmented reality experiences are typically experienced using displays at a distance from the eye, that criterion can be taken into account for distant displays. For augmented reality head-mounted displays, virtual reality headsets, or other wearable displays close to the eye, a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch is probably 7 to 8 times higher than the retina display criterion.
  Q How do supported degrees of freedom in a virtual world connect to the frame-rate requirements for motion perception in an immersive environment?  [28/S2/F0, 28/S2/F2, 28/S2/F3, 28/S3/F1, 28/S3/F8; virtual world, translational movement, rotational movement, six degrees of freedom, yaw, roll, pitch, x axis, y axis, z axis, motion, temporal resolution, frame rate, jitter, immersive environment]
    A In three-dimensional space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: yaw, roll, and pitch rotation, plus movement along the x, y, and z axes. A virtual world may allow translational movement for navigating in three-dimensional space and rotational movement for moving at different angles, and motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported. Temporal resolution is the frame rate, and it must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter; for motion perception in an immersive environment, a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second or 60 frames per second.

===== lecture 29: Auditory Sense & Immersive Experience

29/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (3 facts, 3 concepts)
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

29/A1  quiz  29/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q Why should an immersive XR system combine audio with visual input?  [29/S0/F1]
    - Vision alone is sufficient, and audio is mainly for gaming and entertainment.
    - Audio is added because the outer-ear canal boosts every frequency.
    * Vision alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, and audio enhances immersion.
    - Audio is added because sound can propagate in a vacuum, unlike light.
    because: The visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, while augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience.
  Q Which properties of a virtual environment are reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects?  [29/S0/F3]
    - Color, brightness, clarity, movement, and speed
    * Size, volume, material, intensity, and distance
    - Weight, temperature, smell, taste, and motion
    - Shape, color, brightness, motion, and speed
    because: Combining sound with vision affects perception of the environment's size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and those perceptions are reinforced by auditory effects.
  Q How can audio make a virtual experience more believable and emotionally engaging?  [29/S0/F4]
    - It increases the amount of visual detail shown on the display.
    * It brings the experience closer to everyday reality and helps create an emotional connection.
    - It removes unrealistic visual artifacts from the scene.
    - It replaces visual information with recorded speech.
    because: Audio reinforces the virtual experience as believable, closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection.
  Q What two requirements are needed for presence in a virtual environment?  [29/S0/F5]
    * Believability of the experience and attachment to it
    - High-fidelity audio and visual realism
    - Attachment and low-latency tracking
    - Believability and high-resolution graphics
    because: Presence requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience.
  Q How can audio recording and audio reproduction be considered a VR experience?  [29/S0/F2]
    * They can themselves provide a VR experience even when other senses are missing.
    - They are a VR experience only when presented in a cave-like environment.
    - They are a VR experience only when synchronized with motion tracking.
    - They are a VR experience only when combined with a wearable display.
    because: Audio recording and reproduction can itself be considered a VR experience even if other senses are missing, and it can support better surround sound in cave-like or headset versions.

29/A2  recap  29/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  High-fidelity audio technologies clearly improve the immersive experience in VR. Augmenting vision with audio enhances immersion because vision alone may not give a full picture. Combining sound with vision reinforces the perception of properties like size and distance, making virtual experiences believable and helping to create an emotional connection. The auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence by reinforcing believability and attachment.
  - High-fidelity audio technologies clearly improve the immersive experience in VR.
  - Augmenting vision with audio enhances immersion because vision alone may not give a full picture.
  - Combining sound with vision reinforces the perception of properties like size, volume, and distance.
  - Audio makes a virtual experience believable and helps create an emotional connection.
  - Audio plays a very important role in increasing presence by reinforcing believability and attachment.

29/A3  quiz  29/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q Why can sound not propagate in a vacuum?  [29/S1/F0]
    - It needs a vacuum to carry pressure variations.
    - It needs a light wave to create pressure variations.
    - It needs a surface point to reflect pressure variations.
    * It needs a medium for pressure variations to propagate.
    because: Sound is vibration in a medium and requires a medium to propagate. A vacuum has no medium, unlike light, which can propagate without one.
  Q What physical variation carries sound through a medium?  [29/S1/F1]
    - Temperature alternates between hot and cold extremes.
    - Sensor signals alternate between input and output states.
    - Light intensity alternates on a surface point.
    * Pressure alternates between compression and rarefaction.
    because: Sound propagation is caused by pressure variations in the medium, ranging from high-pressure compression to low-pressure rarefaction.
  Q What does the frequency of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F5]
    * The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    - The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Frequency is the number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second, measured in hertz.
  Q What does the amplitude of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F7]
    - The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    * The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
  Q What does the phase of a sound wave describe?  [29/S1/F8]
    - The maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.
    * The start position of a cycle of the wave.
    - The number of alternations between one maximum and another maximum per second.
    - The pressure variation at the human eardrum as a function of time.
    because: Phase is the start position of a cycle of the wave.

29/A4  recap  29/S1  "Recap"  (9 facts, 17 concepts)
  Sound is a vibration in a medium, usually air, but it requires a medium to propagate. Pressure variations are converted by the human eardrum into auditory experiences and can be represented as sound waves plotted against time. These waves are primarily characterized by frequency, amplitude, phase, and the human audible frequency range.
  - Sound is a vibration in a medium, usually air, but it requires a medium to propagate.
  - Pressure variations in a medium are converted by the human eardrum into auditory experiences.
  - Sound waves are plots of pressure variation against time.
  - Sound waves are primarily characterized by frequency, amplitude, phase, and the human audible frequency range.

29/A5  quiz  29/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 22 concepts)
  Q The human hearing system is divided into which three parts?  [29/S2/F0]
    - The receiver, the canal, and the eardrum
    * The outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear
    - The canal, the eardrum, and the ossicles
    - The eardrum, the ossicles, and the cochlea
    because: The hearing system contains three main parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.
  Q In the outer ear, what does the receiver part do with an incoming sound wave?  [29/S2/F1]
    * It receives the wave and sends it into the outer-ear canal
    - It vibrates and transfers motion to three ossicles
    - It converts the wave's energy into neural impulses
    - It boosts the wave's pressure for a range of frequencies
    because: The receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the outer-ear canal.
  Q When a sound wave reaches the middle ear, what does the tympanic membrane do?  [29/S2/F3]
    - It converts sound energy into neural impulses
    * It vibrates and transfers motion to three ossicles
    - It attenuates high-frequency sound waves
    - It boosts the sound pressure for a range of frequencies
    because: A sound wave striking the tympanic membrane causes it to vibrate, and that vibration is transferred to the malleus, incus, and stapes.
  Q What is the cochlea's role in hearing?  [29/S2/F4, 29/S2/F5]
    - It boosts the sound pressure for a range of frequencies
    * It converts sound energy into neural impulses for the brain
    - It transfers vibration to the ossicles in the middle ear
    - It attenuates high-frequency sound waves in the canal
    because: The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing, and it converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain.

29/A6  recap  29/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  The human hearing system consists of the outer, middle, and inner ear. The outer ear receives and amplifies sound while attenuating high-frequency waves, which then strike the tympanic membrane in the middle ear to transfer vibrations to three ossicles. Finally, the inner ear's cochlea converts this sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain.
  - The human hearing system contains the outer, middle, and inner ear.
  - The outer ear receives and amplifies sound while attenuating high-frequency sound waves.
  - The middle ear vibrates the tympanic membrane to transfer vibrations to three ossicles.
  - The inner ear's cochlea converts sound energy into neural impulses for the brain.

29/A7  put_in_order  29/S2  "Order the steps of sound processing in the human ear"  (3 facts, 20 concepts)
  Order the steps of sound processing in the human ear: Outer ear receives a sound wave > Tympanic membrane vibration transfers to ossicles > Cochlea converts sound energy into neural impulses > Neural impulses travel to the brain  [29/S2/F1, 29/S2/F3, 29/S2/F5]

29/A13  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why does adding sound to a visually rich virtual environment matter for the immersive experience and for presence?  [29/S0/F1, 29/S0/F5, 8/S2/F0; visual sense, audio component, immersive experience, presence]
    A The visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, so augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. Presence requires reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence.
  Q How does a sound wave move from the air to a signal the brain can use, and why does the medium matter?  [29/S1/F0, 29/S1/F1, 29/S1/F2, 29/S2/F5; sound, medium, pressure variation, eardrum, cochlea, neural impulse, brain]
    A Sound is a vibration in a medium, so it requires a medium to propagate and cannot occur in a vacuum. Its propagation is caused by pressure variations in the medium, and the pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience. The cochlea then converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.
  Q Why can audio change how users judge properties of a virtual environment, and how does that connect to making the experience believable?  [29/S0/F3, 29/S0/F4; audio component, visual sense, virtual environment, size, volume, material, intensity, distance, virtual experience, believable, emotional connection]
    A Combining sound with vision affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and reinforces what visual sense alone only partly gives. Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, meaning closer to reality and everyday experience. Vision coupled with audio also helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment.
  Q How do frequency and amplitude define whether a sound wave is audible to humans and how its level is expressed?  [29/S1/F4, 29/S1/F5, 29/S1/F6, 29/S1/F7; sound wave, frequency, hertz, human audible frequency range, human ear, amplitude, decibel]
    A A sound wave is primarily characterized by frequency, amplitude, and phase. Frequency, measured in hertz, must fall inside the human audible frequency range from 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz for the human ear to perceive it. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave, measured in decibel relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 hertz.
