===== lecture 30: Auditory Sense & Immersive Experience

30/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is frequency? (lecture 29) -> Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.
  What is sound wave? (lecture 29) -> Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

30/A1  quiz  30/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q Which three levels of sound perception are described?  [30/S0/F0]
    - Social, warning, and immersive
    * Social, warning, and primitive
    - Social, spatial, and primitive
    - Warning, background, and primitive
    because: Sound perception occurs at social, warning, and primitive levels, and these levels together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.
  Q What is the main purpose of social-level sound perception?  [30/S0/F1]
    - Perceiving mostly ignored background noises
    - Providing an alert or warning about an event
    * Helping a person carry out social interactions with other individuals
    - Estimating the location of a sound source
    because: Social-level sound perception is the level that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.
  Q What function does warning-level sound perception serve?  [30/S0/F2]
    * Providing an alert or warning about something, such as an event
    - Carrying out social interactions with other individuals
    - Matching auditory and visual cues to locate objects
    - Perceiving intuitive background noises that are mostly ignored
    because: Warning-level sound perception provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event.
  Q Which statement best describes primitive-level sound perception?  [30/S0/F3]
    - It helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.
    - It estimates the location of a sound source by matching auditory and visual cues.
    - It provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event.
    * It is the intuitive perception of naive sounds, such as background noises, that are mostly ignored.
    because: Primitive-level sound perception is the intuitive perception of naive sounds such as background noises, which people mostly ignore and which may not lead to meaningful action.
  Q When generating auditory effects for social-level perception in a VR system, what should a developer do?  [30/S0/F4]
    * Generate stimuli that support social-level perception
    - Generate stimuli that provide warnings about events
    - Generate stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception
    - Generate stimuli that only estimate sound-source location
    because: If social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

30/A2  recap  30/S0  "Recap"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Sound perception occurs at social, warning, and primitive levels, which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings. Social-level perception helps with social interactions, warning-level perception provides alerts, and primitive-level perception involves intuitive sounds that people mostly ignore. Identifying the desired sound perception level helps developers generate suitable auditory effects for VR systems.
  - Sound perception occurs at social, warning, and primitive levels to give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.
  - Social-level sound perception helps an individual carry out social interactions.
  - Warning-level sound perception provides alerts or warnings about an event.
  - Primitive-level sound perception involves intuitive perception of naive sounds that people mostly ignore.
  - Identifying the desired sound perception level helps developers generate suitable auditory effects for VR systems.

30/A3  quiz  30/S1  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q How does psychoacoustics differ from psychophysics?  [30/S1/F0, 30/S1/F1]
    - It studies only the physical properties of sound, not perception.
    - It studies the engineering of virtual reality sound hardware.
    - It studies perceptual phenomena produced by any physical stimulus.
    * It studies perceptual phenomena produced specifically by acoustic stimuli or sound.
    because: Psychophysics is the study of perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli, while psychoacoustics is the more specific area concerned with acoustic stimuli or sound.
  Q In a power-law model of perception, what does the exponent represent?  [30/S1/F2]
    * The relationship between actual stimulus magnitude and perceived magnitude.
    - The minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener.
    - The constant that depends on the units used.
    - The amount of change needed to detect a change in at least half of trials.
    because: In the power-law equation, the exponent is the value that relates the actual magnitude of the stimulus to its perceived magnitude.
  Q In the psychophysical law that captures the just noticeable difference, how does the noticeable change depend on stimulus magnitude?  [30/S1/F4]
    - It is equal to perceived magnitude raised to a constant power.
    - It decreases as the stimulus magnitude increases.
    - It remains a fixed amount for all stimulus magnitudes.
    * It grows in proportion to the stimulus magnitude.
    because: Weber's law expresses the just noticeable difference as delta M / M = C, equivalently delta M = M times C, so the noticeable change grows with stimulus magnitude.
  Q What is the just noticeable difference (JND)?  [30/S1/F3]
    * The stimulus change needed for subjects to perceive a change in at least 50 percent of trials.
    - The amount of change needed for a subject to notice a change in every trial.
    - The minimum frequency difference that can be detected at 10,000 hertz.
    - The minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener.
    because: The JND specifies the amount of change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.
  Q For a pure tone whose perceived loudness follows a power-law exponent less than 1, what happens when pressure level increases a lot?  [30/S1/F2, 30/S1/F6]
    - Perceived loudness increases more rapidly than the pressure level.
    - Perceived loudness increases by the same factor.
    * Perceived loudness increases only a bit.
    - Perceived loudness stays the same no matter how much pressure rises.
    because: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone, the power-law exponent is less than 1, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder.

30/A4  recap  30/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 10 concepts)
  Psychophysics and psychoacoustics are the scientific studies of perceptual phenomena produced by physical and acoustic stimuli. Stevens' power law characterizes the relationship between a stimulus magnitude and its perceived magnitude, while Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND) required for perception. These laws also apply to auditory perception. A change in a stimulus must be above the JND to be perceived.
  - Psychophysics and psychoacoustics are the scientific studies of perceptual phenomena produced by physical and acoustic stimuli.
  - Stevens' power law characterizes the relationship between a stimulus magnitude and its perceived magnitude.
  - Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), which is the change in magnitude required for perception.
  - These laws also apply to auditory perception.
  - A change in a stimulus must be above the JND to be perceived.

    - It is largest at low frequencies
    - It decreases with frequency
    * It increases with frequency
    because: For sound frequency, the just noticeable difference increases as frequency increases, such as from less than 1 Hz at low frequencies to about 100 Hz at 10,000 Hz.
  Q In percentage terms, what is required to notice a frequency difference at higher sound frequencies compared with low frequencies?  [30/S2/F1]

    - A smaller percentage difference
    - The same percentage difference
    - No percentage difference

30/A7  quiz  30/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q In psychoacoustics, what does sound localization estimate?  [30/S3/F0]
    - The loudness difference between the two ears
    * The location of a sound source from hearing it
    - The arrival-time difference between the two ears
    - The pitch of a sound wave from its frequency
    because: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.
  Q Why is sound localization important in virtual reality?  [30/S3/F1]
    - It lets the user ignore visual position and locate objects using only sound
    - It helps auditory and visual cues disagree in a way that strengthens presence
    - It fixes virtual objects in a global direction independent of the user
    * It helps auditory and visual cues agree about object position and orientation
    because: In VR, sound localization helps the user perceive object orientation and position by matching auditory and visual cues; a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness.
  Q What is the minimum audible angle in sound localization?  [30/S3/F2]
    * The smallest angular change a listener can detect
    - The smallest distance change a listener can detect
    - The smallest frequency change a listener can detect
    - The smallest loudness change a listener can detect
    because: The minimum audible angle is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference concept to sound localization.
  Q Which three parameters represent a sound source location in the spherical coordinate system used for sound localization?  [30/S3/F3]
    - Pitch, loudness, and radius
    * Azimuth, elevation, and radius
    - Azimuth, elevation, and pitch
    - Azimuth, loudness, and radius
    because: The spherical coordinate system uses azimuth for the horizontal-plane angle, elevation for the angle relative to the horizontal plane, and radius for the distance from the listener's head to the source.
  Q How does the minimum audible angle vary?  [30/S3/F4]
    - It depends only on the loudness of the sound
    * It depends on the sound's frequency and the source direction
    - It depends only on the listener's distance to the source
    - It is the same for all frequencies and source directions
    because: The minimum audible angle depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source; at some combinations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at others localization can be very difficult.

30/A8  recap  30/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Sound localization estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it, which is crucial in VR for matching auditory and visual cues to maintain presence and prevent cybersickness. To represent sound source locations, a spherical coordinate system uses azimuth, elevation, and radius. The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the smallest detectable angular variation, and it depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source.
  - Sound localization estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.
  - Localization is crucial in VR because matching auditory and visual cues helps users perceive orientation and prevents cybersickness.
  - The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the smallest angular variation a human listener can detect, represented in a spherical coordinate system.
  - A spherical coordinate system uses azimuth, elevation, and radius to represent sound source location.
  - The MAA depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source.

30/A9  quiz  30/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q Which feature distinguishes binaural sound localization cues from monaural ones?  [30/S4/F0]
    * They use information from both ears
    - They use information from the listener's visual focus
    - They use information from the sound source's distance
    - They use information from a single ear
    because: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving one ear, or binaural, involving both ears.
  Q What does interaural level difference (ILD) refer to?  [30/S4/F1]
    - A difference in sound arrival time at the two ears
    - A difference in perceived pitch between the two ears
    * A difference in sound magnitude received by the two ears
    - A difference in frequency produced by the sound source
    because: ILD is a binaural cue based on the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the unobstructed ear receiving a stronger sound.
  Q How does interaural time difference (ITD) help a listener locate a sound source?  [30/S4/F3]
    - The sound reaches both ears at exactly the same time
    - The sound is louder at one ear than at the other
    - The sound changes pitch as it moves around the head
    * The sound reaches the two ears at slightly different times
    because: ITD is a binaural cue caused by different sound arrival times at the ears, and that small time difference can be used to locate the source.
  Q Why do XR systems often use an HRTF for an average listener instead of measuring every user's HRTF?  [30/S4/F6, 30/S4/F7]
    - HRTFs depend only on the size and shape of the sound source
    - Every listener has the same HRTF, so personal measurement is unnecessary
    * Each person's HRTF is unique and obtaining it for every user is impractical
    - HRTFs can be derived from the user's visual display settings
    because: HRTFs depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, so each person has a unique HRTF, making individual measurement impractical and leading to an average-listener HRTF.
  Q How can a pair of HRTFs be used in an XR audio system?  [30/S4/F8]
    - To produce a single monaural sound for both ears
    - To calculate the minimum audible angle before rendering sound
    * To synthesize binaural sound that creates a localization effect
    - To replace audio localization with visual tracking of the source
    because: A pair of HRTFs for both ears can synthesize binaural sound, and generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF implements a localization effect.

30/A10  recap  30/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 9 concepts)
  Sound localization uses monaural or binaural cues, including interaural level difference (ILD) and interaural time difference (ITD). Auditory components in XR systems should be non-stationary, move with the user, and be interactive. Because individual head-related transfer functions (HRTF) are impractical to determine, XR systems use average HRTFs to synthesize binaural sound.
  - Sound localization uses monaural or binaural cues, including interaural level difference (ILD) and interaural time difference (ITD).
  - Auditory components in XR systems should be non-stationary, move with the user, and be interactive.
  - Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound based on their unique head and ear shape.
  - XR systems use average HRTFs to synthesize binaural sound because individual HRTFs are impractical to determine.

  Order the steps for binaural sound localization using HRTFs: Use an HRTF for an average listener > Use a pair of HRTFs for both ears > Generate sound effects or place sound receivers  [30/S4/F7, 30/S4/F8]

30/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q Why is accurate sound localization important for maintaining presence and avoiding cybersickness in virtual reality?  [30/S3/F1, 8/S2/F0, 10/S0/F0; virtual reality, sound localization, presence, cybersickness]
    A In virtual reality, sound localization helps the user perceive the orientation and position of objects by matching auditory and visual cues. Presence is the psychological side that captures whether the user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated. When auditory and visual cues mismatch, that presence can break and the user may experience cybersickness.
  Q How does the just noticeable difference concept lead to the minimum audible angle in sound localization?  [30/S1/F3, 30/S3/F2, 30/S3/F3; just noticeable difference, minimum audible angle, sound localization, spherical coordinate system]
    A The just noticeable difference specifies the amount of change in a stimulus required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials. Applying that concept to sound localization gives the minimum audible angle, the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener. That angle is represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin.
  Q How can interaural level difference and interaural time difference be combined with head-related transfer functions to support sound localization in extended reality?  [30/S4/F0, 30/S4/F1, 30/S4/F3, 30/S4/F8; sound localization cue, binaural sound localization cue, interaural level difference, interaural time difference, head-related transfer function, binaural sound, sound localization, extended reality]
    A Sound localization cues include binaural sound localization cues that use both ears. The interaural level difference is a binaural sound localization cue based on the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, while the interaural time difference is based on different sound arrival times at the ears. A pair of head-related transfer functions can synthesize binaural sound, and generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF can implement a localization effect in extended reality.
  Q How do psychophysical results apply to auditory perception, and what does Stevens' power law imply about the perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone?  [30/S1/F0, 30/S1/F1, 30/S1/F5, 30/S1/F2, 30/S1/F6; psychophysics, psychoacoustics, physical stimulus, acoustic stimulus, Stevens' power law, perceived loudness, pure tone, pressure level]
    A Psychophysics studies perceptual phenomena produced by physical stimuli, and its laws also apply to psychoacoustics when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli. Psychoacoustics is the more specific area that studies perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli. For perceived loudness of a 3000 Hz pure tone, Stevens' power law has an exponent of 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder.

===== lecture 31: Other Senses & Full Immersion

31/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is neuron? (lecture 26) -> Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.
  What is proprioception? (lecture 26) -> Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

    - Conscious awareness of velocities, accelerations, and forces during body movement
    - Perception of the overall geometric shape of an object through touch
    - Determination of a viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor
    * Conscious awareness of the pose and movement of body parts relative to other body parts
    because: Proprioception is defined as conscious awareness of the pose and movement of movable body parts relative to other body parts.
  Q What kind of information does kinesthesis provide?  [31/S0/F2]
    * Information about velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement
    - Perception of an object's overall geometric shape from touch
    - Information about the pose of a body part relative to other body parts
    - Determination of a viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor
    because: Kinesthesis is the awareness of parameters associated with moving body parts, including velocities, accelerations, and forces.
  Q In which body structures are the receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis found?  [31/S0/F6]
    * Muscles, tendons, and joints
    - Muscles and tendons only
    - Joints and tendons only
    - The epidermis and dermis
    because: The proprioceptive and kinesthetic receptors are found in muscles, tendons, and joints: muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors, respectively.
  Q How does the somatosensory system transform touch into perception and corrective action?  [31/S0/F7]
    - Receptors send impulses directly to muscles without involving the brain
    - The brain perceives touch by determining the object's pose relative to an anchor
    * Receptors send neural impulses to the brain, which perceives touch and can send messages back for corrective action
    - Force feedback devices replace skin receptors by stimulating the visual system
    because: Activated receptors transform input into neural impulses sent to the brain, and the brain can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions.

    * The epidermis and dermis
    - The hypodermis only
    - The epidermis and hypodermis
    - The dermis and hypodermis

31/A2  recap  31/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 43 concepts)
  The somatosensory system handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis through at least nine major types of receptors. Proprioception is the conscious awareness of body part pose and movement, while kinesthesis provides information on movement parameters like velocity and force. These receptors transform inputs into neural impulses that the brain processes into perception and can send back to cause corrective motor actions.
  - The somatosensory system handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.
  - Proprioception is the awareness of body part pose, while kinesthesis is the awareness of movement parameters like velocity and force.
  - At least nine major types of receptors in the skin and muscles detect touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.
  - Receptors transform inputs into neural impulses that the brain processes into perception and can send back to cause corrective motor actions.

  Order the steps of touch perception and response: Hand touches an object > Somatosensory receptors are activated > Neural impulses travel to the brain > Brain processes impulses into touch perception > Brain sends corrective motor messages  [31/S0/F7]

31/A5  recap  31/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 28 concepts)
  Haptic perception is the perception of an object's geometric shape through touch, while haptic exploration involves manipulating objects to infer that shape. Different types of haptic exploration are used to create a geometric mental model of an object's properties. By allowing users to feel the virtual environment, haptic perception and exploration increase the immersive experience.
  - Haptic perception is the perception of an object's geometric shape through touch.
  - Haptic exploration involves manipulating objects to infer their shape.
  - Different types of haptic exploration are used to create a geometric mental model of an object's properties.
  - Incorporating haptic perception and exploration increases immersion by allowing users to feel the virtual environment.

31/A7  recap  31/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Touch sensation in XR can be provided by engineered force feedback devices, although precisely controlling haptic pin arrays to simulate surface textures is challenging. Real-world objects are sometimes called tangible user interfaces and are used as avatars to provide touch feedback, which is generally considered less challenging than creating computer-controlled haptic devices. These tangible user interfaces work by aligning the real and virtual worlds.
  - Touch sensation in XR can be provided by engineered force feedback devices.
  - Haptic pin arrays can simulate surface textures, but controlling them precisely enough is challenging.
  - Real-world objects are sometimes called tangible user interfaces and are used as avatars to provide touch feedback.
  - Using real objects for touch is generally considered less challenging than creating computer-controlled haptic devices.
  - Tangible user interfaces work by aligning the real and virtual worlds.

  Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses that have much less research and fewer devices than vision, audio, and touch. Olfactory displays usually use pumps to provide smells that are relatively easier to deliver for personal experiences than on a room scale and may help reduce cybersickness to some extent. Taste interfaces use electrodes but are generally quite difficult to develop without people eating food.
  - Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses that respond to chemical stimuli.
  - There is much less research and fewer devices for these senses than for vision, audio, and touch.

31/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How does haptic exploration help a virtual world support the kind of mental-model building that makes an experience feel immersive?  [31/S1/F5, 31/S1/F6, 31/S1/F7; haptic exploration, mental model, immersive experience, virtual reality, haptic perception, geometric mental model, somatosensory signals]
    A Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience. Haptic exploration integrates somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of shape, size, weight, and hardness is learned. In virtual reality, haptic perception and haptic exploration add an extra dimension by letting users feel the virtual environment through touch, and because real-world immersion also involves haptic exploration, adding it increases the immersive experience.
  Q Why is it not enough to apply a single kind of touch input for all object properties when simulating haptic perception?  [31/S1/F3, 31/S1/F4, 31/S1/F5; haptic exploration, lateral motion, pressure, enclosure, static contact, unsupported holding, contour following, texture perception, hardness perception, global shape perception, temperature perception, weight perception, local shape perception, receptor, spatial information, temporal information, somatosensory signals, geometric mental model]
    A The six types of haptic exploration are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception. Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information. The overall goal is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model is learned in terms of shape, size, weight, and hardness.
  Q Why might a tangible user interface be a less challenging path than a fully computer-controlled haptic device when a see-through display is used to combine real and virtual objects?  [31/S2/F3, 31/S2/F4, 31/S2/F5, 31/S2/F6, 31/S2/F7; tangible user interface, virtual avatar, virtual world, haptic device, somatosensory system, touch feedback, see-through display, Microsoft HoloLens, virtual object]
    A A tangible user interface uses a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in the virtual world, and it can be used in place of a computer-controlled haptic device to provide feedback to the somatosensory system. Using real objects for touch feedback is generally considered less challenging than creating a computer-controlled haptic device, and the basic implementation aligns the real world and the virtual world. A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens lets users see and interact with the physical world while wearable device sensors detect the real object and virtual objects are added to the real world.
  Q Why are personal smell interfaces easier to implement than room-scale smell delivery, and what effect can successful smell effects have on an extended reality experience?  [31/S3/F3, 31/S3/F4, 31/S3/F5; smell interface, odor, air pump, micropump, chemical compound, room-scale delivery, odor intensity, uniformity, odor concentration, localization, immersive experience, visually induced motion sickness, extended reality]
    A A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose. Delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than room-scale delivery, because room-scale delivery makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization. When olfactory displays generate odor effects, they can induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness.

===== lecture 32: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

32/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 5 concepts)
  What is interaction design? (lecture 25) -> In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.
  What is extended reality system? (lecture 24) -> Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
  What is user-centered design (UCD)? (lecture 24) -> User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

32/A1  quiz  32/S0  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q In user-centered design, how are users involved in developing an application?  [32/S0/F0]
    - Users are involved only during requirements analysis.
    - Users are involved only after the system is deployed.
    * They are actively or passively involved throughout the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation.
    - Users are involved only in final usability testing.
    because: User-centered design actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of producing usable software.
  Q What is the core design concern for user-centered XR application software?  [32/S0/F1, 32/S0/F2]
    - Designing systems that minimize users' involvement in the design lifecycle.
    - Designing systems that expose the hardware and software internals to laypersons.
    - Designing systems primarily for expert developers of the XR platform.
    * Designing usable interactive systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.
    because: The core concern is designing usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons, and the XR application software is interactive software intended for laypersons.
  Q What is required to obtain usable application software instead of a haphazard or ad hoc manner?  [32/S0/F3]
    - Skipping to final coding after the first idea.
    - Following an unstructured brainstorming process.
    - Using intuition alone to pick the best valid design.
    * Following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle.
    because: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

32/A2  recap  32/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 8 concepts)
  User-centered design involves users in the design and implementation to create usable software that meets the needs of laypersons. Since XR software is intended for users who may not need to know how the hardware or software works, it requires a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle. Software engineering provides this systematic approach by building software in connected stages.
  - User-centered design involves users in the design and implementation to make software usable.
  - XR software is intended for laypersons who may not need to know how the hardware or software works.
  - Obtaining usable software requires a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle.
  - Software engineering is a systematic process of building software in connected stages.

    - It has a fixed and small number of elements to be displayed

    - Only one valid design choice remains
    - No valid design choices can remain

    - It chooses the design that uses the fewest development stages
    * It helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability
    because: A systematic software development life cycle helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone.

  A design space is the set of all possible designs, and a calendar application has a very large design space. A software development life cycle (SDLC) is a systematic approach that helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability.
  - A design space is the set of all possible designs.

32/A5  quiz  32/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q In interactive system design, during which stages must users be taken into account?  [32/S2/F1]
    - Only the deployment and maintenance stage
    * All stages of the development lifecycle
    - Only the design and prototyping stages
    - Only the requirement-gathering stage
    because: Users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.
  Q Why does user-centric design of interactive systems require a highly iterative lifecycle?  [32/S2/F2]
    * To allow developers to return to earlier stages when user needs change
    - To proceed only to the next stage without returning to previous stages
    - To keep the stage sequence fixed after user needs are included
    - To avoid loops between earlier and later stages
    because: Including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage.
  Q In an interactive system development lifecycle, what is meant by user feedback in stage iterations?  [32/S2/F3]
    * Involving users in different ways, not only through feedback
    - Involving users only after the system is deployed
    - Involving users only through feedback
    - Involving developers in different ways, not only through feedback
    because: Iterations between stages account for user feedback, which means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.
  Q Which part of the iterative interactive system development lifecycle can iterate back to requirement gathering?  [32/S2/F5]
    - The feasibility study stage
    - The code testing stage
    * The design-prototype-evaluate cycle
    - The deployment and maintenance stage
    because: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle has iterations among its stages and also an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.
  Q What does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle consist of?  [32/S2/F4]
    - Code testing, deployment, and maintenance
    * Design, prototyping, and early evaluation
    - Requirement gathering, analysis, and specification
    - Design, coding, and empirical usability study
    because: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle consists of design, prototyping, and early evaluation.

32/A6  recap  32/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 24 concepts)
  A software development lifecycle is a set of stages followed in a sequence where users must be involved in every stage of interactive system design. A highly iterative lifecycle is required for user-centric design because user needs and expectations create loops back to previous stages. These iterations account for user feedback in different ways, including a design-prototype-evaluate cycle that can iterate back to requirement gathering.
  - A software development lifecycle is a set of stages followed in a sequence.
  - Users must be involved in every stage of interactive system design.
  - A highly iterative lifecycle is required for user-centric design because user needs create loops back to previous stages.
  - Iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback in different ways.
  - The lifecycle includes various stages, such as a design-prototype-evaluate cycle that iterates back to requirement gathering.

32/A7  put_in_order  32/S2  "Order the key stages of the interactive system development lifecycle"  (1 facts, 18 concepts)
  Order the key stages of the interactive system development lifecycle: Feasibility study > Requirement gathering > Design-prototype-evaluate cycle > Code design > Coding and implementation > Code testing > Empirical study > Deployment and maintenance  [32/S2/F4]

32/A8  quiz  32/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In the development of interactive systems, who must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards?  [32/S3/F0]
    - End users only after the design stage
    * End users together with the customer or client
    - Only the customer or client
    - The client only during the feasibility study
    because: For interactive systems, end users must be involved from requirement gathering onwards along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the client's requirements.
  Q Which methods are used for gathering end-user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage?  [32/S3/F1]
    - Contextual inquiry, empirical study, and ethnographic studies
    - Ethnographic studies, code design, and cultural probes
    * Contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes
    - Contextual inquiry, code testing, and cultural probes
    because: The requirement-gathering stage uses methods such as contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes to gather end-user requirements.
  Q In the design-prototype-evaluate loop, when can the design be stabilized and the next stage begin?  [32/S3/F2]
    - After the empirical study confirms final usability
    - After code testing confirms the code is bug-free
    * After evaluation no longer identifies many significantly different problems
    - After the first prototype has been evaluated
    because: The design is stabilized and the next stage can begin once iterations have continued until evaluation no longer reveals many significantly different problems.
  Q Why should each stage of the design-prototype-evaluate loop be completed quickly?  [32/S3/F3]
    - To move directly to code design after a single evaluation
    * To allow many iterations within a reasonable overall time
    - To reduce the need for user feedback in every iteration
    - To allow only one iteration within a reasonable overall time
    because: The loop and its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time; otherwise the overall turnaround time increases significantly.
  Q Which design activity is carried out in the design-prototype-evaluate loop?  [32/S3/F4]
    * Interface and interaction design from the user's point of view
    - Empirical study after system deployment
    - Hardware selection for the final XR system
    - Code design before the prototype is evaluated
    because: The loop includes interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view, while code design is a separate later activity.

32/A9  recap  32/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  End users and the client must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards using methods like contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes. The design-prototype-evaluate loop then uses user feedback to iteratively refine interface and interaction designs until they are stabilized. Because code design is a separate later activity, these loops must be completed quickly to avoid significant increases in overall turnaround time.
  - End users and the client must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards.
  - Requirements can be gathered using contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.
  - The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines interface and interaction designs using user feedback until they are stabilized.
  - Each loop must be completed quickly to prevent the overall turnaround time from increasing significantly.

32/A10  quiz  32/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q What is the initial sequence for coding and code testing in interactive system development?  [32/S4/F0]
    - Coding and implementation, then code testing, then code design
    - Code testing, then code design, then coding and implementation
    * Code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing
    - Code design, then code testing, then coding and implementation
    because: The traditional sequence is code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.
  Q Why are fewer iterations between code design, coding, and code testing preferred?  [32/S4/F1]
    * Because code design is highly skilled and costly, and late problems are costly to rewrite and test
    - Because code testing guarantees usability, so fewer design changes are needed
    - Because code testing is highly skilled and costly, and early designs are easy to change
    - Because empirical studies are inexpensive, so coding loops are unnecessary
    because: Fewer iterations are preferred because code design is highly skilled and costly, and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.
  Q What are the three evaluation points in the iterative software development life cycle for usable interactive systems?  [32/S4/F2]
    * Early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study
    - Early evaluation, code design, and code testing
    - Requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study
    - Code testing, empirical study, and user requirement gathering
    because: Early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study are the three evaluation points.
  Q What does code testing fail to establish?  [32/S4/F3]
    - Proper execution of the code
    - Bug-freeness of the code
    - Executability of the code
    * Usability from the end user's point of view
    because: Code testing ensures the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish usability from the end user's point of view.
  Q Why is the empirical study stage a distinguishing feature of interactive system development?  [32/S4/F4, 32/S4/F5]
    - Because it only checks that the code is bug-free before release
    * Because it systematically tests usability with end users, an activity typically absent when end users are not involved
    - Because it replaces the early evaluation of interface and interaction design
    - Because it evaluates code executability during coding and implementation
    because: Empirical study systematically tests usability with end users, and it is typically not part of other software development where end users are not involved.

32/A11  recap  32/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  Coding and code testing follow traditional software engineering, where fewer iterations are preferred because code design is costly. The iterative life cycle includes three evaluation points: early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study. While code testing ensures the system is executable, empirical studies are required to ensure usability and typically distinguish interactive systems from other software development.
  - Coding and code testing follow traditional software engineering, where fewer iterations are preferred because code design is costly.
  - The iterative software development life cycle includes three evaluation points: early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study.
  - Code testing ensures the system is executable and bug-free, but empirical studies are required to ensure usability with end users.
  - Empirical studies are typically not part of other software development and differentiate interactive systems by involving end users.

    - The loop between code design, coding, and code testing

    because: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly. The other listed loops should not be frequent.

    - Because frequent repetition can reduce the need to involve end users early
    - Because frequent repetition can allow more quick design-prototype-evaluate iterations
    * Because frequent repetition can escalate development cost, delay turnaround, and lead to project abandonment
    because: Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate loop can significantly affect project outcome and turnaround time. They can also escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.
  Q How should development stages be completed when building a usable extended reality system?  [32/S5/F2]
    - Quickly, so that the design-prototype-evaluate loop can be repeated often
    - Repeatedly, so that coding can be tested many times
    - After empirical study, so that usability can be confirmed
    * Carefully, so that there is no need to return to previous stages
    because: The development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

Frequent loops other than this cycle significantly affect a project's outcome, cost, and turnaround time. Development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.
  - The design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly.
  - Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate cycle significantly affect a project's outcome, cost, and turnaround time.
  - Development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

32/A22  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 39 concepts)
  Q Why does building usable XR software as interactive software for laypersons require a highly iterative software development lifecycle, and what role do iterations play?  [32/S0/F0, 32/S0/F2, 32/S2/F2, 32/S2/F3; user-centered design, extended reality software, interactive software, software development lifecycle, iteration, user feedback]
    A User-centered design involves users in the overall design lifecycle to produce usable application software, and the XR application software being developed is interactive software for laypersons. A highly iterative lifecycle is required because users' needs and expectations change the stage sequence and create loops in which a developer can return to a previous stage. Iterations between stages account for user feedback, which means involving users in different ways rather than only through feedback.
  Q Why is the design-prototype-evaluate loop expected to be performed quickly and repeatedly, while loops involving code design, coding, code testing, or empirical study should not be frequent?  [32/S3/F2, 32/S3/F3, 32/S5/F0, 32/S5/F1; design-prototype-evaluate loop, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code design, coding, implementation, code testing, empirical study, turnaround time, development cost]
    A The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs by prototyping a design, evaluating it to identify problems, and refining it through many iterations until few significantly different problems remain. Its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise turnaround time increases significantly. Other loops, such as the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent because they significantly affect the project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.
  Q Why is an empirical study needed in interactive system development even when code testing shows that the code executes properly?  [32/S4/F3, 32/S4/F4, 32/S4/F5; code testing, empirical study, executability, usability, usability testing, interactive system development, end user]
    A Code testing tests executability by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view. The empirical study is a usability-testing stage that uses systematic testing with end users to ensure that the interactive system product conforms to usability. This stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development, in which end users are not involved.
  Q Why must requirement gathering in an interactive-system development lifecycle involve end users as well as the client, and what methods can be used for this stage?  [32/S3/F0, 32/S3/F1, 32/S6/F0; requirement gathering, end user, client, requirement analysis, contextual inquiry, ethnographic study, cultural probe, interactive system development lifecycle]
    A In interactive system development, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the client, while typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client. Methods for gathering end-user requirements include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes. Requirement gathering is one stage in which building interactive software differs from building regular software.


===== lecture 33: Introduction to Majuli case study

33/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is extended reality system? (lecture 24) -> Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is immersive technology? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is digital heritage preservation? (lecture 2) -> The major current application domains for virtual reality (VR) discussed are gaming and entertainment, healthcare, education, the automobile industry, travel and tourism (including virtual tourism and digital heritage preservation), real estate and architecture, and defense.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is virtual reality system? (lecture 4) -> A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

33/A8  recap  33/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Traditional methods for preserving cultural heritage include oral traditions, museums, and documentation. Digital heritage preservation involves using digital media, archiving, and immersive technologies like VR and AR to preserve various types of heritage. These technologies can recreate physical spaces as virtual worlds where users can interact with entities, allowing a global audience to explore heritage sites remotely and promoting preservation for future generations.
  - Traditional methods for preserving cultural heritage include oral traditions, museums, and documentation.
  - Digital heritage preservation involves using digital media, archiving, and immersive technologies like VR and AR to preserve various types of heritage.
  - Immersive technologies can recreate physical spaces as virtual worlds, allowing users to interact with entities.
  - VR allows a global audience to explore heritage sites remotely and plays a pivotal role in preserving heritage for future generations.

    because: Heritage preservation means creating an archive of heritage information, ideally a multimedia archive with images, videos, audio, and text.
  Q How is heritage experience provided in the Majuli VR system?  [33/S3/F2]
    - As a non-immersive video watched on a computer screen

    - As a traditional museum exhibit about the island
    * As an immersive virtual tour or exploration using the archive
    because: Experiencing heritage is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the heritage archive.

33/A10  recap  33/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 11 concepts)
  The VR system for Majuli River Island aims to preserve heritage and allow users anywhere on Earth to experience it. Preservation involves creating a multimedia archive of images, videos, audio, and text, ideally in 2D and 360-degree forms. This archive is then used to provide users with an immersive virtual tour or exploration of the island.
  - The VR system for Majuli River Island aims to preserve heritage and provide global access to it.
  - Heritage preservation involves creating a multimedia archive of images, videos, audio, and text, ideally in 2D and 360-degree forms.
  - Users can experience this heritage through an immersive virtual tour or exploration of the island using the archive.

33/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 45 concepts)
  Q Why can the Majuli case study be treated as the development of an interactive system, and how does the proposed system satisfy the definition of a virtual reality system?  [33/S0/F0, 33/S0/F1, 4/S1/F0; Majuli case study, extended reality system, interactive system, system development lifecycle, virtual reality system]
    A Extended reality systems are interactive systems, so the same system development lifecycle used for interactive systems can essentially be followed to build them. The Majuli case study focuses on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system for digital heritage preservation. A virtual reality system is identified by an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment.
  Q How do floods and river erosion make digital heritage preservation necessary for Majuli, and what kinds of heritage need to be preserved?  [33/S1/F3, 33/S1/F4, 33/S1/F10, 33/S2/F2; flood, river erosion, cultural resource, tangible heritage, intangible heritage, ecological heritage, digital heritage preservation]
    A Severe annual floods and erosion endanger Majuli's cultural resources and its material existence, and river erosion consumes the island, reducing its habitable area until formerly habitable areas become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas. Because there is a real possibility that the island may disappear, its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage must be preserved. Digital heritage preservation uses digital media to preserve heritage and includes archiving, digitizing, and immersive technologies such as virtual reality and augmented reality.
  Q How do the preservation and experience goals of the Majuli VR system connect to the components of digital heritage preservation?  [33/S2/F2, 33/S3/F0, 33/S3/F1, 33/S3/F2; digital heritage preservation, virtual reality system, heritage preservation, multimedia archive, virtual tour, Majuli River Island]
    A Digital heritage preservation involves using digital media to preserve heritage, including archiving, digitizing, and immersive technologies. The preservation goal of the Majuli VR system is to create an archive of heritage information, ideally a multimedia archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in two-dimensional and 360-degree forms. The experience goal is an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses that archive.
  Q Why can immersive technology help a global audience engage with the heritage that the Majuli VR system aims to preserve?  [33/S2/F6, 33/S2/F7, 33/S3/F0; immersive technology, virtual reality, heritage site, artifact, intangible cultural heritage, heritage preservation]
    A Virtual reality and other immersive technologies permit a global audience to explore heritage sites, artifacts, and intangible cultural heritage remotely from home without visiting the physical site. Their use in heritage preservation is known to play a pivotal role in promoting the preservation of heritage for future generations. The Majuli VR system therefore has two clear-cut goals: to preserve heritage and to let users anywhere on Earth experience that heritage.

===== lecture 34: Introduction to Majuli case study

34/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is code testing? (lecture 32) -> Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.
  What is virtual tour? (lecture 33) -> Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.
  What is Majuli case study? (lecture 33) -> The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.
  What is satra? (lecture 33) -> Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.
  What is tangible heritage? (lecture 33) -> Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.
  What is intangible heritage? (lecture 33) -> Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.

34/A10  quiz  34/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What is the main purpose of the Majuli VR tour?  [34/S4/F0]
    - To preserve a large collection of 360-degree drone videos for real estate applications.
    - To create an augmented reality system for healthcare applications in cultural sites.
    - To demonstrate a gaming and entertainment application of virtual reality for a mass audience.
    * To recreate Majuli island in virtual space and provide an immersive interactive heritage experience.
    because: The Majuli VR tour was created by recreating the island in virtual space to provide an immersive interactive experience of its tangible and intangible heritage.
  Q Why is developing the Majuli VR tour considered a classical interactive system development challenge?  [34/S4/F1, 34/S4/F2]
    - It is driven mainly by the large average file sizes in the multimodal heritage archive, not by user needs.
    * It is for lay users and requires understanding users, requirements, and implementable design ideas.
    - It is for technical experts and requires choosing and configuring the right VR headset.
    - It requires only code testing, because usability testing is not part of interactive development.
    because: The tour is an interactive system for lay persons, and a key challenge is understanding users and their requirements, then converting those requirements into implementable design ideas.
  Q In the Majuli VR tour, what is the primary meaning of testing the design?  [34/S4/F3]
    * Usability testing, with code testing included as a part.
    - Only code testing, because user experience cannot be measured during development.
    - Only verifying that the 3D models are visually accurate.
    - Only checking the resolution and file size of the captured media.
    because: Testing whether the design meets user requirements means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.
  Q What makes the scale of Majuli a challenge compared with typical virtual museum tours?  [34/S4/F4]
    - The tour is difficult because it covers only a single room-sized cultural landscape.
    - The archive's lack of 3D models makes the spatial scale impossible to show.
    * The tour must cover a large island's geography and heritage in a usable immersive experience, not a small enclosed space.
    - The challenge is that the island's heritage is only tangible, not intangible.
    because: A challenge is combining vast tangible and intangible heritage information into a usable immersive tour that covers the island's large geography, unlike typical virtual tours of small places.
  Q Why can exploring the large Majuli VR tour increase the risk of cyber sickness?  [34/S4/F5]
    - The 24 numbered hotspots force the user to look rapidly in all directions.
    * It can involve longer session duration and increased interactivity during in-depth exploration.
    - The high-definition 360-degree image resolution directly causes motion discomfort.
    - The use of drone videos for cultural preservation creates visual conflict.
    because: Covering the huge island while experiencing heritage may lead to cyber sickness because of longer duration and increased interactivity when a user explores in depth.

34/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 39 concepts)
  Q Why is minimizing cybersickness a particular design concern for the Majuli Island virtual reality tour?  [34/S0/F0, 34/S4/F4, 34/S4/F5; Majuli Island virtual reality tour, cybersickness, interactivity, duration]
    A Minimizing cybersickness is a key concern while users explore the virtual island. The tour must cover almost 427 square kilometers as 24 spots, unlike typical virtual tours of small museums or places. Deeper exploration can therefore involve longer duration and increased interactivity, which may lead to cybersickness.
  Q How are the 24 Majuli hotspots used to represent different parts of the island's cultural heritage?  [34/S2/F0, 34/S2/F1, 34/S2/F3; hotspot, cultural landscape, village, town, tribal culture, mixed culture, tangible heritage, intangible heritage]
    A The island's cultural landscape is represented by a map of 24 numbered hotspots. Capturing the tangible and intangible heritage at these hotspots is taken to capture the island's cultural landscape and cultural heritage. Villages are used to capture tribal culture, while towns and other places are used to capture mixed culture.
  Q How do three-dimensional models, drone material, and two-dimensional videos in the Majuli multimodal heritage archive support different heritage aspects in the virtual tour?  [34/S3/F2, 34/S3/F3, 34/S3/F4, 34/S3/F5; three-dimensional model, two-dimensional drone shot, drone video, two-dimensional video, virtual landscape, virtual tour, ecological heritage, cultural heritage, architectural heritage, intangible heritage]
    A Three-dimensional models are created from captured images to recreate the landscape, preserve ecological heritage, and recreate tangible architectural heritage. Drone shots and drone videos showcase the landscape and top view while digitally recreating and preserving cultural and ecological heritage. Two-dimensional videos capture intangible cultural aspects, and the archive is used to recreate a more expansive virtual landscape and a virtual tour of the island.
  Q Why is testing the Majuli Island virtual reality tour treated as usability testing rather than only code testing?  [34/S4/F1, 34/S4/F3, 32/S4/F0; interactive system, usability testing, code testing, design, user requirement]
    A The tour is an interactive system intended for lay persons, so a key challenge is understanding users and their requirements. Testing therefore checks whether the design meets those user requirements, with usability testing as the main form. Code testing is still part of the process, carried out in the traditional software engineering way after coding and implementation.

===== lecture 35: Usability requirement gathering and specification

35/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is user-centered design (UCD)? (lecture 24) -> User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
  What is interface design? (lecture 32) -> The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.
  What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)? (lecture 32) -> In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

35/A1  quiz  35/S0  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q In the interactive system development life cycle, what does the requirement gathering stage mainly address?  [35/S0/F0]
    - Functional requirements that specify black-box outputs
    - System-centered decisions driven by developer interest
    * End-user requirements that ensure usability
    - Client requirements that define business goals
    because: The requirement gathering stage concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements and is aimed at ensuring usability.
  Q Requirement specification is required for which development activity?  [35/S0/F1]
    - Programming language selection
    - Database storage design
    * System implementation
    - User group icon selection
    because: Requirement specification is required for system implementation.

35/A2  recap  35/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 7 concepts)
  The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements to ensure usability. Additionally, a requirement specification is required for system implementation.
  - Requirement gathering focuses on end-user requirements to ensure usability.
  - Requirement specification is needed for system implementation.

35/A3  quiz  35/S1  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 2 concepts)
  Q In a system-centered design approach, what mainly guides what should be built?  [35/S1/F0]
    * What developers can easily build with available tools and what interests them
    - What user context and goals require for the task
    - What client requirements specify for the project
    - What end users need and expect from the system
    because: System-centered design is driven by the developer's skill and interest, what can be easily built on the platform, and what can be created from available tools, rather than by the user's needs and expectations.
  Q A user-centered design approach bases its design primarily on what?  [35/S1/F1]
    - Developers' skills, interests, and programming convenience
    * Users' abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations
    - Available tools, platform features, and resource limits
    - Client requirements, business goals, and project constraints
    because: User-centered design is a design approach based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view.
  Q What is the main concern in system-centered design, as opposed to user-centered design?  [35/S1/F0]
    - The end user, rather than the client
    * The system, rather than the user
    - The programmer, rather than the designer
    - The user, rather than the system
    because: System-centered design is a design approach in which the main concern is the system rather than the user.

35/A4  recap  35/S1  "Recap"  (2 facts, 2 concepts)
  System-centered design is a design approach where development is driven by the developer's skills, interests, and what can be easily built on the platform. In contrast, user-centered design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, ideally driven from the user's point of view.
  - System-centered design is driven by the developer's skills and what can be easily built on the platform rather than the user's needs.
  - User-centered design is based on the user's goals, needs, and abilities rather than the programmer's convenience.

    because: Requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application treats a requirement as an end-user requirement.

    - An interface-design decision
