35/A6  recap  35/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Requirements refer specifically to end-user requirements. Platform and programming language choices are feasibility issues, while data storage decisions are code-design decisions. Some developer questions are design decisions rather than requirements. The objective is to identify usability requirements to be converted into plans for design, implementation, and deployment.
  - Requirements refer specifically to end-user requirements.
  - Platform and programming language choices are feasibility issues.
  - Data storage decisions are code-design decisions rather than usability requirements.
  - Some developer questions are design decisions rather than requirements.
  - Identifying usability requirements helps create plans for design, implementation, and deployment.

35/A7  quiz  35/S3  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q How are functional requirements characterized in software requirements?  [35/S3/F1, 35/S3/F2]
    * They specify system features that carry out tasks as black-box functions producing output from input.
    - They specify system characteristics related to quality attributes that cannot be expressed as functions.
    - They specify how hardware and software are interfaced with each other.
    - They specify the economic cost of developing and operating the system.
    because: Functional requirements are task features expressed as functions treated as black boxes, while non-functional requirements are quality-related characteristics not expressible as functions.
  Q What type of requirement is a usability requirement?  [35/S3/F3]
    * A non-functional requirement about the user interface design and qualities that make the interface usable.
    - An external system interface requirement between hardware and software.
    - A performance-related requirement about system speed or resource use.
    - A functional requirement about the tasks the system can perform.
    because: Usability requirements are a kind of non-functional requirement concerned with user interface design and usability qualities.
  Q Which category of non-functional requirements includes the user interface where usability issues arise?  [35/S3/F4, 35/S3/F5, 35/S3/F6]
    - Performance-related requirements
    - Lifecycle requirements
    * Interface issues.
    - Economic considerations
    because: Interface issues cover the design or qualities of interfaces that make them usable, and include the user interface where usability issues arise.
  Q Why is usability particularly important for some interactive systems?  [35/S3/F7]
    - They are specified by functional black-box requirements.
    - They have economic operating constraints.
    - They include an external hardware-software interface.
    * They are intended for non-experts or users unaware of how the system works.
    because: Usability matters when interactive systems are intended for non-experts or users who do not know how the system works.

35/A8  recap  35/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Requirements are divided into functional requirements, which are system features, and non-functional requirements, which are system characteristics typically related to quality attributes. Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities that make an interface usable. Usability is important for interactive systems intended to be used by non-experts or users who are unaware of how the system works.
  - Requirements are divided into functional and non-functional requirements.
  - Functional requirements are system features that produce an output from an input.
  - Non-functional requirements are system characteristics typically related to quality attributes.
  - Usability requirements are non-functional requirements concerning the qualities that make an interface usable.
  - Usability is important for systems intended to be used by non-experts or users unaware of how the system works.

35/A9  quiz  35/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q Why must end-user requirement gathering begin by specifying or categorizing the users of the system?  [35/S4/F0]
    - Because usability is important for systems used by non-experts.
    * Because end-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users.
    - Because functional requirements must be defined before interface requirements.
    - Because platform and language choices belong to the feasibility stage.
    because: Specifying or categorizing users is the first step because end-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users.
  Q What does the ISO definition of usability require a usable product to have?  [35/S4/F1]
    - A specified user group.
    - A specified performance benchmark.
    * A specified context of use.
    - A specified functional requirement.
    because: The ISO definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use.
  Q How is contextual inquiry often described?  [35/S4/F5]
    - As an optimization method that measures navigation time and paths.
    - As a requirement method that separates functions from quality attributes.
    * As a semi-structured interview process combining interviews and observations.
    - As a hardware method that checks display quality and tracking.
    because: Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.
  Q What is the primary objective of contextual inquiry?  [35/S4/F6]
    - To ask users questions that clarify certain behaviors or activities.
    * To observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting.
    - To categorize users into pilgrims, students, or tourists for the tour.
    - To decide the platform and programming language for implementation.
    because: The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gain insight into behavior and requirements.
  Q What do observations and interaction with users help designers learn in contextual inquiry?  [35/S4/F9]
    - The input-output functions that a system must perform once implemented.
    - The user group chosen before the virtual tour experience begins.
    * The task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints.
    - Performance-related requirements, economic considerations, and lifecycle requirements.
    because: Observations and interaction enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace.

35/A10  recap  35/S4  "Recap"  (8 facts, 16 concepts)
  Requirement gathering must begin by specifying users and their context of use because usability is defined relative to a specific work context. Contextual inquiry is a semi-structured interview process that combines observations and interviews. This method involves watching users in their natural work settings to learn about user behaviors, work culture, and physical or social constraints.
  - Requirement gathering must begin by specifying users and their context of use.
  - Contextual inquiry is a semi-structured interview process that combines observations and interviews.
  - The goal is to watch users in their natural work settings to learn about behaviors and constraints.

35/A11  quiz  35/S5  "Quick quiz"  (2 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Why is contextual inquiry important in system development?  [35/S5/F0]
    - It divides end-user requirements into functional and non-functional categories.
    - It provides a standardized ISO definition of a specified context of use.
    * It studies users in their work setting and helps refine the design.
    - It ensures lay users keep control of the system during interaction.
    because: Contextual inquiry studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting and reveals their unique behavioral traits, enabling design refinement; without it, designers may treat essential user activities as equally important as unnecessary features.
  Q What must happen to user activities observed in contextual inquiry?  [35/S5/F1]
    - They should be classified only as non-functional requirements.
    - They should be recorded but need not become system features.
    - They should be ranked below optional features.
    * They must be supported as features in the system design.
    because: Observed user activities, such as setting meeting dates and reminders in a managerial staff calendar app, must be supported as features to make the system usable for that user group.

35/A12  recap  35/S5  "Recap"  (2 facts, 9 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users in their work settings, revealing unique behavioral traits and enabling design refinement. User activities observed in this process must be supported as features in the system design to ensure designs are valid and do not prioritize unnecessary features over essential ones.
  - Contextual inquiry is important because it studies users in their work setting to reveal behavioral traits and enable design refinement.
  - Observed user activities must be supported as features in the system design.

35/A19  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 38 concepts)
  Q Why are usability requirements considered a type of non-functional requirement rather than a functional requirement?  [35/S3/F0, 35/S3/F1, 35/S3/F2, 35/S3/F3; requirement, functional requirement, non-functional requirement, quality attribute, usability requirement, user interface]
    A Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements are system features and abilities, treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input once implemented. Non-functional requirements are system characteristics, typically related to quality attributes of software. Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement because they concern the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.
  Q How does specifying users and their context of use support the gathering of end-user usability requirements?  [35/S4/F0, 35/S4/F1, 35/S4/F2, 35/S4/F3, 35/S4/F6; user group, end-user requirement, usability, context of use, user behavior, contextual inquiry, usability requirement]
    A Users must first be specified or categorized because end-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users. The ISO definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use, and knowing user behavior in that work context is essential. Contextual inquiry observes users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. In usability requirement gathering, those end-user requirements are treated as usability requirements.
  Q Why are decisions about a mobile platform, a programming language, or a relational database management system not treated as end-user usability requirements in the calendar app case?  [35/S0/F0, 35/S2/F1, 35/S2/F2, 35/S2/F3; requirement gathering, end-user requirement, usability requirement, mobile platform, programming language, Java, JavaScript, feasibility stage, relational database management system, my structured query language, code design, interface design, design stage, calendar app]
    A Requirement gathering concerns end-user requirements and is aimed at ensuring usability. In the calendar app, choosing a mobile platform or a programming language such as Java or JavaScript is related to the feasibility stage rather than to end-user usability requirements. Choosing a relational database management system such as MySQL is a code-design decision rather than an interface-design decision or an end-user usability requirement. Some developer questions are therefore part of the design stage rather than being requirements.
  Q How does contextual inquiry connect observed user activities in a work context to features in a system design?  [35/S4/F6, 35/S4/F9, 35/S5/F1; contextual inquiry, user behavior, end-user requirement, task domain, work culture, physical constraint, social constraint, design decision, user activities, feature, system design, calendar app, user group]
    A Contextual inquiry watches users performing tasks in their natural work setting to gather insight about user behavior and end-user requirements. Through observation and interaction, designers learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints that support design decisions. User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design. In the calendar app for managerial staff, observed activities such as setting meeting dates and reminders must be supported to make the app usable for that user group.

===== lecture 36: Usability requirement gathering and specification

36/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (1 facts, 1 concepts)
  What is contextual inquiry (CI)? (lecture 35) -> Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

36/A1  quiz  36/S0  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  Q What is contextual inquiry?  [36/S0/F0]
    * A usability requirement-gathering method that observes users in their natural work setting.
    - A usability requirement-gathering method that observes users in a laboratory setting.
    - A usability requirement-gathering method that records users and never interacts with them.
    - A usability requirement-gathering method that only asks users what they want.
    because: Contextual inquiry observes targeted or specified users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.
  Q In active mode of contextual inquiry, what is true about the observer?  [36/S0/F1]
    - The observer only watches recorded activities after the work is finished.
    * The observer is physically present where users perform their tasks.
    - The observer is absent while user activities are recorded.
    - The observer tells users how they should complete their tasks.
    because: Active mode means the observer is physically present in the environment where users are doing their tasks.
  Q Which statement best describes passive mode of contextual inquiry?  [36/S0/F1]
    - User activities are performed while an observer is physically present.
    - User activities are performed in a laboratory while the observer watches directly.
    - User activities are recorded and analyzed without later interaction with the users.
    * User activities are recorded, later observed, and clarified through interaction with the users.
    because: Passive mode has no observer present; user activities are recorded or videotaped, later observed, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.
  Q In genuine contextual inquiry, how should the observer treat the users?  [36/S0/F2]
    - As students who need to be taught how to behave.
    - As customers who should request design changes during the task.
    - As employees who should follow the observer's instructions.
    * As masters or teachers, while the observer acts as an apprentice or learner.
    because: The observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, learning how they behave rather than advising or teaching them.

36/A2  recap  36/S0  "Recap"  (3 facts, 4 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement-gathering method that observes targeted or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave. It can be performed in active mode, where the observer is physically present, or passive mode, where user activities are recorded and observed later. In this process, the observer must act as an apprentice while treating the users as masters or teachers.
  - Contextual inquiry involves observing users in their natural work settings.
  - Contextual inquiry can be performed in active or passive modes.
  - The observer must act as an apprentice learning from the user as a master.

36/A3  quiz  36/S1  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q In contextual inquiry, which stage involves performing the actual observations and recording data?  [36/S1/F3]
    - The close stage
    - The initiate stage
    - The plan stage
    * The execute stage
    because: The execute stage is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through observations and recording data.
  Q During the initiate stage of contextual inquiry, why is communication opened with end users?  [36/S1/F2]
    - To script and rehearse the observation procedure
    - To send messages of gratitude for future usability testing
    - To obtain permissions from relevant authorities
    * To remove anxieties so they behave naturally
    because: In the initiate stage, communication with end users is opened to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
  Q Which activity is a helpful practice in the plan stage of contextual inquiry?  [36/S1/F1]
    - Sending thank-you notes to observed users
    * Scripting and rehearsing the procedure
    - Analyzing collected data to identify design goals
    - Performing the actual observations and recording data
    because: The plan stage includes identifying goals and arrangements, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.
  Q In the close stage of contextual inquiry, why are thank-you notes or messages sent to users and possibly authorities?  [36/S1/F4]
    - To obtain permissions before observing employees
    * Because they may be useful for future activities such as usability testing
    - To remove anxieties so users behave naturally
    - To arrange the date, time, and place of observation
    because: The close stage ideally sends thank-you notes or a message of gratitude because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.
  Q How is the affinity diagram method used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry?  [36/S1/F5, 36/S1/F6]
    - It performs the actual observations and records new data
    - It obtains necessary permissions from relevant authorities
    * It arranges collected data so patterns can be found more easily
    - It sends gratitude messages to users after the inquiry
    because: The reflect stage analyzes the data collected during execution, and the affinity diagram method arranges that data so patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of design goals.

36/A4  recap  36/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Contextual inquiry is a systematic process consisting of five stages: plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect. These stages involve planning goals and logistics, obtaining permissions, performing observations, and formally closing the inquiry. During the reflect stage, the team analyzes collected data and uses affinity diagrams to find patterns and identify design goals.
  - Contextual inquiry is a systematic process consisting of five stages: plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect.
  - The process involves planning goals and logistics, obtaining permissions, performing observations, and formally closing the inquiry.
  - During the reflect stage, the team analyzes collected data and uses affinity diagrams to find patterns and identify design goals.

36/A5  put_in_order  36/S1  "Order the stages of contextual inquiry"  (6 facts, 10 concepts)
  Order the stages of contextual inquiry: Identify goals and arrange observation > Obtain permissions and communicate with users > Perform observations and record data > Thank users and authorities > Analyze data and identify design goals  [36/S1/F0, 36/S1/F1, 36/S1/F2, 36/S1/F3, 36/S1/F4, 36/S1/F5]

36/A6  quiz  36/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 7 concepts)
  Q Which sequence describes the affinity diagram method?  [36/S2/F0]
    - Display ideas, create a group header, sort ideas, generate ideas, and draw the finished diagram
    - Plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect on the contextual inquiry data, then prepare the finished diagram
    * Generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a group header, and draw the finished diagram
    - Generate ideas, draw the finished diagram, display ideas, sort ideas, and create a group header
    because: The affinity diagram method has the five steps: generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a header or name for each group, and draw the finished diagram.
  Q Why are ideas sorted into groups in the affinity diagram method?  [36/S2/F2]
    * To find patterns among ideas that may look random by placing similar ideas together
    - To remove duplicate notes before drawing the finished affinity diagram from the board
    - To assign development tasks to programmers after system design is approved and implementation begins
    - To count the ideas recorded by each observer during the execute stage before grouping
    because: Sorting ideas into groups is done to find patterns among seemingly random ideas by moving similar ideas into the same group so meaningful conclusions can be drawn.
  Q What is a group header in an affinity diagram?  [36/S2/F3]
    - A usability requirement written directly from the user's stated goals before design and specifications
    - An original contextual inquiry note selected as the most representative idea for the group
    - A software module name created during the code design stage for later implementation
    * A name assigned after sorting that identifies the pattern binding the ideas in the group
    because: A group header is a name or identifier assigned after the ideas have been sorted; it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas and is not present in the initial ideas.
  Q After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, what does reflection involve?  [36/S2/F5]
    - Coding the system and testing it in the traditional software engineering way
    - Returning to the execute stage to record more observations from the users
    * Deciding what to do with the data and formulating design recommendations based on it
    - Choosing the final layout screens during the design-prototype-evaluate cycle
    because: Reflection after the finished affinity diagram means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.
  Q A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility is best described as what?  [36/S2/F7]
    - A diagram header labeling the group of notes about content correction on the board
    - A code design decision specifying the programming structure and tests for erasing notes
    * A requirement stating what must be done for usability, not how to implement it
    - An implementation guideline produced by following a traditional software development lifecycle without inquiry
    because: Such a design recommendation is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable and does not specify how to implement it.

36/A7  recap  36/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 9 concepts)
  The affinity diagram method analyzes contextual inquiry notes through five steps, including sorting ideas into groups to identify patterns and assigning headers to those groups. Reflection on these diagrams produces informed design recommendations based on the inquiry data. These recommendations serve as requirements for what must be done to make the system usable rather than prescriptions for implementation.
  - The affinity diagram method analyzes contextual inquiry notes through five steps.
  - Sorting ideas into groups identifies patterns to draw meaningful conclusions.
  - Group headers are assigned to identify the patterns binding the ideas.
  - Reflection on the diagram produces informed design recommendations based on inquiry data.
  - Design recommendations are requirements for what must be done, not prescriptions for implementation.

36/A8  put_in_order  36/S2  "Order the steps of the affinity diagram method"  (4 facts, 3 concepts)
  Order the steps of the affinity diagram method: Collect final observer notes > Put notes on a wall or board > Move similar notes into groups > Add a header to each group > Draw the completed diagram  [36/S2/F0, 36/S2/F1, 36/S2/F2, 36/S2/F3]

36/A9  quiz  36/S3  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In the calendar app affinity diagram, which observations are placed under the reminder setting group?  [36/S3/F0]
    - Observations that users check upcoming deadlines, meeting dates, and lecture schedules
    - Observations that users check the date and then check the timetable
    - Observations that users check meeting schedules and lecture schedules on a particular day
    * Observations that users set reminders, including using a mobile app to check the day and date and set an assignment-submission reminder
    because: The reminder setting group contains observations about setting reminders, including using a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission. The other listed observations were scheduling-related, not reminder-setting observations.
  Q How were the calendar app observations that did not relate to reminder setting organized in the affinity diagram?  [36/S3/F1]
    - They were kept as a single work scheduling group in the finished diagram
    - They were first grouped under reminder setting and then refined into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling
    * They were first grouped under work scheduling and then refined into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling
    - They were divided directly into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling without an earlier work scheduling group
    because: The five observations that did not relate to reminder setting were initially grouped under work scheduling and later refined into the final scheduling groups overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling.
  Q In an affinity diagram, what is true about the grouping of observations?  [36/S3/F2]
    - There is only one correct way to group the observations
    - The grouping must follow the order in which the observations were recorded
    - The finished diagram must always contain the same groups as any other analyst would produce
    * Different groupings of the same observations are possible
    because: There is no unique way to group observations in an affinity diagram, so more than one grouping can be possible.

36/A10  recap  36/S3  "Recap"  (3 facts, 9 concepts)
  Observations related to setting reminders are grouped under a specific header. Other observations can be grouped and then refined into specific categories. There is no unique way to group observations in an affinity diagram.
  - Observations related to setting reminders are grouped under a specific header.
  - Other observations can be grouped and then refined into specific categories.
  - There is no unique way to group observations in an affinity diagram.

36/A16  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q How does the reflect stage of contextual inquiry use an affinity diagram method to move from recorded observations to a design specification and design recommendations?  [36/S1/F5, 36/S1/F6, 36/S2/F5; contextual inquiry, reflect stage, affinity diagram method, design goal, design specification, design recommendation]
    A In the reflect stage, the observer analyzes data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals. The affinity diagram method arranges the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals. After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations.
  Q Why is a design recommendation derived from contextual inquiry, such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application, considered an informed requirement rather than a prescription for implementation?  [36/S2/F6, 36/S2/F7; contextual inquiry, design recommendation, informed design choice, uninformed design choice, class note-taking application, requirement, implementation]
    A A design recommendation derived from contextual inquiry is an informed design choice because it is produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices. The erase-content facility recommendation is a requirement because it states what must be done to make the system usable. It does not specify how the system should implement that facility.
  Q Why must an observer in genuine contextual inquiry act as an apprentice rather than a teacher, and how does this role relate to active and passive modes?  [36/S0/F1, 36/S0/F2; contextual inquiry, master-apprentice model, active mode, passive mode, observation]
    A In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, so advice or teaching is prohibited. Contextual inquiry can be performed in active mode, where the observer is physically present, and passive mode, where user activities are recorded and later clarified through interaction. In both modes, the observer is learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave.
  Q Why can an affinity diagram for a calendar app refine a group header from work scheduling into overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling without treating the first grouping as simply wrong?  [36/S3/F1, 36/S3/F2; calendar app, affinity diagram, observation, header, work scheduling, overall scheduling, day-wise scheduling, reminder setting]
    A In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry observations that do not relate to reminder setting were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling. There is no unique way to group the observations in an affinity diagram, so different groupings are possible. The finished diagram has three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

===== lecture 37: Usability requirement gathering and specification

37/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is contextual inquiry (CI)? (lecture 35) -> Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.
  What is requirement? (lecture 36) -> A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.
  What is design recommendation? (lecture 36) -> After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

    - It can be used only as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles.
    * It can be used as design guidelines, design recommendations, design principles, or functional requirements.
    - It can be used only as code design documents, implementation plans, and code testing records.
    - It can be used only as functional requirements.
    because: Contextual inquiry outcomes can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.
  Q Which statement explains why functional requirements are easier to convert into code?  [37/S0/F1]
    - They are collected from field trips, interviews, and observations.
    * They are specified as functions with well-defined inputs and well-defined outputs.
    - They are non-functional usability requirements written in prose.
    - They are specified only with an optional description of their purpose.
    because: Functional requirements are specified in terms of functions with well-defined input and output, and this functional specification makes conversion to code and the transition to code design easier.

37/A2  recap  37/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 13 concepts)
  The outcome of contextual inquiry can be used as design guidelines or functional requirements. Functional requirements are specified in terms of functions with well-defined inputs and outputs. This specification makes them easy to convert to code, making the transition to code design easier.
  - Contextual inquiry outcomes can be used as design guidelines or functional requirements.
  - Functional requirements have well-defined inputs and outputs, making them easy to convert to code.

37/A5  quiz  37/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q Which description matches a functional requirement?  [37/S2/F0]
    * A system feature specified as a black-box function with a defined input and output
    - A user goal described without a clear system output
    - A usability preference expressed as a design guideline
    - A hardware component selected for the project
    because: A functional requirement is formally specifiable because it describes a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output, and an optional purpose.
  Q Why can usability requirements be converted into functional requirements?  [37/S2/F1]
    - To remove non-functional requirements from the software requirements specification
    - To replace contextual inquiry with a usability evaluation
    - To assign each requirement to a specific user group
    * So usability is directly incorporated into the system through code and supports code design
    because: Usability requirements, as non-functional requirements, can be converted into functional requirements so they are directly incorporated through code and support code design.
  Q What does a software requirements specification contain?  [37/S2/F2]
    - Only the optimization metrics for the final build
    - Only the tested features of the implemented system
    - Only the user groups identified during contextual inquiry
    * All functional and non-functional requirements, including the formal specification of functional requirements
    because: A software requirements specification is the textual document that specifies all functional and non-functional requirements and includes the formal specification of functional requirements.
  Q How are requirements generally organized in a software requirements specification?  [37/S2/F3]
    - In chronological order of implementation tasks
    - In separate documents for each user group
    - In alphabetical order by stakeholder name
    * In a hierarchy of identifiers, with each identifier naming a function with a defined input and output
    because: In an SRS, requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers, and each identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, output, and optional description.
  Q What is the output of contextual inquiry?  [37/S2/F4]
    - A single list of user goals without group organization
    - A final test report verifying all usability requirements
    * A group-wise organization of observation notes that can guide design and sometimes become functional requirements
    - A complete formal specification of every functional requirement
    because: Contextual inquiry produces group-wise organized notes that can serve as design guidelines and, for some items, be converted into functional requirements that can be implemented as code.

37/A6  recap  37/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Functional requirements specify system features as black-box functions with well-defined inputs and outputs. Usability requirements can be converted into functional requirements to be directly incorporated into the code. These requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy within a software requirements specification (SRS). Additionally, notes from contextual inquiry can be used as design guidelines or converted into functional requirements.
  - Functional requirements specify system features as black-box functions with well-defined inputs and outputs.
  - Usability requirements can be converted into functional requirements to be directly incorporated into the code.
  - Requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy within a software requirements specification (SRS).
  - Contextual inquiry notes can be used as design guidelines or converted into functional requirements.

  Q How did the Majuli VR Tour address the large-geography and cyber-sickness challenge?  [37/S3/F5, 37/S3/F6, 37/S3/F7]
    - By giving all users access to the entire collected data set
    * By giving each user group access only to a data subset relevant to its typical activities
    - By asking users to explore every place in detail
    - By giving each group only data unrelated to its typical activities
    because: Group-specific data subsets reduced the amount of information to explore and lowered the risk of cyber sickness, whereas full access to all data could confuse users and increase sickness.

37/A8  recap  37/S3  "Recap"  (12 facts, 33 concepts)
  Usability requirements for the Majuli VR Tour were gathered through field trips, interviews, and observations. The system targets three non-resident user groups: students, tourists, and pilgrims, using contextual inquiry to identify their specific needs and design challenges. To prevent cybersickness and confusion, information is restricted to subsets tailored to each group's activities. Contextual inquiry also highlighted the importance of location awareness and interaction aids to provide a seamless experience.
  - Usability requirements were gathered through field trips, interviews, observations, and notes.
  - The tour targets three non-resident user groups: students, tourists, and pilgrims.
  - Contextual inquiry was used to identify group-specific needs, features, and design challenges.
  - Data is restricted to subsets per group to reduce confusion and cybersickness.
  - Contextual inquiry also identified the need for location awareness and interaction aids.

37/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why can usability requirements gathered by contextual inquiry for the Majuli VR Tour be made more suitable for implementation by converting them into functional requirements?  [37/S0/F0, 37/S0/F1, 37/S2/F1; contextual inquiry, usability requirement, non-functional requirement, functional requirement, code design]
    A Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement gathering method, and its outcome can be used as design guidelines, recommendations, or principles, and also as functional requirements. Usability requirements are non-functional requirements, but when they are converted into functional requirements and added to the existing set, they are directly incorporated into the system through code and support code design. A functional requirement specifies a feature as a function with a well-defined input and output, and this functional specification makes conversion to code easier.
  Q How did the Majuli VR Tour use the identified user groups to make a large multimodal virtual tour less likely to cause cybersickness?  [37/S3/F2, 37/S3/F5, 37/S3/F6, 37/S3/F7; Majuli virtual reality tour, user group, large geographical area, multimodal data, cybersickness, data subset restriction]
    A The three potential user groups were students or learners, tourists, and pilgrims. A key design challenge was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cybersickness. The tour addressed this by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, based on what that group typically does, which reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail. This reduced the possibility of cybersickness and increased interest for each group.
  Q Why is location awareness important in a virtual reality tour of a large geographical area, and how can that insight become part of the system design?  [37/S0/F1, 37/S3/F8, 37/S3/F9; location awareness, location information, virtual reality tour, large geographical area, functional requirement, system design]
    A Accurate location information is crucial in a virtual reality tour, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space. In the Majuli VR Tour, location awareness was identified during contextual inquiry as an issue for users exploring a large space. A possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature and later convert it into functional requirements during system design, which are easier to turn into code because they specify well-defined inputs and outputs.
  Q How does a software requirements specification help organize functional requirements so that each requirement remains clear for later coding?  [37/S2/F0, 37/S2/F2, 37/S2/F3; software requirements specification, functional requirement, requirement hierarchy, requirement identifier, top-level requirement, sub-requirement, input, output]
    A A software requirements specification is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements. In an SRS, requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement. Each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does, which supports conversion to code.

===== lecture 38: System Design

38/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is design-prototype-evaluate cycle? (lecture 32) -> The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.
  What is interface design? (lecture 32) -> The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.
  What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)? (lecture 32) -> In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

38/A4  recap  38/S1  "Recap"  (6 facts, 16 concepts)
  Designing an immersive experience involves a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements. The design process can start from creativity aided by intuition and expertise, or from guidelines that range from generic high-level rules to detailed micro details. Because interface design requires a design language that is generally different from code design, a prototype can be used as a language for expressing design ideas.
  - Designing an immersive experience involves a design-prototype-evaluation cycle to incorporate user requirements.
  - Design can start from creativity aided by intuition, expertise, experience, and domain knowledge, or from guidelines like checklists and heuristics.
  - Design guidelines can be generic high-level rules or detailed specific specifications for micro details.
  - A design language is used to specify interface design, which is generally different from the language used to specify code design.
  - A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.

38/A8  quiz  38/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What does Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design require?  [38/S3/F0]
    - Provide informative feedback
    - Design for universal usability
    - Design dialogues to yield closure
    * Strive for consistency
    because: The first golden rule is to strive for consistency in system and interface design.
  Q In Shneiderman's consistency rule, what does internal consistency mean?  [38/S3/F1, 38/S3/F2]
    - Matching virtual-world elements and interactions to the user's real-world experience
    * Using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts and usage instances
    - Providing informative feedback whenever the user performs an action
    - Using separate objects and interactions for each part of a design
    because: Internal consistency uses the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances.
  Q What is external or environmental consistency in system design?  [38/S3/F3]
    - Hotkey options should be preferred because they rely on recognition rather than recall
    * Virtual-world elements and interactions should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge
    - A system should provide facilities for all user categories
    - The same elements and interactions should be used for the same task across different parts
    because: External or environmental consistency means virtual-world elements and interactions closely match real-world experience and knowledge so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world.
  Q What does Shneiderman's second golden rule, universal usability, require?  [38/S3/F4]
    * A system should provide facilities for and support different user categories rather than only specific ones
    - A system should use the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts
    - A system should match virtual-world elements to the user's real-world experience
    - A system should provide informative feedback after every user action
    because: Universal usability means a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific ones.
  Q Why can menu-based options be preferable to hotkey options for some users?  [38/S3/F5]
    * Menu options rely on recognition rather than recall
    - Recall is a less skilled task than recognition
    - Menu options are faster for users who do not want slower hotkey options
    - Hotkeys rely on recognition while menus rely on recall
    because: Menu options can help users who may not remember hotkey combinations because they rely on recognition rather than recall, while recall is a skilled task. Hotkeys can be faster for users who prefer them over slower menu-based options.

38/A9  recap  38/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 14 concepts)
  Strive for consistency in system and interface design by using internal and external consistency. Design for universal usability to support all user categories. Menu-based options may be preferable to hotkeys because they rely on recognition rather than recall.
  - Strive for consistency in system and interface design.
  - Use internal consistency for tasks and external consistency to match real-world experience.
  - Design for universal usability to support all user categories.
  - Menu options rely on recognition while hotkeys rely on recall.

  - Design dialogues to yield closure by organizing tasks into beginning, middle, and end parts with feedback for each group.

38/A12  put_in_order  38/S4  "Order the parts of task execution in a dialogue"  (1 facts, 3 concepts)
  Order the parts of task execution in a dialogue: Task is started > Task is executed > Task is completed  [38/S4/F3]

38/A13  quiz  38/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q What should a system design offer to help users deal with errors?  [38/S5/F0]
    * Error prevention and simple error handling
    - Dialogues that yield closure
    - Short-term memory load reduction
    - Informative feedback for every user action
    because: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.
  Q Why should close and start options for the same interface not be placed side by side?  [38/S5/F1]
    - To maintain consistency with external interfaces
    - To reduce the amount of information held in short-term memory
    * To reduce accidental selection of the wrong action
    - To provide informative feedback after the user acts
    because: Placing close and start options side by side can cause a user to accidentally choose the wrong action.
  Q What should error handling provide when an error occurs?  [38/S5/F2]
    * Simple, easy-to-understand information
    - A progress bar showing task completion
    - A hexadecimal status code
    - Complicated technical error messages
    because: Error handling should give simple, easy-to-understand information rather than complicated error messages.
  Q What are undo and redo facilities primarily meant to permit?  [38/S5/F3, 38/S5/F4]
    - A lower short-term memory load
    - Informative feedback about system state
    * Easy reversal of actions
    - A feeling of user control over the system
    because: The sixth rule permits easy reversal of actions, and undo and redo are primarily facilities for that purpose.

38/A14  recap  38/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  System design should offer error prevention and simple error handling, which includes keeping error rates low by avoiding placing options side by side that could lead to the wrong action. Error messages should be simple and easy to understand to avoid confusing or scaring the user. Additionally, systems should permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available, through undo and redo facilities which are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.
  - Offer error prevention and simple error handling.
  - Keep error rates low by avoiding placing options side by side that could lead to the wrong action.
  - Provide simple, easy-to-understand information instead of complicated error messages.
  - Permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available.
  - Use undo and redo facilities, which are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

38/A15  quiz  38/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What does the keeping-users-in-control usability rule require?  [38/S6/F0]
    - Lay users should be forced to remember more than nine chunks during an interaction.
    * Lay users should feel in control, perceive that their interaction changes system state, and receive feedback.
    - Lay users should be limited to a single hand-gesture input modality for every task.
    - Lay users should depend only on permanent long-term memory for day-to-day information.
    because: Keeping users in control means lay users feel in control, see that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on actions and results; without this they feel at a loss and usability is reduced.
  Q In the broad sense of human memory, what is short-term memory?  [38/S6/F1]
    - An AR headset that tracks eye movements as input data.
    * A non-permanent, note-like store used to bring long-term memory content into day-to-day activities.
    - A permanent store that replaces long-term memory for day-to-day activities.
    - A set of five to nine input modalities used to operate an interface.
    because: Human memory broadly includes short-term and long-term memory, and short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.
  Q Why should an interface avoid forcing users to remember too many chunks?  [38/S6/F2, 38/S6/F3]
    - Because the chunk limit applies to long-term memory, not short-term memory.
    * Because too many chunks overutilize short-term memory and are harmful.
    - Because chunks become harmful only when they are reduced to single letters.
    - Because too many chunks underutilize short-term memory and improve recall.
    because: Short-term memory is limited to five to nine chunks at a time, and holding more than that overutilizes it and is harmful.
  Q Why can the generic usability rules be analyzed for extended reality systems?  [38/S6/F5]
    - They apply only to non-immersive voice-command interfaces.
    - They require a particular tracking hardware setup to be valid.
    - They were designed specifically for Microsoft HoloLens AR headsets.
    * They are not specific to a particular product or system.
    because: The generic usability rules are not tied to one product or system, so they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

38/A16  recap  38/S6  "Recap"  (5 facts, 17 concepts)
  Keeping users in control requires that users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback. Because short-term memory is a non-permanent store limited to five to nine chunks of information, designers should reduce short-term memory load by keeping interface information within that range. These generic usability rules can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.
  - Keeping users in control requires that users feel in control, perceive state changes, and receive feedback.
  - Short-term memory is a non-permanent store used to aid day-to-day activities.
  - Short-term memory is limited to holding five to nine chunks of information at a time.
  - Reducing short-term memory load requires keeping interface information between five and nine chunks.
  - These generic usability rules can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

38/A17  quiz  38/S7  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q Familiar touch and gesture are similar to interaction in which context?  [38/S7/F0]
    - Immersive virtual reality
    - System control in an immersive environment
    * Non-immersive augmented reality
    - Object interaction in a virtual environment
    because: Interaction in non-immersive settings such as augmented reality is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.
  Q What does using suitable interaction techniques in immersive VR or MR design aim to enhance?  [38/S7/F1]
    - Error handling
    * Presence
    - Action reversal
    - Feedback
    because: For immersive VR or MR experiences, suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.
  Q Which three broad categories cover interaction in immersive environments?  [38/S7/F2]
    - Presence, feedback, and error prevention
    - Touch, gesture, and object selection
    * Object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control
    - Virtual world, headset, and immersive technology
    because: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control.
  Q What does object interaction in an immersive environment involve?  [38/S7/F2]
    * Selecting and manipulating objects in the virtual environment
    - Moving from one point to another in the virtual environment
    - Changing system-related settings
    - Using touch and gesture in augmented reality
    because: Object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment.
  Q What does navigation in an immersive environment involve?  [38/S7/F2]
    - Changing system-related settings
    - Selecting and manipulating objects in the virtual environment
    * Moving from one point to another in the virtual environment
    - Enhancing presence through interaction techniques
    because: Navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment.

38/A18  recap  38/S7  "Recap"  (3 facts, 14 concepts)
  Interaction in non-immersive settings is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture. For immersive virtual reality or mixed reality experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. Interaction in these immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control.
  - Non-immersive interaction is similar to familiar touch and gestures.
  - Immersive experiences use specialized techniques to enhance presence.
  - Immersive interaction is categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

  11 across: A way to express a concept so it can be brainstormed and refined. (6,8) = DESIGNLANGUAGE
  1 down: Providing ways to manage mistakes in a system. (5,8) = ERRORHANDLING
  2 down: Permitting easy ways to return from an erroneous situation. (8,6) = REVERSALOPTION

38/A23  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (8 facts, 32 concepts)
  Shneiderman's rules | *Prototype | Apple's guidelines | Norman's principles  (Shneiderman's rules, Norman's principles, and Apple's guidelines are design guidelines; a prototype is a way of expressing design ideas, not a design guideline.)  [38/S1/F3, 38/S1/F4, 38/S1/F6]
  Consistency | *Presence | Feedback | Closure  (Consistency, closure, and feedback are Shneiderman golden-rule design concepts; presence is a user psychological quality enhanced by interaction techniques, not one of those rules.)  [38/S2/F2, 38/S3/F0, 38/S4/F3, 38/S7/F1]
  *Selection | Navigation | System control | Object interaction  (Object interaction, navigation, and system-control interaction are the broad categories of immersive-environment interaction; selection is a type of object interaction, not a separate broad category.)  [38/S7/F2]

38/A24  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q How do the two design stages in the interactive system development lifecycle differ in purpose, and why is the design stage placed in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?  [38/S0/F0, 38/S0/F1, 38/S1/F0; interactive system development lifecycle, design stage, code design, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, design-prototype-evaluation cycle, non-interactive software development, immersive experience, user requirement]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design. Code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development. The design stage is in the design-prototype-evaluation cycle, which is involved in designing an immersive experience in order to incorporate user requirements.
  Q Why is having a design language important for interface and interaction design, and how can a prototype serve that role?  [38/S1/F1, 38/S1/F5, 38/S1/F6; interface and interaction design, design process, design language, prototype, interface design, code design]
    A Interface and interaction design involves how to start the design process and how to express a design so it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language. A design language is a specification of design, and the language used to specify interface design is generally different from the language used to specify code design. A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.
  Q Why can Shneiderman's eight golden rules guide an extended reality system, while some virtual reality-specific guidelines are not automatically transferable to augmented reality?  [38/S2/F0, 38/S2/F1, 38/S2/F2; Shneiderman's eight golden rules, generic design rule, extended reality system, interactive system, graphical user interface, specific design guideline, virtual reality, augmented reality, cybersickness, immersion, immersive system]
    A Shneiderman's eight golden rules are generic design rules that are applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems, although they are mostly rather than fully applicable to extended reality systems. They were originally developed primarily for graphical user interfaces, but they can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces. Specific design guidelines for avoiding or minimizing cybersickness are typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems and may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality systems because augmented reality immersion differs from virtual reality immersion.
  Q How does interaction design in an augmented reality setting differ from design for immersive virtual reality or mixed reality, and what broad categories cover interaction in immersive environments?  [38/S7/F0, 38/S7/F1, 38/S7/F2; augmented reality, touch, gesture, virtual reality, mixed reality, interaction technique, presence, object interaction, navigation, interaction for system control, selection, manipulation, virtual environment]
    A Interaction in non-immersive settings such as augmented reality is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture. For immersive virtual reality or mixed reality experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence. Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means changing system-related settings.

===== lecture 39: System Design

39/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is interaction? (lecture 23) -> Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
  What is degree of freedom? (lecture 28) -> The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.
  What is six degrees of freedom? (lecture 28) -> In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.
  What is object interaction? (lecture 38) -> Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.
  What is augmented reality system? (lecture 5) -> The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

    - Selection changes object properties; manipulation specifies objects from a virtual set.
    * Selection specifies objects; manipulation changes properties of an already selected object.
    - Selection moves the user's viewpoint; manipulation changes object properties.
    because: Object interaction includes selection for specifying one or more objects and manipulation for changing the properties of selected objects.
  Q Which variable can determine which object-selection technique is suitable, alongside target distance and direction?  [39/S1/F1]

    - The matched-zone alignment of the target with the real world
    * The density of objects around the target object

    - It requires no specialized technique because occlusion is irrelevant.
    * The user must first be made aware that the object is present.
    - It is usually the majority case in object selection.
    - It becomes easier than selecting a partially visible object.
    because: Partly occluded targets are challenging, and fully occluded targets require awareness of their presence before they can be selected.

39/A5  quiz  39/S2  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What characterizes the virtual hand hand-selection technique?  [39/S2/F2]
    - A virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
    - A virtual hand is guided by a ray that selects the first object it intersects
    * A visible virtual hand follows the physical hand through a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation
    - A visible virtual hand changes the virtual arm length to reach distant objects quickly
    because: The virtual hand technique uses a visible hand as an avatar of the physical hand, tied to it by a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation.
  Q In go-go hand selection, why can selecting a distant small object be imprecise?  [39/S2/F4, 39/S2/F5]
    * As distance increases, small physical hand movements are mapped to larger and faster virtual hand movements
    - The physical and virtual hands maintain a fixed one-to-one mapping at all distances
    - The virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
    - The virtual hand moves more slowly when the target object is farther away
    because: Go-go maps smaller physical movements to larger and faster virtual movements for farther objects, so a small movement can miss or cross a distant small target.
  Q How does the prism technique improve on go-go for distant objects?  [39/S2/F6, 39/S2/F7]
    * It slows or stops the virtual hand when the physical hand moves below specified velocity thresholds
    - It bends a virtual ray toward the closest selectable object before selection
    - It requires the user to position virtual fingers around the object to refine the selection
    - It keeps the virtual hand moving at full speed even when the physical hand is stopped
    because: Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves slowly and keeps the virtual hand still below a minimum velocity, giving a control benefit not present in go-go.
  Q What does intent-driven selection use to refine which object is selected?  [39/S2/F9, 39/S2/F10]
    - A one-to-one mapping of physical hand motion to a visible virtual hand
    - A scaled mapping in which small physical movements move the virtual hand faster
    * Hand or finger postures that progressively reduce proximity spheres around the target
    - A ray from the head or eye that selects the first intersected object
    because: Intent-driven selection uses virtual hand movement and finger postures, often with proximity spheres that shrink as the user gets closer, to refine the selection.

39/A6  recap  39/S2  "Recap"  (11 facts, 15 concepts)
  Hand selection involves reaching out to directly touch and grab virtual objects. While the virtual hand technique uses one-to-one mapping, go-go and prism are travel techniques that scale movements to reach distant objects. Intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique using finger postures and proximity spheres that can be combined with these travel techniques.
  - Hand selection involves reaching out to directly touch and grab virtual objects.
  - The virtual hand technique uses a one-to-one mapping but can be tiring for distant objects.
  - Go-go and prism are travel techniques that scale movements for distant objects, with prism offering better control by allowing the hand to stop.
  - Intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique using finger postures and proximity spheres that can be combined with travel techniques.

39/A7  quiz  39/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In basic pointing-based object selection, how does the user select a virtual object?  [39/S3/F0]
    - Choosing the object nearest to the controller regardless of the ray
    * Extending a visible ray and triggering the controller to select the first intersected object
    - Moving a virtual hand until it directly touches the object
    - Pointing at an object and holding it until it automatically selects
    because: Pointing-based selection works by extending a visible ray into the virtual world and using a controller trigger to select the first object intersected by that ray.
  Q How can the pointing ray be moved without the user using a hand?  [39/S3/F1]
    - By moving the body in place
    * By moving the head or changing the eye gaze
    - By pressing a selection button on a wristband
    - By moving a hand-held controller
    because: Pointing can be done with head movement from a head-mounted display or with eye-gaze tracking, both without hand use.
  Q Why can selecting a small distant object be difficult in ray casting?  [39/S3/F5]
    * It requires precise pointing, especially when other objects surround it
    - It requires the ray to automatically bend toward the object
    - It requires a depth marker to be placed at the object
    - It requires the user to physically reach the object
    because: In ray casting, the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when a small object is surrounded by other objects.
  Q How does bend cast help a user select an object?  [39/S3/F6]
    * It bends the ray toward the closest selectable object
    - It selects the largest object intersected by the ray
    - It extends the ray only to a fixed distance
    - It uses a depth marker to choose among objects
    because: Bend cast improves basic ray casting by bending the ray toward the closest selectable object, so the user does not need to point as precisely.
  Q What does the depth ray technique add to basic ray casting?  [39/S3/F8]
    - An eye-gaze estimate that replaces the pointing ray
    * A user-controlled depth marker that selects the intersected object closest to the marker
    - A circular arc that visually bends the ray
    - A timer that selects the first highlighted object
    because: Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the intersected object closest to the marker.

39/A8  recap  39/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 18 concepts)
  Pointing-based selection uses a virtual ray from the hand, head, or eye to select objects in a virtual world. Ray casting is the basic method, but it can be difficult to select small or distant objects. Bend cast and depth ray are improvements that help with precision and disambiguating multiple intersected objects.
  - Pointing-based selection uses a virtual ray from the hand, head, or eye to select the first object intersected by the ray.
  - Some methods combine gaze pointing for target estimation with hand pointing to trigger selection.
  - Ray casting is the basic method, but it can make selecting small or distant objects difficult.
  - Bend cast improves on ray casting by bending the ray toward the closest object, but it works best when few objects are nearby.
  - Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects.

39/A9  quiz  39/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q Which description best matches image-plane selection?  [39/S4/F1, 39/S4/F2]
    - A 3D selection made by shaping a box around the object with both hands
    - A selection made by pointing a ray and choosing the first intersected object
    * A 2D selection made by aligning an object with a hand between the eye and the object
    - A selection made by casting a cone and choosing the objects inside it
    because: Image-plane selection is a 2D selection on a view plane. The user holds a hand or finger between the eye and the object and signals when the object lines up with the hand and eye.

    - By letting the user select an object directly under a single finger
    * By letting the user select a 3D region so objects inside it are selected
    because: Volumetric selection allows selection of a 3D region in virtual space, with objects within that region selected. The region can be a box, sphere, or cone.

    - It uses both hands to shape and reduce a box around a 3D region
    because: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection method that extends ray casting by casting a cone and selecting objects inside that cone.
  Q What is two-handed box selection?  [39/S4/F12]
    - A technique in which a sphere is cast onto a surface and objects inside the sphere are selected
    - A technique in which a hand is held between the eye and an object to align it
    - A technique in which a cone is cast to a distance and objects inside the cone are selected
    * A bimanual technique in which both hands position, orient, and shape a box to select a 3D region
    because: Two-handed box selection uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube, and progressively reduces it to select a specified 3D region.
  Q When is a volumetric selection technique less effective for selecting smaller objects?  [39/S4/F13]
    - When the pointing ray intersects only a single object
    * When the virtual environment is complex and contains many objects
    - When the user is selecting on a two-dimensional view plane
    - When the target object is small, well-defined, and isolated
    because: Volumetric selection is most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment. Selecting smaller objects becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.

39/A10  recap  39/S4  "Recap"  (13 facts, 24 concepts)
  Image plane selection is a 2D technique where a user selects an object on a view plane by positioning a hand between the eye and the object. This category includes techniques such as the head crusher, sticky finger, lifting palm, and framing hands. Volumetric selection extends this to 3D regions like cones, spheres, or boxes, including a bimanual technique where both hands are used to shape a region. These volumetric techniques are most useful for selecting small or well-defined isolated objects in less complex virtual environments.
  - Image plane selection is a 2D technique where the user selects an object on a view plane by positioning a hand between the eye and the object.
  - Image plane selection includes techniques such as the head crusher, sticky finger, lifting palm, and framing hands.
  - Volumetric selection allows for selecting 3D regions, such as cones, spheres, or boxes.
  - Two-handed box selection is a bimanual technique where the user uses both hands to shape a 3D region.
  - Volumetric selection is most useful for selecting small or well-defined isolated objects in less complex environments.

  - Indirect manipulation is sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects by manipulating other objects mapped to them.
