    - Ray-casting selection and navigation.
    - Indirect manipulation and bimanual manipulation.
    because: HOMER integrates ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation so that selection and manipulation are not performed separately.
  Q In HOMER, when the selected ray intersects the desired object, what happens next?  [39/S8/F2]
    * The user's virtual hand automatically moves to the object and attaches to it.
    - The object automatically moves to the user's virtual hand.
    - The ray automatically attaches to the object.
    - The virtual hand remains in its original position.
    because: In HOMER, the virtual hand moves automatically to the intersected object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object.
  Q After the virtual hand attaches to an object in HOMER, what does the user do with the object?  [39/S8/F3]
    - The user performs system control with familiar computer controls.
    * The user changes its position and orientation through hand manipulation.
    - The user controls the scene through a 3D widget.
    - The user navigates to another point in the virtual world.
    because: After the virtual hand attaches to the object, HOMER switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation.
  Q What ends the manipulation phase in HOMER?  [39/S8/F4]
    - The object reaches a predefined position.
    - The ray no longer intersects the selected object.
    * The user indicates that the job is done with a trigger or a specific hand gesture.
    - The virtual hand stops moving for a set period.
    because: Manipulation ends when the user indicates completion through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.

39/A18  recap  39/S8  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  Integrated hybrid manipulation automatically switches between selection and manipulation modes without explicit user signals. HOMER is a technique that combines ray casting and hand manipulation by automatically attaching the virtual hand to an object once selected by a ray. Users can then change the object's position and orientation before ending the task with a trigger or gesture.
  - Integrated hybrid manipulation automatically switches between selection and manipulation without explicit user signals.
  - HOMER is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that combines ray casting selection with hand manipulation.
  - In HOMER, selecting an object with a ray causes the virtual hand to automatically move to and attach to that object.
  - Once attached, the system switches to manipulation mode, allowing users to change the object's position and orientation.
  - Manipulation ends with a trigger or gesture, which returns the virtual hand to its original position.

39/A19  put_in_order  39/S8  "Order the steps of HOMER object manipulation"  (1 facts, 4 concepts)
  Order the steps of HOMER object manipulation: The user selects an object with ray casting > The ray intersects the desired object > The virtual hand moves to the object > The virtual hand attaches to the object  [39/S8/F2]

39/A20  quiz  39/S9  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Why can augmented reality systems use regular interaction techniques?  [39/S9/F0]
    * Because the user's senses are not blocked
    - Because the user is completely cut off from the real world
    - Because the user's senses are blocked
    - Because the interaction requires bimanual synchronized movement
    because: Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques to be used with the virtual augmentation of the real world because the user's senses are not blocked.
  Q Why do immersive environments need improved interaction techniques?  [39/S9/F1]
    * Because they block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world
    - Because they depend only on ordinary computer-system controls
    - Because they leave the user's real-world senses fully available
    - Because they allow regular interaction with the real-world augmentation
    because: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed for a better immersive experience.
  Q Which pair of interaction techniques is typically used in immersive environments and related to virtual objects?  [39/S9/F2]
    - Object selection and navigation
    - Navigation and system control
    - Object manipulation and system control
    * Object selection and object manipulation
    because: Object selection and object manipulation are the two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.
  Q What is the purpose of navigation techniques?  [39/S9/F3]
    - Changing settings on a computer system
    - Selecting virtual objects with a pointing ray
    - Matching virtual content with real-world surfaces
    * Moving from one point to another in a virtual world
    because: Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.
  Q What does system control interaction primarily rely on?  [39/S9/F4]
    - Techniques for manipulating virtual objects with both hands
    - Improved techniques required for fully immersive environments
    * Regular interaction techniques familiar from ordinary computer systems
    - Techniques for moving between locations in a virtual world
    because: System control interaction primarily relies on regular interaction techniques that are familiar when dealing with any computer system.

39/A21  recap  39/S9  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques because the user's senses are not blocked. Immersive environments block senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, requiring improved techniques such as object selection and manipulation for virtual objects. Navigation techniques are used to move from one point to another in a virtual world, while system control interaction primarily relies on regular techniques familiar to any computer system.
  - Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques because the user's senses are not blocked.
  - Immersive environments block senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, requiring improved interaction techniques for a better experience.
  - Object selection and manipulation are interaction techniques used for virtual objects in immersive environments.
  - Navigation techniques are used for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.
  - System control interaction primarily relies on regular techniques familiar to any computer system.

39/A27  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q In immersive interaction design, why might head pointing or eye-gaze pointing be useful for selecting virtual objects when hand tracking is unavailable?  [39/S3/F1, 39/S3/F2; pointing-based selection, virtual ray, hand tracking, head position, eye gaze, head-mounted display, eye tracker, hand pointing, eye-gaze pointing, virtual hand]
    A Pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing, head pointing with a head-mounted display, or eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. A virtual ray can be attached to the virtual hand, head position, or eye gaze, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.
  Q How do the go-go and prism techniques change virtual hand selection for distant objects, and why might prism still be preferable to go-go?  [39/S2/F3, 39/S2/F4, 39/S2/F7, 39/S2/F8; virtual hand technique, go-go technique, prism technique, virtual arm length, hand velocity, one-to-one mapping]
    A A direct virtual hand can require a long duration of physical hand movement to reach distant objects, so the go-go technique changes the virtual arm length and maps smaller physical hand movements to faster virtual hand movement. Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves below a specified speed and leaves the virtual hand still when the physical hand is slower than a specified minimum speed. Prism can therefore be a better solution for distant objects because the virtual hand slows or stops when the physical hand slows or stops, although it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.
  Q Why can selecting small or tightly grouped objects be difficult in both ray casting and volumetric selection, even though they use different selection geometries?  [39/S3/F5, 39/S4/F10, 39/S4/F13; ray casting, volumetric selection, cone casting flashlight technique, virtual ray, object selection technique, virtual environment]
    A Ray casting requires precise pointing of a virtual ray, so selecting small distant objects is difficult, especially when the small object is surrounded by other objects. The cone casting flashlight technique is volumetric and selects the objects within a cone, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects can be difficult. Volumetric selection is most useful for small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment and becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.
  Q Why might a single three-dimensional widget not be enough to fully manipulate a virtual object, and how does that follow from the idea of degrees of freedom?  [28/S2/F1, 28/S2/F2, 39/S6/F2; three-dimensional widget, degree of freedom, six degrees of freedom, three-dimensional, virtual object, manipulation]
    A Degrees of freedom describe the different ways an object can move in space, and in three-dimensional space an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch. A three-dimensional widget is typically responsible only for a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom. Therefore, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using individual widgets rather than one widget for all properties.

===== lecture 40: System Design

40/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is location awareness? (lecture 37) -> Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.
  What is go-go technique? (lecture 39) -> Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.
  What is object manipulation? (lecture 39) -> Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.
  What is three-dimensional widget? (lecture 39) -> Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.

40/A2  recap  40/S0  "Recap"  (2 facts, 6 concepts)
  The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move a user from one point to another by changing their viewpoint. This movement is composed of two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
  - Navigation in a virtual world moves the user from one point to another.
  - Navigation movement has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.

40/A3  quiz  40/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)

    * The actual movement between two locations
    - The creation of the virtual environment
    - The rendering of objects in the virtual environment
    - The planning of how to reach a destination
    because: The travel part of navigation is the motor component and refers to the actual movement between two locations.
  Q What are locomotion techniques, or travel techniques, used to do?  [40/S1/F1]
    * Let a user travel from one place to another and perceive that travel has taken place
    - Let a user plan a route without moving in the virtual world
    - Let a user render a virtual scene from a fixed position
    - Let a user create objects in the virtual environment
    because: Locomotion techniques are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.
  Q Which statement correctly describes the three ways travel in navigation can be done?  [40/S1/F2]
    - Exploration changes the viewpoint continuously, search has no explicit goal, and maneuvering moves around to see, learn, or explore.
    * Exploration has no explicit goal or target point, search moves to a specified target location, and maneuvering uses short, precise movements.
    - Exploration moves to a specified target location, search has no explicit goal, and maneuvering uses continuous control of direction and speed.
    - Exploration uses short, precise movements, search moves around to see, learn, or explore, and maneuvering moves to a specified target location.
    because: Travel can be done by exploration, which has no explicit goal, search, which moves to a specified target, or maneuvering, which comprises short, precise movements.
  Q Which four broad types of locomotion techniques are used to accomplish travel in navigation?  [40/S1/F3]
    - Full gait, partial gait, gait negation, and spatial steering
    * Walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based
    - Exploration, search, maneuvering, and wayfinding
    - Physical steering, selection-based, manipulation-based, and panoramic video
    because: Travel in navigation can be accomplished using walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based locomotion techniques.
  Q Which broad locomotion technique type involves navigating by manipulating certain things?  [40/S1/F4]
    - Steering-based locomotion
    - Selection-based locomotion
    * Manipulation-based locomotion
    - Walking-based locomotion
    because: Manipulation-based locomotion involves navigating by manipulating certain things, while object manipulation may not be involved in walking-based, steering-based, or selection-based locomotion.

40/A4  recap  40/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  Locomotion is the motor component of navigation referring to actual movement between locations. Locomotion techniques let users travel and perceive that travel in a virtual world through exploration, search, or maneuvering. There are four broad types of locomotion: walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based. While manipulation-based locomotion involves manipulating objects, navigation usually involves no object manipulation.
  - Locomotion is the motor component of navigation referring to actual movement between locations.
  - Locomotion techniques let users travel and perceive that travel in a virtual world.
  - Travel can be done through exploration, search, or maneuvering.
  - Locomotion techniques are categorized into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based types.
  - Manipulation-based locomotion involves manipulating objects, but navigation usually involves no object manipulation.

    - Selection-based travel
    - Manipulation-based travel
    because: Walking-based locomotion is divided into full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques.
  Q Why is physical walking restricted in full-gait techniques?  [40/S2/F2, 40/S2/F3]
    - Because the user must walk in place to avoid changing position
    - Because specialized pressure sensors are needed to detect the walking pattern
    * Completely free walking is impractical, so restricted physical walking is mapped to potentially unlimited virtual movement
    - Because natural lateral movement is difficult to map to focused virtual movement
    because: Although actual walking is the most natural form of travel, completely free walking is not practical, so physical walking is limited while virtual movement can be much larger.
  Q In a partial gait technique, how is virtual movement created?  [40/S2/F4, 40/S2/F5]
    - The user's actual walking in a bounded physical space is translated to virtual movement
    - The user's continuous direction and speed control a virtual vehicle
    * The user's walking-in-place pattern is mapped to virtual movement using specialized devices
    - The user's lateral movement is canceled by a fixed-position setup
    because: In partial gait techniques, the user walks in place without changing physical position, and specialized input devices map that walking pattern to movement in virtual space.
  Q Why does a gait-negation setup cancel the user's lateral movements?  [40/S2/F6]
    - To make full gait the most natural way to travel
    * Natural lateral walking is hard to map to focused virtual movement, so removing it helps the system infer intended travel
    - To map a single-place walking pattern to different virtual walking types
    - To let the user change physical position while moving in the virtual environment
    because: Gait-negation setups cancel lateral movement and keep the user's physical position fixed, making it easier for the system to understand the intended virtual movement.

40/A6  recap  40/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 10 concepts)
  Walking-based locomotion maps physical movement in the real world to movement in a virtual environment and is categorized into full gait, partial gait, and gait negation. Full gait translates real-world walking into virtual movement, although physical walking is often restricted. Partial gait involves walking in place with specialized devices, while gait negation uses specialized setups to cancel lateral movements to map the user's intended navigation.
  - Walking-based locomotion maps physical movement in the real world to movement in a virtual environment.
  - These techniques are broadly divided into full gait, partial gait, and gait negation.
  - Full gait techniques translate real-world walking into virtual movement, though physical walking is often restricted.
  - Partial gait involves walking in place with specialized devices, while gait negation uses specialized setups to cancel lateral movements.

40/A7  quiz  40/S3  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q Which feature defines steering-based navigation?  [40/S3/F0]
    - Instant movement to a chosen target
    - Selection of a destination without continuous control
    * Continuous control of direction and speed
    - Cancellation of lateral physical movement
    because: Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another.
  Q Steering-based navigation is divided into which two types?  [40/S3/F1]
    * Spatial steering-based and physical steering-based
    - Gaze-directed and hand-directed
    - Full gait and gait negation
    - Target selection and route planning
    because: Steering-based navigation has spatial steering-based navigation and physical steering-based navigation.
  Q In gaze-directed spatial steering-based navigation, how does movement occur?  [40/S3/F2]
    * Looking at a target moves the user continuously in that direction
    - Leaning the body cancels the user's lateral movement
    - Looking at a target instantly moves the user there
    - Hand gestures determine the direction of travel
    because: In gaze-directed spatial steering-based navigation, looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking.
  Q Which of the following is an example of physical steering-based navigation?  [40/S3/F1, 40/S3/F3]
    * A VR simulator for cars, boats, and spaceships
    - A gaze-directed travel technique
    - A hand-directed travel technique
    - A body-leaning directed travel technique
    because: Physical steering-based navigation uses vehicular props or additional hardware, such as VR simulators for cars, boats, and spaceships.

40/A8  recap  40/S3  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  Steering-based navigation involves continuously controlling direction and speed while moving. This navigation is divided into spatial steering-based navigation, which can be gaze-directed, hand-directed, or body-leaning directed, and physical steering-based navigation, which uses hardware or physical setups.
  - Steering-based navigation involves continuously controlling direction and speed while moving.
  - Navigation is categorized into spatial and physical steering-based types.
  - Spatial steering-based navigation includes gaze-directed, hand-directed, and body-leaning directed types.
  - Physical steering-based navigation involves using hardware or physical setups to control travel in a virtual world.

40/A9  quiz  40/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 10 concepts)
  Q What is the main idea behind selection-based locomotion?  [40/S4/F0]
    - The user continuously controls direction and speed while moving
    * The user selects where to go rather than continuously steering movement
    - The user's body leaning determines the travel direction
    - The user manipulates the virtual world's scale with gestures
    because: Selection-based locomotion lets the user choose the destination instead of continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking.
  Q What are the two types of selection-based locomotion?  [40/S4/F1]
    * Target selection-based and route planning-based
    - Spatial steering-based and physical steering-based
    - Target teleportation and map dragging
    - Gaze-directed and body-leaning directed
    because: Selection-based locomotion is divided into target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.
  Q In target selection-based locomotion, what happens after the user selects a destination?  [40/S4/F2]
    * The virtual viewpoint changes so the user feels moved to the target
    - The virtual world's scale changes to make the target appear closer
    - The user continues to steer direction and speed until arriving
    - The virtual viewpoint changes gradually along a preselected route
    because: In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to it.
  Q How does route planning-based locomotion differ from target selection-based teleportation?  [40/S4/F4]
    - The user manipulates objects to change the virtual viewpoint
    - The user continuously steers direction and speed during movement
    * The user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint
    - The user selects only the endpoint and the viewpoint jumps instantly
    because: Route planning-based locomotion selects a route to the target, allowing movement along a path and more granular control than merely teleporting to a target.
  Q Which implementation idea for manipulation-based locomotion works by changing the virtual viewpoint when certain objects are moved?  [40/S4/F6, 40/S4/F7]
    - The homer technique
    * The world in miniature metaphor
    - The go-go technique
    - Target selection-based teleportation
    because: In the world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects causes a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, as if the user moves.

40/A10  recap  40/S4  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Selection-based locomotion involves choosing a destination rather than continuously steering or looking to move. This category includes target selection-based locomotion, which instantly changes the viewpoint, and route planning-based locomotion, which provides more granular and natural movement. Alternatively, manipulation-based locomotion uses gestures to change the viewpoint or the world, such as the world in miniature metaphor where manipulating objects causes a change in the virtual viewpoint.
  - Selection-based locomotion involves choosing a destination rather than continuously steering or looking.
  - Target selection-based locomotion instantly changes the viewpoint to a selected destination.
  - Route planning-based locomotion involves selecting a path to provide more granular and natural movement.
  - Manipulation-based locomotion uses gestures to manipulate the viewpoint or the virtual world.
  - In the world in miniature metaphor, manipulating certain objects causes a change in the virtual viewpoint.

40/A11  quiz  40/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q What are the two components of navigation?  [40/S5/F0]
    - Steering-based navigation, and selection-based locomotion
    * Locomotion or travel, and wayfinding
    - Landmark knowledge, and map knowledge
    - Rendering, and tracking
    because: Navigation has a motor component, locomotion or travel, and wayfinding.
  Q What does wayfinding refer to?  [40/S5/F1]
    - Creating and updating a real-world map while localizing positions
    * Location awareness, path-finding to a destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world
    - Continuous control of direction and speed while moving between points
    - Selecting a target and changing the virtual viewpoint instantly
    because: Wayfinding involves location awareness, ascertaining a path to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.
  Q What can happen when an XR environment's design does not support the creation of a mental map?  [40/S5/F3]
    * Many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates
    - A world in miniature display automatically provides the missing spatial knowledge
    - The user no longer needs to know landmarks or follow procedural knowledge
    - Locomotion or travel alone becomes sufficient for efficient navigation
    because: The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; without that support, problems may occur and the user experience deteriorates.
  Q Which types of spatial knowledge form the essential knowledge base of a wayfinding mental model?  [40/S5/F4]
    - Steering-based navigation, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion
    * Landmark knowledge, procedural knowledge, and topological or map-like knowledge
    - Translational movement, rotational movement, and panoramic video
    - Material surface property, physical surface property, and triangular mesh
    because: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge, procedural knowledge, and topological or map-like knowledge.
  Q How does breadcrumb support help wayfinding?  [40/S5/F10]
    - It uses colors to show multiple paths through a single space
    * It leaves a trail of markers along a path already followed by predecessors
    - It specifies directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space
    - It displays the entire virtual world, the current position, and routes in miniature
    because: Breadcrumb support leaves a trail of markers along a path followed by predecessors, helping users recognize an explored path and avoid getting lost.

40/A12  recap  40/S5  "Recap"  (9 facts, 28 concepts)
  Navigation has two components: locomotion and wayfinding. Wayfinding is a mental model used to build a cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment. Wayfinding support is essential and can be provided through landmarks, maps, path following, breadcrumbs, and compasses.
  - Navigation has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.
  - Wayfinding is a mental model used to build a cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment.
  - Wayfinding support is essential and can be provided through landmarks, maps, path following, breadcrumbs, and compasses.

40/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (16 facts, 61 concepts)
  Q How do locomotion and wayfinding work together in navigation through a virtual world, and why is wayfinding support important for user experience?  [40/S0/F1, 40/S1/F0, 40/S5/F1, 40/S5/F2, 40/S5/F6; virtual world, navigation, travel, locomotion, wayfinding, mental model, user experience]
    A Navigation in a virtual world includes travel and wayfinding, and locomotion is the motor component that moves the user from one point to another. Wayfinding refers to location awareness and to building a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment. Locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, because without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use travel techniques efficiently or effectively in a complex virtual environment.
  Q Why can full gait techniques create a mismatch between physical and virtual movement, and how do partial gait and gait negation techniques handle the user's physical movement?  [40/S2/F3, 40/S2/F4, 40/S2/F5, 40/S2/F6; walking-based locomotion, full gait technique, partial gait technique, gait negation technique, virtual navigation]
    A In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical, so walking is restricted in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in virtual space, creating a mismatch. In partial gait techniques, the user walks in place and specialized devices or active walking interfaces map the in-place walking pattern to different types of virtual movement. In gait negation techniques, a specialized setup cancels lateral movement and keeps the user's physical position fixed before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation.
  Q How does target selection-based locomotion differ from route planning-based locomotion, and why can route planning give a more gradual sense of movement?  [40/S4/F0, 40/S4/F1, 40/S4/F2, 40/S4/F4; selection-based locomotion, target selection-based locomotion, route planning-based locomotion, teleportation, virtual viewpoint]
    A Target selection-based locomotion lets the user select a destination, and the virtual viewpoint changes so the user feels moved to the target, as in teleportation, map dragging, or the jumper technique. Route planning-based locomotion lets the user select a route to the target rather than only the endpoint. Different viewpoint changes while moving through the selected route make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.
  Q How is interaction for system control different from navigation and object interaction in an immersive environment?  [40/S6/F0, 40/S6/F1, 38/S7/F2; interaction for system control, navigation, object manipulation, system state, system mode, command]
    A Object interaction in immersive environments means selecting and manipulating objects that are part of the virtual environment, while navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment. Interaction for system control issues commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file. It can use physical controllers, graphical menus, voice commands, gesture commands, tools, or multimodal interaction techniques.

===== lecture 41: System Design

41/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
  What is virtual tour? (lecture 33) -> Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.
  What is navigation? (lecture 38) -> Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.
  What is locomotion technique? (lecture 40) -> Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.
  What is wayfinding? (lecture 40) -> Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

41/A15  quiz  41/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In the island tour, how does movement from one place to another happen?  [41/S6/F0]
    - By walking continuously through a 3D island model
    - By switching between two minimap views
    - By changing the camera position inside one image
    * By transitioning from one 360-degree image to another
    because: Each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.
  Q What does view interpolation do during a transition between two 360-degree images?  [41/S6/F1]
    - It changes the surrounding scenes to create motion
    - It guides the user from one image to another
    - It gives the user a seated viewpoint inside a vehicle
    * It blurs the image boundaries to make the transition smooth and avoid jerks
    because: View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition by blurring the boundaries between two 360-degree images, preventing sudden movement or jerks.
  Q Why was a different travel technique required for exploring the entire island?  [41/S6/F4]
    * Because walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness
    - Because walking-based navigation is unavailable for any place on the island
    - Because view interpolation cannot link 360-degree images
    - Because the virtual vehicle cannot be selected by the user
    because: Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness.
  Q How does the virtual vehicle travel technique determine the movement path?  [41/S6/F6]
    - The system plans the path from the user's walking speed
    - The user selects a visible target and moves there instantly
    * The user selects a destination, which selects a pre-planned route
    - The user draws a free path for the vehicle to follow
    because: The technique is selection-based and uses pre-planned routes: the user selects a destination to select a route, not a target or an instantaneous movement.
  Q How does the virtual vehicle travel technique create the feeling of motion?  [41/S6/F5]
    - Navigation arrows point from one spot to another
    - View interpolation blurs the boundaries of two images
    - The user walks through the 360-degree images
    * The surrounding scenes change as the vehicle moves
    because: When the vehicle is selected, the user has a seated viewpoint inside it, and the surrounding scenes change as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion.

41/A16  recap  41/S6  "Recap"  (7 facts, 19 concepts)
  Moving between locations in the tour involves transitioning between 360-degree images using view interpolation to ensure smooth visual transitions. Navigation arrows guide the user between images to prevent random movement. To avoid the time and cybersickness of walking, a virtual vehicle metaphor is used for long-distance travel. This technique provides a seated viewpoint and allows for selection-based movement along pre-planned routes.
  - Moving between locations in the tour involves transitioning between 360-degree images.
  - View interpolation blurs boundaries to ensure smooth transitions and prevent jerks.
  - Navigation arrows guide the user between images to prevent random movement.
  - A virtual vehicle metaphor facilitates long-distance travel to avoid the time and cybersickness associated with walking.
  - The virtual vehicle technique provides a seated viewpoint and uses ray casting for selection-based movement on pre-planned routes.

41/A19  quiz  41/S8  "Quick quiz"  (3 facts, 12 concepts)
  Q How does the controlled navigation technique reduce cybersickness in the XR tour?  [41/S8/F0]
    - It removes visual cues so the user receives less sensory information.
    - It speeds up viewpoint changes to shorten travel time.
    * It uses joystick-based navigation or teleportation to prevent abrupt movements.
    - It encourages users to walk freely through every scene at any speed.
    because: The joystick-based controlled navigation supports smooth movement and avoids abrupt movements that can cause discomfort.
  Q Why must the speed of vehicular movement be chosen carefully?  [41/S8/F1]
    - Because slow movement always produces the most immersive feeling.
    - Because speed changes alter the joystick's teleported destination.
    - Because faster movement reduces the need for visual cues.
    * Because an inappropriate speed of viewpoint change can cause cybersickness.
    because: In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not carefully chosen.
  Q What role do consistent visual cues and smooth transitions play in the XR design?  [41/S8/F2]
    - They hide distant landmarks to simplify the virtual environment.
    - They replace joystick input with direct vehicle control.
    - They increase motion speed by shortening each viewpoint change.
    * They maintain spatial orientation and reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts.
    because: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help users keep orientation, improve awareness, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and help avoid severe cybersickness effects in the long term.

41/A20  recap  41/S8  "Recap"  (3 facts, 12 concepts)
  Controlled navigation via joystick use or teleportation minimizes cybersickness by avoiding abrupt movements. Additionally, the speed of change of viewpoint in vehicular movement must be chosen carefully to avoid causing discomfort. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help maintain spatial orientation and reduce sensory conflicts.
  - Controlled navigation using a joystick or teleportation minimizes cybersickness by avoiding abrupt movements.
  - Vehicle movement speeds must be chosen carefully to avoid causing cybersickness.
  - Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions maintain spatial orientation and reduce sensory conflicts.

41/A28  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 43 concepts)
  Q How does identifying pilgrims, students, and tourists as user categories shape what a user sees in the Majuli VR tour before and during the experience?  [41/S1/F0, 41/S1/F1, 41/S2/F2, 41/S7/F1; user categories, user experience design, contextual inquiry, user group, icon, tablet interface, video player, user type, video]
    A In user experience design, the first stage is to identify the users so the experience can be designed accordingly. The tour identifies pilgrims, students, and tourists, whose preferences were collected through contextual inquiry, and before the tour the user chooses one of these groups using icons. During the tour, the tablet interface lists videos available for the current spot, and the corresponding material is added in a way that depends on the user type, so relevant information is tailored to that user.
  Q How do the virtual vehicle travel technique and the dual maps address the two components of navigation in the Majuli VR tour?  [40/S5/F0, 40/S1/F1, 41/S6/F6, 41/S5/F5, 41/S5/F6; navigation, locomotion technique, wayfinding, virtual vehicle travel technique, selection-based locomotion technique, route, destination, virtual world, dual maps, global map, minimap, orientation awareness]
    A Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding. The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which a route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route, allowing the user to travel in the virtual world and perceive that travel has occurred. The dual maps, made of a global map and a local minimap, support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the world in miniature and reducing clutter.
  Q Why is view interpolation important when a place in the Majuli VR tour is built from separate 360-degree images, and how does that choice support user comfort?  [41/S6/F0, 41/S6/F1, 41/S8/F2; 360-degree image, view interpolation, smooth transition, spatial orientation, anxiety, sensory conflict, cybersickness]
    A Each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another. View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause. Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions help maintain spatial orientation, reduce anxiety and sensory conflict, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

===== lecture 42: System Implementation

42/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC)? (lecture 32) -> In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.
  What is design? (lecture 41) -> In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is computer? (lecture 13) -> Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

  Q In an interactive system development lifecycle, what does empirical evaluation assess?  [42/S0/F0]
    - The usability of a single prototype
    * The usability of the whole system
    - The performance of the code after testing
    - The appearance of the interface design
    because: Empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.
  Q At what point in the interactive system development lifecycle is empirical usability evaluation performed?  [42/S0/F2]
    - After every quick evaluation of a prototype
    - During the initial feasibility study
    * After the code is bug-free or runs smoothly
    - Before requirement gathering is complete
    because: The lifecycle places the empirical or usability evaluation stage finally, after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.
  Q Why is the design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle repeated?  [42/S0/F3]
    * To refine the design until it stabilizes
    - To rewrite the requirements after each evaluation
    - To replace final usability evaluation with quick checks
    - To finish the full coded system as early as possible
    because: In this cycle, the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.
  Q Which stage of interactive system development is described as standard software development work with nothing special for VR or AR?  [42/S0/F4]
    - Quick evaluation of a design prototype
    - Final usability evaluation of the whole system
    - Repeated interface design until users are satisfied
    * Coding and implementation after code design
    because: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation are standard software development stages, with nothing special or distinct for VR or AR.
  Q Why should cycles in the interactive system development lifecycle generally be kept infrequent?  [42/S0/F6]
    - To reduce the need for usability evaluation
    * To avoid cost and time overrun
    - To keep the code from being tested too early
    - To let the design stabilize after one pass
    because: Frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, so cycles should generally be kept infrequent.

42/A2  recap  42/S0  "Recap"  (6 facts, 22 concepts)
  The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to XR systems and includes a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation to stabilize the design. Coding and implementation follow standard software development lifecycle stages. Finally, an empirical usability evaluation assesses the whole system from a usability perspective once the code is bug-free.
  - The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.
  - The design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle that repeats until the design stabilizes.
  - Code design, coding, implementation, and code testing are standard software development lifecycle stages.
  - Empirical evaluation, or usability evaluation, assesses the whole system from a usability perspective once the code is bug-free.
  - Cycles should generally be kept infrequent to avoid cost and time overruns, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

42/A7  quiz  42/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q What are prototyping techniques mainly used for?  [42/S2/F0]
    - Producing a final product without later refinement or testing
    - Building a complete full implementation before any evaluation
    - Replacing design guidelines with a final verdict on usability
    * Quickly building and evaluating design ideas to collect usability feedback
    because: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.
  Q Why can a prototype be preferred over a full implementation when testing whether a design will work?  [42/S2/F2]
    - It already proves the design is usable without any evaluation
    - It is a full implementation with similar resource, manpower, and cost demands
    - It implements all functionalities in depth before collecting user feedback
    * It is a lightweight implementation with much lower resource, manpower, and cost demands
    because: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, used to test whether a design idea will work in practice.
  Q Why are design guidelines alone not enough to judge whether a design will work?  [42/S2/F1]
    * They are only a starting point and do not show whether the design is usable or unusable
    - They provide a quick evaluation of the design after implementation
    - They list the final functional requirements that guarantee a usable design
    - They define the user groups that must be tested in the system
    because: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable.
  Q What is a risk of developing a full software implementation before testing the design idea?  [42/S2/F3]
    - The full system is guaranteed to be usable once every function is built
    * Money and time spent on programmers and resources can be wasted if the idea is not good
    - The project avoids cost components such as resource procurement and manpower engagement
    - The design is accepted as good without needing empirical evaluation
    because: A full implementation involves highly skilled manpower and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted.
  Q What can happen to a prototype after it has been used to test design ideas?  [42/S2/F4]
    - It must always be replaced by a separately built full implementation
    - It must remain a horizontal prototype for feedback on appearance
    * It can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it becomes the final product
    - It cannot be changed after its first evaluation has been completed
    because: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

42/A8  recap  42/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 8 concepts)
  Prototyping techniques are typically used for quick evaluation and to collect feedback on usability. Since design guidelines are only a starting point, designs must be implemented and tested to see if they work. A prototype is a lightweight implementation used to test if a design idea works in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first, and it can be discarded or, in the best case, refined into the final product.
  - Prototyping techniques are typically used for quick evaluation and to collect feedback on usability.
  - Because design guidelines are only a starting point, designs must be implemented and tested to see if they work.
  - A prototype is a lightweight implementation used to test if a design idea works in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.
  - Full implementation involves highly skilled manpower and many cost components, so money and time can be wasted if an idea is later found not good.
  - A prototype can be discarded after testing or, in the best case, refined into the final product.

42/A9  quiz  42/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q Which description best matches a horizontal prototype?  [42/S3/F1]
    - An in-depth implementation of selected features from first to last screen
    - A series of sketches showing the sequence of actions in a task
    - A complete implementation of every feature in the system
    * A surface-level depiction of the entire interface's look, feel, and appearance
    because: A horizontal prototype shows how the interface appears to the user at a surface level, without functionality or interaction.
  Q What is a horizontal prototype most suitable for?  [42/S3/F2]
    - Capturing the sequence of user actions in a task
    - Testing whether every feature works in the full system
    - Analyzing interactions implemented in selected features
    * Eliciting feedback about whether the interface's appearance is understandable and intuitive
    because: Horizontal prototypes are used to discuss and collect user feedback on the look, feel, and appearance of an interface.
  Q Which description best matches a vertical prototype?  [42/S3/F3]
    * An in-depth implementation of selected commonly used features, from first screen to last
    - A surface-level depiction of the whole interface without interaction
    - A single sketch showing only the layout of one screen
    - A complete implementation of every feature in the system
    because: A vertical prototype implements a few selected features in depth, from the first screen to the last screen after the final action.
  Q Why are vertical prototypes suitable for analyzing interactions and features?  [42/S3/F3, 42/S3/F4]
    - Because they avoid implementing any functionality
    - Because they represent every feature in the full system
    * Because they implement interactions for a few selected features
    - Because they show the entire interface only at a surface level
    because: Vertical prototypes are suitable for analyzing interactions and features because they implement those interactions, rather than merely showing appearance.
  Q Which statement about the terms in a vertical prototype description is correct?  [42/S3/F5]
    - The term 'implemented' means building the full final system, and 'screen' means only a paper sketch
    - The term 'implemented' always means writing code, and 'screen' means only a physical display
    - The term 'implemented' means only VR rendering, and 'screen' means only a virtual scene
    * The term 'implemented' may not mean writing code, and 'screen' may be a 2D screen or an immersive scene
    because: In a vertical prototype, implemented and screen are generic: implementation does not require code, and a screen can be a 2D screen or a virtual or immersive scene.

42/A10  recap  42/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  Prototypes can be categorized as horizontal or vertical. Horizontal prototypes depict the entire interface's look and feel without functionality, making them suitable for gathering feedback on appearance and usability. Vertical prototypes focus on implementing the most commonly used features in depth to analyze interactions, using the terms "implemented" and "screen" generically.
  - Prototypes can be categorized as horizontal or vertical.
  - Horizontal prototypes depict the entire interface's look and feel without any functionality.
  - Horizontal prototypes are suitable for gathering feedback on appearance and usability.
  - Vertical prototypes implement the most commonly used features in depth to analyze interactions.
  - In vertical prototypes, the terms "implemented" and "screen" are generic.

    * It is made without a computer, code, or programming, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.
    - It is made using a computer program, as reduced-scale actual software development.
    - It is made with digital animation or a slideshow that simulates interaction.
    - It is made on a computer with simple static screens, but no coding is involved.
    because: A low-fidelity prototype is created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.
  Q What is the primary use of low-fidelity prototyping?  [42/S4/F1]
    - To make a computer-based static interface or simple animation for testing interaction.
    - To use programming to create a reduced-scale version of the actual software system.
    * To make and modify prototypes quickly and cheaply, brainstorm designs, and obtain user feedback on usability.
    - To implement a few selected features in depth from the first screen to the last screen.
    because: Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes and is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.
  Q How are low-fidelity prototypes related to horizontal and vertical prototypes?  [42/S4/F2]
    - They are used only for horizontal prototypes because they cannot represent interactions.
    - They are used only for vertical prototypes because they always implement functionality.
    - They are primarily associated with high-fidelity implementation because they require programming.
    * They are intuitively associated with horizontal prototypes but can also be used for vertical prototypes.
    because: Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.
  Q What is an interface sketch?  [42/S4/F3]
    - A working software build that implements selected features in depth.
    - A hardware specification describing input devices that track user actions.
    - A computer-generated animation of a full interface task from beginning to end.
    * A simple paper drawing of major interface components, their appearance, and their layout.
    because: An interface sketch is a simple drawing, often on paper, that depicts the major components of an interface, including screen elements, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout.
  Q How does a storyboard represent interaction in low-fidelity prototyping?  [42/S4/F5, 42/S4/F6]
    * It uses a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, to show user actions and screen appearances from task start to end.
    - It uses a single keyframe to show only the final result of the task.
    - It uses one detailed interface sketch to show the final appearance of the main screen.
    - It uses a computer program to run the complete system and test actual performance.
    because: A storyboard uses a series of interface sketches, with each sketch as a keyframe snapshot, to capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances from the beginning of a task to its end.

42/A12  recap  42/S4  "Recap"  (7 facts, 13 concepts)
  Low-fidelity prototypes are created without technological intervention using non-digital materials to primarily brainstorm designs and obtain user feedback. While an interface sketch depicts major components and layout, storyboarding uses a series of sketches as keyframes to capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances for a task. Because these prototypes allow for the evaluation and revision of ideas, an interface sketch need not be replicated exactly in the final design.
  - Low-fidelity prototypes are created without technological intervention using non-digital materials to primarily brainstorm designs and obtain user feedback.
  - An interface sketch depicts major components and layout but is not sufficient to prototype interaction sequences.
  - Storyboarding uses a series of sketches as keyframes to capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances for a task.
  - These prototypes allow for the evaluation and revision of ideas, so an interface sketch need not be replicated exactly in the final design.

42/A13  quiz  42/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q Which statement best distinguishes medium-fidelity prototyping from low-fidelity prototyping?  [42/S5/F0]
    * Medium-fidelity uses a computer without coding, while low-fidelity does not use computers or digital media.
    - Medium-fidelity uses programming to create reduced-scale software, while low-fidelity uses paper mockups.
    - Medium-fidelity uses no digital media, while low-fidelity uses simple computer animations.
    - Medium-fidelity relies on a hidden wizard, while low-fidelity uses static cardboard mockups.
    because: Medium-fidelity creates simple prototypes on a computer without coding, whereas low-fidelity does not rely on computers or digital media.
  Q What characterizes a high-fidelity prototype?  [42/S5/F1]
    - It uses a computer to make static sketches without any real functionality.
    - It relies on an unseen human operator to produce the displayed response.
    * It uses computer programs or programming, making it reduced-scale software development.
    - It is made from non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.
    because: A high-fidelity prototype is created with computer programs or programming, so it is effectively actual software development, possibly on a reduced scale.
  Q Why does high-fidelity prototyping require much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping?  [42/S5/F2]
    - It must be built without digital tools to keep the process simple.
    - It only represents static screens and does not include interaction.
    * It is more sophisticated and needs skilled programmers with programming expertise.
    - It needs a hidden wizard to simulate all user responses.
    because: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.
  Q In medium-fidelity prototyping, what can an animation video or a slideshow with simple key presses or timers create?  [42/S5/F3]
    - A low-fidelity prototype by using paper storyboards.
    * A vertical prototype by simulating interaction.
    - A full implementation by completing the entire software system.
    - A horizontal prototype by showing static interface sketches.
    because: In medium-fidelity prototyping, simple animated interaction can simulate a vertical prototype, while static interface sketches produce only a horizontal prototype.
  Q Which prototyping approach is primarily meant for vertical prototypes?  [42/S5/F4]
    - Medium-fidelity prototyping approaches.
    * High-fidelity prototyping approaches.
    - Hidden-wizard prototyping approaches.
    - Low-fidelity prototyping approaches.
    because: High-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, while low-fidelity is primarily horizontal and medium-fidelity is primarily both.

42/A14  recap  42/S5  "Recap"  (5 facts, 20 concepts)
  Medium-fidelity prototyping uses computers without coding, while low-fidelity prototyping does not rely on computers or digital media. High-fidelity prototyping involves computer programming and is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale, requiring much more effort and skilled programmers with programming expertise. Medium-fidelity approaches can produce both horizontal and vertical prototypes, whereas low-fidelity prototypes are primarily for horizontal prototypes and high-fidelity approaches are primarily for vertical prototypes.
  - Medium-fidelity prototyping uses computers without coding, while low-fidelity prototyping does not rely on computers or digital media.
  - High-fidelity prototyping uses computer programs or programming and is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.
  - High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort and skilled programmers with programming expertise.
  - Medium-fidelity approaches can produce horizontal prototypes through static sketches and vertical prototypes through simulated interaction.
  - Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity for both horizontal and vertical, and high-fidelity primarily for vertical prototypes.

42/A15  quiz  42/S6  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In a Wizard of Oz prototype, who actually produces the response received by the user?  [42/S6/F0]
    * An unseen human operator called the wizard
    - The visible computer screen
    - A hidden camera
    - An autonomous computer
    because: The Wizard of Oz technique makes the user believe they are interacting with an autonomous computer, while an unseen human operator, the wizard, controls the response.
  Q Why was the Wizard of Oz approach used in the listening typewriter experiment?  [42/S6/F1]
    - To demonstrate a complete virtual reality hardware system
    - To test the accuracy of an existing speech recognizer
    * To test a speech recognition idea before the recognizer technology existed
    - To build a high-fidelity prototype with programmed software
    because: The approach was used to test the acceptability of a speech recognition idea before committing resources to build a recognizer, because the required technology was not yet available.
  Q What arrangement in the listening typewriter setup allowed the user to believe the computer was autonomous?  [42/S6/F2]
    - A single computer directly connected to the microphone
    * A hidden wizard separated from the user by a wall
    - A user sitting next to the hidden wizard
    - A wizard visible to the user through a window
    because: The setup placed a hidden wizard behind a wall, while the user faced a computer and believed it was operating on its own.
  Q How did the hidden wizard create the illusion that speech was automatically converted into text?  [42/S6/F3]
    - By having the computer convert the speech itself
    * By typing characters that were transmitted to the user's screen
    - By speaking the characters into the microphone
    - By having the user type the characters onto the screen
    because: The wizard heard the user's speech, typed the corresponding characters, and sent them to the user's screen, so the user believed speech had been automatically converted.

42/A16  recap  42/S6  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  The Wizard of Oz approach involves a hidden human operating a computer that a user believes is autonomous. This allows developers to test if a technology is acceptable before the actual technology exists. In this setup, a hidden operator receives user input and manually provides a response to simulate an automated system.
  - The Wizard of Oz approach involves a hidden human operating a computer that a user believes is autonomous.
  - This approach can test if a technology is acceptable before the actual technology exists.
  - A hidden operator receives user input and manually provides a response to simulate an automated system.

42/A22  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (21 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q How does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle fit into the development of an extended reality system, and why must its evaluation be quick?  [42/S0/F1, 42/S0/F2, 42/S0/F3, 42/S1/F1, 42/S1/F2, 42/S1/F3, 32/S6/F0; interactive system development lifecycle, extended reality system, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, interface design, interaction design, usability evaluation, quick evaluation, turnaround time, cost overrun, prototype]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality systems, and building interactive software is broadly similar to regular software, with differences in requirement gathering, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical study stages. The lifecycle includes a design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle that is repeated until the design stabilizes, where design means interface and interaction design rather than code design. Quick usability evaluation is required because the cycle may need many repetitions; if evaluation is slow, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun, while a quick prototype and quick evaluation method keep the cycles within a reasonable timeframe.
  Q Why can a prototype be a better way to test a design idea than immediately doing a full implementation, especially when design guidelines are available?  [42/S2/F1, 42/S2/F2, 42/S2/F3, 42/S2/F4; design guideline, prototype, full implementation, usability, testing, programmer, final product]
    A Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is usable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested. A prototype is a lightweight implementation with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, so it can test whether a design idea will work before programmers and expensive resources are committed. A full implementation uses highly skilled programmers and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted. After serving its purpose, the prototype can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it evolves into the final product.
  Q How do horizontal and vertical prototypes differ, and why can a storyboard support the kind of prototype that a single interface sketch cannot?  [42/S3/F1, 42/S3/F2, 42/S3/F3, 42/S3/F4, 42/S4/F4, 42/S4/F5, 42/S4/F6; horizontal prototype, vertical prototype, interface, user feedback, interaction, feature, functionality, interface sketch, storyboard, keyframe, user action, task, screen]
    A A horizontal prototype depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is suitable for obtaining user feedback about appearance. A vertical prototype primarily represents selected interactions or features by implementing them in depth from the first screen to the last screen, so it is suitable for analyzing interaction. A single interface sketch is primarily a horizontal prototype because it does not show the sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes. A series of interface sketches forms a storyboard, whose keyframes can capture the sequence of user actions from the beginning to the end of a task and thus give a vertical prototype.
  Q Why can the Wizard of Oz approach be useful for testing an interaction idea, and what did the IBM listening typewriter experiment use it to do?  [42/S2/F2, 42/S6/F0, 42/S6/F1, 42/S6/F3; prototype, interaction, wizard of oz approach, wizard, international business machines, listening typewriter experiment, speech recognition system, microphone, computer]
    A A prototype is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice before full implementation is committed. In the Wizard of Oz approach, a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen wizard operates the computer and returns the requested response. In the 1984 IBM listening typewriter experiment, the user spoke into a microphone, the hidden wizard heard the speech, typed corresponding characters, and transmitted them to the user's screen, making the user believe speech had been automatically converted. IBM used this to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system before committing resources to build one, because the automatic technology was not yet available.
