===== lecture 46: System Implementation

46/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is empirical study? (lecture 32) -> The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
  What is controlled experiment? (lecture 45) -> A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.
  What is experiment? (lecture 45) -> An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.
  What is level? (lecture 45) -> The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.
  What is test condition? (lecture 45) -> Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.
  What is usability? (lecture 24) -> Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

46/A1  quiz  46/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In experiment design, why should the selected participants be representative of all potential users?  [46/S0/F0]
    * To make the conclusions about that user group valid and reliable
    - To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design
    - To make a between-subjects design easier to manage
    - To ensure the task set covers common interface tasks
    because: Participants are a subset of all potential users, so if the subset is not representative, the conclusions drawn from it are not valid or reliable.
  Q When is it acceptable to use a homogeneous group of experiment participants?  [46/S0/F1]
    * When the system is intended for that homogeneous user group
    - When the system is intended for heterogeneous users
    - When the task sequence is randomized to reduce practice effects
    - When the task set is limited to commonly used tasks
    because: A homogeneous user subset is acceptable when the system is for that homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions about a heterogeneous user group.
  Q In experiment design, what is a user profile?  [46/S0/F2]
    - The objective data collected while participants perform tasks in the interface
    * A set of well-defined characteristics used to define the user before selecting participants
    - The allocation of test conditions to participants in a within-subject design
    - A small subset of tasks that participants perform during the experiment
    because: A user profile is a set of well-defined user characteristics; the user is first defined by that profile, and participants are selected only on its basis.
  Q Why should age and computer-use frequency be considered when selecting participants for a typing task?  [46/S0/F3]
    - Because they indicate whether a random text is representative for the typing task
    - Because they determine whether a between-subjects design is needed
    * Because they can lead to different typing behavior and typing speeds
    - Because they determine how many participants are needed for reliable conclusions
    because: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users.

46/A2  recap  46/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 16 concepts)
  Participants must be a representative sample of the whole user group so that the conclusions drawn from the subset are valid. A homogeneous subset is acceptable for a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group. Participants are selected based on a user profile of well-defined characteristics, which must include factors like age and experience that are likely to influence behavior.
  - Participants must be a representative sample of the whole user group for conclusions to be valid.
  - Homogeneous subsets are only reliable for drawing conclusions if the system is for a homogeneous group.
  - Participants are selected based on a user profile of well-defined characteristics.
  - User profiles must include characteristics like age and experience that are likely to influence behavior.

46/A3  quiz  46/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q In a controlled empirical experiment, why can conclusions from a very small participant group be questionable?  [46/S1/F0]
    - They fail because the selected tasks are not representative of the interface.
    * They may not be reliable and may change if the participant count is increased.
    - They rely on subjective user preferences instead of task performance data.
    - They are confounded mainly by a practice effect from repeated practice.
    because: With a small participant group, the conclusions may be unreliable and can change if the number of participants is increased.
  Q In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, what type of task data is typically collected from users?  [46/S1/F1]
    - Mostly system resource usage data.
    - Mostly user profile characteristics.
    - Mostly subjective user preference data.
    * Mostly objective task performance data.
    because: In such an experiment, users perform tasks, and the collected task performance data are mostly objective.
  Q In a controlled interface experiment, why may researchers use only a small subset of all tasks supported by the system?  [46/S1/F2]
    - Because random tasks are more reliable for judging usability.
    - Because subjective data cannot be collected for some tasks.
    * Because testing all tasks may be limited by time or practicality.
    - Because each participant must learn the whole system before starting.
    because: Only a small subset can be used because of less time or practicality, and it must be chosen carefully.
  Q What distinguishes a representative task set for an interface from an arbitrary set of tasks?  [46/S1/F3]
    * It contains the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use in practice.
    - It is chosen only to minimize the time needed for implementation.
    - It contains every task supported by the system, regardless of use.
    - It consists of tasks that are performed by only a few expert users.
    because: A representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks used by everybody most of the time.
  Q When comparing typing interfaces in an experiment, which typing task is representative?  [46/S1/F4]
    - A text string selected only for one user profile.
    * Text strings selected using metrics that indirectly cover the interface and typing skills.
    - A random piece of text selected from any document.
    - A text string selected only because it is short.
    because: A random piece of text is not representative, while representative typing tasks are chosen based on metrics that indirectly encompass the interface and typing skills.

46/A4  recap  46/S1  "Recap"  (4 facts, 9 concepts)
  A participant count between 12 and 25 is generally assumed to be sufficient to draw reliable conclusions in a controlled empirical experiment. Evaluation relies on analyzing objective data collected from users performing specific tasks. Because only a small subset of tasks can be used, these must be chosen carefully from a representative set of tasks that users most frequently use to ensure the data reflects overall usability.
  - A participant count between 12 and 25 is generally assumed to draw reliable conclusions.
  - Interface evaluation relies on analyzing objective data collected from user tasks.
  - A representative subset of tasks that users most frequently use must be chosen carefully to ensure the data is useful for drawing reliable conclusions about overall usability.

46/A5  quiz  46/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Q In a between-subjects experimental design, how are the tasks for the test conditions assigned?  [46/S2/F0]
    - Every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions.
    * They are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
    - Tasks are assigned according to participants' user characteristics.
    - Each participant receives the same numbered task sequence.
    because: In a between-subjects design, the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.
  Q Why may a between-subjects design be selected even when a within-subject design is easier to manage?  [46/S2/F1]
    - Because it lets every participant perform all test conditions.
    - Because it requires the same task sequence for all participants.
    * Because the availability of participants and resources may force it.
    - Because it makes the practice effect statistically zero.
    because: Choosing between within-subject and between-subjects designs depends on circumstances, and participant or resource availability may force a between-subject design.
  Q In a within-subject design, what is the practice effect?  [46/S2/F2]
    * An improvement in task performance from repeated practice.
    - A decrease in task performance from repeated practice.
    - A variation in performance caused by differences in user characteristics.
    - An improvement in task performance caused by the interface under test.
    because: The practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice, and it can confound analysis by making gains appear due to practice rather than the interface.
  Q In a within-subject design, how can the practice effect be reduced?  [46/S2/F3]
    - By assigning tasks according to participants' user characteristics.
    * By randomizing or systematically varying the task sequence.
    - By assigning the same task sequence to every participant.
    - By selecting only the tasks most commonly used in practice.
    because: Random or systematic variation of the task sequence is used to nullify the practice effect in a within-subject design.
  Q What does a Latin square design do in task assignment?  [46/S2/F4]
    * It systematically varies the task sequence by shifting it one position for each successive participant.
    - It gives the same task sequence to every participant.
    - It divides the tasks for all conditions among subsets of participants.
    - It randomly changes the task sequence independently for each participant.
    because: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered sequence one position for each successive participant.

46/A6  recap  46/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 9 concepts)
  Tasks can be assigned using a within-subject design, where every participant performs all tasks, or a between-subjects design, where tasks are divided among subsets. While within-subject designs are easier to manage, the choice between them depends on participant and resource availability. To reduce the practice effect in within-subject designs, task sequences can be randomized or systematically varied using a Latin square design.
  - Tasks can be assigned using a within-subject design or a between-subjects design.
  - Within-subject designs are easier to manage, but the choice depends on participant and resource availability.
  - Repeated practice in a within-subject design can create a practice effect that confounds the analysis.
  - Randomizing or systematically varying the task sequence can reduce the practice effect.
  - A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence for each participant.

46/A7  quiz  46/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Q What is the role of the data analysis stage in system implementation?  [46/S3/F0]
    - Comparing interfaces using only absolute text-entry speed values
    - Assigning tasks using a within-subject or between-subjects design
    * Processing empirical data and testing it for statistical significance before drawing conclusions
    - Collecting empirical data from the actual population of users
    because: The data analysis stage is where empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions about a design's efficacy are drawn.
  Q In empirical interface studies, what is the relationship between the data collected and the conclusions of interest?  [46/S3/F1]
    - The data come from the actual population, while the conclusions concern the sample of users
    * The data come from a sample of users, while the conclusions concern the larger population
    - The data come from one participant, while the conclusions concern the larger population
    - The data come from the sample of users, while the conclusions concern the sample of users
    because: Empirical interface studies obtain data from a sample of users, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population.
  Q What does a statistically significant difference between observed data values indicate?  [46/S3/F3]
    - It indicates that the participants are the actual population rather than a sample
    - It indicates that the two groups have exactly the same absolute mean value
    * It indicates that the difference is not due to chance but to the tested conditions
    - It indicates that the difference is due to chance rather than the tested conditions
    because: A statistical significance test shows whether an observed difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a significant difference is not due to chance.
  Q When comparing two text-entry interfaces, what does the analysis focus on?  [46/S3/F4]
    * The relative difference between the mean text-entry speeds of the groups
    - The absolute text-entry speed of each individual participant
    - The practice effect caused by repeated task performance
    - The number of tasks assigned to each participant
    because: The analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between those means rather than absolute values.
  Q Why is a higher mean text-entry speed by itself not enough to conclude that one interface is better?  [46/S3/F5]
    * The higher mean may be due to chance, so a statistically significant difference is required
    - The higher mean may be due to the tested conditions, so no significance test is required
    - The higher mean may be due to a randomized task sequence, so a longer experiment is required
    - The higher mean may be due to chance, so an absolute mean comparison is required
    because: A higher mean alone may be due to chance; a statistically significant difference between the means is needed to conclude that one design is better in speed or efficiency.

46/A8  recap  46/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 18 concepts)
  Empirical data must be tested for statistical significance in the data analysis stage because observed results may be due to chance. These tests show whether differences are reliable for a larger population rather than just a sample. To conclude one design is better than another, there must be a statistically significant difference between the means of the groups.
  - Empirical data must be tested for statistical significance in the data analysis stage before drawing conclusions.
  - Results from a sample of users are used to draw conclusions about a larger population.
  - Direct conclusions can be misleading because observed results may be due to chance.
  - Statistical significance tests show whether differences are reliable or due to chance.
  - A statistically significant difference between the means of groups is required to conclude one design is better than another.

46/A9  put_in_order  46/S3  "Order the steps of experimental data analysis"  (1 facts, 6 concepts)
  Order the steps of experimental data analysis: Empirical data are processed > Data are tested for statistical significance > Conclusions about the design are drawn  [46/S3/F0]

46/A10  quiz  46/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q What determines which statistical significance test should be selected for an experiment?  [46/S4/F0]
    - The nature of the input data and the size of the observed difference
    - The design of the experiment and the number of participants
    * The design of the experiment and the nature of the input data
    - The number of participants and the availability of resources
    because: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.
  Q In a statistical significance test, what is the p-value?  [46/S4/F2]
    - The probability that the tested conditions are true
    - The absolute difference between the group means
    * The probability of obtaining the data by chance
    - The probability that the observed result is practically important
    because: The p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.
  Q For an experimental design with one factor having two levels, which parametric test is used for a within-subject design?  [46/S4/F5]
    - One-way analysis of variance
    * Paired sample t-test
    - Independent samples t-test
    - Repeated measures analysis of variance
    because: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels, a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test.
  Q For a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels, which parametric test is used?  [46/S4/F6]
    - Factorial analysis of variance
    - Independent samples t-test
    - Repeated measures analysis of variance
    * One-way analysis of variance
    because: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance is used for one factor with more than two levels.
  Q For a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, which non-parametric test can be used?  [46/S4/F7]
    * Friedman test
    - Kruskal-Wallis test
    - McNemar's test
    - Mann-Whitney U test
    because: For a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

46/A11  recap  46/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 23 concepts)
  The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data. Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests. Depending on the design, scale of measurement, and number of factors or levels, specific parametric or non-parametric tests can be used.
  - The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.
  - Statistical significance tests fall into two groups: parametric tests and non-parametric tests.
  - For a nominal scale of measurement and one factor with two levels, specific non-parametric tests are used.
  - For designs with one factor and two levels, specific parametric or non-parametric tests can be used.
  - For designs with more factors or levels, various parametric and non-parametric tests can be used.

46/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 37 concepts)
  Q Why must both the participants and the tasks in an empirical interface study be representative of real users and real use?  [46/S0/F0, 46/S1/F2, 46/S1/F3; sample, user group, task, representative task set, interface, usability]
    A Participants are a sample of the whole user group, so if the sample is not representative, the conclusions drawn from the experiment are not valid or reliable. The experiment can use only a small subset of all tasks, so it should choose from the representative task set of tasks that users commonly use; otherwise the observed data may not support a reliable conclusion about the overall usability of the interface.
  Q When comparing two text-entry interfaces, why is a statistically significant difference between mean text-entry speeds required rather than simply noticing that one mean is higher?  [46/S3/F2, 46/S3/F3, 46/S3/F5; mean text-entry speed, statistical significance test, observed data difference, statistically significant difference, text-entry interface, efficiency]
    A A straightforward conclusion from experimental data can be misleading because an observed data difference may be due to chance, and changing the participants or conditions may produce different data and a different conclusion. A statistical significance test indicates whether the observed data difference is reliable by showing whether it is due to chance or to the tested conditions. Therefore, a higher mean text-entry speed alone is not enough; a statistically significant difference is required to conclude that one text-entry interface is better in speed or efficiency.
  Q What is one practical reason to prefer a within-subject design, and what method can be used to reduce its main confounding effect?  [46/S2/F0, 46/S2/F1, 46/S2/F2, 46/S2/F3, 46/S2/F4; within-subject design, between-subjects design, practice effect, confounding variable, task sequence, Latin square design, interface]
    A In a within-subject design every participant performs the tasks for all test conditions, while a between-subjects design divides the tasks for all test conditions among different participants, so within-subject designs are easier to manage. Repeated practice can improve task performance, creating a practice effect that is a confounding variable and may be mistaken for an effect of the interface. To reduce this effect, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied, for example by using a Latin square design, and these variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.
  Q How does data analysis in stage 4 of the system implementation process support a conclusive usability assessment of a fully implemented system?  [46/S3/F0, 45/S1/F1, 45/S4/F3, 24/S2/F0; data analysis, system implementation process, usability, controlled experiment, empirical data, text entry speed, objective data]
    A Data analysis is stage 4 of the system implementation process, where empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before conclusions are drawn about a design, such as text entry speed. A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data. For a text entry speed question, the experiment can collect objective data by having all users input the same text and logging speed as characters per minute. This allows data analysis to turn objective behavioral data from the implemented system into evidence for a usability judgment.

47/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ)? (lecture 11) -> The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).
  What is questionnaire? (lecture 44) -> In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.
  What is statistically significant difference? (lecture 46) -> A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is head-mounted display (HMDs)? (lecture 6) -> The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

  - Cybersickness is measured using the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ).
  - The SSQ uses a 0 to 3 scale to measure and compare symptoms before and after exposure.

    - Pre-exposure simulator sickness

    - To choose the hardware and software for the setup

47/A8  recap  47/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Pre-experiment training can reduce familiarity or prior-experience bias. Evaluations use questionnaires to measure cybersickness and presence, with exploration lasting 45 to 50 minutes to provide sufficient time for exploration while minimizing the possibility of cybersickness. Controlled experiments require defining users, preparing setups, and establishing procedures that eliminate biases.
  - Pre-experiment training can reduce familiarity or prior-experience bias.
  - Evaluations use questionnaires to measure cybersickness and presence.
  - Exploration lasts 45 to 50 minutes to provide sufficient time for exploration while minimizing the possibility of cybersickness.
  - Controlled experiments require defining users, preparing setups, and establishing procedures that eliminate biases.

47/A13  recap  47/S5  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  The cyber sickness evaluation of the Majuli virtual tour used the SSQ questionnaire to collect pre- and post-exposure data. While box plots showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test revealed statistically significant differences for oculomotor and total sickness items. This significant change in total sickness indicates that the Majuli virtual tour design had some effect on total sickness.
  - The SSQ questionnaire was used to collect pre- and post-exposure data for cyber sickness.
  - Box plots showed little difference in nausea and disorientation, but some difference in total and oculomotor severity.
  - A Wilcoxon signed-rank test revealed statistically significant differences in oculomotor and total sickness items.
  - The statistically significant change in total sickness indicates that the Majuli virtual tour design had some effect on total sickness.

47/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 40 concepts)
  Q Why did the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation ask participants to complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exploration, while the questionnaire for environmental presence was completed only after exploration?  [47/S0/F1, 47/S2/F0, 47/S2/F1, 47/S2/F5, 47/S3/F1, 47/S3/F3; usability, presence, cybersickness, simulator sickness questionnaire, questionnaire for environmental presence, exposure, Majuli virtual reality tour]
    A The evaluation aimed to measure usability aspects such as presence and comfort and to identify potential improvements by analyzing cybersickness symptoms. Presence is a psychological state measured by standard questionnaires, and the questionnaire for environmental presence was used as the presence measure after exploration. Because cybersickness depends on exposure, the simulator sickness questionnaire was completed before exploration and after the session so pre- and post-exposure scores could be compared to assess the tour's effect.
  Q How do the presence results and the Welch t-test finding on prior exposure explain the risk of prior virtual reality experience biasing the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?  [47/S1/F2, 47/S3/F0, 47/S4/F4, 47/S4/F5, 47/S6/F0; virtual reality experience, pre-experiment training session, prior-experience bias, presence, Welch t-test, statistically significant difference, prior exposure, digital avatar, Majuli virtual reality tour]
    A Twenty-one of the 27 participants had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output, and a pre-experiment training session can reduce or nullify such prior-experience bias. The presence measure gave mostly good results, and a Welch t-test revealed a statistically significant difference between users with and without prior exposure to digital or virtual tours, supporting that prior exposure helps users gain a better experience. Previous visitors gave more favorable presence ratings despite higher expectations, suggesting they felt comfortable with digital exploration, that the system reasonably well mimicked the physical island environment in its design elements, interaction, and implementation, and that the digital avatar was close to reality.
  Q What do the simulator sickness questionnaire box plots and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test together suggest about which parts of cybersickness the Majuli virtual tour affected?  [47/S5/F1, 47/S5/F2, 47/S5/F3, 47/S6/F1; cybersickness, simulator sickness questionnaire, box plot, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, statistically significant difference, total sickness, oculomotor component, nausea, disorientation, Majuli virtual tour]
    A The box plots showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour did not generally induce cybersickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test found a statistically significant difference between pre- and post-exposure outcomes for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item. This indicates that the tour design had some effect on total sickness, with the oculomotor component possibly being affected.

===== lecture 48: System Implementation

48/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is empirical study? (lecture 32) -> The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.
  What is cognitive walkthrough? (lecture 43) -> Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.
  What is heuristic evaluation? (lecture 43) -> Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.
  What is integration? (lecture 16) -> The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.
  What is interaction design? (lecture 25) -> In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.
  What is iteration? (lecture 32) -> The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

48/A1  quiz  48/S0  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 23 concepts)
  Q Why is an empirical study needed after code testing in interactive system development?  [48/S0/F4]
    - To confirm that all unit, integration, and system tests have passed
    - To verify that the system is executable after unit and integration testing
    - To replace the design-prototype-evaluate cycle once a stable interface is reached
    * To estimate usability, which code testing does not show.
    because: Code testing can show that the system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable, so usability testing or an empirical study is needed to estimate usability.
  Q What rule in the traditional interactive system development lifecycle can lead to time and cost overruns?  [48/S0/F7]
    * Completing every activity and requirement in a stage before starting the next stage.
    - Starting deployment after every successful interface prototype
    - Removing unnecessary documentation from the project
    - Delivering usable features in short successive sprints
    because: The traditional lifecycle is rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts, and this strict stage completion can lead to time and cost overruns.
  Q Why can a stage in the standard interactive system development lifecycle take longer than the stage's actual work?  [48/S0/F9]
    - Because every prototype must be rebuilt after each code review
    - Because sensor orientation must be re-registered for each stage
    * Because documentation for the stage must also be prepared.
    - Because new participants must be found for every stage
    because: Each stage requires a long time not only because of executing the stage but also because documentation for the stage must be prepared.
  Q When is the interface design-prototype-evaluate cycle complete in interactive system development?  [48/S0/F1]
    * When the interface design is stable and further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.
    - When the first prototype passes a cognitive walkthrough
    - When the client signs the software requirement specification
    - When all code units have passed system-level testing
    because: The cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.
  Q In interactive system development, from whom do usability requirements primarily come?  [48/S0/F0]
    * End users.
    - Both clients and end users equally
    - The development team's design guidelines
    - Clients
    because: Usability requirements primarily come from end users, while other non-functional requirements may come from clients and functional requirements may come from both.

48/A2  recap  48/S0  "Recap"  (11 facts, 47 concepts)
  Interactive system development involves specific cycles for gathering requirements, prototyping, and iterations across multiple stages. Implementation includes coding and systematic testing, followed by empirical studies to estimate usability. Because the traditional lifecycle is rigid and requires full completion and extensive documentation for each stage, the process can lead to significant time and cost overruns before deployment.
  - Requirement gathering, interface design, and code design involve specific cycles for gathering requirements, prototyping, and iterations.
  - Implementation includes coding and systematic testing, followed by empirical studies to estimate usability.
  - The traditional lifecycle is rigid because each stage requires full completion and extensive documentation before moving forward.
  - Because each stage takes a long time, this strict process can lead to significant time and cost overruns before deployment.

  Order the stages of the traditional interactive system development lifecycle: Gather functional and usability requirements > Run design-prototype-evaluate cycles for the interface > Create the code design > Code the system > Test the code > Conduct an empirical usability study > Deploy the system  [48/S0/F0, 48/S0/F1, 48/S0/F2, 48/S0/F3, 48/S0/F4, 48/S0/F6, 48/S0/F7, 48/S0/F8]

48/A4  quiz  48/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
  Q How does agile development differ from the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle in delivery?  [48/S1/F1]
    - It delivers the system only after all stage documents are prepared
    * It delivers usable features over successive deliveries
    - It delivers a finished system only after all requirements are collected
    - It completes the whole system before making the first delivery
    because: Agile development keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, whereas the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle first completes the system and then delivers it.
  Q Which sequence best represents the work inside an agile sprint?  [48/S1/F4]
    - Testing, development, requirements from stakeholder feedback, then delivery to production
    * Requirements from the product sprint backlog and feedback, development, testing with training and documentation, then delivery to production
    - Development, requirements from the product sprint backlog, testing, then deployment after all documentation is approved
    - Requirements, deployment to production, development, then testing and training
    because: An agile sprint includes requirements based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development, then testing including training and documentation, and then delivery to production.
  Q Which practice in agile development lets the team address stakeholder needs quickly during sprints?  [48/S1/F5]
    - Waiting until the end of the project to collect customer comments
    - Complete documentation of every stage before any feedback is shared
    * Live demonstrations after iterations and quick feedback shared before the next sprint
    - A final usability study after all coding is completed
    because: The development team provides a live demonstration after each iteration and regularly collects quick feedback from stakeholders and customers, which is shared with the team before the next sprint so it can be addressed.
  Q Why does agile development avoid trying to do everything from the beginning?  [48/S1/F0]
    - To test the whole system only after all features are coded
    * To eliminate unnecessary elements and documentation and achieve a quick, client-acceptable turnaround
    - To identify every end-user requirement before a sprint starts
    - To complete all requirements and documentation before development starts
    because: Agile development starts small, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, and eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation to ensure a quick project turnaround.
  Q In contrast to agile methods, what is the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle primarily meant for?  [48/S1/F7]
    - Delivering short sprints with live demonstrations
    * Understanding the overall development flow for pedagogical purposes
    - Building practical systems within a reasonable time frame
    - Collecting quick customer feedback before every development step
    because: The Interactive System Development Life Cycle is primarily meant for understanding the overall flow and for pedagogical purposes, rather than for building practical systems within a reasonable time frame.

48/A5  recap  48/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 20 concepts)
  Agile development is a framework for fast development that starts small and reduces unnecessary documentation. It delivers features through successive deliveries, unlike the ISDLC method where the system is finished first. An agile sprint typically lasts four to six weeks and uses daily meetings and stakeholder feedback to make quick changes. While ISDLC helps understand the overall flow, agile methods are better for building practical products in a reasonable time frame.
  - Agile development is a framework for fast development that starts small and reduces unnecessary documentation.
  - Agile delivers features through successive deliveries, unlike the ISDLC method where the system is finished first.
  - An agile sprint typically lasts four to six weeks and covers requirements, development, testing, and delivery.
  - Teams maintain agility through daily meetings, live demonstrations, and frequent stakeholder feedback.
  - Agile methods are better for practical product development, whereas ISDLC is primarily for pedagogical purposes.

  Order the activities in an agile sprint: Collect requirements from backlog and feedback > Develop sprint features > Test, train, and document > Deliver to production  [48/S1/F4]

48/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 50 concepts)
  Q How do the sources of requirements in the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development compare with the way requirements are formed in an agile sprint?  [48/S0/F0, 48/S1/F4, 48/S1/F5; requirement gathering, requirement, functional requirement, non-functional requirement, usability requirement, end user, client, sprint backlog, feedback, sprint]
    A In the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development, functional requirements may come from both clients and end users, usability requirements primarily come from end users, and other non-functional requirements may come from clients. In an agile sprint, requirements are based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback. Quick feedback from stakeholders and customers is collected regularly and shared with the team before the next sprint.
  Q Why can deployment in an interactive system development lifecycle take a very long time?  [48/S0/F7, 48/S0/F8, 48/S0/F9, 48/S0/F10; deployment, documentation, interactive system development lifecycle, feasibility study report, software requirements specification, design document, code testing document, usability study report]
    A The interactive system development lifecycle can be rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts and before deployment. Deployment is reached only after requirement gathering, coding, code testing, and usability testing, and each stage also needs time for documentation. Before deployment, it requires a feasibility study report, a software requirements specification, design documents, a code testing document, and a usability study report.
  Q Why is code testing not enough to establish that an interactive system is usable, and how does empirical study fit with earlier prototype evaluation?  [48/S0/F4, 32/S4/F2, 43/S2/F0, 43/S3/F0; code testing, usability testing, empirical study, design-prototype-evaluate cycle, quick evaluation, prototype, cognitive walkthrough, heuristic evaluation]
    A Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable, so an empirical study is needed to estimate usability. In the iterative software development life cycle, early evaluation in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code testing, and empirical study are the evaluation points. Early quick evaluation can use cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation to inspect a prototype and identify usability problems.
  Q How does agile development keep delivering value without first developing the entire interactive system?  [48/S1/F0, 48/S1/F1, 48/S1/F4, 48/S1/F5; agile development, sprint, delivery, development, testing, training, documentation, feedback, sprint backlog, daily meeting, demonstration, production]
    A Agile development starts small and does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning. It keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries. In a sprint, requirements come from the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, followed by testing including training and documentation and delivery to production, while daily meetings or brainstorming, demonstrations, and quick feedback keep the team able to change quickly.

===== lecture 49: VR experience optimisation

49/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is gait negation technique? (lecture 40) -> Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

49/A1  quiz  49/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 8 concepts)
  Q What two perspectives are used to describe optimization in virtual reality?  [49/S0/F0]
    - Visual perception optimization and auditory perception optimization
    - Augmented reality optimization and mixed reality optimization
    - Hardware optimization and software optimization
    * Psychophysiological experience optimization and technological resource utilization
    because: Optimization in virtual reality can be viewed as optimizing psychophysiological experience or optimizing technological resource utilization.
  Q In virtual reality, what does experience optimization roughly mean?  [49/S0/F1]
    - Designing the experience to maximize user-controlled navigation
    * Designing the experience to minimize cybersickness or its possible induction
    - Designing the experience to reduce resource requirements
    - Designing the experience to reduce hardware display latency
    because: Experience optimization in virtual reality is roughly about minimizing cybersickness or the chance that it is induced.
  Q Why do high resource requirements matter for virtual reality products?  [49/S0/F2]
    - They make immersive experiences more appealing to a wider range of people
    - They make systems more affordable for the masses
    - They make mass-market products easier to create
    * They make systems less affordable and harder to create for mass markets
    because: Virtual reality and extended reality systems are generally resource-hungry, and too high resource requirements can prevent affordability and mass-market products.
  Q What does effective resource optimization in virtual reality require?  [49/S0/F3]
    - Maximizing immersive experience regardless of resource requirements
    - Eliminating all resource requirements without affecting the experience
    * Balancing trade-offs to reduce resource requirements while preserving immersive experience and quality
    - Reducing resource requirements by accepting a lower immersive experience
    because: Effective resource optimization minimizes resource requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it, and ideally without reducing quality.

49/A2  recap  49/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 8 concepts)
  VR optimization can be considered from two perspectives: psychophysiological experience and technological resource utilization. Experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the VR experience to minimize cybersickness, while XR systems are generally resource-hungry and may become unaffordable for the masses if requirements are too high. Effective resource optimization requires balancing the trade-offs between minimizing resource requirements and maximizing immersive experience without compromising its quality.
  - VR optimization can be considered from two perspectives: psychophysiological experience and technological resource utilization.
  - Experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the VR experience to minimize cybersickness.
  - XR systems are generally resource-hungry, and high resource requirements can make them unaffordable for the masses.
  - Effective resource optimization involves balancing the trade-off between minimizing resource requirements and maximizing immersive experience without compromising quality.

49/A3  quiz  49/S1  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q What is cybersickness in virtual reality?  [49/S1/F0]
    - A hardware malfunction caused by display resolution
    * A visually induced motion sickness with multiple contributing factors
    - A temporary visual defect caused only by field of view
    - A single-factor effect caused only by visual motion
    because: Cybersickness, or visually induced motion sickness, can occur during VR use and is not a single-factor effect because many factors can influence it.
  Q Which option correctly identifies one internal and one external factor that can induce cybersickness?  [49/S1/F1]
    - Latency is internal, and visual motion is external.
    * User susceptibility to motion sickness is internal, and latency jitter is external.
    - Field of view is internal, and emotional condition is external.
    - Display resolution is internal, and the user's age is external.
    because: User susceptibility to motion sickness is listed among internal factors, while latency jitter is listed among hardware factors in external factors.
  Q Why can cybersickness mitigation strategies sometimes reduce presence?  [49/S1/F3]
    - They may reduce the difference between the virtual and physical environments.
    * They may make the environment feel more artificial and less immersive.
    - They may make the user feel less aware of the artificial environment.
    - They may make the environment feel more real and more immersive.
    because: Reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real one and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.
  Q What is the central challenge when developing cybersickness mitigation strategies?  [49/S1/F4]
    - Maximizing all hardware specifications.
    - Eliminating every source of visual motion.
    - Reducing only the user's exposure duration.
    * Avoiding any compromise to presence.
    because: The challenge is to develop mitigation strategies while avoiding compromising presence, which is indirectly related to user experience.

49/A4  recap  49/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 26 concepts)
  Cybersickness is a multi-factor condition caused by various internal user factors and external hardware or content factors. While reducing this sickness is important for improving the user experience, mitigation strategies can often compromise the sense of presence by making the environment feel artificial. The primary challenge is to develop solutions that mitigate cybersickness without compromising the user's sense of presence.
  - Cybersickness is a multi-factor condition that can affect individuals interacting with VR.
  - The condition is caused by internal factors like user susceptibility and external factors like hardware and VR content.
  - Reducing cybersickness is important to improve the user experience and make VR more appealing.
  - Mitigation strategies can often come at the cost of presence by making the environment feel more artificial.
  - The challenge is to develop mitigation strategies that do not compromise the sense of presence.

49/A5  quiz  49/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Q In VR experience optimization, reducing which factors can minimize cybersickness while preserving presence?  [49/S2/F0]
    - Cognitive demand or visual complexity
    * Exposure duration or navigation distance
    - Optic-flow speed or field of view
    - Display latency or display resolution
    because: Cybersickness is minimized by reducing either the duration of exposure to the virtual world or the distance covered during navigation, while presence is preserved or maximized.
  Q Which VR locomotion technique category includes full gait, partial gait, and gait negation methods involving physical walking?  [49/S2/F1]
    - Selection-based techniques
    - Manipulation-based techniques
    - Steering-based techniques
    * Walking-based techniques
    because: Virtual locomotion techniques involving physical walking are walking-based techniques, which include full gait, partial gait, and gait negation.
  Q What is the key difference between system-controlled and user-controlled VR tours?  [49/S2/F2]
    * The system controls the user's movement
    - The user selects the next movement target
    - The user controls the navigation path
    - The user steers the virtual avatar
    because: In a user-controlled tour, the user controls how and where to navigate, while in a system-controlled tour the system controls the user's movement.
  Q Why can a system-controlled VR tour have reduced cognitive demands?  [49/S2/F3]
    - The user must plan each navigation step
    - The user continuously chooses a movement target
    * The system decides how and where the user moves
    - The user must adjust the locomotion speed
    because: System-controlled tours reduce cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to focus on the experience.
  Q Why can lack of user involvement in a system-controlled VR tour undermine presence?  [49/S2/F4]
    - The user has too many movement choices
    - The user can choose a new path at will
    * The user is unable to control the movement
    - The user controls movement with controllers
    because: Lack of user involvement makes system-controlled tours less realistic and defeats presence because the user cannot control the movement.

49/A6  recap  49/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 15 concepts)
  Cybersickness is minimized by reducing navigation duration or distance while preserving presence. Virtual locomotion techniques are categorized into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based techniques. VR tours are categorized into user-controlled and system-controlled tours. System-controlled tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands, but they are less realistic and can defeat the purpose of presence.
  - Cybersickness is minimized by reducing navigation duration or distance while preserving presence.
  - Virtual locomotion techniques are categorized into walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based techniques.
  - VR tours are categorized into user-controlled and system-controlled tours.
  - System-controlled tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands, but they are less realistic and can defeat the purpose of presence.

49/A7  quiz  49/S3  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q In a VR tour, what does a system-controlled tour mean?  [49/S3/F0]
    * The system forces the user to move from one place to another.
    - The user controls the movement with a hand controller.
    - The user chooses each destination before the tour.
    - The user stays in place while the system changes the scene.
    because: A system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system, not the user, moves the user from one place to another.
  Q Why is a realistic walking experience important in a system-controlled VR tour?  [49/S3/F1]
    - It requires the user to walk at a constant speed.
    - It lets the user ignore the realism of the walking motion.
    - It makes the user feel more aware of system control.
    * It helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system.
    because: Realistic walking helps the user feel present instead of being controlled and reduces awareness of unrealistic elements.
  Q What is optic flow in a VR tour?  [49/S3/F3]
    - The user's real-world walking speed.
    - The number of visual objects in the scene.
    * The speed at which the visual scene changes.
    - The distance between two places in the VR tour.
    because: Optic flow is the speed of change in the visual scene through which movement is perceived.
  Q When a system-controlled VR tour assumes walking, what should its optic flow match?  [49/S3/F4, 49/S3/F5]
    * The user's instantaneous real-world walking speed.
    - The speed of the system-controlled tour path.
    - The user's preferred VR walking speed.
    - A single constant scene-change speed.
    because: The scene-change speed should match the user's real-world walking speed, and a model of typical walking behavior can make it follow the user's instantaneous walking speed.
  Q Why is a constant optic flow not very realistic in a system-controlled walking tour?  [49/S3/F5]
    - Because users cannot perceive scene-change speed.
    - Because the virtual scene does not change continuously.
    * Because people rarely walk at constant speed.
    - Because system-controlled tours require a fixed movement speed.
    because: A more realistic tour uses a walking-behavior model because people rarely walk at a constant speed, so constant optic flow is less realistic.

49/A8  recap  49/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 15 concepts)
  System-controlled tours are navigation modes where the system forces the user to move. Although realistic walking helps users feel present, it is difficult to achieve in automated tours that lack continuous user input. To make movement look realistic, the optic flow should match real-world walking speeds rather than VR walking speeds. Because people rarely walk at constant speeds, the optic flow must be matched to the user's instantaneous walking speed.
  - System-controlled tours are navigation modes where the system forces the user to move.
  - Realistic walking is important for feeling present, but it is difficult to achieve in automated tours that lack continuous user input.
  - Optic flow should match real-world walking speeds rather than VR walking speeds to appear realistic.
  - Optic flow must match the user's instantaneous walking speed because people rarely walk at constant speeds.

49/A14  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 26 concepts)
  Q Why can a virtual reality optimization choice that lowers cybersickness still weaken the immersive experience, and why does that matter for user experience?  [49/S0/F1, 49/S1/F3, 49/S1/F4, 8/S2/F0; virtual reality, cybersickness, cybersickness mitigation strategies, presence, immersive experience, user experience]
    A In virtual reality, experience optimization is often about designing the experience to minimize cybersickness. Cybersickness mitigation strategies can make the environment feel more artificial, so they may reduce presence, which is the psychological side of perceiving immersive qualities. Because presence is indirectly related to user experience, the challenge is to reduce sickness without compromising presence.
  Q Why can a system-controlled virtual reality tour feel easier for a user while also making presence harder to achieve, and how can a realistic walking experience address that problem?  [49/S2/F2, 49/S2/F3, 49/S2/F4, 49/S3/F1; system-controlled virtual reality tour, virtual reality tour, presence, realistic walking experience]
    A A system-controlled virtual reality tour is a tour where the system controls the user's movement, often along a predetermined path. It can feel effortless and reduce cognitive demands because the user does not decide how or where to move, but this lack of user involvement makes it less realistic and can defeat presence. A realistic walking experience helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of unrealistic elements.
  Q Why should a system-controlled virtual reality tour that simulates walking match the user's real-world walking speed rather than a constant virtual walking speed, and why is instantaneous matching more realistic?  [49/S3/F2, 49/S3/F3, 49/S3/F4, 49/S3/F5; system-controlled virtual reality tour, system-controlled tour, user input, walking speed, optic flow, real-world walking speed, virtual reality walking speed, instantaneous walking speed, walking speed model, constant optic flow]
    A System-controlled tours typically do not allow continuous user input, so it is difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural. Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and user movement in a virtual reality tour appears as a constantly changing scene. If the tour assumes walking, its optic flow should match the user's actual or typical real-world walking speed rather than virtual reality walking speed; constant optic flow is not very realistic because people rarely walk at constant speed, so a more realistic tour matches instantaneous walking speed using a walking speed model.
  Q Why does technological optimization in virtual reality connect resource requirements with affordable mass-market products, and how must it be balanced with immersive experience?  [49/S0/F0, 49/S0/F2, 49/S0/F3; virtual reality, extended reality, technological optimization, resource requirement, immersive experience, optimization]
    A Virtual reality optimization can be considered from the perspective of technological optimization, which in virtual reality concerns resource requirements and immersive experience. Extended reality and virtual reality systems are generally resource-hungry, and if their resource requirements are too high, products will not be affordable for the masses. Effective resource optimization therefore means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience without compromising it, which requires balancing the trade-off between resource requirements and immersive experience.

50/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is practice effect? (lecture 46) -> In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.
  What is p-value? (lecture 46) -> The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.
  What is optic flow? (lecture 49) -> Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is Oculus Rift? (lecture 6) -> Oculus Rift is an inexpensive virtual reality (VR) headset created by Palmer Luckey in 2012.

50/A8  quiz  50/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 11 concepts)

    - As a Fourier series whose weights are fixed by the display refresh rate.
    * As a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids whose weights are calculated from empirical data.
    - As a square pulse wave whose amplitude is set by the user's maximum speed.
    - As a constant average speed maintained between the source and destination.
    because: The pattern is similar to a Fourier approximation of a square pulse wave, and the model uses a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids with weights calculated from empirical data.
  Q Why should a virtual tour not simply move the scene at the user's actual walking velocity?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4]
    - Because the virtual scene must remain unchanged until the user reaches the destination.
    - Because a constant average speed is required to make virtual walking feel natural.
    * Because users generally perceive optic flow more slowly than actual movement, so the perceived scene-change speed must be adjusted.
    - Because perceived scene-change speed already matches the actual walking speed in most users.
    because: Actual and perceived movement speeds need not be the same, and the tour should make perceived scene-change speed differ from actual movement to support natural walking behavior.
  Q How is the desired perceived scene-change speed calculated in the visual gain model?  [50/S3/F5]
    - By dividing the actual instantaneous walking speed by the visual gain.
    - By using the average walking speed over the entire route.
    - By adding the visual gain to the instantaneous step frequency.
    * By multiplying the visual gain by the actual instantaneous walking speed.
    because: The perceived scene-change speed is computed as the visual gain times the actual instantaneous walking speed.
  Q Why is the visual gain usually chosen greater than one?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4, 50/S3/F5, 50/S3/F6]
    - To reduce the number of Fourier terms needed to approximate the walking pattern.
    - To make the perceived scene-change speed identical to the actual walking speed.
    * To compensate for users generally perceiving optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.
    - To keep the user's physical walking speed at a constant value.
    because: A visual gain of 2.10 is commonly used to give natural walking behavior, and because users generally perceive optic flow more slowly, the perceived speed is scaled from the actual speed.

50/A9  recap  50/S3  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled using a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids based on empirical data. Because users typically perceive visual flow more slowly than actual movement, the perceived scene-change speed must differ from the actual speed to ensure natural behavior. This is achieved by multiplying the actual walking speed by a visual gain g, which is typically set to 2.10.
  - The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled using a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids based on empirical data.
  - A Fourier series can approximate any continuous periodic function with arbitrary precision using its first few terms.
  - To create natural walking behavior, the perceived scene-change speed must differ from the actual movement speed.
  - Perceived speed is computed by multiplying the actual walking speed by a visual gain g, which is typically set to 2.10.

50/A17  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (23 facts, 59 concepts)
  Q How does the corridor experiment with paintings support the development of a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality navigation?  [50/S0/F0, 50/S0/F1, 50/S1/F0, 50/S1/F3, 50/S1/F4, 50/S1/F5, 50/S2/F0; realistic walking behavior model, corridor experiment, point of interest, system-controlled virtual reality navigation, speed estimation model, empirical research]
    A The corridor experiment is the empirical-research step used to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another to propose a speed estimation model. Placed paintings simulated points of interest, and the instruction to stop and click a photograph made participants stop after predefined distances. Analyzing the recorded foot-strike timestamps and distances produces step-frequency data for creating and validating the model. The resulting realistic walking behavior model can then be used for system-controlled virtual reality navigation.
  Q Why is a Fourier series an appropriate mathematical way to model the slow-in-slow-out step-frequency pattern observed in natural walking?  [50/S2/F1, 50/S3/F0, 50/S3/F1, 50/S3/F2, 50/S3/F8; slow-in-slow-out pattern, fourier series, square pulse wave, continuous periodic function, instantaneous step frequency, empirical data]
    A The observed step-frequency pattern starts low, rises, plateaus, and decreases to zero, which resembles a square pulse wave. A Fourier series can approximate continuous periodic functions by adding harmonically related sinusoids, and a practical approximation can be obtained from the first few terms. Thus the slow-in-slow-out pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion whose sinusoid weights are calculated from empirical data to compute instantaneous step frequency.
  Q How does visual gain change the scene-change speed in a virtual tour relative to a user's actual movement speed?  [50/S3/F3, 50/S3/F4, 50/S3/F5, 50/S3/F6, 49/S3/F3; visual gain, virtual tour, actual movement speed, perceived movement speed, optic flow]
    A Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and in virtual walking a user generally perceives optic flow more slowly than actual movement speed. Because of this, a virtual tour should not change the scene at the actual walking velocity; instead the perceived scene-change speed should differ from the actual movement speed. The perceived speed is computed as v_visual = g x v_actual, with g typically set to 2.10, so the user perceives natural walking behavior.
  Q What role do randomized order and paired sample t-tests play in validating the natural walking speed model?  [50/S4/F1, 50/S4/F4, 50/S4/F5, 50/S4/F6, 46/S2/F2, 46/S4/F1; randomized order, paired sample t-test, natural walking speed model, practice effect, statistical significance, perceived realism, user preference]
    A The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model enhances perceived realism compared with constant speed. Participants experienced constant speed and instantaneous speed in a randomized order, with breaks, to avoid the practice effect and bias in a within-subject comparison. Box plots showed higher realism and user preference for instantaneous speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed that these differences were statistically significant.

===== lecture 51: VR experience optimisation

51/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is visual gain? (lecture 50) -> The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.
  What is natural walking speed model? (lecture 50) -> The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is presence? (lecture 8) -> Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
  What is cybersickness (CS)? (lecture 10) -> Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

51/A1  quiz  51/S0  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 13 concepts)
  Q What is the natural walking model for a system-controlled VR tour intended to achieve?  [51/S0/F0]
    - Reducing cybersickness by limiting total VR exposure duration
    - Providing instantaneous movement between two virtual locations
    - Choosing a shortest path between points of interest
    * Providing a realistic walking experience by matching optic flow to the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed
    because: The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow, that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed.
  Q What does the natural walking model itself provide with respect to VR experience optimization?  [51/S0/F1]
    * It provides no optimization; it can only enhance presence in the virtual world
    - It chooses a path that minimizes total navigation time
    - It increases virtual travel speed to shorten travel time
    - It limits exposure duration to reduce cybersickness
    because: The natural walking model does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.
  Q What does the VR navigation optimization approach that uses the natural walking model do to address cybersickness?  [51/S0/F2]
    - It enhances presence in the virtual world to reduce sickness
    * It controls the duration of exposure in the virtual world
    - It increases virtual travel speed arbitrarily to reduce sickness
    - It uses instantaneous teleportation to reduce sickness
    because: The optimization approach that uses the natural walking model addresses cybersickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.
  Q Why can a shorter VR exposure duration help eliminate or minimize the onset of cybersickness?  [51/S0/F3]
    * Because the degree of cybersickness symptoms rises proportionally as VR session duration increases
    - Because shorter sessions reduce the amount of visual speed shown to the user
    - Because shorter sessions make the optic flow match the perceived walking speed better
    - Because shorter sessions allow arbitrary virtual travel speeds to be used
    because: Cybersickness in VR is correlated with exposure duration, and the degree of symptoms rises proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so shorter exposure can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset.

51/A2  recap  51/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 13 concepts)
  The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience and produce the perception of movement, but it does not provide experience optimization and can only be used to enhance presence. Optimization can be achieved by using the natural walking model to control exposure duration and address cybersickness. Since cybersickness symptoms rise proportionally with session duration, shorter exposure durations can help eliminate or at least minimize these symptoms.
  - The natural walking model is intended to provide a realistic walking experience and produce the perception of movement.
  - The natural walking model does not provide experience optimization and can only be used to enhance presence.
  - Optimization can be achieved by using the natural walking model to control exposure duration and address cybersickness.
  - Shorter exposure durations can help eliminate or at least minimize cybersickness because symptoms rise proportionally with session duration.

    - Travel time if directly connected, otherwise a very large value

51/A8  recap  51/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 12 concepts)
  The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph where points of interest are vertices and edges represent paths between them. Edge weights are assigned based on Euclidean distance, meaning the graph does not have to be complete. The objective is to find a path that covers all POIs in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed.
  - The virtual world is represented as a weighted graph where points of interest (POIs) are vertices and edges represent paths.
  - The graph does not need to be complete because there may not always be a direct path between certain POIs.
  - Edge weights are assigned as Euclidean distances for connected POIs and infinity for those that are not directly connected.
  - Each point of interest is a node, while a single structure may contain multiple nodes.
  - The goal is to find a path covering all POIs in the shortest time while maintaining a realistic speed.

51/A9  quiz  51/S4  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 16 concepts)
