    - Mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation
    because: The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.
  Q How does point-sample rendering create a synthetic image?  [55/S3/F1, 55/S3/F2, 55/S3/F3]
    * It processes captured real-world points, each carrying attributes, and maps them to pixels.
    - It partitions the scene into spatial regions, then renders only the visible regions.
    - It defines synthetic objects with polygonal surfaces, then renders the connected mesh.
    - It computes pixel intensities from implicit surface equations instead of captured points.
    because: In point-sample rendering, real-world scene information is captured as points with attributes and then processed or mapped to pixels to generate an image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.
  Q What distinguishes boundary representation from other object representations?  [55/S3/F4]
    - Objects are represented directly by the pixel intensities stored in a frame buffer.
    - Objects are represented by dividing the scene into hierarchical spatial regions.
    * Objects are represented by the surfaces that define their boundary, which may be polygonal or curved.
    - Objects are represented as isolated raw data points that carry scene attributes.
    because: Boundary representation represents objects by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.
  Q What is the role of mesh representation in a rendered computer-graphics scene?  [55/S3/F5, 55/S3/F8]
    - It is the only form used to store raw points captured by range scanners.
    * It is the basic object form, made of connected polygons, to which other representations are converted before rendering.
    - It is a partition of space used to skip invisible objects before pixel calculation.
    - It is a higher-level curve representation that stores spline pieces for curved surfaces.
    because: Mesh representation assumes polygonal surfaces connected into a mesh, and it is the most basic form for objects in a rendered scene; other representations are converted to mesh before rendering.
  Q What trade-off is involved when using a greater number of polygons in a mesh?  [55/S3/F7]
    - Lower storage requirements with fewer surface details.
    * Better surface approximation with a more complex vertex list that is harder to construct.
    - Simpler reconstruction with fewer boundary surfaces.
    - Faster pixel mapping with less realistic object detail.
    because: In mesh representation, more polygons give a better approximation of the surfaces but make the vertex list more complex and harder to construct.

55/A9  recap  55/S3  "Recap"  (9 facts, 24 concepts)
  Object representation categories include point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation. Point sample rendering maps real-world sensor data to pixels, while boundary representation defines objects by their surfaces. Mesh representation approximates these surfaces with polygons, requiring a trade-off between quality and complexity, and all other representations are converted to mesh before rendering.
  - Broad representation categories include point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.
  - Point sample rendering captures real-world information as raw data points and maps them to pixels to generate synthetic images.
  - Boundary representation defines objects by their surfaces, which can be polygonal or curved.
  - Mesh representation approximates surfaces with polygons, requiring a trade-off between approximation quality and complexity.
  - All other representations are converted to a mesh representation before the objects are rendered.

55/A10  quiz  55/S4  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q What type of object representation is spline representation?  [55/S4/F0, 55/S4/F6]
    - A point sample rendering technique
    * A higher-level parametric boundary representation
    - A basic mesh boundary representation
    - A space partitioning tree method
    because: Spline representation falls under parametric representation and is a higher-level boundary representation. Mesh is the most basic boundary representation, while higher-level forms can be implicit or parametric.
  Q Why would a scene designer choose spline representation for curved surfaces?  [55/S4/F1]
    - To capture real-world points using range scanners
    * To create quality rendered scenes for complex artificial surfaces
    - To partition object space into disjoint regions
    - To represent objects by connected polygonal triangles
    because: Spline representation is typically used by developers or designers to construct quality rendered scenes and to represent complex artificial surfaces that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.
  Q How is a complete curve represented in a spline?  [55/S4/F3]
    - As connected triangles forming a mesh
    * As several lower-degree polynomial pieces, each called a blending or basis function
    - As a list of raw points from sensors
    - As one higher-degree polynomial covering the entire curve
    because: In spline representation, a complete curve is made of several lower-degree polynomial pieces rather than one higher-degree polynomial, and each piece is a blending function or basis function.
  Q What is the main computational advantage of using lower-degree pieces in a spline?  [55/S4/F2, 55/S4/F3]
    - It captures real-world points directly from sensors
    - It partitions the object's volume into non-overlapping regions
    * Point computation on each curve segment is simpler and less time-consuming
    - It reduces the number of polygons in a mesh
    because: Computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming, while spline pieces use simpler lower-degree polynomials to compute points on their curve segments.
  Q What must be true about the polynomial pieces in a spline curve?  [55/S4/F5]
    - They must divide the scene into disjoint spatial regions
    - They must be stored as a complete vertex and edge list
    * They must join smoothly and satisfy required geometric and other properties
    - They must each be a single high-degree polynomial
    because: The polynomial pieces that make up a complete spline curve must join smoothly, and each piece must satisfy certain geometric and other properties.

55/A11  recap  55/S4  "Recap"  (6 facts, 17 concepts)
  Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces that falls under parametric representation. It is typically preferred for constructing quality scenes and representing complex surfaces that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations. In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces that must join smoothly and satisfy certain properties, avoiding the more time-consuming computation of a single higher-degree complex polynomial.
  - Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces that falls under parametric representation.
  - It is typically preferred for constructing quality scenes and representing complex surfaces that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.
  - Spline representation uses several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, which is more time-consuming to compute.
  - These pieces, which are most commonly third-order polynomials, must join smoothly and satisfy certain geometric and other properties.

55/A12  quiz  55/S5  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 6 concepts)
  Q In a space partitioning representation, how is an object represented?  [55/S5/F0]
    * By dividing the 3D space it occupies into disjoint, non-overlapping regions and representing the occupied regions
    - By describing the object as self-repeating structures that repeat in larger parts
    - By storing only the object surface as a set of triangular meshes for the graphics pipeline
    - By collecting raw data points from the real-world scene and mapping those points to pixels
    because: Space partitioning representation divides the 3D space occupied by an object into disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so the object is represented by the occupied regions.
  Q What is a space partitioning tree?  [55/S5/F1]
    - A set of disjoint, non-overlapping regions used directly to represent an object
    - A non-hierarchical collection of raw data points captured from a real-world scene
    - A skeletal model that captures a complex character's appearance and motion behavior
    * A hierarchical, tree-like structure used to create a space partitioning representation
    because: A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.
  Q When are specialized sophisticated representation techniques often required?  [55/S5/F3]
    - For basic surfaces that can be represented by simple polygons or polynomial equations
    - For curves that are constructed from lower-degree polynomial pieces that join smoothly
    - For simple scenes that can be rendered from a set of raw captured data points
    * For application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects where broader boundary or space partitioning categories are insufficient
    because: Specialized sophisticated representation techniques are often needed for application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects rather than the broader boundary or space partitioning categories.
  Q Which specialized representation method is suited to self-repeating structures such as a leaf?  [55/S5/F4]
    - Space partitioning representation
    - Skeletal model representation
    * Fractal representation
    - Particle system representation
    because: Fractal representation is the specialized method for self-repeating structures, such as a leaf whose individual parts repeat in the larger part.
  Q Which specialized representation method relies on simulating physical properties for objects such as a waterfall?  [55/S5/F5]
    - Skeletal model representation
    - Point sample rendering
    * Particle system representation
    - Fractal representation
    because: Particle system representation is the specialized method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.

55/A13  recap  55/S5  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Space partitioning representation divides an object's 3D space into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions, which can be organized into a hierarchical space partitioning tree. Examples include octree, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods. For complex photorealistic objects, specialized techniques such as fractal representations, particle systems, and skeletal models are often required.
  - Space partitioning representation divides an object's 3D space into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions.
  - These regions are organized into a hierarchical, tree-like structure called a space partitioning tree.
  - Examples of space partitioning include octree, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.
  - Specialized sophisticated representation techniques are often required for complex photorealistic objects.
  - Specific specialized techniques include fractal representations, particle systems, and skeletal models.

55/A21  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (14 facts, 47 concepts)
  Q How do the coordinate systems in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline connect object definitions to the final pixel-level description?  [55/S1/F2, 55/S1/F3, 55/S1/F7, 55/S1/F8, 55/S1/F9; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, local coordinate system, modeling transformation, world coordinate system, viewing pipeline, three-dimensional view coordinate system, two-dimensional view coordinate system, device coordinate system, scan conversion, screen coordinate system, pixel]
    A The pipeline first defines objects in their local coordinate systems, then modeling transformation places them into the common world coordinate system to construct the scene. The viewing pipeline maps the scene from the world coordinate system through the three-dimensional and two-dimensional view coordinate systems to the device coordinate system. Finally, scan conversion changes the continuous device-coordinate description into the discrete screen coordinate system, where each pixel has integer coordinates. Together, these transformations use the local, world, three-dimensional view, two-dimensional view, device, and screen coordinate systems to turn object definitions into pixel-level scene descriptions.
  Q How does scan conversion prepare the scene for the frame buffer and pixels of a raster scan display?  [55/S1/F0, 55/S1/F8, 54/S4/F0; scan conversion, device coordinate system, screen coordinate system, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, frame buffer, pixel, video controller, display mechanism]
    A Scan conversion transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can have real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer. The three-dimensional graphics pipeline then computes and stores intensity values for these pixels in the frame buffer, which drives the display mechanism through the video controller. In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory that stores one intensity value for each pixel as a bit string of 0s and 1s.
  Q Why is no single three-dimensional object representation technique sufficient for all rendered scenes, and why is mesh representation especially important at the end of the pipeline?  [55/S2/F2, 55/S2/F3, 55/S3/F8; three-dimensional object representation technique, point sample rendering, boundary representation, space partitioning based representation, mesh representation, pipeline, computer graphics, rendering]
    A A single representation technique is not sufficient because different techniques are available and the appropriate one must be chosen for a particular problem. The broad categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation. Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before objects are rendered.
  Q Why can spline representation make complex curves more practical to compute than representing them with a single high-degree polynomial?  [55/S4/F2, 55/S4/F3, 55/S4/F4, 55/S4/F5; polynomial representation, spline representation, polynomial, polynomial piece, basis function, curve segment, third-order polynomial, spline curve, curve]
    A In polynomial representation, a more complex curve is represented by a higher-degree polynomial, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming. In spline representation, the complete curve is made of several lower-degree polynomial pieces, each called a blending function or basis function, so simpler polynomials can compute points on each curve segment. The pieces must join smoothly, and third-order polynomials are the most common form used to construct spline curves.

    - As Ks times Is times (N dot L) raised to Ns
    * As Ks times Is times (V dot r) raised to Ns
    because: The specular component is the specular coefficient Ks multiplied by the source intensity Is and the dot product V dot r raised to the power Ns, provided V dot r is greater than 0.
  Q How is the ideal specular reflection direction vector r represented?  [56/S7/F8]
    * As 2(L dot N)N - L
    - As 2(V dot N)N - V
    - As V - 2(V dot N)N
    - As 2(N dot L)L - N
    because: The ideal specular reflection direction vector r is represented by twice the dot product of the light direction L and the surface normal N multiplied by N, minus L.

56/A18  recap  56/S7  "Recap"  (9 facts, 23 concepts)
  Reflection coefficients Ka, Kd, and Ks determine the fraction of incident light reflected from a surface based on its properties. The ambient component is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity by Ka, while the diffuse component uses Kd, source light intensity, and the dot product of the surface normal and light direction. The specular component is computed using the Phong model, which relies on the Ks coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the viewer direction and the ideal specular reflection direction.
  - Reflection coefficients Ka, Kd, and Ks determine the fraction of incident light reflected from a surface based on its properties.
  - The ambient component is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity by the ambient reflection coefficient Ka.
  - The diffuse component is computed using the Kd coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the surface normal and the light direction.
  - The specular component is computed using the Phong model, which involves the Ks coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the viewer direction and the ideal specular reflection direction.

56/A19  quiz  56/S8  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 17 concepts)
  Q In a lighting model, what form is the radial intensity attenuation factor typically computed in?  [56/S8/F1]
    - A constant factor determined by the spotlight angular limit theta
    * An inverse quadratic function of the distance d, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2
    - The cosine of phi raised to the positive exponent A1
    - An inverse linear function of the distance d, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2
    because: The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of distance using coefficients a0, a1, and a2.
  Q Why is angular intensity attenuation included in a lighting model?  [56/S8/F2]
    * To create spotlight effects in which points inside the cone are bright and points outside are darker
    - To multiply the ambient light intensity by the ambient reflection coefficient
    - To calculate the ideal specular reflection direction from the normal and light vectors
    - To account for the reduction in light intensity as the distance from the source increases
    because: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, where elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.
  Q What values does the commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor take for a spotlight cone?  [56/S8/F3]
    * 0 outside the angular limit theta, and cos phi to the power A1 inside it
    - 0 inside the angular limit theta, and cos phi to the power A1 outside it
    - A constant inside the angular limit theta, and 0 outside it
    - 1 outside the angular limit theta, and an inverse quadratic function of d inside it
    because: The commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, and within that limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1.
  Q In the modified simple lighting model, which intensity components are scaled by radial and angular attenuation factors?  [56/S8/F4]
    - The ambient component, with the diffuse and specular components unchanged
    - Only the diffuse component, with the ambient and specular components unchanged
    * The sum of the diffuse and specular components, with the ambient component unchanged
    - All three components: ambient, diffuse, and specular
    because: The I_M ambient component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse component I_D and the specular component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors.

56/A20  recap  56/S8  "Recap"  (5 facts, 18 concepts)
  Intensity attenuation factors are needed because light intensity typically diminishes with distance from a source. Radial intensity attenuation typically uses an inverse quadratic function of the distance to model this diminishing light. Angular intensity attenuation is primarily used to generate spotlight effects, with factors varying based on whether a point is inside or outside a spotlight cone. In the modified model, these factors multiply the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components while the I_M component remains unchanged.
  - Intensity attenuation factors are needed because light intensity typically diminishes with distance from a source.
  - Radial intensity attenuation typically uses an inverse quadratic function of the distance to model this diminishing light.
  - Angular intensity attenuation is primarily used to generate spotlight effects.
  - Angular attenuation factors are 0 outside a spotlight cone and vary as the cosine of the angle raised to a power inside it.
  - These factors multiply the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components while the I_M component remains unchanged.

56/A21  quiz  56/S9  "Quick quiz"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Q In a colored light source model, how is the intensity of a light source represented?  [56/S9/F0]
    - As a four-element vector including an alpha channel
    - As a single scalar intensity value
    * As a three-element vector of red, green, and blue intensities
    - As a two-element vector of luminance and chrominance
    because: The model represents the emitted light intensity with three components corresponding to red, green, and blue, forming the vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).
  Q What does a colored light source model do to the red, green, and blue parts of the source intensity?  [56/S9/F1]
    - Averages all color components into one monochrome intensity
    - Computes the combined color first and then splits it into components
    - Uses the red component alone to estimate the perceived color
    * Computes each color component individually and combines them to produce perceived color
    because: The red, green, and blue components are computed individually, and their combination gives the perception of any color.
  Q In a colored light source model, how are the reflection coefficients k, kd, and ks specified?  [56/S9/F2]
    - As two-element vectors for brightness and saturation
    - As single scalar values shared by all colors
    - As four-element vectors including a separate ambient term
    * As three-element vectors with a value for each red, green, and blue component
    because: The reflection coefficients are specified as three-element vectors, corresponding to the red, green, and blue components.
  Q How does a lighting model handle multiple light sources?  [56/S9/F3]
    - All source contributions are multiplied together and then added to the ambient intensity
    * Ambient intensity plus the sum of separately calculated source contributions, computed per RGB component
    - The source contributions are averaged once before being added to the ambient intensity
    - Only the brightest light source is used, and the others are ignored
    because: For n light sources, the model adds the ambient intensity to the summation of contributions from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and, for colored sources, computed separately for red, green, and blue.

56/A22  recap  56/S9  "Recap"  (4 facts, 11 concepts)
  Colored light sources use red, green, and blue components that are computed individually to create any color. Reflection coefficients are specified as three-element vectors where each component has a value of one. The total light intensity is the sum of ambient light and the contributions from all light sources, with each contribution calculated separately for the red, green, and blue components.
  - Colored light sources have red, green, and blue components that are computed individually to produce any color.
  - Reflection coefficients are three-element vectors where each component has a value of one.
  - Total intensity is the sum of ambient light and the contributions from all light sources, calculated separately for each color.

56/A23  quiz  56/S10  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Q In intensity mapping, how do lighting-model intensities differ from device-supported intensities?  [56/S10/F0]
    - The model and display both support an infinite range, so no mapping is needed.
    * The model can produce any value from 0 to 1, while a display supports only a finite set of values.
    - The model produces only integer bit patterns, while a display can represent any real value from 0 to 1.
    - The display supports more intensity values than the lighting model can compute.
    because: A lighting model computes pixel intensities over an infinite 0-to-1 range, whereas a display has only a finite set of supportable intensity values.
  Q Why are successive device-supported intensity levels related by a multiplicative factor r?  [56/S10/F3]
    * Because humans perceive relative changes between intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity.
    - Because the lighting model computes only absolute intensity values.
    - Because a display stores absolute bit patterns for each pixel.
    - Because a photometer can measure only absolute intensity values.
    because: The multiplicative factor reflects the psychophysiological property that perception is based on relative changes between intensities, not absolute intensity changes.
  Q What information is used to determine the device-supported intensity values?  [56/S10/F1]
    - The number of pixels, the minimum reflection coefficient Ka, and the maximum reflection coefficient Ks.
    - The source intensity vector Is, the colored reflection coefficient vectors, and the ambient intensity.
    - The distance d, the radial coefficients a0, a1, and a2, and the angular limit theta.
    * The number of levels n, the measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.
    because: Device-supported values are determined from the number of levels, the photometer-measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.
  Q How is a lighting-model pixel intensity stored for display?  [56/S10/F4]
    - It is mapped to the next higher table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    * It is mapped to the nearest table intensity, and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    - It is mapped to the next lower table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
    - It is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location as the unmodified model intensity.
    because: A table stores the device-supported intensities and their bit patterns; the model intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and its bit pattern is written to the frame buffer.
  Q How is the multiplicative factor r for the device-supported intensity levels found?  [56/S10/F1, 56/S10/F2]
    - By taking the average of the minimum intensity I0 and the maximum intensity value.
    * By using the relation In = r^n I0 with the known maximum intensity value.
    - By measuring each intermediate intensity value with a photometer.
    - By using the reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model.
    because: Successive levels are I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0, so r is obtained from that relation using the maximum intensity.

56/A24  recap  56/S10  "Recap"  (5 facts, 19 concepts)
  Lighting models produce an infinite range of intensities, but displays support only a finite set of values determined by the number of levels, minimum intensity, and maximum intensity. Successive device-supported values are calculated using a multiplicative factor because humans perceive relative changes in intensity. Lighting intensities are then mapped to the nearest supported value in a table to store the corresponding bit pattern in the frame buffer.
  - Lighting models produce an infinite range of intensities, but displays support only a finite set of values.
  - Device-supported intensity values are determined by the number of levels, the minimum intensity value, and the maximum intensity value.
  - Successive intensity values are calculated using a multiplicative factor because humans perceive relative changes in intensity.
  - Lighting intensities are mapped to the nearest supported value in a table to store the corresponding bit pattern in the frame buffer.

  *Projection | Scaling | Rotation | Translation  (Translation, rotation and scaling are basic modeling transformations; projection is a transformation in the viewing pipeline, not a basic modeling transformation.)  [56/S2/F2, 56/S1/F0]
  Specular reflection intensity | *Source light intensity | Ambient light intensity | Diffuse reflection intensity  (Ambient light intensity, diffuse reflection intensity and specular reflection intensity are the three intensities summed in the simple lighting model; source light intensity is a factor used to compute reflection components, not one of those summed intensities.)  [56/S6/F2, 56/S7/F4]
  Specular reflection coefficient | Diffuse reflection coefficient | *Angular attenuation exponent | Ambient reflection coefficient  (Ambient, diffuse and specular reflection coefficients are the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model; the angular attenuation exponent is a spotlight parameter, not a reflection coefficient.)  [56/S7/F1, 56/S8/F3]

56/A30  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (15 facts, 54 concepts)
  Q How does modeling transformation connect object representation with lighting in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline?  [55/S1/F2, 55/S1/F3, 56/S2/F0, 56/S1/F0; object representation, modeling transformation, local coordinate system, world coordinate system, lighting, three-dimensional graphics pipeline]
    A Object representation defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system. Modeling transformation then maps those local descriptions into a common world coordinate system so multiple objects can be assembled into a scene. Because lighting takes place in the world coordinate reference frame, it can use the assembled scene after modeling transformation.
  Q Why is the right-to-left order of transformation matrices important when forming a composite transformation matrix?  [56/S4/F0, 56/S4/F3, 56/S4/F6; composite transformation matrix, transformation matrix, basic transformation, matrix multiplication, order of application, world coordinate scene]
    A A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic transformations. It is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, and subsequent transformations are placed to its left. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.
  Q How are lighting models related to shading models, and why can shading be useful in a graphics rendering pipeline?  [56/S5/F0, 56/S5/F1, 56/S5/F2; color computation, lighting model, shading model, depth, quality of experience, computer graphics pipeline]
    A In the computer graphics pipeline, color computation uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene. If a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced. Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models and involve less computation, so they can reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience.
  Q Why does intensity mapping need device-supported intensity levels when a lighting model has already produced pixel intensities?  [56/S10/F0, 56/S10/F1, 56/S10/F2, 56/S10/F3, 56/S10/F4; lighting model, pixel intensity, intensity mapping, 8-bit display, device-supported intensity value, multiplicative factor, psychophysiological property, table, bit pattern, frame buffer]
    A A lighting model can compute a pixel intensity as any continuous value between 0 and 1, but a display such as an 8-bit display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel. Device-supported intensity values are determined from the number of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value, and the known maximum value, using a multiplicative factor based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes rather than absolute changes. A table stores these device-supported intensity values and their bit patterns, so the continuous pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer.

57/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 55) -> The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
  What is viewing pipeline? (lecture 55) -> The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
  What is viewing transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is projection transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is window-to-viewport transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

    - It changes scene objects from world coordinates to view coordinates.
    - It converts an arbitrary view volume into a canonical unit cube.
    - It projects scene objects inside the view volume onto the view plane.
    because: Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection.
  Q Which shape describes the view volume for parallel projection?  [57/S2/F1, 57/S2/F6, 57/S2/F8]

    - A normalized unit cube
    - A perspective frustum
    * A rectangular parallelepiped
    because: For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped. A frustum is the perspective view volume, a normalized unit cube is a canonical view volume, and a view plane is a rectangular area.
  Q How is a canonical view volume obtained for perspective projection?  [57/S2/F8, 57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10]
    * By scaling and shearing the frustum into a unit cube.
    - By transforming the world coordinate system into the 3D view coordinate system.
    - By scaling a rectangular parallelepiped into a unit cube.
    - By computing intersections between object and view volume boundaries.
    because: For perspective projection, the frustum is converted to a normalized unit cube using scaling and shearing. Parallel projection only scales a rectangular parallelepiped, while intersection computation describes clipping.
  Q In what order are matrices multiplied to project a point from world coordinates to the view plane?  [57/S2/F13]

    * World-to-view, canonical view volume, projection
    - Canonical view volume, world-to-view, projection
    because: The point is first transformed from world coordinates to the 3D view coordinate system, then the view volume is transformed to a canonical view volume, and finally the point is projected. The matrices are multiplied in that order.

57/A7  recap  57/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 12 concepts)
  Projection transformation maps objects from a 3D view coordinate system to a 2D view plane. Perspective projection provides realistic rendering with converging projectors, whereas parallel projection uses parallel projectors. By converting view volumes into a canonical view volume, which is a normalized unit cube, the system simplifies calculations before transforming points from the world coordinate system to the 2D view plane through a sequence of matrices.
  - Projection transformation maps objects from a 3D view coordinate system to a 2D view plane.
  - A view volume defines the portion of the scene to be projected, while clipping discards objects outside that volume.
  - Perspective projection uses converging projectors for realistic rendering, while parallel projection uses parallel projectors.
  - View volumes are converted into a canonical view volume, which is a normalized unit cube, to simplify calculations.
  - Points are transformed from the world coordinate system to the 2D view plane through a sequence of matrices.

57/A9  recap  57/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 11 concepts)
  A window is an abstract intermediate representation, while a viewport is a specific portion of the final screen defined in device space. The window-to-viewport transformation maps points from the window to the viewport using a three by three matrix based on their respective dimensions. To find the final viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by this matrix and divided by the homogeneous factor W.
  - A window is an abstract intermediate representation also known as a normalized clipping window or view plane.
  - A viewport is a portion of the final screen defined in device space using the display's dimensions and origin.
  - The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation.
  - This transformation uses a three by three matrix defined by the dimensions of both the window and the viewport.
  - The transformed viewport point is obtained by multiplying the window point vector by the transformation matrix and dividing by the homogeneous factor W.

57/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 42 concepts)
  Q Why does virtual reality place a larger resource burden on the viewing pipeline than augmented reality, and which two operations in the viewing pipeline reduce that burden?  [57/S0/F0, 57/S4/F0, 57/S4/F1; virtual reality, augmented reality, viewing pipeline, clipping, hidden surface removal]
    A Realistic scene generation is more important in virtual reality than in augmented reality and requires more resources in virtual reality. Clipping discards objects or portions outside the view volume before projection, so projection is applied to fewer vertices. Hidden surface removal removes occluded objects, surfaces, or surface points before rendering, reducing computational complexity and supporting a realistic image.
  Q As the fourth stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline, how do the viewing transformation and projection transformation work together to produce the image shown on a head-mounted display?  [55/S1/F1, 57/S0/F2, 57/S1/F1, 57/S2/F0; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, viewing pipeline, viewing transformation, projection transformation, three-dimensional view coordinate system, view plane, head-mounted display, three-dimensional scene, two-dimensional display]
    A The viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline, and it produces an image on a head-mounted display by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional scene and projecting that portion onto a two-dimensional display or view plane. The three-dimensional viewing transformation transforms the scene from world coordinates to a three-dimensional view coordinate system to simulate looking at the scene with a camera viewing mechanism. The projection transformation then maps objects in the three-dimensional view coordinate system to the two-dimensional view plane.
  Q Why is a perspective view volume converted into a canonical view volume before clipping, and how does that conversion differ from the parallel projection case?  [57/S2/F6, 57/S2/F7, 57/S2/F8, 57/S2/F9, 57/S2/F10; perspective projection, parallel projection, frustum, canonical view volume, unit cube, clipping, naive clipping method, scaling, shearing]
    A For perspective projection the view volume is a frustum, and naive clipping that computes intersections with arbitrarily shaped volumes is computationally intensive. Converting the frustum to a canonical normalized unit cube simplifies pipeline computations. For parallel projection the view volume can be scaled into the unit cube, whereas the perspective frustum requires scaling and shearing and thus more computation.

===== lecture 58: VR resource optimization

58/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is clipping? (lecture 21) -> Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.
  What is world coordinate system? (lecture 55) -> The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.
  What is viewing transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is projection transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is window-to-viewport transformation? (lecture 55) -> The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  What is hidden surface removal? (lecture 57) -> Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

58/A2  recap  58/S0  "Recap"  (4 facts, 17 concepts)
  Rendering is the most challenging part of generating immersive experiences from the point of view of the system. The 3D graphics pipeline has five stages, the first four being object representation, modeling, lighting, and viewing transformation. After viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation. The fifth stage is scan conversion, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.
  - Rendering is the most challenging part of generating immersive experiences from the point of view of the system.
  - The 3D graphics pipeline has five stages, the first four being object representation, modeling, lighting, and viewing transformation.
  - After the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
  - The fifth stage is scan conversion, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

    - It maps visible and hidden surfaces in a three-dimensional view coordinate system to determine occlusion
    * It maps continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates to a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels
    - It maps a three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional view coordinate system using projection transformation
    - It maps objects from a local coordinate system to a world coordinate system using geometric transformation
    because: Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, transforms continuous two-dimensional viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.

58/A5  recap  58/S1  "Recap"  (3 facts, 13 concepts)
  The device coordinate system used to define the 2D viewport is continuous, but display devices use a pixel grid where points can only have integer coordinates. Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is the fifth stage of the process. It uses mapping algorithms to transform continuous viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels.
  - The device coordinate system for the 2D viewport is a continuous coordinate system.
  - A display device uses a pixel grid where points can only have integer coordinates.
  - Scan conversion maps continuous viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system.

58/A6  quiz  58/S2  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 20 concepts)
  Q What operation is used to render a point with real-number coordinates?  [58/S2/F0]
    * Round it to the nearest integer coordinate values
    - Apply a decision parameter to choose between x and y pixels
    - Color every pixel along a line segment passing through the point
    - Keep it in continuous device coordinates until lighting is applied
    because: Point rendering maps a point from device space to discrete space by rounding its real-number coordinates to the nearest integer coordinate values.
  Q Why do efficient line-rendering algorithms aim to avoid floating-point operations?  [58/S2/F1]
    * Floating-point operations slow down the computer
    - Floating-point operations speed up the computer
    - Floating-point operations reduce the number of line segments to draw
    - Floating-point operations make anti-aliasing unnecessary
    because: A naive line-rendering method needs many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, efficient algorithms try to avoid them.
  Q What makes Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm efficient?  [58/S2/F2, 58/S2/F5]
    - It removes aliasing by averaging neighboring pixel intensities
    * It selects pixels with integer arithmetic while avoiding floating-point operations
    - It shortens the input line before finding the pixels
    - It computes exact real-valued coordinates for every point on the line
    because: Bresenham's algorithm identifies the pixels that approximate a line without floating-point operations, using integer arithmetic such as addition and multiplication to speed up line rendering.
  Q Why is fast line rendering especially important in interactive virtual reality?  [58/S2/F6]
    * User input can change the scene and require redrawing many line segments
    - The number of line segments is fixed regardless of user input
    - Headset resolution removes the need for fast line rendering
    - Virtual reality displays accept only continuous real-number pixel coordinates
    because: A system may need to render a large number of line segments at once, and in interactive virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.
  Q How does line rendering differ from rendering other geometric shapes in terms of floating-point operations?  [58/S2/F9]
    - Floating-point operations are unnecessary for all scan-converted shapes
    - Floating-point operations can be completely eliminated for circles and polygons
    * Floating-point operations can be completely eliminated for lines
    - Floating-point operations can only be minimized for lines
    because: For lines, floating-point operations can be completely eliminated, whereas for other shapes they may not be completely eliminated but can be minimized.

58/A7  recap  58/S2  "Recap"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  While point rendering uses rounding, naive line-rendering is slow because it requires many floating-point operations. The basic idea for rendering a shape is to map it to a set of pixels as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations. Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm achieves this by using integer arithmetic to avoid slow operations like rounding and division, which is necessary for interactive graphics like virtual reality.
  - Point rendering uses rounding, but naive line-rendering is slow because it requires many floating-point operations.
  - The basic idea for rendering a shape is to map it to a set of pixels as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations.
  - Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm identifies pixels for a line without using floating-point operations.
  - Bresenham's algorithm is efficient because it uses integer arithmetic to avoid slow operations like rounding and division.
  - Efficient line-rendering is necessary for interactive graphics like virtual reality, where a system may need to redraw hundreds of thousands of lines.

58/A8  put_in_order  58/S2  "Order the steps of Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm"  (2 facts, 10 concepts)
  Order the steps of Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm: Two endpoints are given > Differences and decision parameter are computed > An endpoint pixel is added > Pixel coordinates are updated  [58/S2/F3, 58/S2/F4]

58/A9  quiz  58/S3  "Quick quiz"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q Why can aliasing occur when a shape is scan-converted to pixels?  [58/S3/F0]
    - Because anti-aliasing adds operations to the other rendering stages
    - Because a simple lighting model cannot represent realistic VR content
    - Because user input changes the content of a dynamic virtual world
    * Because pixels are rendered near, but not exactly at, points on the original shape
    because: Aliasing is distortion that can occur after scan conversion because the rendered pixels approximate, rather than exactly match, points on the original shape.
  Q What is a consequence of leaving aliasing unaddressed?  [58/S3/F1]
    * Distortion can become visible when resolution changes and reduce quality of experience
    - Dynamic VR content becomes simpler to compute
    - The need for anti-aliasing operations can be removed
    - The rendered line can exactly match the original line
    because: If aliasing is left unaddressed, it may lead to visible distortion when resolution changes and reduce the quality of experience.
  Q What do anti-aliasing operations do in rendering?  [58/S3/F2]
    - They render pixels exactly at the points of the original shape
    * They remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing
    - They remove the extra computation from other rendering stages
    - They make motion appear in a static virtual world
    because: Anti-aliasing operations use complex algorithms to remove or reduce aliasing distortion so that the final effect is better.
  Q Why does anti-aliasing add to rendering cost?  [58/S3/F3]
    - Because it avoids complex algorithms for computing pixel intensities
    - Because it replaces rich realistic VR content with static content
    - Because it removes the other rendering stages from the overall computation
    * Because it is an essential additional computation for pixel intensities
    because: Anti-aliasing is essential and adds further computation to the overall computation of pixel intensities along with the other rendering stages.
  Q What is the challenge in VR rendering?  [58/S3/F4, 58/S3/F5]
    * To handle a computationally complex, dynamic rendering process without the user perceiving lag or distortion
    - To remove user interaction so the virtual world remains static
    - To make every pixel exactly match the original shape
    - To avoid anti-aliasing because it adds operations
    because: VR rendering becomes computationally complex because of realistic content, dynamic user input, high interaction, motion, and lighting limitations; the challenge is to handle this without perceived lag or distortion.

58/A10  recap  58/S3  "Recap"  (6 facts, 21 concepts)
  Aliasing is distortion caused by scan conversion when pixels do not exactly match original shapes, which can lead to visible distortion and reduced quality of experience. Anti-aliasing uses complex algorithms to reduce this distortion but adds to the overall computation. Because realistic dynamic content manifoldly increases rendering complexity in VR, the challenge is handling these processes without the user perceiving lag or distortion.
  - Aliasing is distortion caused by scan conversion when pixels do not exactly match original shapes.
  - Unaddressed aliasing can lead to visible distortion and reduce the quality of experience.
  - Anti-aliasing uses complex algorithms to reduce distortion but adds to the overall computation.
  - Realistic dynamic content in VR manifoldly increases rendering complexity.
  - The challenge is to handle this complexity without the user perceiving lag or distortion.

    * Predefined sets of functions that perform specific tasks when invoked with appropriate parameters.
    - Undefined sets of tasks that programmers must define and implement for every project.
    because: Graphics-library APIs are predefined function sets that carry out specific tasks when called with the right arguments or parameters.
  Q Which underlying system or platform details are examples of details that using graphics library APIs removes the need to know?  [58/S4/F3]
    - Only operating-system details, not processor details or memory details.
    - Only memory details, not processor details or operating-system details.

    * Processor details, memory details, and operating-system details.
    because: Graphics-library APIs eliminate the need to know every underlying system detail, including processor, memory, and operating-system details, in order to build a graphics application.

58/A12  recap  58/S4  "Recap"  (3 facts, 10 concepts)
  A computer graphics programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can use graphics libraries and their APIs to deal with lower-level tasks. By using these APIs, a programmer eliminates the need to know every detail of the underlying system or platform in order to build a graphics application.
  - Programmers do not always need to implement a graphics pipeline from scratch because they can use graphics libraries and their APIs to handle lower-level tasks.
  - APIs are predefined sets of functions that perform specific tasks when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters.

58/A15  quiz  58/S6  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 27 concepts)
  Q Why are GPUs especially suited to real-time computer graphics and virtual reality?  [58/S6/F0]
    - Graphics operations are mostly sequential, so a single fast core is sufficient.
    - GPUs have no dedicated memory, so all intermediate data must be kept in CPU memory.
    - GPUs generally are not designed for large-scale parallel activities.
    * Their architecture is designed to exploit the inherent parallelism of highly parallel graphics operations.
    because: Graphics operations are highly parallel, and GPUs are used to exploit that parallelism, while CPUs generally are not designed for large-scale parallel activities.
  Q What happens during the GPU modeling transformation stage?  [58/S6/F3]
    - The CPU completes the vertex transformations and sends finished world-space triangles to the GPU.
    * The same transformation matrix is multiplied with each vertex vector simultaneously, producing transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates.
    - The GPU rasterizes the scene first and then applies the modeling transformation to the resulting pixels.
    - A different lighting matrix is multiplied with each pixel vector sequentially, converting world coordinates into screen coordinates.
    because: Modeling transformation applies transformations such as rotation by multiplying the same transformation matrix with all vertex vectors at once, converting local coordinates into world coordinates.
  Q What computation does the GPU perform simultaneously for multiple vertices to compute vertex color in the simple lighting model?  [58/S6/F6]
    - Depth-buffer comparisons
    - Composite projection matrix multiplications
    * Vector dot products
    - Texture-image lookups
    because: Vertex color is computed by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.
  Q What property makes rasterization able to determine pixel colors in parallel?  [58/S6/F8]
    - The color of one pixel depends on the colors of all other pixels in the triangle.
    - A pixel can be processed only after every other pixel in the triangle has been completed.
    * Each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels.
    - The pixels of a triangle must be processed in a fixed sequential order.
    because: Rasterization exploits the fact that each pixel can be treated independently, so the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously.
  Q Which two activities occur in the GPU pixel processing stage?  [58/S6/F9]
    - Rasterization and hidden surface removal
    - Projection transformation and rasterization
    - Vertex assembly and vertex lighting
    * Surface texturing and hidden surface removal
    because: In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

58/A16  recap  58/S6  "Recap"  (12 facts, 59 concepts)
  GPUs are multicore systems that exploit parallelism to perform simple arithmetic simultaneously. They process triangular meshes by transforming vertices and computing vertex colors simultaneously, then calculate the colors of overlapped pixels in parallel during rasterization. Finally, the GPU performs surface texturing and hidden surface removal to complete pixel processing.
  - GPUs are multicore systems that exploit parallelism to perform simple arithmetic simultaneously.
  - The GPU processes triangular meshes by transforming vertices and computing vertex colors simultaneously.
  - Rasterization determines which pixels are overlapped by triangles and calculates their colors in parallel.
  - The GPU finishes pixel processing by performing surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

58/A21  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (6 facts, 42 concepts)
  Projection transformation | *Modeling transformation | Viewing transformation | Viewport transformation  (Viewing, projection and viewport transformations are combined in the GPU projection stage; modeling transformation is an earlier graphics-pipeline stage.)  [58/S6/F7, 58/S0/F1]
  Circle | Ellipse | Polygon | *Line  (Circle, ellipse and polygon are the other geometric shapes whose efficient rendering algorithms are more complex than line rendering; a line is the simpler case.)  [58/S2/F7, 58/S2/F9]

58/A22  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (24 facts, 96 concepts)
  Q Why can a mathematically defined line become distorted after scan conversion, and why is anti-aliasing still computationally expensive?  [58/S1/F0, 58/S1/F1, 58/S1/F2, 58/S3/F0, 58/S3/F1, 58/S3/F2, 58/S3/F3; device coordinate system, display device, pixel grid, scan conversion, line, aliasing, anti-aliasing, quality of experience, pixel intensity, rendering stage]
    A The device coordinate system that defines the viewport is continuous, so coordinate values can be real numbers, but a display device uses a pixel grid whose points have integer coordinates. Scan conversion maps continuous viewport coordinates to the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a rendered line approximates rather than exactly matches the original shape. This approximation can produce aliasing, a distortion that can be visible with a change in resolution and can reduce quality of experience. Anti-aliasing removes or reduces that distortion, but it adds further computation to the overall calculation of pixel intensities along with the other rendering stages.
  Q How does the GPU process a scene from vertices to pixels, and which parts of the graphics pipeline can be performed in parallel?  [58/S6/F3, 58/S6/F4, 58/S6/F5, 58/S6/F6, 58/S6/F7, 58/S6/F8; graphics processing unit, scene, triangle, triangular mesh, vertex, modeling transformation, vertex color, dot product, projection stage, rasterization, pixel, parallelism]
    A Most graphics systems assume a scene is made of triangles, and the GPU assembles vertices sent through graphics-library APIs into triangles. It applies modeling transformation by multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously and computes vertex color by performing dot products for multiple vertices at once. The projection stage combines viewing, projection, and viewport transformations into a composite matrix, producing triangles in continuous screen coordinates. Rasterization then determines the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles, treating each pixel independently so pixel colors can be determined simultaneously.
  Q Why can a VR developer rely on SDK and engine layers instead of writing direct low-level graphics code, and where do native rendering libraries fit in the layered architecture?  [58/S4/F0, 58/S4/F1, 58/S4/F2, 58/S4/F3, 58/S5/F0, 58/S5/F1; layered virtual reality software architecture, virtual reality application layer, software development kit, virtual reality engine, native rendering library, application programming interface, operating system layer, hardware layer, graphics processing unit, processor, memory, operating system, graphics application]
    A In the layered VR software architecture, the VR application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK calls the VR engine, and the engine calls the APIs of native rendering libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan, and Direct3D. Those native libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, which sits on top of the hardware layer that includes the GPU. Because APIs are predefined functions that perform lower-level tasks, they eliminate the need to know every processor, memory, or operating-system detail while building a graphics application. This lets the developer use the SDK to access the engine and avoid directly accessing the native rendering libraries.
  Q How do depth-buffer hidden surface removal and surface texturing in the GPU pixel processing stage relate to hidden surface removal in the view pipeline?  [55/S1/F6, 57/S4/F1, 58/S6/F9, 58/S6/F10, 58/S6/F11; view pipeline, hidden surface removal, pixel processing stage, depth buffer, depth, surface texturing, texture, pixel, three-dimensional scene, two-dimensional plane]
    A The view pipeline includes hidden surface removal, which removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are occluded from a particular viewer position before the scene is rendered. In the GPU pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer that stores the viewer's distance, or depth, for points in the three-dimensional scene before projection onto a two-dimensional plane. The same pixel processing stage also performs surface texturing, replacing computed pixel colors with texture colors from stored texture images. Thus the pixel stage depends on stored depth and texture data for each pixel.

===== lecture 59: VR resource optimization

59/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is three-dimensional graphics pipeline? (lecture 55) -> The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
  What is latency? (lecture 10) -> Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
  What is teleportation? (lecture 11) -> The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
  What is rendering? (lecture 19) -> Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

    because: The case study aims to create an immersive, interactive VR tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage.
  Q Why does the Majuli virtual tour combine walking with teleportation or a vehicle metaphor?  [59/S0/F3]
    * The island is geographically large, so one navigation technique alone may not work well
    - Walking is required for every immersive virtual reality application
    - Teleportation alone gives a more realistic sense of movement between towns
    - A vehicle metaphor is used because the tour contains only indoor spaces
    because: Because the island's large geographical spread means that a single technique such as walking or teleportation alone may not be good, the tour uses walking within points and teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between points.
  Q What creates two levels of extensive content in the Majuli virtual tour?  [59/S0/F2]
    * Many geographically spread information points, each containing many points of interest
    - Two user roles, a guide and a visitor, in the tour
    - Two separate applications for ecological heritage and cultural heritage
    - Two display resolutions for desktop and mobile deployment
    because: The tour has many geographically spread information points, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.
  Q Why was resource optimization necessary for the Majuli virtual reality application?  [59/S0/F6, 59/S0/F7]
    - Its static 360-degree photographs need to be streamed from a local server
    - Its navigation system requires a high-refresh-rate display to avoid cybersickness
    * Its rich multimodal content can be interactively changed and needs far more computation and storage than regular systems can support
    - Its 3D models require a proprietary processor found only in high-end headsets
    because: Rendering the application's rich, interactively changed multimodal content has computational and storage requirements far beyond rendering a simple static image, and regular systems cannot support it.

59/A2  recap  59/S0  "Recap"  (7 facts, 23 concepts)
  The Majuli case study aims to provide an immersive VR tour of the island's ecological and cultural heritage. The application contains extensive multimodal content including images, videos, and 3D models totaling almost 10 gigabytes. Because rendering this content requires a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a simple static image, resource optimization is necessary because regular systems cannot support the application.
  - The Majuli case study aims to provide an immersive VR tour of the island's ecological and cultural heritage.
  - The application contains extensive, geographically spread information points with two levels of content.
  - The tour uses a multimodal archive of images, videos, and 3D models totaling almost 10 gigabytes.
  - Rendering this content requires a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a simple static image.
  - Resource optimization is necessary because regular systems cannot support the Majuli application.

59/A3  quiz  59/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 33 concepts)
  Q Which hardware configuration describes the Oculus Quest 2?  [59/S1/F0]
    * A standalone headset and controllers with its own processor and memory, not tethered to a fixed computer
    - A cardboard housing for a smartphone that displays stereoscopic views
    - A room-scale augmented reality device that tracks an entire physical room
    - A high-end graphics workstation connected to an external headset
    because: The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device with a headset and handheld controllers, its own processor and memory, and no need for a fixed computer.
  Q Why did the Oculus Quest 2 application require resource optimization?  [59/S1/F1]
    - Because the full system had to be deployed on a smartphone in cardboard
    * Because the standalone device has less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation
    - Because eye tracking devices added extra sensor data and rendering requirements
    - Because the application stored all images, not videos, on a cloud server
    because: The Quest 2 has less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so reducing size reduces rendering requirements and memory access.
  Q When a user selected a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest 2 video player, where did the application obtain the video?  [59/S1/F2]
    - From a smartphone inside a cardboard headset, to reduce local size
    * From the cloud server, not from local storage
    - From the headset's local storage, to avoid network latency
    - From a high-end graphics workstation, to reduce storage requirements
    because: All videos, not images, were stored in the cloud; when a video thumbnail was selected, the video was loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally.
  Q What local benefit did the Oculus Quest 2 deployment gain from moving videos to the cloud?  [59/S1/F3]
    - The client needed local video playback to keep the experience realistic
    - The client size increased because thumbnails were cached locally
    - The client required a tethered workstation for high-quality video rendering
    * The client size and associated computations were reduced
    because: Storing the videos in the cloud reduced the deployed client size and produced a corresponding computational reduction.
  Q What network conditions were necessary for cloud-based video-loading on the Oculus Quest 2 to be useful?  [59/S1/F4]
    - Compressed images, removed video playback, and smartphone storage
    - Large local storage, fast memory access, and offline video files
    * High bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency
    - A high-end workstation, eye tracking, and haptic feedback
    because: The cloud-based video-loading optimization required high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

59/A4  recap  59/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 33 concepts)
  The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone device with its own processor and memory. Because it has less computing power and storage than a high-end workstation, the application required optimization to reduce size and computational demands. By storing videos in the cloud and loading them on demand, the application size was reduced to 5.1 GB. However, this optimization relies on high bandwidth, network coverage, and low latency to load high-quality content in real time.
  - The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone device with its own processor and memory.
  - The Quest 2 requires optimization because it has less computing power and storage than a high-end workstation.
  - Cloud-based optimization stores videos in the cloud and loads them on demand to reduce local storage and data-access requirements.
  - This optimization reduced the application size to 5.1 GB and decreased computational requirements.
  - Cloud-based optimization requires high bandwidth, network coverage, and low latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

59/A6  quiz  59/S2  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Q What is a cardboard virtual reality headset?  [59/S2/F0]
    - A standalone headset with its own processor and handheld controllers
    - A glass-based display that overlays virtual objects on the real world
    - A tethered headset connected to a high-end graphics workstation
    * A cardboard housing that holds a smartphone displaying stereoscopic views
    because: A cardboard VR headset is a cardboard housing for a smartphone, and the smartphone's stereoscopic display provides the immersive view.
  Q Why did the Majuli VR system need optimization for deployment on a smartphone placed in a cardboard headset?  [59/S2/F1]
    - Because the cardboard housing reduced the smartphone's available computing power
    - Because average smartphones cannot display stereoscopic views
    - Because the full system depended on a cloud server for video playback
    * Because its full version's size and computation exceeded what average smartphones typically support
    because: The full Majuli VR system was too large and computationally demanding for average smartphones, so a resource-constrained deployment required optimization.
  Q What optimization strategy was used for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli VR system?  [59/S2/F2]
    - Videos were stored in the cloud and loaded when selected
    - The system was moved to a standalone headset with its own processor
    - Images were compressed and video playback support was retained
    * Images were compressed and video playback support was removed
    because: For the smartphone/cardboard version, images were compressed to reduce storage and video playback was removed because most videos could not be used.
  Q What trade-off resulted from compressing images and removing video playback in the Majuli smartphone/cardboard system?  [59/S2/F3]
    - The system could retain more video content than the full version
    - The overall size of the system increased
    - The experience required a high-bandwidth cloud connection
    * The experience became less realistic than the full version
    because: Compressing images and removing video support reduced resource use but made the experience less realistic than the full implementation.
  Q Which general approach is described as allowing video playback to be retained when an immersive VR system has computational limits?  [59/S2/F5]
    * Cloud-based services
    - Removing some features entirely
    - Compressing images to reduce storage
    - Replacing video with static 2D drone shots
    because: Cloud-based services are identified as an approach that can allow video playback to be retained, whereas compression and feature removal are different trade-offs.

59/A7  recap  59/S2  "Recap"  (7 facts, 17 concepts)
  Cardboard headsets provide a low-cost option for VR on smartphones, but the full Majuli VR system exceeds the capabilities of average smartphones. Optimization techniques like image compression and removing video playback can significantly reduce system size, although these trade-offs make the experience less realistic. If a device cannot perform the rendering, developers may need to use cloud-based services or remove features entirely.
  - Cardboard headsets provide a low-cost option for VR on smartphones.
  - The Majuli VR system exceeds the computation and storage capabilities of average smartphones.
  - Optimization techniques like image compression and removing video playback can significantly reduce system size.
  - These trade-offs make the VR experience less realistic than the full version.
  - If a device cannot perform the rendering, developers may use cloud-based services or remove features.
