59/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (13 facts, 52 concepts)
  Q Why would the Majuli virtual tour application need different resource optimizations for an Oculus Quest 2 headset and for a smartphone placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset?  [59/S0/F5, 59/S0/F6, 59/S0/F7, 59/S1/F1, 59/S1/F2, 59/S1/F3, 59/S2/F1, 59/S2/F2, 59/S2/F4; Majuli virtual tour application, Oculus Quest 2, smartphone, cardboard virtual reality headset, resource optimization, cloud-based video loading optimization, image compression, video playback, gigabyte]
    A The Majuli virtual tour application is almost 10 gigabytes in size because its collected multimodal content is vast, and its interactive videos and animations make rendering much more demanding than rendering a static image. Regular systems cannot support the application, and the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so the Quest 2 application was optimized by storing videos in the cloud and loading them on demand, reducing it to 5.1 gigabytes. The smartphone/cardboard deployment had to compress images and remove video playback because the full system's size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support. That strategy reduced the overall size of the Majuli virtual reality system to about 0.7 gigabytes.
  Q How can cloud-based video loading reduce the storage needed on the Oculus Quest 2 while still depending on network conditions for the Majuli virtual tour?  [59/S1/F2, 59/S1/F3, 59/S1/F4, 10/S2/F3; cloud-based video loading optimization, Oculus Quest 2, video, cloud, storage, bandwidth, network coverage, latency, real time, gigabyte, network connectivity]
    A In the Oculus Quest 2 application, videos were not stored locally because videos take up more storage, and a video is loaded from the cloud when the user selects its thumbnail, reducing the deployed application to 5.1 gigabytes. This cloud-based video loading optimization requires high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time. Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world, so if network connectivity issues are not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.
  Q How does the three-dimensional graphics pipeline explain why a platform that cannot render the required immersive content cannot host the whole Majuli virtual reality system?  [55/S1/F0, 59/S0/F6, 59/S2/F6; three-dimensional graphics pipeline, rendering, Majuli virtual tour application, Majuli virtual reality system, computational requirement, static image, real-time interactive rendering, platform, device]
    A The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller. Rendering the Majuli virtual tour application's rich multimodal content involves a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a static image and requires fast storage and retrieval support for real-time interactive rendering. When such rendering cannot be performed on the device, deploying the whole Majuli virtual reality system on that platform is not possible.

===== lecture 60: Linking theory to practice

60/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is application programming interface (API)? (lecture 58) -> A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is immersive experience? (lecture 1) -> An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

    - A fundamental object that acts as a container for components implementing its functionality.
    - A view that shows the scene while it is being built and manipulated.
    because: A Unity prefab is a template made by configuring and storing a game object and allows instances of that object in a scene.

60/A9  recap  60/S4  "Recap"  (7 facts, 22 concepts)
  Unity assets are items used to create applications and can be imported from outside or created internally. A scene is a specific type of asset containing parts of an application that can be edited through a scene interface. Game objects act as containers for components to define functionality, while prefabs serve as templates to make instances of those objects in a scene.
  - Unity assets are items used to create applications and can be imported from outside or created internally.
  - A scene is a specific type of asset containing parts of an application that can be edited through a scene interface.
  - Game objects are fundamental objects that act as containers for components to define their functionality.
  - Prefabs are templates of game objects used to create instances in a Unity scene.

60/A15  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (12 facts, 32 concepts)
  Q How does Unity help a developer build an immersive extended reality experience without implementing every stage of the computer graphics pipeline from scratch?  [60/S1/F0, 60/S1/F2, 60/S2/F2, 58/S4/F0; Unity, extended reality, immersive experience, computer graphics pipeline, application programming interface]
    A Unity is a programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems, and it is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and rendering. Its editor allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement that pipeline. This is similar to using graphics libraries and their APIs instead of implementing pipeline stages from scratch.
  Q Why does Unity provide both a scene view and a game view when a developer is creating a Unity scene?  [60/S3/F2, 60/S3/F3; scene view, game view, game object, scene, camera]
    A The scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene while it is being built, and it lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that comprise the scene. The game view is the final view used to preview the developed scene, and it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.
  Q How do Unity game objects and prefabs help a developer assemble a scene in the Unity editor?  [60/S3/F2, 60/S4/F4, 60/S4/F7; Unity game object, component, Unity prefab, scene view, Unity scene, instance]
    A A Unity game object is a fundamental container for components, and the scene view lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects that together comprise the scene. A prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object. This lets the developer make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.
  Q How does the Unity preference tab reflect the distinction among virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality under the broader term extended reality?  [60/S3/F0, 1/S1/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F3; preference tab, virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, extended reality]
    A The Unity preference tab lets the developer select extended reality settings for virtual reality, mixed reality, and augmented reality. Extended reality is an umbrella term covering augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality. Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while mixed reality is the broader space between the real and virtual extremes, and Unity's mixed reality setting lets Unity's own environment and the user's real world environment interact.

===== lecture 61: Linking theory to practice

61/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is scene? (lecture 60) -> The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.
  What is Unity? (lecture 60) -> Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.
  What is unity editor? (lecture 60) -> Unity Hub is a standalone application that is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine; installing Unity Hub gives the Unity Editor interface and the Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects and installations.
  What is component? (lecture 60) -> A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.
  What is platform? (lecture 19) -> In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.
  What is graphics processing unit (GPU)? (lecture 20) -> A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

61/A2  recap  61/S0  "Recap"  (8 facts, 29 concepts)
  Unity is an implementation platform and editor for creating and deploying XR systems. It provides render pipeline support for various graphics components and offers three pre-built pipelines, including the built-in, URP, and HDRP. While the built-in pipeline has limited customization, URP provides optimized graphics for many platforms and HDRP is designed for high-fidelity graphics on high-end hardware.
  - Unity is an implementation platform and editor used to create, build, and deploy XR systems.
  - Unity's render pipeline support handles graphics components while allowing for customized control over individual pipeline stages.
  - Unity offers three pre-built render pipelines and custom APIs, though the built-in pipeline has limited customization.
  - The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) provides optimized graphics for a wide range of platforms.
  - The High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) provides photorealistic graphics for high-end hardware.

61/A3  quiz  61/S1  "Quick quiz"  (5 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q What is a model in Unity's built-in render pipeline?  [61/S1/F0]
    * A file containing data on a 3D object's shape and appearance
    - A pipeline stage that performs lighting and view transform
    - A transform component that places a mesh in world coordinates
    - A skybox cube that forms a 360-degree background
    because: Models are files containing data on the shape and appearance of 3D objects, and they serve as the object representation.
  Q What are Unity's main graphics primitives?  [61/S1/F3]
    - Render pipelines made of camera and lighting stages
    * 3D meshes made of triangles or quadrangles
    - Terrain objects made of landforms and vegetation
    - Skyboxes made of textured cube faces
    because: Unity treats 3D meshes as its main graphics primitives, and it supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes.
  Q What happens in Unity's mesh rendering workflow?  [61/S1/F4]
    - The mesh renderer takes pose data from a tracker and registers virtual content
    - The mesh renderer takes material data from a model file and defines the object's shape
    - The mesh renderer takes skybox textures from the scene and applies them to a mesh
    * The mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the object's transform position
    because: The mesh renderer receives geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.
  Q In a Unity model file, how do materials differ from meshes?  [61/S1/F5]
    - Materials create a skybox, while meshes store animation data
    - Materials define the object's shape, while meshes reference textures and color tints
    - Materials store pose data, while meshes define tracking coordinates
    * Materials specify how a surface is rendered, while meshes describe the object's shape
    because: Materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how it should be rendered, whereas meshes describe the object's shape.
  Q What are textures in Unity?  [61/S1/F6]
    - Shader scripts that create a custom render pipeline
    - Polygonal meshes that define an object's geometric shape
    - Transform components that place a rendered object in the world
    * Bitmap images applied over a mesh surface to represent color and other surface properties
    because: Textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface to assign colors and can also represent surface aspects such as reflectivity and roughness.

61/A4  recap  61/S1  "Recap"  (7 facts, 30 concepts)
  Unity models are files containing data on the shape and appearance of 3D objects, which can be imported from over 10 different formats. 3D meshes serve as the main graphics primitives, which the mesh renderer uses to place geometry at the position defined by the game object's transform. Materials and textures further define the surface appearance of these meshes by providing details such as color, reflectivity, and roughness.
  - Unity models are files containing data on the shape and appearance of 3D objects.
  - Unity supports more than 10 model formats, allowing models created in different formats to be imported.
  - 3D meshes are the main graphics primitives.
  - The mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform.
  - Materials describe surface appearance by referencing textures, which are bitmap images used for color and properties like reflectivity and roughness.

61/A9  recap  61/S3  "Recap"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Unity uses native rendering libraries to implement the graphics pipeline, meaning developers do not need to manage the implementation themselves. Depending on platform availability, Unity supports various native graphics libraries like DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan. By enabling the AutoGraphics API option, Unity automatically selects the best supported API at runtime; otherwise, it searches the API list until it finds a match.
  - Unity uses native rendering libraries to implement the graphics pipeline, meaning developers do not need to manage the implementation themselves.
  - Unity supports various native graphics libraries like DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan depending on platform availability.
  - Enabling the AutoGraphics API option allows Unity to automatically select the best supported graphics API at runtime.
  - Without the AutoGraphics API option, Unity searches through the API list until it finds a supported match for the platform.

61/A11  quiz  61/S4  "Quick quiz"  (7 facts, 21 concepts)
  Q What does a rigid body component allow a Unity game object to do?  [61/S4/F2]
    - Configure friction and bounce for the object's surface
    - Connect the object to another rigid body with limits
    * Respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing appears realistic.
    - Define the object's shape for physical collisions
    because: A rigid body is attached to a game object so that it responds to gravity, making falling or bouncing appear realistic.
  Q What does setting isKinematic on a Unity rigid body do?  [61/S4/F3]
    - Make the object automatically follow gravity and behave as a solid object
    - Add a joint that applies forces and limits to the object
    * Remove the object from physics engine control so a script can move it without automatic gravity.
    - Turn the object's collider into a trigger that other colliders pass through
    because: The isKinematic property removes a rigid body from the physics engine's automatic control, allowing script-based kinematic movement without automatic gravity.
  Q What does a joint component do in Unity physics?  [61/S4/F8]
    - Define the collision shape of a game object for other objects to hit
    * Connect a rigid body to another rigid body or a fixed point and apply forces with limits on movement.
    - Configure the friction and bounce of a surface
    - Remove a game object from physics engine control so a script can move it
    because: A joint connects rigid bodies or a rigid body to a fixed point, can apply forces, and uses limits to restrict movement.
  Q What is an advantage of using an articulation body for a jointed structure in Unity?  [61/S4/F9, 61/S4/F10, 61/S4/F11]
    - It requires the developer to set forces and limits for every joint manually
    * It automatically implements joint constraints in a logical tree, so individual joints need not be controlled separately.
    - It represents each joint as an independent collider with no parent-child relationship
    - It moves the whole structure by script without using physics constraints
    because: Physics articulation describes the overall movement of a jointed structure, and the articulation body automatically implements the joint constraints represented as a logical tree.
  Q In Unity, what is the effect of configuring a collider as a trigger with isTrigger?  [61/S4/F7]
    - The collider connects the game object to another rigid body
    - The collider makes the game object respond to gravity
    - The collider defines a more accurate but processor-intensive collision shape
    * The collider does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.
    because: A collider configured as a trigger does not act as a solid object; it simply allows other colliders to pass through it.

61/A12  recap  61/S4  "Recap"  (11 facts, 30 concepts)
  Unity's physics engine uses components like rigid bodies, colliders, joints, and articulation to simulate physical laws. Rigid bodies allow objects to react to gravity, but can be set to kinematic to be moved by scripts. Colliders define collision shapes and can be configured as static objects or triggers, while joints and articulation bodies manage complex movements by connecting objects and using a logical tree of joints.
  - Unity's physics engine uses components like rigid bodies, colliders, joints, and articulation to simulate physical laws.
  - Rigid bodies allow objects to react to gravity, but can be set to kinematic to be moved by scripts.
  - Colliders define collision shapes and can be configured as static objects or triggers.
  - Joints and articulation bodies manage complex movements by connecting objects and using a logical tree of joints.

    - Manage transitions and interactions between animation clips with a visual tool
    * Apply an animation from one character model onto another
    - Align animation clips in a simplified workflow before previewing them
    because: Humanoid animation retargeting in Unity is the ability to apply animations from one character model onto another.
  Q How does Unity's animation processing relate to the 3D graphics pipeline?  [61/S5/F2]
    * It involves similar stages, but lets a developer work directly with animations without implementing those stages
    - It replaces the 3D graphics pipeline with a rigid body and collider so the physics engine moves the animation
    - It requires a developer to implement every 3D graphics pipeline stage before an animation clip can play
    - It is unrelated to the 3D graphics pipeline, so animation clips are processed independently of any pipeline stages
    because: Animation processing in Unity involves stages similar to the 3D graphics pipeline stages, but Unity lets a developer work directly with animations without implementing those stages or their computations.
  Q What is the role of an audio listener in Unity?  [61/S5/F5]
    - It stores a standard audio file, such as an MP3 or WAV, for later playback
    * It listens to all audio in the scene and transfers it to the computer speakers
    - It attaches to a game object to make that object play an audio clip
    - It modifies the output of an audio source to generate various sound effects
    because: The Unity audio listener listens to all audio playing in the scene and transfers it to the computer speakers, with heard audio relative to its positioning.
  Q What do Unity audio filters do?  [61/S5/F6]
    - They define the shape of a game object for physical collisions with other objects
    - They listen to all audio playing in the scene and transfer it to the computer speakers
    - They attach to a game object to make that object play a sound clip
    * They modify the output of an audio source or the intake of an audio listener to generate sound effects
    because: Unity audio filters are components that modify the output of an audio source or the intake of an audio listener to generate various sound effects.
  Q In Unity, what is the primary component attached to a game object to make it play a sound?  [61/S5/F4]
    - The audio filter
    * The audio source
    - The rigid body
    - The audio listener
    because: The Unity audio source is the primary component attached to a game object to make it play a sound.

61/A14  recap  61/S5  "Recap"  (7 facts, 20 concepts)
  Unity provides an animation system that supports importing clips, humanoid retargeting, and managing complex interactions. While animation processing involves 3D graphics pipeline stages, Unity allows developers to work with animations directly without implementing those computations. Additionally, Unity supports immersive audio through dedicated components for sound sources, listeners, and filters to manage playback and effects.
  - Unity's animation system supports importing clips, humanoid retargeting, and managing complex interactions.
  - Unity allows developers to work with animations directly without implementing 3D graphics pipeline stages.
  - Unity supports audio through dedicated components for sound sources, listeners, and filters.

61/A19  odd_one_out  lecture  "Odd one out"  (5 facts, 25 concepts)
  Capsule collider | *Mesh collider | Box collider | Sphere collider  (Box, sphere, and capsule colliders are primitive colliders, while a mesh collider is a collider type but not a primitive collider.)  [61/S4/F4]
  *Audio clip | Audio source | Audio listener | Audio filter  (Audio source, audio listener, and audio filter are dedicated Unity audio components, while an audio clip is a sound file played by an audio source.)  [61/S5/F3, 61/S5/F4, 61/S5/F6]
  Universal render pipeline | High Definition render pipeline | *Custom render pipeline | Built-in render pipeline  (The built-in, Universal, and High Definition render pipelines are Unity's pre-built render pipelines, while a custom render pipeline is created by a developer using scriptable render pipeline APIs.)  [61/S0/F2]

61/A20  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (17 facts, 53 concepts)
  Q Why might a developer choose Unity's Universal Render Pipeline rather than High Definition Render Pipeline for an XR experience that must run on varied or resource-constrained platforms?  [61/S0/F4, 61/S0/F5, 61/S0/F6, 61/S0/F7; Universal Render Pipeline, High Definition Render Pipeline, resource requirement, high-end platform]
    A URP is a quick and easy way to customize graphics and create optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms. It has many pipeline stages optimized by the pipeline implementation, so it minimizes resource requirements. HDRP is meant for high-fidelity photorealistic graphics but requires a good amount of resources and is typically for high-end platforms with good GPU support.
  Q Why does the camera component matter for both the rendered view and the audio heard by a user in a Unity XR scene?  [61/S2/F9, 61/S2/F10, 61/S2/F11, 61/S5/F5; camera, camera component, view transformation, three-dimensional graphics pipeline, audio listener]
    A View transformation is an important stage in the 3D graphics pipeline, and Unity supports it through its camera concept after the developer sets up a camera. The camera is created by adding a camera component to a game object. The audio listener, which by default is attached to the camera, determines the positioning with respect to which all scene audio is heard.
  Q How do rigid bodies, colliders, and physics materials combine to make object interactions feel physical in Unity, and what changes when a collider is made a trigger?  [61/S4/F0, 61/S4/F2, 61/S4/F4, 61/S4/F6, 61/S4/F7; Unity physics engine, rigid body, collider, physics material, friction, bounce, trigger, collision, gravity]
    A The Unity physics engine simulates physical laws so objects accelerate and respond to collisions, with rigid bodies making game objects respond to gravity. A collider defines the shape of a game object for collisions, and a physics material configures surface friction and bounce. If the collider is configured as a trigger, it does not behave as a solid object and allows other colliders to pass through.
  Q How does Unity's reliance on native graphics libraries relate to the earlier idea that a developer may rely on platform-specific SDKs rather than handling all lowest-level operations directly?  [61/S3/F0, 61/S3/F1, 61/S3/F5, 19/S2/F5; native graphics library, application programming interface, autographics application programming interface, Unity]
    A In practical VR development, a developer may use a platform-specific SDK to handle lowest-level operations, while still needing to understand that SDK. Unity does not implement the graphics pipeline itself; it uses functions of native rendering libraries such as DirectX, Metal, OpenGL, and Vulkan. With the AutoGraphics API option, a Unity player build includes built-in graphics APIs and selects the appropriate one at runtime, so the developer does not manually choose the platform-specific API.

===== lecture 62: Linking theory to practice

62/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (6 facts, 6 concepts)
  What is Vuforia? (lecture 22) -> Vuforia is a tracking library that has an augmented reality (AR) plugin that works with Unity three-dimensional (3D) and can be used to create AR applications, particularly mobile AR applications for iOS and Android platforms.
  What is trigger? (lecture 61) -> A collider in Unity configured as a trigger using the isTrigger property does not behave as a solid object and simply allows other colliders to pass through.
  What is collider? (lecture 61) -> The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling.
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is marker? (lecture 3) -> Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
  What is virtual reality (VR)? (lecture 4) -> Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

  Q Why would a developer write scripts in Unity instead of relying only on built-in support?  [62/S0/F0]

    - To replace the Unity package with a different development environment
    - To turn a game object into a separate visual asset
    because: Built-in support gives only the experience that the system provides, so scripts or small pieces of code are used to change it to match the programmer's expectations and needs.
  Q How is Unity's C# scripting environment initially available in a project?  [62/S0/F1]

    - It replaces the game object with a prefab before execution

  To obtain a more customized experience, programmers must write scripts to change the built-in support. Unity supports the object-oriented language C# and usually includes an integrated development environment. These scripts can be attached as components to game objects to control behavior and respond to user input. Scripts are usually created directly within the Unity environment.
  - Custom scripts are needed to provide a more customized experience than the built-in support provides.
  - Unity supports C#, an object-oriented programming language, and usually includes an integrated development environment.
  - C# scripts function as components that can be attached to game objects to control behavior and respond to user input.
  - Scripts are usually created directly within Unity using the Assets menu.

  Q In a Unity script, what is the role difference between prebuilt functions and user-defined functions?  [62/S2/F1]
    - Prebuilt functions are optional improvements, while user-defined functions are required for the script to work.
    - Prebuilt functions are defined by the user, while user-defined functions are supplied automatically by Unity.
    - Prebuilt functions are used only for initialization, while user-defined functions are used only for update events.
    * Prebuilt functions are critical for making the script work, while user-defined functions are defined by the user and are typically part of a good script.
    because: Unity scripts use prebuilt functions that are critical for making a script work, and user-defined functions, which are defined by the user and are typically part of a good script.
  Q What happens when a Unity gameplay event occurs for an event function?  [62/S2/F2]
    - The event function's body executes and then retains control instead of returning it to Unity.
    - Unity executes the event function before the gameplay event occurs, so it can prepare in advance.
    * Unity passes control to the event function, executes its body, then returns control to Unity.
    - The developer manually calls the event function after detecting the gameplay event.
    because: An event function is activated by Unity in response to a gameplay event: Unity passes control to the function, its body executes, and then control is passed back to Unity.
  Q When are OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit functions called in Unity?  [62/S2/F3]

  Q How can Unity event functions be used to impose realistic behavior?  [62/S2/F4]
    - Physics-event functions can impose visual behavior, while GUI event functions can impose user-input behavior.
    - Physics-event functions can impose interactive behavior, while GUI event functions can impose physical behavior.
    - Physics-event functions can impose rendering behavior, while GUI event functions can impose physical behavior.
    * Physics-event functions can impose physical behavior, while GUI event functions can impose interactive behavior.
    because: Unity's event functions can impose realistic behavior, such as physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in GUI event functions.

62/A6  recap  62/S2  "Recap"  (5 facts, 38 concepts)
  Unity scripts use prebuilt and user-defined functions, including the Destroy function which destroys a game object from the scene after a specified delay. Event functions are activated by Unity in response to gameplay events such as regular updates, initialization, graphical user interface, and physics events. These functions are used to impose realistic and interactive behaviors.
  - The Destroy function destroys a game object from the scene after a specified delay.
  - Unity scripts use both prebuilt functions and user-defined functions.
  - Event functions are activated by Unity in response to gameplay events, where Unity passes control to the function and then back to Unity.
  - Common gameplay events include regular updates, initialization, graphical user interface, and physics events.
  - Event functions can be used to impose realistic and interactive behaviors.

    * Its condition is checked after the body, so the body runs at least once
    - Its condition is checked before the body, so the body may not run
    - It is used to work directly with a collection of homogeneous data types
    - It is entry-controlled because its condition is checked after the body
    because: For and while loops are entry-controlled because their condition is checked before the body executes, while a do-while loop is exit-controlled because its body executes at least once and its condition is checked after the body.
  Q What is a foreach loop used for in the scripting environment?  [62/S3/F4]
    * Working directly with an array or collection of homogeneous data types
    - Pausing execution and continuing on the following frame
    - Working directly with a single transform component's position, rotation, and scale
    - Checking a loop condition before any loop body executes
    because: A foreach loop can be used for arrays or collections of homogeneous data types, allowing the programmer to work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types.

62/A8  recap  62/S3  "Recap"  (5 facts, 24 concepts)
  To instantiate a prefab at runtime, a script needs a reference that is attached in the editor by dragging the prefab into a script component's field. Script behavior can be controlled using standard if-else statements and various loop types, including entry-controlled for and while loops, exit-controlled do-while loops, and foreach loops for collections of homogeneous data types.
  - A script needs a reference to a prefab to instantiate it at runtime.
  - Prefabs are attached in the editor by dragging them into a script component's field.
  - The scripting environment supports standard if-else statements.
  - For and while loops are entry-controlled, while do-while loops are exit-controlled.

    - Calibration and registration values
    - Initial delay and repeat interval
    - Viewer pose and anchor position

  Q How does a Unity coroutine spread a task over several frames?  [62/S4/F1]
    - It starts a separate thread for each task.
    - It registers virtual content by determining the viewer's pose.
    - It calls a function after a delay and then at fixed intervals.
    * It pauses execution, returns control to Unity, and resumes on a later frame.
    because: A coroutine spreads work across frames by pausing, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off.
  Q Which statement correctly distinguishes coroutines from threads?  [62/S4/F2]
    - A coroutine spawns one thread for each paused operation.
    * Coroutines execute on the main thread and do not spawn individual threads.
    - A coroutine is designed to behave like a thread for background work.
    - A coroutine pauses the main thread so other threads can run.
    because: Coroutines are not threads; synchronous operations inside them still run on the main thread.
  Q What makes a gradual opacity fade visible?  [62/S4/F3]

    * Reducing the alpha or opacity value over a sequence of frames.
    - Calling the fade function once with the final opacity value.
    - Invoking the fade method on a separate thread.
    because: A fade is perceivable only when its alpha or opacity changes frame by frame so Unity renders intermediate values.
  Q What do the two times passed to InvokeRepeating specify?  [62/S4/F4]

    - The object's local scale and rotation values.
    because: InvokeRepeating takes a function name and two times: the initial start time and the repeat interval.

  FixedUpdate function | *Start function | Update function | LateUpdate function  (Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate are Unity regular update event functions; Start is an initialization event function.)  [62/S2/F3]

  OnCollisionStay function | *OnTriggerEnter function | OnCollisionEnter function | OnCollisionExit function  (OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit are physics event functions for contact being made or broken; OnTriggerEnter is a physics-related event function called for a collider configured as a trigger.)  [62/S2/F3]

62/A26  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (11 facts, 41 concepts)
  Q Why can a basic virtual or augmented reality system be built in Unity without scripting, while a customized experience requires scripting?  [62/S0/F0, 62/S8/F0; Unity, scripting, integrated development environment, programming, virtual reality, augmented reality]
    A Unity's built-in support gives a good-quality experience, but only what the system provides, so a programmer must write scripts to change it. Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems are primarily programming tasks, with the amount depending on required functionality. A basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment support, whereas a customized experience requires scripting and therefore more programming.
  Q How does a C# script attached to a Unity game object let a developer create realistic interactive behavior during game execution?  [62/S0/F3, 62/S0/F4, 62/S2/F4; C#, script, component, game object, interactive behavior, user input, event function]
    A A C# script can be attached as a component to a game object, and creating the script is essentially creating a new type of component that behaves as the developer wants. Once attached, it starts working when the game is executed, allowing the developer to trigger game events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input. Unity event functions can then impose realistic behavior, such as interactive behavior in graphical user interface event functions.
  Q Why must a gradual opacity fade of a Unity object be implemented as a coroutine rather than a fade function that is called only once?  [62/S4/F1, 62/S4/F3; Unity, coroutine, opacity fade, frame]
    A A coroutine is a method that spreads tasks across several frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off on the following frame. A gradual opacity fade is visible only when its opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so Unity can render the intermediate values. A fade function called only once is not perceivable, so the fade must be defined as a coroutine and started so the change is spread frame by frame.
  Q How does Vuforia enable marker-based augmented reality in Unity when Unity's built-in support for object recognition is limited?  [62/S6/F3, 62/S7/F0, 62/S7/F9, 3/S2/F2; Unity, Vuforia, augmented reality, object recognition, computer vision, marker-based augmented reality, three-dimensional model, marker]
    A Unity's built-in support for object recognition or computer vision operations is not extensive and not very good, so seamless and efficient performance requires external packages. Vuforia is an augmented reality software development kit that supports advanced computer vision for recognizing images and objects and interacting with spaces in the real world. In marker-based augmented reality, a marker triggers the experience, and when the Vuforia engine recognizes the matching image, it displays a three-dimensional model in place of the marker.

===== lecture 63: Concluding remarks

63/A0  recall  lecture  "Before you start: recall"  (4 facts, 4 concepts)
  What is augmented reality (AR)? (lecture 1) -> Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
  What is mixed reality (MR)? (lecture 1) -> Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.
  What is extended reality (XR)? (lecture 1) -> Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).
  What is internet of things (IoT)? (lecture 23) -> In the development of computer systems, people have tried to make technology disappear from the user's point of view, and the current stage defined by popular technological products such as wearable devices, mobile devices, flexible devices, and connected devices is referred to as Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing, in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear.

63/A2  recap  63/S1  "Recap"  (5 facts, 14 concepts)
  Computer vision is an enabling technology with huge potential for building better applications in augmented reality (AR) and mixed reality (MR). Cloud and edge computing concepts are relevant for scalable and affordable extended reality systems and for addressing resource optimization concerns. Machine learning and deep learning concepts are currently ubiquitous for building better experiences and more intelligent systems. Large language models (LLMs) or generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used for enhanced interactivity, while IoT, robotics, and blockchain technology are relevant technologies for extended reality applications.
  - Computer vision is an enabling technology for building better AR and MR applications.
  - Cloud and edge computing are relevant for scalable XR systems and resource optimization.
  - Machine learning and deep learning are ubiquitous for building intelligent XR systems.
  - LLMs or generative AI can be used for enhanced interactivity.
  - IoT, robotics, and blockchain are relevant technologies for XR applications.

63/A7  open_question  lecture  "Think it through"  (9 facts, 24 concepts)
  Q How do cloud and edge computing relate to resource optimization and affordability in extended reality systems?  [63/S1/F1, 1/S1/F0; extended reality, cloud computing, edge computing, resource optimization]
    A Extended reality is an umbrella term covering immersive technologies such as augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality. Cloud and edge computing are relevant for making such extended reality systems scalable and affordable, and for addressing resource optimization concerns.
  Q How does computer vision relate to the way augmented reality and mixed reality combine real and virtual content?  [63/S1/F0, 1/S2/F1, 1/S2/F3; computer vision, augmented reality, mixed reality]
    A Augmented reality is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content, while mixed reality broadly spans the space between the real and virtual extremes. Computer vision is an enabling technology with huge potential for building better applications in both augmented and mixed reality.
  Q How can machine learning, deep learning, large language models, and generative artificial intelligence change the experience and interactivity of extended reality systems?  [63/S1/F2, 63/S1/F3; machine learning, deep learning, large language model, generative artificial intelligence, extended reality]
    A Machine learning and deep learning are currently ubiquitous for building better experiences and more intelligent systems in extended reality. Large language models or generative artificial intelligence can be used for enhanced interactivity in extended reality applications.
  Q How do the Internet of Things, robotics, and blockchain relate to extended reality applications, and how does the Internet of Things connect to making technology disappear?  [63/S1/F4, 23/S0/F5; internet of things, robotics, blockchain, extended reality]
    A The Internet of Things, robotics, and blockchain are relevant technologies for extended reality applications. The Internet of Things is the current ubiquitous-computing stage in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear.
